When polite and casual Korean registers got mixed, a rule now enforces the polite register. When content not found in the source crept in, a rule now limits the text to what the source supports. The earlier curations on anti-slop skillsand the slop-rewrite editing agentfollow the same idea: they turn AI writing habits people kept deleting by hand into rules.
By the manifesto’s definition, though, style correction alone cannot stop slop. A smooth sentence that makes a claim the source never made still leaves the reader to check it against the source. If review scope follows risk, as resolution 9 suggests, the first things to check in a curation are numbers, quotes, and whether the source actually says what the post claims.
Further reading The manifesto links these resources at the bottom of the page.
No More Slop: swyx declares war on slop at AIE Code Summit, November 2025 Please stop the slop: Tejas Kumar on keeping slop out of his own writing Vibe Coding Our Way to Disaster: Jake Nations on why thinking can’t be handed to AI, only amplified by it Ghostty AI Usage Policy: the Ghostty terminal maintainers on human understanding and care Why Software Factories Fail: Dex Horthy asking people to keep reading at least some of the code To sign, leave a comment on the GitHub Gistwith any of your name, company, X handle, or LinkedIn. The maintainers say they pull signatures into the page regularly.
Summary The manifesto defines slop as output that asks the reader to spend more effort understanding it than the author spent making it. Whether AI was involved is not the test. Producing output now costs almost nothing while review costs stay the same, so slop piles up fast and the next agent reads and copies it. Signers commit to owning what they ship: they disclose agent-written content, scale review to the stakes, and turn repeated mistakes into linter rules and guardrails.
summary: A plain-language walkthrough of the No AI Slop manifesto written by AIE Code Summit 2026 speakers and attendees: its definition of slop, the asymmetry behind it, five values, and twelve resolutions, with practical examples and a check against this blog’s own curation pipeline.
title: You Own What You Ship: Reading the No AI Slop Manifesto

content:
Developers frequently assign long-running tasks to coding agents like Claude Code or Codex before stepping away or traveling. Closing a MacBook lid typically pauses running processes or risks severe device overheating. The open-source menu bar app ClamDown keeps background workloads running while actively managing system cooling with the lid closed.
Limitations of Traditional Keep-Awake Tools and How ClamDown Works Standard tools like caffeinate or virtual display plugins often require an external display or fail to regulate thermal conditions. When a MacBook lid closes, default macOS behavior caps fan speeds at minimal levels regardless of CPU temperature spikes. ClamDown detects the closed-lid state and takes direct control of fan speeds. On Apple Silicon MacBooks, it keeps fans at minimum speed when the CPU stays at 50°C and ramps fans to maximum speed once temperatures reach 75°C.
Safety Mechanisms and Watchdog Architecture ClamDown includes built-in safeguards to prevent battery depletion and overheating. If the battery drops below 10% or the thermal state passes the serious threshold, the app halts operations and puts the MacBook to sleep. If a user steps away, the app confirms one minute of user inactivity before triggering sleep mode to prevent accidental heat buildup.
The app uses a root helper and watchdog architecture for system stability. The main app sends a heartbeat signal to the helper every 30 seconds. If the helper receives no response for 90 seconds, it immediately returns sleep configuration and fan control to macOS. ClamDown requires macOS 13 or later and root helper authorization during setup. Intel Macs can only read temperature data, while Apple Silicon Macs get full cooling control.
ClamDown provides practical convenience for developers executing heavy local agent workflows. A simple menu bar toggle keeps intensive tasks running safely without hardware risks.
Summary Performs direct fan and thermal control with the lid closed, overriding limitations of caffeinate and virtual display plugins. Triggers automatic sleep mode upon reaching low-battery or high-thermal thresholds to prevent overheating in bags. Restores default macOS controls safely via a 30-second watchdog helper if the main app crashes.
summary: ClamDown is an open-source menu bar app that manages CPU temperatures and battery levels to safely run coding agents while your MacBook lid is closed.
title: ClamDown: Run Coding Agents Safely on MacBooks with the Lid Closed

content:
AI coding tools have dramatically accelerated how fast diffs get written, yet unverified speed brings subtle bugs and mid-session context collapse. To add structural guardrails ahead of code generation, Google open-sourced the Elephant-Goldfish Model (EGM) plugin under the Apache 2.0 license.
Splitting Long-Horizon Elephants from Stateless Goldfish EGM separates AI sessions into two strict roles: Elephant and Goldfish. The Elephant is a long-lived session holding overarching architectural vision and project memory under a strict No Code rule - focusing exclusively on spec design and capturing subtle trade-offs without writing implementation code.
The Goldfish, by contrast, is a stateless session with zero shared conversation history. Because it does not inherit the Elephant’s sunk-cost context or blind spots, the Goldfish acts as an independent critic hunting for gaps and edge cases in the written design doc.
Three-Stage Adversarial Review Inside Antigravity Built to automate this workflow inside Antigravity, the open-source EGM plugin runs across three stages:
egm-brainstorm: Loads system context to explore trade-offs and assumptions with the developer without touching application code. egm-draft: Produces a structured Markdown design spec covering problem statement, technical plan, alternatives considered, and exact target file paths. egm-review: Spawns stateless Goldfish sessions to run the adversarial Goldfish Protocol. The Goldfish Protocol runs three distinct checks: a Comprehension Check where a fresh Goldfish restates the spec to expose ambiguity, an Antagonistic Review where multiple Goldfish personas attack logical flaws, and an Implementation Readiness Check verifying that file paths and function signatures are concrete enough to code against.
From Internal Google Workflow to Apache 2.0 Open Source Originally used daily by Google engineers shipping production code, the EGM plugin packages custom Markdown rules and subagent personas under Apache 2.0 - shifting developers out of line-by-line prompt micromanagement and into architectural review.
Summary Splits AI sessions into a long-horizon, no-code Elephant architect and stateless Goldfish critics to eliminate context bias. Runs specs through a three-part Goldfish Protocol: Comprehension Check, Antagonistic Review, and Implementation Readiness Check. Open-sourced from Google’s internal production workflow under Apache 2.0 with ready-to-run support for environments like Antigravity.
summary: Google open-sourced its internal Elephant-Goldfish Model (EGM) plugin under Apache 2.0, pairing a no-code long-horizon architect session with stateless adversarial reviewers.
title: Google's Open-Source Elephant-Goldfish Model Plugin for AI Software Design

content:
Waiting on terminal coding agents like Claude Code or Codex makes it tempting to spin up another task in a second tab. Before long, follow-up questions and half-finished branches multiply into 20 concurrent threads, burning mental energy just remembering what each session was doing. One developer shared a clean personal experiment that replaces tab juggling with a priority queue backed by Git.
Git-Committed Markdown Tickets and Clear Role Boundaries To eliminate lost state across closed terminals, the Git repository itself serves as the single source of truth. Tasks live right beside the code as committed Markdown ticket files along with board state. Background agents poll the board on a schedule to investigate new tickets, implement approved specs, and run test suites plus browser checks. Risky code changes stay isolated on feature branches awaiting sign-off, and production deployments remain strictly human-triggered.
Closing Mental Loops with an Owner Inbox and Artifact Viewers Only items genuinely blocked on human judgment surface in a prioritized owner inbox. A small script scans the board and groups diffs needing review, trade-off calls, and open questions. Each cycle also generates a visual Claude artifact from Git state so the owner can inspect what changed and why from a single link instead of scrolling raw terminal logs, recording the decision straight back onto the Git ticket card.
Pull One Ticket, Decide, and Return It to the Queue Working strictly one ticket at a time - making a call or requesting a revision and returning the card to the queue - closes the mental loop before picking up the next item. Remaining open items on the author’s roadmap include a tighter summary view to cut context-reload time from 20 minutes down to 1 minute, plus circuit breakers to stop blocked tickets from looping while awaiting human input.
Scaling personal throughput with coding agents depends less on opening more terminal tabs than on designing a queue that lets human attention cleanly close one decision at a time.
Summary Replaces fragmented terminal agent sessions with a Git-backed Markdown priority queue that preserves state across restarts. Delegates research, coding, and verification to agents while keeping risky branch merges and production deploys gated on human approval. Pairs an owner inbox with generated Claude artifact views so developers process and close one ticket at a time without context thrash.
summary: A solo experiment replacing 20 scattered AI coding terminal threads with Git-committed Markdown tickets, an owner inbox, and single-ticket context closure.
title: Taming Multi-Agent Context Overload with a Git Priority Queue

content:
Full speech transcript summary of Jang PM’s video “Sharing a Free Copy-Editing Agent That Strips AI Tells | Using Claude Code / Codex Agents” (slop-rewrite).
[00:00] Intro: AI-generated drafts often read vaguely right up to the final paragraph or insert forced metaphors that muddy the point. Existing Korean editing skills that mechanically swap banned phrases strip obvious AI tells yet flatten the writing’s natural voice. Rather than doing line-by-line regex replacements, slop-rewrite flags weak spots via code rules and lets the LLM rewrite for full-paragraph flow. Shared free on GitHub, it installs into Claude Code, Codex, or Antigravity by cloning the repo and asking the agent to register it as a global (user-scope) skill so it works from any folder.
[01:58] How slop-rewrite Works: Code checks pinpoint AI-sounding words and phrasing while the LLM handles rewriting across three layers: 1) universal AI-tell removal principles, 2) a selectable Style Guide matching the target format, and 3) accumulated personal preferences learned from user feedback.
[03:36] Demo 1 - Polishing an LLM Wiki Blog Draft: Running slop-rewrite on an AI-drafted company blog post converts hesitant rhetorical questions into direct statements, cuts filler phrases and stray emoji, and replaces vague lines like “you do not need many prerequisites” with concrete specifics.
[05:18] Demo 2 - Editing an Agent Engineering Trends Post: On a draft comparing prompt, context, harness, and graph engineering, the original text leaned on cliched pendulum metaphors (“where does the pendulum swing next?”). slop-rewrite drops unhelpful metaphors automatically, tightens repetitive three-part framings into crisp sentences, and cuts manual editing effort ahead of final human review.
[07:00] Building Custom Style Guides and Saving Taste: Alongside built-in presets (Jang PM style, Toss style, and Korean bullet-report style), the bundled Style Guide Builder skill ingested 82 past issues of the Danggeun Mail productivity newsletter to register a new custom style guide. Beyond style guides, users can ask the agent to render drafts as commentable artifacts, leave red-pen margin notes explaining what worked or missed, and save those subjective preferences (such as preferring a sharper thesis up front) for future runs.
[09:37] Improving Agents 1 - Inductive Refinement: Passing human-written gold examples or detailed inline margin critiques lets the agent infer its own evaluation rules inductively, producing much stronger gains than abstract instructions.
[10:40] Improving Agents 2 - Light-Touch Deductive Refinement: Micromanaging step-by-step agent procedures often degrades output on modern models. Leave procedural planning to the agent at first; later, ask it to visualize its workflow as an HTML diagram splitting Human, Code, and LLM responsibilities so you can nudge high-level boundaries (such as moving a rigid code check to the LLM).
[12:37] Wrap-Up: Set clear goals and quality criteria rather than micromanaging every step - acting like a smart, high-trust lead when collaborating with AI agents.
Drafts written with AI often have clean grammar while still reading unnaturally - burying the main point or wedging in strained metaphors that blur meaning. Editing skills built on mechanical word-replacement lists strip surface cliches yet leave prose flat. slop-rewrite is an open-source Korean copy-editing agent built to fix AI-sounding prose while keeping natural rhythm.
Rewriting for Flow Across Three Layers of Standards Instead of relying on rigid find-and-replace scripts, slop-rewrite uses code rules only to flag suspect passages and delegates actual rewriting to the LLM so paragraph flow stays intact.
Edits apply three layers in sequence:
Shared AI-slop removal rules strip forced metaphors, filler transitions, and translationese. A target Style Guide sets tone and structure for the document type. Saved personal taste rules apply subjective preferences gathered from prior artifact comments and edits. Alongside built-in presets, an included Style Guide Builder skill analyzes existing newsletters or past articles you provide to generate custom style profiles that sharpen as feedback accumulates.
Cloning the Repo and Registering as a User-Scope Skill Published on GitHub, slop-rewrite plugs directly into CLI agents like Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity. Clone the repository into a local folder and ask your agent to register it as a user-scope (global) skill so you can invoke it on blog drafts or executive memos from any project directory.
Inductive vs. Deductive Feedback for Better Agent Output Creator Jang PM highlights two complementary ways to tune agent quality over time.
Inductive refinement feeds the agent finished human examples or inline margin comments on an artifact so it reverse-engineers concrete editing rules from real judgments.
Deductive refinement inspects an HTML diagram of the agent’s pipeline - separating Human, Code, and LLM steps - to adjust high-level boundaries without micromanaging every step. With capable models, defining clear goals and quality standards beats scripting rigid step-by-step instructions.
Summary slop-rewrite pairs code-based slop detection with LLM rewriting so prose keeps natural flow rather than reading like mechanical word swaps. Combines three layers - universal AI-tell rules, custom Style Guides, and saved user feedback - to match an author’s voice. Tunes agent quality best through example-driven inductive feedback and high-level goal setting rather than step-by-step micromanagement.
summary: Jang PM’s open-source slop-rewrite agent strips awkward AI metaphors and translationese using anti-slop rules, style guides, and saved user feedback.
title: slop-rewrite: Polishing AI-Generated Korean Prose Without Losing Voice

content:
In KakaoTalk Gift’s seller contract-termination workflow, the manual time required for one operations specialist to process a single seller dropped from 1 hour to 10 minutes. What stands out in Kakao’s Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE) talk is how they achieved that number. Here are five practical lessons on how embedded engineers reshaped frontline operations.
1. Faster Individual Drafting Still Hits Review and Handoff Bottlenecks Speeding up document drafting or search with AI leaves total lead time unchanged if work still sits in queues waiting on reviews, sign-offs, and cross-team handoffs. As the talk illustrates, if four out of five stages process 100 items an hour while one stage processes 20, end-to-end throughput stays stuck at 20 items an hour. What to measure: Track idle wait time alongside individual task speed. Once engineering accelerates, product planning, design, QA, or operations often becomes the new bottleneck. Talk from 05:402. Picking Automation Targets by Metrics, Repetition, and Downstream Impact Kakao’s FDE team filtered candidate workflows against three criteria:
Does a hard metric move? Cost savings, revenue lift, or risk reduction must be quantifiable. Is manual repetition or error rate high? Look for tasks where scaling volume currently requires adding headcount. Does fixing this step unblock downstream work? Improving one stage should shorten end-to-end cycle time across follow-on tasks. At the time of the talk, the team had selected 34 short-term improvement tasks and 15 multi-workflow strategic initiatives. Embedded FDEs sit directly with business teams, owning discovery, planning, UI design, engineering, and stakeholder alignment until the operational bottleneck actually clears. Talk from 09:353. Going from 1 Hour to 10 Minutes Required Unifying Lookup, Judgment, and Action Closing out a KakaoTalk Gift seller contract spanned seven steps, from pulling scattered records to mailing certified legal notices and tracking statutory hold periods:
Prior workflow: Specialists manually queried separate systems into spreadsheets and docs, relied on tribal knowledge in their heads for edge-case rules, and walked over to a shared Windows PC just to dispatch certified notices. Redesigned workflow: Connected seller, product, order, and contract tables into a single screen showing status alongside explicit decision evidence, letting operators trigger actions directly while logging every outcome back to the system. Automation boundary: Workflow triggers, AI summary reports, certified-notice dispatch, and 90-day statutory wait monitoring were automated, while settlement conditions, formal sign-off drafts, and final contract closure stayed with human specialists. What the metric means: The 90-day legal waiting period itself stays fixed by law; the semi-automated pipeline cut active human handling time per case from 60 minutes to 10. Case study from 12:04, Results from 21:184. Statistics and Explicit Rules Handled 80% of Decisions Status classification: Roughly 80% of automated status classifications ran on statistics, trend analysis, thresholds, and deterministic business rules - surfacing the exact rule evidence alongside each label. UI automation without APIs: Because the certified-notice system lacked an API and followed identical click sequences every time, the team chose deterministic RPA via Power Automate on Windows rather than asking an LLM to interpret screen pixels. Where the AI agent sits: The LLM agent interprets natural-language operator questions and routes them to data lookups and action tools, while pulling ground-truth facts from business databases and enforcing hard procedural guardrails via code. Tool choice followed task structure: fast, auditable rules and RPA for fixed logic and repetitive clicks, and LLMs strictly where natural-language intent needed routing. Decision logic from 17:04, Tool selection from 18:345. Validate on One Narrow Workflow, Then Reuse as a Shared Platform Start with shared domain vocabulary: Defining core entities and relationships - such as how a “Seller” binds to a “Contract” - formed a practical ontology so neighboring teams stopped interpreting the same business terms differently. Keep initial scope minimal: Instead of spending months building a company-wide ontology platform up front, the team modeled only the seller, contract, and termination rules needed to prove value on this single workflow first. Next horizon: Package data connectors, ontology definitions, rule engines, action runners, and agents into a reusable “AI Workspace as a Service” so other business units can adopt field-tested building blocks. Rewiring data pipelines and business rules from scratch for every new automation project creates unsustainable maintenance debt. When applying Kakao’s FDE playbook internally, ask which pieces of today’s workflow can be reused unchanged on the very next ops problem. Start-small architecture from 14:27, Platform roadmap from 24:57
summary: Kakao’s Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE) team embedded directly with business ops to connect scattered data, rules, RPA, and AI agents into reusable workflows.
title: How Kakao's Forward Deployed Engineers Cut a 1-Hour Ops Workflow to 10 Minutes

content:
A wild new AI video tool just dropped. Viral videos that took creators days to assemble can now be broken down frame by frame by AI - covering shot framing, camera movement, captions, sound effects, transitions, and even reconstructed AI video prompts, finishing with a ready-to-shoot replication blueprint. Studying viral video craft no longer relies on pure guesswork.
Anyone dissecting a viral video usually ends up stepping through frames by hand to guess how shots, pacing, and effects were put together. The open-source tool rea-video replaces guesswork with structured analysis, breaking down input videos shot by shot and outputting an actionable replication blueprint.
Supporting formats ranging from talking-head clips and tabletop shoots to AI-generated videos and 3D animation, rea-video inspects visual effects, subtitle timing, edit cuts, and audio layering across every scene before generating a step-by-step production plan.
Format-Specific Breakdown Across Video Types For live-action footage, rea-video identifies camera framing, composition, lighting gear checklists, and color grading profiles. On AI-generated clips, it reconstructs per-shot generation prompts alongside recommended models for batch creation, and for avatar or 3D videos it flags suitable video models versus rendering pipelines.
On code-driven UI demos and motion graphics, it extracts layout hierarchy and motion timing curves so developers can rebuild scenes as Remotion projects. Hybrid edits mixing screen recordings with live footage get classified shot by shot, and passing --lang outputs the entire analysis report in your preferred language.
Turning Video Breakdowns into Repeatable Workflows Structured shot breakdowns take the trial-and-error out of studying reference videos, turning ad-hoc creative research into a repeatable production playbook.
Summary rea-video decomposes live-action, AI-generated, 3D, and code-based UI videos shot by shot. Outputs camera setups, lighting lists, color profiles, reconstructed per-shot AI prompts, and Remotion-ready motion specs. Supports localized reports via --lang, making it easy to wire into automated creative agent pipelines.
summary: rea-video breaks down live-action, AI-generated, 3D, and motion-graphics videos frame by frame into camera setups, prompts, audio cues, and replication blueprints.
title: rea-video: Open-Source Shot-by-Shot Video Reverse Engineering

content:
Bottom line: The model featured in the demo is NVIDIA’s RE-USE. It is a strong STT preprocessing candidate, provided you use the commercially licensed weights and benchmark it on Korean audio first.
What It Is and How It Performs
Promoted by NVIDIA on October 30 (model card dated October 22), RE-USE is a 9.6M-parameter multilingual speech enhancement model. Beyond simple denoising, it removes background noise, reverb, clipping, codec artifacts, packet loss, and mic distortion while preserving intelligibility and speaker timbre. In NVIDIA’s benchmarks, it outperforms 250M (Sidon) and 500M (UniPASE) models across PESQ, speaker similarity, and ASR character accuracy - lifting ASR accuracy from 81.29% on raw noisy audio to 89.17%. Checks Before Production Adoption
Licensing (most important): The original nvidia/RE-USE repo released in March uses the NVIDIA One-Way Noncommercial License (NSCLv1). Commercial deployments must use NVIDIA-NemotronLabs-RE-USE (including its laughter-preserving variant) under OpenMDW-1.1, after reviewing its exact terms. Korean support: Marketed as language-agnostic, its training corpus covers English, German, Spanish, French, and Mandarin only - test directly on real Korean meeting recordings. Real scope of “local execution”: Official benchmarks ran on Linux with an NVIDIA A100 and Mamba CUDA kernels. Small parameter count alone does not guarantee real-time CPU or edge speed, and while a community MLX port exists for Mac, check whether derived weights inherit NSCLv1. Meeting Transcription Pipeline Perspective In a field-recording -> RE-USE -> STT -> ontology extraction pipeline, RE-USE fits cleanly ahead of ASR while preserving speaker identity for diarization. The fastest validation is comparing Character Error Rate (CER) on raw STT vs. RE-USE + STT across a few noisy recordings, or testing samples in the Gradio demo.
Reference links: nvidia/RE-USE on Hugging Face, AlphaSignal coverage, Hermes overview, Digg spotlight, and faraday/re-use-mlx.
Architecturally, NVIDIA-NemotronLabs-RE-USE (~9.61M parameters, ~38MB FP32 weights) stacks 30 bidirectional time-frequency Mamba (SEMamba) blocks for universal speech enhancement and bandwidth extension across 8kHz-48kHz audio.
1. Pipeline Ordering Pitfalls on Meeting Audio
Overlapping speech suppression: Because NVIDIA-NemotronLabs-RE-USE is trained to keep the dominant speaker and suppress simultaneous secondary voices as noise, running it over an unsegmented multi-speaker file erases interjections. Run Speaker Diarization (such as Pyannote) and VAD first, then pass individual speaker segments to RE-USE. Chunking to prevent OOM: Trained on clips under 10 seconds, feeding 30+ second recordings whole spikes VRAM/Unified Memory or degrades output. Split long turns into 10-second chunks with 1-second overlap. Weight provenance: Verify commercial deployments pull nvidia/NVIDIA-NemotronLabs-RE-USE (OpenMDW-1.1) rather than third-party ports of noncommercial nvidia/RE-USE (NSCLv1). 2. Local Runtime Options
Option A (Apple Silicon / MLX): Run natively without CUDA mamba-ssm or causal-conv1d via pip install mlx-audio huggingface_hub soundfile librosa and huggingface-cli download nvidia/NVIDIA-NemotronLabs-RE-USE --local-dir ./models/reuse. Option B (C++ / GGUF via audio.cpp): Run audiocpp_cli --task s2s --family reuse --model ./models/RE-USE-GGUF/reuse-f32.gguf --backend metal --audio meeting_raw.wav --out meeting_clean.wav --request-option audio_chunk_duration_sec=10 --request-option audio_chunk_overlap_sec=1 (swap --backend cuda on NVIDIA GPUs, processing 5s of audio in ~0.27s at RTF 0.05). Option C (Official Python / Docker on NVIDIA GPUs): Download nvidia/NVIDIA-NemotronLabs-RE-USE, place 30s+ files under long_noisy_audio, and run sh inference_chunk.sh. 3. Diarization + RE-USE + Whisper Pipeline
Audio normalization and VAD/diarization: Load meeting audio as 16kHz mono, tag speech segments and speaker IDs via pyannote.audio or Silero VAD, and split monologues longer than 15s into 10s chunks with 1s overlap. Per-segment RE-USE speech enhancement: Pass each waveform array through RE-USE to strip HVAC hum, vehicle noise, and room reverb while sharpening muffled far-field phoneme contours. STT transcription and structuring: Transcribe cleaned segments with a local ASR model such as Whisper-large-v3-turbo to cut silence hallucinations and feed speaker-tagged text downstream. import subprocess import tempfile import soundfile as sf import librosa def enhance_audio_segment(audio_array, sr, gguf_model_path, backend="metal"): """Denoise a single speech segment with the RE-USE model.""" with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix=".wav") as temp_in, \ tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix=".wav") as temp_out: sf.write(temp_in.name, audio_array, sr) cmd = [ "audiocpp_cli", "--task", "s2s", "--family", "reuse", "--model", gguf_model_path, "--backend", backend, "--audio", temp_in.name, "--out", temp_out.name, "--request-option", "audio_chunk_duration_sec=10", "--request-option", "audio_chunk_overlap_sec=1" ] subprocess.run(cmd, check=True, stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL) clean_audio, _ = librosa.load(temp_out.name, sr=16000, mono=True) return clean_audio def process_meeting_recording(audio_path, diarization_segments, stt_model, gguf_path): """ diarization_segments: [{'speaker': 'SPEAKER_01', 'start': 0.5, 'end': 8.2}, ...] """ raw_audio, sr = librosa.load(audio_path, sr=16000, mono=True) transcript_results = [] for seg in diarization_segments: start_sample = int(seg["start"] * sr) end_sample = int(seg["end"] * sr) segment_audio = raw_audio[start_sample:end_sample] # Skip segments shorter than 0.2 seconds if len(segment_audio) < int(0.2 * sr): continue # 1. Strip noise and room reverb with RE-USE clean_segment = enhance_audio_segment(segment_audio, sr, gguf_path) # 2. Run STT on cleaned audio (e.g., faster-whisper or mlx-whisper) text = stt_model.transcribe(clean_segment, language="ko") transcript_results.append({ "speaker": seg["speaker"], "start": round(seg["start"], 2), "end": round(seg["end"], 2), "text": text.strip() }) return transcript_results 4. Production Tip (Bandwidth Extension): When field recordings come from 8kHz phone lines or budget Bluetooth mics that smear high-frequency sibilant consonants (such as Korean s, j, and ch), enabling RE-USE Bandwidth Extension (BWE) restores 8kHz audio up to 16kHz-48kHz and lowers Korean syllable-final consonant CER.
Background noise and room reverb in field meetings or phone recordings remain a leading cause of STT transcription errors. NVIDIA’s RE-USE packs universal speech enhancement into just 9.6M parameters - here is how its architecture works and how to wire it into a production STT pipeline without losing multi-speaker turns.
Parameter Efficiency and Mamba Architecture Weighing roughly 38MB in FP32, RE-USE stacks 30 bidirectional time-frequency Mamba (SEMamba) blocks for efficient sequence modeling. Despite its compact footprint, it beats much larger models including Sidon (250M) and UniPASE (500M) on PESQ, speaker similarity, and downstream ASR character accuracy - lifting noisy-audio ASR accuracy from 76-81% up to 87-89%. It supports 7 sampling rates from 8kHz to 48kHz alongside bandwidth extension. While acoustic restoration is language-agnostic in principle, its training set covers English, German, Spanish, French, and Mandarin, so teams processing Korean meetings should benchmark CER on real internal audio before rollout.
Pipeline Ordering Rules for Multi-Speaker Meetings Running RE-USE blindly over a full hour-long meeting file introduces two failure modes. First, when two or more people talk at once, RE-USE is trained to isolate the loudest voice and suppress secondary speakers as background noise - wiping out overlapping remarks in group discussions. Always slice speaker turns first using VAD or diarization tools like Pyannote, then run RE-USE per segment. Second, because training used clips under 10 seconds, feeding 30+ second streams whole risks memory spikes or quality drop-offs, making VAD segmentation or 10-second chunking (with 1-second overlap) mandatory. Finally, double-check weight licensing: the March nvidia/RE-USE checkpoint carries a noncommercial license (NSCLv1), whereas commercial pipelines must use NVIDIA-NemotronLabs-RE-USE under OpenMDW-1.1.
Runtime Options and End-to-End Preprocessing Flow On Apple Silicon Macs, mlx-audio runs converted weights locally with Metal acceleration, while Linux GPU servers and C++ backends can pair audio.cpp with 37.8MB GGUF weights to keep compute overhead minimal. In a Python ingestion pipeline, VAD-sliced waveforms pass through RE-USE first to strip HVAC hum, vehicle noise, and room echo before hitting an ASR model such as Whisper-large-v3-turbo - sharply reducing Whisper’s habit of hallucinating repeated phrases during noisy pauses. When ingesting 8kHz phone calls or muffled Bluetooth mic audio, turning on Bandwidth Extension restores high-frequency consonant contours and cuts Korean recognition errors.
For data engineers dealing with noisy field audio, testing segment-level RE-USE preprocessing on a sample batch via the Gradio demo or audio.cpp is a fast way to measure downstream STT gains.
Summary At 9.6M parameters (~38MB FP32), Mamba-based RE-USE outperforms 500M-class baselines on speech quality and downstream ASR accuracy. Multi-speaker meeting pipelines must run VAD / Diarization -> per-segment RE-USE (<=10s chunks) -> STT so overlapping remarks are not suppressed as noise. Commercial deployments must use OpenMDW-1.1 NVIDIA-NemotronLabs-RE-USE weights rather than noncommercial NSCLv1 checkpoints.
summary: How NVIDIA’s 9.6M-parameter Mamba speech enhancement model RE-USE works, what license rules apply, and how to pair diarization and chunking ahead of Whisper STT.
title: NVIDIA RE-USE: 9.6M Speech Enhancement and STT Preprocessing Pipelines

content:
As AI coding agents write a growing share of production code, engineers face a subtle risk: losing the sharp judgment needed to review it. Addy Osmani, an engineer on Anthropic’s Claude Code team, argues that developers have to deliberately protect critical thinking as agent output improves. Here are the core takeaways on why verification skills dull and how to counter that drift.
Cognitive Surrender and the Paradox of Supervision Better AI models paradoxically weaken human oversight. Early coding assistants made obvious syntax and logic blunders that kept developers alert. Today, polished-looking diffs invite Cognitive Surrender - rubber-stamping generated code without checking underlying assumptions.
An internal Anthropic study of 132 engineers and researchers surfaced the Paradox of Supervision: supervising Claude effectively requires strong coding instincts, yet heavy reliance on AI steadily erodes those exact instincts. Andrej Karpathy noted a similar effect firsthand, observing his own raw coding fluency dip after shifting roughly 80% of his coding workflow to AI.
Comprehension Debt and the Orchestration Tax Code review intuition fades fast without hands-on problem solving and mental models of the system. Even when green test suites let diffs merge smoothly today, skipping structural understanding piles up Comprehension Debt - making production incidents and architectural changes far harder to debug months later.
Running parallel agent fleets adds an Orchestration Tax as well. Agent code generation easily outpaces human review bandwidth, and when an agent writes both the implementation and the tests under the same flawed premise, a passing test suite proves very little.
Deliberate Verification Habits That Keep Humans in Charge Rather than arbitrarily banning AI tools, teams need explicit verification steps wired into their workflow. Write down expected behavior and acceptance criteria before handing a task to an agent, and periodically build core pieces without AI assistance to keep foundational instincts sharp.
Developers no longer need to type every line by hand, yet they always need to know what they do and do not understand in their own system. As Anthropic’s engineering guidance emphasizes, technical ownership and accountability cannot be delegated to a model.
Judgment is a muscle: keeping critical review habits active even when agent output looks effortless separates durable engineering teams from passive operators.
Summary Rising AI output quality lowers perceived review urgency, triggering cognitive surrender and rubber-stamped merges. Heavy agent delegation accumulates comprehension debt and an orchestration tax when code volume outstrips human review capacity. Setting acceptance criteria before prompting and practicing key tasks unassisted preserve engineering judgment.
summary: Anthropic engineer Addy Osmani warns that better AI code increases cognitive surrender, comprehension debt, and orchestration tax unless teams build deliberate review habits.
title: Avoiding the Paradox of Supervision and Cognitive Surrender with AI Agents

content:
When LLM agents query enterprise databases directly, hallucinated joins or invented metrics create immediate business risk. Accurate, auditable numbers matter far more than fast guesses. NVIDIA’s open-source Auto-Ontology sits alongside existing databases to ground agents in verified context, compiling raw schema metadata into business glossary terms, certified SQL formulas, and join graphs.
Turning Database Metadata into a Certified Ontology Building an ontology starts with source ingestion across three stages: an ingestion service profiles database catalogs and maps tables to business concepts, infers join paths and schema relationships from foreign keys and data patterns, and stores the resulting graph in PostgreSQL with pgvector embeddings.
Operationally, the framework follows five stages: Discover, Ground, Certify, Validate, and Expose. Ground assigns a single canonical definition per business concept across tables. Certify lets data teams edit and approve business terms and SQL expressions via web UI or API. Validate checks whether an incoming question can actually be answered before running queries and returns both generated SQL and reasoning steps. Expose serves that context to agents over MCP (Model Context Protocol) and REST APIs - pairing human sign-off with structured retrieval to curb SQL hallucinations.
Selective Ontology Retrieval vs. Raw Schema Dumping Standard Text-to-SQL pipelines stuff entire database schemas into the prompt context window. As table counts grow, token costs spike and agents guess join conditions from ambiguous column names alone. Auto-Ontology retrieves only the glossary terms, formulas, and tables relevant to the specific question.
It also handles unanswerable questions differently. Ask a naive schema-stuffed agent for Return on Ad Spend (ROAS) against the Wide World Importers sample database - which contains zero ad-spend tables - and it will often fabricate a plausible-looking query anyway. An Auto-Ontology agent runs check_answerable first, detects missing schema coverage, and asks the user for clarification instead of returning bogus numbers.
Deployment Setup and Benchmark Evaluation The companion auto-ontology-eval repository benchmarks ontology-grounded agents against raw schema-in-prompt baselines across BIRD, BEAVER, and FDABench-Lite, scoring exact execution match to quantify accuracy gains.
Local deployment spins up PostgreSQL, pgAdmin, and the web UI via Docker Compose. After adding an NVIDIA API key and database connection string to .env, running semantic compilation indexes the target database - so a query asking for June 2015 product revenue in Pennsylvania resolves business relationships through the ontology and returns both verified SQL and step-by-step reasoning.
For enterprise data teams, putting a human-certified semantic layer in front of Text-to-SQL agents turns database access into a governable engineering workflow.
Summary Replaces full-schema prompt stuffing with targeted retrieval of certified ontology terms and join paths, cutting both token spend and SQL hallucinations. Uses check_answerable coverage checks to catch unsupported metrics up front and ask follow-up questions rather than fabricating SQL. Exposes the semantic layer over MCP and REST APIs for clean integration into existing LLM agent stacks.
summary: NVIDIA’s open-source Auto-Ontology compiles database metadata into human-certified business terms, verified SQL formulas, and join graphs exposed over MCP.
title: NVIDIA Auto-Ontology: A Semantic Context Layer for Enterprise Text-to-SQL

content:
X’s lead designer released a new skill aimed at higher-craft UI generation. Stageshow helps AI agents produce polished visual interface artifacts, including UI mockups and screen concepts, interface animations, Bento Grid layouts, and other visual design assets. Worth exploring if you want sharper visual execution from coding agents.
Interfaces generated by AI coding agents often work functionally while falling flat visually. To close that gap, X lead designer Benji Taylor open-sourced Stageshow, an agent skill built to guide coding agents toward production-grade visual design.
React UI Generation Paired with Video Self-Verification Rather than shipping a static component library, Stageshow bundles composition rules with an automated visual inspection loop. Using React, agents generate static hero visuals, feature cards, animated cursor walkthroughs, and Bento Grid layouts backed by explicit motion and framing guidelines. Crucially, the skill records video captures of rendered output so the agent can review its own animations and layout polish before finishing.
One-Line CLI Installation Adding Stageshow to an agent workspace takes a single terminal command:
npx skills add benjitaylor/skills --skill stageshow Once installed, coding agents reference the bundled examples and composition guides automatically, with clear licensing and asset specs suited for real product work.
Where It Fits for Frontend Engineers and Technical PMs Stageshow fits engineers and product builders who need polished product mockups or interactive launch demos fast. Adding visual framing rules and self-recorded video checks gives logic-heavy coding agents a practical design eye, producing near-production React components in far fewer iterations.
Summary Guides AI agents to build static UI mockups, Bento Grids, cursor demos, and motion sequences in React. Includes a video-capture verification loop so agents inspect their own rendered UI output. Installs into coding agent workspaces with a single npx skills add CLI command.
summary: Released by X lead designer Benji Taylor, Stageshow equips coding agents to build React UI mockups, Bento Grid layouts, and cursor animations with video self-verification.
title: Stageshow: An AI Agent Skill for Production-Grade React UI and Motion

content:
Q Labs published Dust, a method for pretraining Transformer language models without backpropagation. Instead of computing exact derivatives over a backward computation graph, Dust updates weights using forward passes alone through zeroth-order optimization - offering an alternative training path on hardware bottlenecked by memory capacity and bandwidth.
Token-Level Node Perturbation and Gradient Estimation Dust applies Node Perturbation, injecting independent random noise into activations at each token position. Rather than propagating exact errors via the chain rule, it measures how perturbations shift loss values to estimate gradients statistically. Because each token acts as an independent virtual population sample, a single forward pass evaluates perturbations across the sequence in parallel. As the number of noise trials K grows, the estimated update direction converges cleanly toward the true backpropagation gradient.
Trading Compute for Memory Savings Dropping the backward pass eliminates storing full Activation graphs and heavy optimizer states in VRAM, and removes the requirement that every network operation be differentiable. The trade-off is raw forward compute: matching backpropagation’s gradient signal quality requires substantially more forward-pass FLOPs.
Compared against prior weight-space evolutionary strategies such as EGGROLL, Dust improves compute efficiency by 10^3 to 10^4x, maintaining stable gradient estimates up to 243M-parameter Transformers trained on 1B tokens. Crucially, effective population efficiency improves as model scale increases.
Implications for Memory-Bound AI Hardware Modern LLM training and inference hit memory bandwidth and capacity walls well before exhausting raw GPU arithmetic throughput. On hardware with spare compute headroom, trading extra forward FLOPs for a fraction of the memory footprint opens an intriguing design space beyond standard backpropagation.
Summary Dust trains Transformers via forward-only per-token activation perturbation without maintaining backward computation graphs. Achieves 10^3 to 10^4x higher compute efficiency than weight-space ES baselines like EGGROLL, validated up to 243M parameters and 1B tokens. Trades extra forward compute for sharp reductions in activation and optimizer memory on memory-bandwidth-bound AI hardware.
summary: Q Labs’ Dust paper trains Transformer language models using forward-only activation noise perturbation, trading extra FLOPs for lower memory bandwidth and state overhead.
title: Dust: Pretraining Transformers Without Backpropagation via Node Perturbation

content:
When AI agents generate thousands of lines of code a day, human line-by-line review becomes the bottleneck. Founded by former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke, Entire is a new software development platform built around agent collaboration, pairing high-speed code hosting with automated verification.
Replacing Pull Requests with Trails Entire replaces traditional Pull Requests with a review workflow called Trails. Whenever an AI agent pushes changes, the platform automatically generates quality evaluations and rubric scores. Instead of reading every diff line by hand, developers inspect the agent’s execution trail and evaluation scores, merging immediately once verification thresholds pass.
Cutting Token Spend with Continuous Memory Preserving cross-session context relies on Continuous Memory. Under the hood, a Codebase Graph maps structural dependencies to cut agent token consumption by up to 71%, while an Agentic Brain records prior failures so agents stop repeating the same mistakes. Entire pairs these memory layers with a custom distributed Git hosting backend tuned for fast pushes.
Automated CI Integration and Data Residency To shrink verification latency, Entire integrates directly with Continuous Integration (CI) runners from Buildkite and Depot. Pushing agent code triggers builds automatically and streams results straight back into the Trails view. Built-in migration tooling converts existing GitHub Actions workflows, and repository setup supports explicit data-residency regions including the US and EU.
As code authoring, review, and CI shift around agent throughput, human engineering effort moves upstream from writing every diff to defining evaluation gates and auditing system behavior.
Summary Replaces manual line-by-line Pull Request reviews with automated, score-backed Trails for agent-generated changes. Uses Codebase Graph and Agentic Brain memory layers to cut token spend by up to 71% and block repeated agent mistakes. Pairs high-speed distributed Git hosting with Buildkite and Depot CI plus GitHub Actions migration tools and US/EU data residency.
summary: Founded by former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke, Entire replaces traditional pull requests with AI-scored Trails, codebase graphs that cut token use by 71%, and integrated CI.
title: Entire and Trails: Former GitHub CEO's AI-Native Alternative to Pull Requests

content:
Teams building AI coding agents often pack execution harnesses with dense system prompts and specialized tools, assuming richer scaffolding translates into higher patch accuracy. Empirical benchmarks tell a different story.
Harness Complexity vs. Coding Accuracy Researchers from Shandong University and UC Berkeley benchmarked three agent harnesses - Claude Code, OpenCode, and mini-SWE-agent - across open-weight and API models including Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash alongside Claude Opus 5 as a frontier reference. Evaluations ran on 492 tasks from SWE-bench Verified, including 45 hard issues estimated to take human engineers over an hour.
Across the board, heavier harnesses failed to consistently outperform minimal ones. Switching harnesses flipped pass/fail outcomes on roughly 13% of hard tasks, yet re-running the exact same harness produced comparable run-to-run variance - showing most apparent accuracy swings were execution noise rather than structural advantage.
What actually moved scores was basic error recovery. In OpenCode, hitting the 32,000 output Token cap truncated runs before the agent finished writing its patch, dragging down accuracy. Claude Code automatically prompted continuation whenever outputs hit the token limit, keeping long patch generations intact.
Fixed Context Overhead and the 3x Cost Gap While accuracy barely budged, inference spend diverged sharply: running the exact same model on the same benchmark cost up to 3x more depending on the harness. Fixed prompt overhead from system instructions and tool schemas drove most of that gap.
Claude Code starts every session with more than 10,000 tokens of fixed system and tool context, whereas mini-SWE-agent uses roughly 800 tokens. Over multi-step debugging trajectories, resending that baseline context on every turn compounds input token bills rapidly.
Lightweight harnesses were not universally cheaper across every model, however. Paired with DeepSeek models, mini-SWE-agent triggered enough extra tool-call turns to invert total cost - underscoring why teams have to measure specific model-and-harness pairs rather than assuming one setup always wins.
Trimming bloated system prompts and unused tool definitions - keeping only guardrails and recovery logic that prove their worth in repeated evaluations - cuts agent operating costs without sacrificing solve rates.
Summary Higher agent harness complexity does not proportionally raise SWE-bench accuracy, with most task-level flips matching normal run-to-run noise. Fixed system-prompt and tool-schema overhead can create up to a 3x inference cost gap on identical tasks, making prompt pruning high-return work. Because tool-call frequency varies by model-harness pairing, teams should benchmark cost and solve rate together under real workloads.
summary: A Shandong University and UC Berkeley study finds complex agent harnesses rarely beat minimal ones on SWE-bench accuracy while raising costs up to 3x.
title: AI Coding Agent Harness Complexity vs. Cost Efficiency

content:
Checking whether a local dev server is up, running a quick command to see your active Git branch, or hunting through browser tabs for a staging dashboard takes only seconds once - yet repeating those checks dozens of times a day breaks focus.
SwiftBar puts that status right into the top macOS menu bar. A compact label like DEV Running sits in the bar, and clicking it expands a dropdown with check timestamps or clickable links. Any script that prints plain text works without building a native macOS app.
Below, we build a minimal date plugin first and then expand into a live local dev-server monitor, cross-checking setup details against the official SwiftBar documentation.
How Script Output Becomes a Menu Bar Item In SwiftBar, a plugin is simply an executable file that prints menu lines. Here we use standard .sh Bash scripts supported out of the box on macOS.
When you run echo "Task Status" in a terminal, it prints text to standard output (stdout). SwiftBar reads that stdout stream and turns it into a menu bar label plus a dropdown menu:
DEV Running --- URL: http://localhost:3000 Checked at: 09:30:00 Everything above the first --- becomes the menu bar Header, and everything below it forms the clickable dropdown Body. In this example, DEV Running stays visible in the menu bar while the URL and timestamp appear when clicked.
Because menu bar width is tight, keep the header to a single short line and push details into the dropdown body. Printing multiple lines above --- makes SwiftBar cycle through them as rotating titles, so stick to one line when starting out.
Installing SwiftBar and Choosing a Dedicated Plugin Folder With Homebrew installed, run:
brew install --cask swiftbar Both the current Homebrew cask formulaand official README require macOS Monterey 12 or later (updated from older guides citing macOS 11+), so verify your macOS version first.
Launch SwiftBar from /Applications. On first launch, it asks for a Plugin Folder where it will scan for executable scripts. Create a dedicated directory in your home folder and select it:
mkdir -p "$HOME/SwiftBarPlugins" All examples below save files inside $HOME/SwiftBarPlugins; adjust paths if you choose another directory.
Keeping the plugin folder dedicated avoids surprises: SwiftBar traverses subdirectories and symbolic links, so pointing it at an entire code repository can accidentally execute unrelated scripts. Hidden directories are ignored automatically, and you can exclude specific files via .swiftbarignore.
Writing Your First Date and Time Plugin Start with a zero-dependency script to verify folder wiring and output syntax.
Encoding Refresh Intervals in the Filename Create date.1m.sh inside SwiftBarPlugins. SwiftBar filenames follow a three-part pattern:
date.1m.sh name.interval.extension date names the plugin, 1m tells SwiftBar to re-run it every 1 minute, and .sh marks a shell script. Supported refresh units include:
Unit Meaning Example Filename ms Milliseconds sample.500ms.sh s Seconds devserver.10s.sh m Minutes date.1m.sh h Hours weather.1h.sh d Days links.1d.sh Note that 500ms above illustrates filename syntax rather than a recommendation to poll external APIs twice a second.
Writing the Date Script Open date.1m.sh in a code editor and save it as plain UTF-8 text (making sure your editor does not silently append .txt):
#!/bin/bash /bin/date '+%m/%d %H:%M' echo '---' echo "Today: $(/bin/date '+%Y-%m-%d')" echo "Last check: $(/bin/date '+%H:%M:%S')" echo 'Refresh now | refresh=true' #!/bin/bash selects the Bash interpreter, /bin/date formats the current system clock, and $(...) substitutes command output inline.
The first date line sets the menu bar title, echo '---' starts the dropdown, and refresh=true on the final item tells SwiftBar to re-run the script immediately when clicked. Because the schedule runs once per minute, Last check shows the last execution timestamp rather than a live-ticking second hand.
Verifying Output in the Terminal Mark the script executable and run it directly in your terminal first:
chmod +x "$HOME/SwiftBarPlugins/date.1m.sh" "$HOME/SwiftBarPlugins/date.1m.sh" echo "Exit code: $?" Although SwiftBar grants execute permissions to new plugins by default, running chmod +x and testing in the terminal verifies both permissions and stdout formatting up front:
10/27 09:30 --- Today: 2026-10-27 Last check: 09:30:00 Refresh now | refresh=true Exit code: 0 Exit code: 0 comes from your terminal check (reading $? right after execution) rather than the plugin file itself. Once SwiftBar picks up the file, the date appears in your menu bar; if not, confirm SwiftBar is running, check your Plugin Folder path, or trigger a manual reload:
open -g 'swiftbar://refreshallplugins' Adding Colors, Icons, and Click Actions with Pipe Parameters Appending | key=value attributes to any output line customizes appearance and click behavior (separating multiple attributes with spaces):
echo 'DEV Running | color=green sfimage=checkmark.circle' echo '---' echo 'Open in Browser | href=http://localhost:3000' echo 'Check Status Now | refresh=true' This renders green text paired with a native macOS SF Symbols icon (sfimage), opens http://localhost:3000 when clicking Open in Browser, and re-runs the check on Check Status Now.
Commonly used parameters include:
Parameter Purpose Example color Sets label text color color=green sfimage Renders an SF Symbols icon sfimage=checkmark.circle tooltip Shows hover text tooltip=localhost:3000 href Opens a URL on click href=http://localhost:3000 refresh Re-runs the plugin on click refresh=true bash Executes a binary or script on click bash=/usr/bin/open terminal Controls whether bash opens a Terminal window terminal=false Because | sits inside single quotes here, the shell prints it literally as SwiftBar’s attribute separator rather than piping commands.
To run a local command on click, pass an absolute executable path to bash and supply arguments via param1, param2, and so on:
echo 'Open Applications Folder | bash=/usr/bin/open param1=/Applications terminal=false' Monitoring a Local Dev Server from the Menu Bar Now let’s monitor whether a local dev server is listening on TCP port 3000 (http://localhost:3000). Save devserver.10s.sh inside SwiftBarPlugins (updating 3000 if your server binds another port):
#!/bin/bash if /usr/sbin/lsof -nP -iTCP:3000 -sTCP:LISTEN >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo 'DEV Running | color=green sfimage=checkmark.circle' else echo 'DEV Stopped | color=gray sfimage=pause.circle' fi echo '---' echo 'Target: TCP port 3000' echo "Last check: $(/bin/date '+%H:%M:%S')" echo 'Open in Browser | href=http://localhost:3000' echo 'Check Status Now | refresh=true' /usr/sbin/lsof checks whether any process is actively listening on TCP port 3000, while >/dev/null 2>&1 discards raw lsof output so stray lines do not corrupt the dropdown menu.
Make it executable and test it once in the terminal:
chmod +x "$HOME/SwiftBarPlugins/devserver.10s.sh" "$HOME/SwiftBarPlugins/devserver.10s.sh" With .10s. in the filename, SwiftBar polls every 10 seconds, so starting or stopping your server can take up to 10 seconds to reflect unless you click Check Status Now.
Keep the scope of this check in mind: it only verifies that a process is listening on TCP port 3000. Another program could occupy that port, or your server could accept sockets while returning HTTP 500 errors. For full application health checks, extend the script with curl against a health endpoint and inspect the HTTP status code.
Extending the Pattern to Everyday Dev Tasks Swapping out the status command adapts the same structure to other daily checks:
Use Case Menu Bar Header Dropdown Body Git branch Active branch of a target repo Repo path and quick links Disk space Free space or usage % on a target volume Total capacity and mount path API health Pass/fail status of last probe HTTP status code and check timestamp Deployment bookmarks Short project label Production, staging, and CI dashboard URLs Static bookmark menus need zero polling logic - save links.1d.sh with your team’s real URLs:
#!/bin/bash echo 'Project Links' echo '---' echo 'Production | href=https://example.com' echo 'Staging | href=https://staging.example.com' echo 'CI Dashboard | href=https://ci.example.com' Note that a static link menu does not probe deployment health; seeing the project name in the bar only provides quick navigation. Match refresh intervals to how often data changes - daily (1d) for static bookmarks, seconds (10s) for local ports, and explicit request timeouts plus conservative intervals whenever calling external APIs to save battery and rate limits.
Troubleshooting Missing or Broken Menus When a plugin misbehaves, run the script directly in Terminal first to separate command errors from SwiftBar formatting issues:
Symptom What to Check First Item never appears in menu bar SwiftBar running state, Plugin Folder path, filename format, and execute bit Script runs with empty output Whether every if/else branch prints a header line (empty stdout hides the plugin) Raw command output floods dropdown Redirecting helper command stdout/stderr away from echo menu lines Works in Terminal, fails in SwiftBar Using absolute binary paths (/opt/homebrew/bin/...), env vars, and macOS permissions Stale status persists Filename interval suffix, Last check timestamp, and manual refresh behavior Menu bar shows an error icon Dropdown Error details and SwiftBar logs in macOS Console.app Standard plugins run, emit stdout, and exit; if a script exits 0 with empty stdout, SwiftBar hides it from the menu bar, and any debug logs should go to stderr so they do not pollute menu items. Also remember GUI apps do not inherit your interactive shell PATH, which is why the scripts above use /bin/date and /usr/sbin/lsof (use command -v tool-name in Terminal to find paths for Homebrew binaries).
Start with the 1-minute date script to confirm your folder setup, then add one high-frequency local check with a short status header and links tucked neatly into the dropdown.
Reference: SwiftBar beginner and practical guide on Tistory, with system requirements and plugin behavior verified against official SwiftBar documentation.
summary: Learn how SwiftBar turns standard shell script output into live macOS menu bar items and dropdown menus for local dev server checks and project links.
title: Putting Shell Scripts in the macOS Menu Bar with SwiftBar

content:
Ask an AI coding agent to build a product landing page and a layout appears in seconds - usually with interchangeable headlines, uniform card grids, and predictable spacing. Other times the visuals look clean, yet visitors cannot tell who the product serves or what action to take next.
Two open-source projects tackle these failure modes from different angles: taste-skill and AI Design Skills. Both guide coding agents through Markdown skill files, yet they start from different questions and prioritize different outputs.
If you want to set a clear visual direction and refine live layouts in a real browser, start with taste-skill. If you need to structure product positioning, section order, and copywriting together, start with landing-page-design in AI Design Skills. And if you want to turn a finished static mockup into an animated product demo, check design-to-motion in AI Design Skills.
The comparison below is based on each repository’s README and published skill instructions rather than head-to-head speed or blind quality benchmarks.
What a Design Skill Actually Does Here, a skill is a structured Markdown instruction set (such as SKILL.md) that tells an AI coding agent what context to gather first, how to choose layout and typography, and what to verify after writing code.
You supply product context, existing source files, or reference visuals, and your coding agent writes or edits code following those rules. Downloading a skill folder does not generate pages or videos by itself - your connected agent and local dev tooling still execute the work.
Both repositories document usage with Claude Code alongside tools like Cursor and Codex, though where skill files live and what browser, file, or design integrations are available vary by editor.
taste-skill: Setting Visual Direction and Refining in the Browser taste-skillpushes agents away from repetitive boilerplate templates by establishing explicit visual direction, pulling reference patterns, and inspecting rendered pages inside a real browser.
Its current v2 workflow reads the task brief, picks a visual direction, composes imagery and layout, and checks rendered output across multiple viewport widths - capturing screenshots and fixing the largest visual regressions first. That makes it better suited for rethinking a page’s overall craft than tweaking a single hex color or font size.
Beyond marketing pages, taste-skill also covers dashboards and admin interfaces. When improving an existing app, it inspects the live screen before editing code, making it a strong first choice when alignment, information density, or mobile responsiveness feels off in a working product.
Older write-ups describe multiple standalone skills bundled in one repo, whereas the main repository now centers on design-taste-frontend after moving several style variants and image-generation skills into separate repos - check the latest README before installing.
AI Design Skills: From Product Positioning to Copy and Motion AI Design Skillsis a modular collection currently centered on two skills: landing-page-design and design-to-motion. The first connects product positioning, UI layout, and copywriting; the second turns static mockups into animated product showcases.
landing-page-design Starts with Audience and Target Action Before drawing a single section, landing-page-designnails down the product’s core offer, target buyer, desired visitor action (such as starting a free trial or booking a demo), and likely objections.
From there, it maps out section order and copy alongside visual rules for typography, spacing, border radii, color palettes, and subtle motion - deciding how the hero headline, product walkthrough, social proof, and FAQ sequence together.
For a B2B reporting tool, for instance, it first clarifies who compiles the reports, what hurts in their current manual workflow, and what questions they need answered before booking a demo - turning a flat feature list into a deliberate narrative sequence.
Whether the resulting copy and layout actually lift sign-ups or purchases still requires post-launch conversion testing.
design-to-motion Turns Static Mockups into Animated Showcases design-to-motiontakes a Figma frame or screenshot, reconstructs the interface in code, and layers choreography such as staggered card entrances, live chart drawing, or list updates.
Deliverables depend on the target channel: standalone promo demos export as HTML scenes plus MP4 or GIF recordings, whereas embedded website sections ship as production component code. Not every web task exports video files automatically.
Because the workflow involves UI reconstruction, browser capture, and video encoding, do not mistake it for an in-Figma animation plugin - and expect preparation steps to differ depending on whether you pass live Figma access or a flat screenshot.
Side-by-Side Comparison Dimension taste-skill AI Design Skills Starting point Visual direction matched to the product and prompt Value proposition, target audience, and primary conversion action Core emphasis Reference-guided UI implementation and live browser inspection Connecting page narrative, copywriting, and visual design rules Auditing existing UIs Built-in inspect-first refinement flow Points to a separate redesign-skill repository in its README Role of motion Handled inline as part of web and app UI polish Dedicated design-to-motion skill for animated product showcases Primary output Multi-viewport web pages and application screens Landing page code, or animated HTML scenes with MP4/GIF exports Capabilities overlap in practice: taste-skill still accounts for product purpose, and AI Design Skills includes detailed visual rules (even crediting taste-skill in its README as inspiration for parts of landing-page-design).
Which Skill Should You Try First? Start with taste-skill if an existing screen looks generic, cramped, or visually uneven. Its inspect-and-fix browser loop pairs naturally with live codebases, especially when you name concrete layout issues and functional constraints rather than asking to “make it look premium”:
Keep all existing functionality and data on the current admin screen. On desktop, numeric table columns are hard to scan, and on mobile the nav menu overlaps body content. Audit the live screen using taste-skill first and propose a prioritized fix list. Start with landing-page-design when launching a new product page where messaging and structure are still open. Supply the target audience, core features, primary call-to-action, and verified proof points up front:
We are building a landing page for an automated reporting tool aimed at small teams. The target buyer is an operations manager compiling weekly reports, and the primary goal is booking a demo. Use landing-page-design to confirm any missing inputs first, then propose section structure and copy. Pick design-to-motion when turning a finished UI design into a launch video or animated product demo. Specify both the source design and whether you need web component code or video files:
Build a looping product-intro animation based on this Figma frame. Preserve the existing background and layout while animating the chart and activity list. Apply design-to-motion and export the final result as both MP4 and GIF. Adapt these example prompts to match your actual product details and assets.
Start with One Skill at a Time Stacking both skill packs together on your first run risks conflicting rules around typography, spacing scales, and animation timing. Pick the single skill that matches your current bottleneck, and if you hand off to a second skill later, state explicitly which design tokens and layout choices are already locked.
Check each repository for runtime prerequisites: taste-skill scripts currently require Node.js 22+ and a Chromium-family browser (Chrome, Edge, or Chromium), while AI Design Skills installs by copying selected skill folders into .claude/skills/ (plus capture and encoding tools if exporting video).
Treat showcase screenshots as directional examples and judge results on your own codebase - replacing any placeholder customer logos, testimonials, or metrics with verified facts before publishing, and checking copy accuracy, mobile usability, and interactive states.
Related resources: Prior taste-skill overview on PyTorch KRand AI Design Skills demo video, cross-referenced against both official GitHub repositories.
summary: A side-by-side comparison of taste-skill and AI Design Skills across visual direction, landing-page copywriting, browser inspection, and motion demos.
title: taste-skill vs. AI Design Skills: Picking the Right Web Design Skill

Fixing a short script in Claude Code calls for a very different setup than untangling a complex refactor. Repetitive edits benefit from concise replies and fewer approval prompts, whereas debugging an unfamiliar failure often needs deeper reasoning and fuller explanations - and working in someone else’s repository may warrant reviewing every edit one by one.
Ultra Config is a Claude Code mod that switches multiple settings together to match those different workflows. Distributed through Daniel San’s claude-code-templates project, it groups model selection, reasoning effort, output style, and approval rules into five selectable profiles.
Based on the author’s introduction postand the project README, here is how each profile works and what to watch out for in practice. Note that this overview is based on project documentation rather than independent cost or quality benchmarks.
What Changes When You Pick a Profile A profile in Ultra Config is a preset bundle of Claude Code settings tailored to a working style. Token Saver pairs Sonnet with low reasoning effort and concise output, while Max Quality selects the strongest available model with maximum reasoning effort.
Here, reasoning effort (effort) controls how much reasoning compute the model spends before answering. Higher effort helps on hard architectural or debugging problems without guaranteeing better results on every task - routine edits rarely need maximum effort.
Before applying a profile, the configuration panel previews current values, proposed values, and why each setting changes, so you can inspect exact diffs rather than relying on profile names alone.
Comparing the Five Profiles Profile Config ID Key Settings and Intended Use Token Saver saver Pairs Sonnet, low reasoning effort, concise output, and Haiku subagents. Built for repetitive tasks where trimming token spend matters. Fast Flow flow Uses Sonnet with medium effort and fewer file-edit prompts. Fits interactive loops where a human reviews small, rapid edits. Max Quality quality Picks the highest-capability available model with xhigh effort and permits large workflows. Suited for deep analysis or complex refactoring. Guarded guarded Enforces default approval prompts, disables bypass mode, and blocks Read access on sensitive paths. Fits repositories needing frequent human sign-off. Autopilot autopilot Enables auto-approval mode, high effort, task summaries, push notifications, and auto context compaction for long runs with minimal prompt interruptions. Subagents are helper agents spawned to handle delegated subtasks. Token Saver sets an environment variable pointing subagents to Haiku, though the author notes that this variable alone does not override built-in Explore or Plan agent models - so a profile name does not guarantee the model or cost of every internal call.
Approval behavior also varies by profile: Fast Flow streamlines file-edit approvals, whereas Autopilot switches on auto-approval mode. Even under Autopilot, do not assume a run requires zero human judgment from start to finish.
Installing and Applying Your First Profile The current README requires Claude Code 2.1.287 or later and a trusted project directory. After checking your version, install the mod inside your target project:
npx claude-code-templates@latest --mod productivity/ultra-config Once installed, open the configuration panel inside Claude Code:
/ultra-config Selecting a profile expands its setting diffs - showing current values, new values, items already matching, and skipped items - before you click Activate.
Starting with a clear-cut profile like Token Saver or Max Quality makes it easy to compare against your baseline setup. To inspect Token Saver’s details without activating it right away, pass its ID directly:
/ultra-config saver That command opens the profile preview screen rather than applying changes.
Distinguishing Apply, Undo, and Close Commands Command Behavior /ultra-config Opens the configuration panel. /ultra-config <profile> Opens the detail preview for the specified profile. /ultra-config apply <profile> Applies the profile and reports changed and skipped settings. /ultra-config undo Reverts the changes made by the last applied profile. /ultra-config close Closes the configuration panel. Replace <profile> with a Config ID from the table above. For example, to apply Max Quality directly:
/ultra-config apply quality To revert the last applied profile:
/ultra-config undo Closing the panel with close does not revert settings; use undo to restore your prior state. Because switching to a new profile only overwrites the keys defined by that profile, switching profiles is different from undoing previous changes.
Ultra Config persists recent apply history across restarts so undo continues to work in later sessions, while preserving any custom read-restriction rules you added separately.
Mid-Session Switches Take Effect at Different Times Although you can switch profiles mid-session, not every setting takes effect the instant you click Activate. The README breaks down timing across three tiers:
Setting Type When It Takes Effect Model, approval mode, output style, and other /config options Immediately upon change Model reasoning effort Starting on the next message request CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL and MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS env vars Read at Claude Code startup, taking effect in the next session Activating Token Saver mid-session, for instance, will not swap the subagent model in your already-running process until you start a fresh session. Always check the apply summary alongside startup-bound environment variables.
Settings locked by organization policy or unsupported by your installed Claude Code version are skipped automatically, so seeing a profile in the UI does not mean every setting inside it took effect - check the changed, unchanged, and skipped indicators in the output.
Checking What Guarded Actually Restricts Guarded adds Read tool deny rules for paths such as .env, secrets/, ~/.ssh, and ~/.aws, and disables permission-bypass mode (Read being Claude Code’s built-in file-reading tool).
As the author’s postexplicitly points out, Read deny rules do not block shell commands from reading those same files if a shell command is approved. Guarded is not a full OS sandbox blocking all secret access across every tool path, so treat “restricts access to secrets” with that tool-level boundary in mind.
Ultra Config is a practical helper when you want to switch existing Claude Code settings by task and see exactly what changed. Pick one recurring workflow first, read the diff preview, apply the profile, and practice reverting with undo.
summary: Ultra Config bundles model, reasoning effort, output style, and permission rules into five Claude Code profiles with diff previews, undo support, and clear scope limits.
title: Switching Claude Code Setups by Task with the Ultra Config Mod
