Technical docs and engineering blogs often rely on Mermaid to illustrate system flows. Writing relationships as plain text like A --> B turns them into shapes and arrows while keeping diagrams easy to version alongside code. On documentation sites with dozens of diagrams, rendering speed and visual styling quickly become noticeable.
Pele is an open-source library that renders Mermaid syntax into SVG. The original Threads posthighlights its rendering speed, bundle size, and theming model. Drawing on the official repositoryand documentation, here is what Pele replaces and what to check before swapping it into existing Mermaid pages.
Turning Mermaid Syntax into SVG Working with Mermaid separates the plain-text diagram definition from the renderer that draws it on screen. Here is a basic Mermaid flowchart:
flowchart LR A[Request Received] --> B{Review Needed?} B -->|Yes| C[Assigned Review] B -->|No| D[Completed] C --> D flowchart LR defines a left-to-right flowchart where square brackets create standard nodes, curly braces mark decision branches, and arrows connect steps. A renderer parses this text into a visual diagram flowing from intake through review to completion.
Pele takes that Mermaid text and outputs SVG - a scalable vector image format for shapes, lines, and text that embeds cleanly in web pages and styles via CSS.
Published under Obsidian’s GitHub organization with kepano listed as package author, Pele is described on its official site as built for Obsidian. Embedding the library into your own website is separate from changing the built-in renderer in your installed Obsidian version, so check Obsidian release notes for app-level adoption.
Bundle Size, Rendering Speed, and CSS Theming The official sitenotes zero runtime dependencies, a smaller bundle, and faster rendering than Mermaid.js. Zero dependencies here refers specifically to Pele’s own npm runtime dependencies rather than your broader web stack.
In the project’s published comparison, gzipped bundle size drops from 1.6MB for Mermaid.js to 230kB for Pele, with rendering reported up to 500x faster. Treat those numbers as author-published benchmarks rather than a guarantee that every diagram or full page load speeds up by the same factor.
In real deployments, test against your own diagram types, node counts per page, font loading behavior, and target browsers, since a small three-node flowchart behaves very differently from a page with several long sequence diagrams.
Theming works through CSS custom properties. You can bind background, text, and connector colors directly to your site’s stylesheet and switch between light and dark modes without re-rendering the SVG - a clean fit for documentation sites with theme toggles.
Testing Pele with Code Examples The fastest way to test existing diagrams is pasting Mermaid source into the official Playgroundto check syntax support and node routing before installing anything.
For a web project, install the package via npm:
npm install pele The core render() API accepts Mermaid source text and returns an SVG string. The snippet below assumes a JavaScript module bundler environment rather than an inline script tag in a raw HTML file:
import { render } from 'pele'; const source = `flowchart LR A[Request Received] --> B[Assigned Review] B --> C[Completed]`; const { svg } = render(source); document.querySelector('#diagram').innerHTML = svg; Pair it with a target container element in the DOM:
<div id="diagram"></div> Here source holds the Mermaid definition, svg holds the rendered markup, and the final line injects it into #diagram (which must already exist when the script runs).
For responsive layouts that adapt to container width changes, check mount() in the API docs:
import { mount } from 'pele'; const container = document.querySelector('#diagram'); const source = `flowchart LR A[Draft] --> B[Review] --> C[Publish]`; mount(container, source); Use render() when you want a raw SVG string and mount() when binding directly to a live DOM element that resizes. Both APIs run synchronously, and Pele also exposes lazy entry points if you prefer loading diagram types on demand.
Matching Light and Dark Site Themes The theming guidesets CSS custom properties on .pele or a parent wrapper element:
.pele { --pele-bg: #ffffff; --pele-fg: #1f1f1f; --pele-line: #6e6e6e; --pele-surface: #f3f3f3; --pele-border: #8a8a8a; } @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { .pele { --pele-bg: #1f1f1f; --pele-fg: #eeeeee; --pele-line: #aaaaaa; --pele-surface: #303030; --pele-border: #777777; } } --pele-bg, --pele-fg, and --pele-line control background, label text, and edge colors. The snippet above follows OS color-scheme preferences; if your site uses a manual theme toggle button, swap the media query for your site’s theme class or data attribute.
Keep color swaps distinct from font changes: changing font families alters glyph widths, which requires recalculating node box dimensions. Inline colors hardcoded inside a Mermaid definition can also override CSS theme variables.
Syntax Compatibility Does Not Mean Identical Visual Layout According to the compatibility docs, Pele supports all built-in diagram types from Mermaid 12.1.0 - including flowcharts, sequence diagrams, class diagrams, state diagrams, ER diagrams, and Gantt charts.
Because Pele uses its own layout engine and visual styling, node positions, spacing, and edge routing will differ from Mermaid.js on the exact same input text. Parsing the same syntax is not the same as pixel-identical rendering:
Area to Check What to Verify Before Migrating Diagram types Whether all diagrams use built-in Mermaid 12.1.0 types rather than external plugins Layout Whether node order, spacing, connector routing, and long CJK or multi-word labels stay readable Styling Whether custom Mermaid theme configs need migrating to Pele CSS variables Interactivity Whether diagrams only need URL links or rely on JavaScript click callbacks Mobile viewports Whether scaled-down SVGs or width-responsive re-layouts fit better Specifically, Pele does not support third-party Mermaid plugins, arbitrary HTML inside node labels, or JavaScript callbacks on click directives. Audit existing docs for those features before switching renderers.
When Pele Is Worth Evaluating Teams already maintaining Mermaid diagrams who want smaller client bundles, faster rendering, or cleaner CSS dark-mode integration have good reason to test Pele on documentation sites, blogs, and product guides.
Rather than swapping your entire site renderer at once, compare a handful of representative diagrams side by side - mixing compact flowcharts, dense architecture graphs, long labels, and narrow mobile sequence diagrams. Note that the snippets above illustrate API usage rather than site-wide performance benchmarks.
Released under the MIT license, Pele is easy to evaluate by testing your existing Mermaid blocks in the Playground and checking the official repository.
Lead image: Project image from the official Pele repository.
summary: Pele renders Mermaid syntax into SVG with zero runtime dependencies, CSS variable theming, and a compact bundle size - here is how it compares to Mermaid.js.
title: Pele: A Fast, Lightweight Library for Rendering Mermaid Diagrams to SVG

When giving detailed instructions to an AI assistant or getting rough ideas down on a Mac, speaking out loud is often faster than typing. Handy is a voice-input app that transcribes spoken audio and inserts the resulting text straight into whatever input field currently holds your cursor.
Dictating Prompts into Your Workflow Working effectively with AI usually spends more time explaining background context and constraints than typing a short command. With Handy, you press a shortcut to record your voice and drop the transcribed sentences directly at the cursor, leaving you free to fix missed constraints or misheard terms before hitting send.
Voice dictation and AI processing stay cleanly separated. Handy stops at converting speech into text - trimming verbal repetition, fixing typos, and deciding what to submit remain entirely up to you.
Picking a Model for Korean and macOS Setup Dictating in Korean requires checking the speech model setting first. Select the multilingual Whisper Large v3 model for accurate Korean transcription, and avoid Parakeet Unified EN 0.6B, which supports English only.
As of release v0.9.8, match the installer package to your Mac architecture: Handy_0.9.8_aarch64.dmg for Apple Silicon Macs and Handy_0.9.8_x64.dmg for Intel Macs. Running the app requires granting both Microphone and Accessibility permissions in macOS.
Local Speech Recognition vs. Cloud AI Data Boundaries Handy is a free open-source app that runs speech recognition entirely on-device on your Mac. Audio recordings never go to an external server, keeping transcription offline and private.
Keep the boundary between local speech-to-text and downstream AI services clear, though: once you submit the text Handy typed into an external AI chat window, that provider’s data retention policies govern the text. Local STT protects raw audio before submission, not what you send afterward.
For Mac users who want to dictate rich AI prompts or draft notes faster, removing the friction of typing long context blocks makes starting tasks noticeably easier.
Summary Handy transcribes recorded speech directly into the active cursor field on macOS, speeding up long AI prompt drafting. Korean dictation requires selecting the multilingual Whisper Large v3 model rather than the English-only Parakeet model. Speech-to-text runs offline on-device, while any text subsequently sent into an AI chat app falls under that AI service’s data policy.
summary: Handy is a free open-source macOS speech-to-text app that inserts dictated text right at the cursor, using Whisper Large v3 locally while keeping data boundaries clear.
title: Handy: Dictating AI Prompts Directly at Your Cursor on macOS

content:
Once agents start writing a large share of your code, pull requests pile up faster than humans can read them line by line. Reading every diff carefully turns the review queue into the team’s main bottleneck, while rubber-stamping PRs leaves nobody sure what just shipped. This post breaks down how the Claude Code team restructured code review around layered automated checks and where they still spend human engineering time.
At a Glance Claude writes roughly 90% of Claude Code’s codebase. Between June and September, merged PR volume more than doubled while the revert rate fell by more than 40%. Rather than dropping review, the team shifted most code reading to machines: six stacked layers—from pre-PR self-verification to post-merge rollback—each catch a slice of defects. Required human approvals depend on change risk rather than whether a human or an agent wrote the code: zero human approvals for low-risk changes, one for medium, and two for high. Convergence rules such as round caps stop author and reviewer agents from trading nitpicks overnight, lifting the single-round pass rate on internal PRs from 65% to 78%. About the Original Post Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang published this 14-minute post on October 15, 2026. It documents the production review pipeline used by the Claude Code team, covering how they evaluate and tune review agents, what decisions stay with humans, and what order other teams should adopt these pieces in. Engineering leads rethinking PR rules for agent-heavy repositories are the primary audience. Source: How the Claude Code team does code review.
Redefining What Code Review Is For Start with the volume numbers. Daily changes landing in Anthropic’s main monorepo grew from roughly 2,500 in May to over 30,000 in September, and the standalone Claude Code repository faces comparable pressure. At that pace, relying on a human to read every line of every diff stops working.
The authors separate code review into two distinct jobs: catching defects before users hit them, and building shared understanding of the codebase across the team. Most of the post tackles the first job. Instead of asking “did a human read this diff?”, the team asks what could go wrong with a change and whether an automated check or a human is better suited to catch it. Changing the question also shifted when review happens. Instead of acting as a final gate after opening a PR and waiting on a teammate, review runs continuously while the change is being built—more like live spellcheck than a pre-press sign-off. By the time a human sees a PR, Claude has usually reviewed and revised it at least once.
The team set an explicit operational target across Claude Code’s CLI, desktop and web apps, and mobile apps: most PRs should merge with at most one human involved—who can be the author—without raising revert or incident rates. They track human cost with three metrics: human approvals per PR (median and 95th percentile), human comments per PR, and time a PR spends waiting on a human. Revert and incident rates serve as guardrails; if time saved during review simply turns into firefighting after release, those guardrail numbers surface it immediately.
The Path Every Change Travels The diagram below traces a change from the author’s laptop to production users. Circles mark automated checks, the orange diamond marks the single risk-based human decision point, and the looping arrow at the bottom marks recovery.
Figure 1. From top to bottom, a change moves through BEFORE THE PULL REQUEST, ON EVERY PULL REQUEST, MERGING, and AFTER THE MERGE. Risk-based approval is the sole human gate in the flow. Source: Original post.
Each layer handles a specific slice of verification:
Pre-PR verification: Give Claude concrete ways to run the code—test suites, builds, or screenshots compared against design specs—and require command output rather than a claim that work is finished. A fresh subagent with clean context then reviews the diff before a PR ever opens. Claude Code creator Boris Cherny estimates that giving the agent self-verification tools improves output quality two to three times. Repository guidance files: Whenever automated review repeats the same complaint, the team updates skills, lint rules, or guidance docs. CLAUDE.md explains what the project is and how to work in it, while REVIEW.md—maintained by code owners—tells reviewers what matters in that directory. Good REVIEW.md files stay short: they state what failure looks like in that repo (factual errors in docs, misrouted traffic in configs), cap minor nitpicks, and require file and line citations as proof. AI review on every PR: Externally, Code Review for Claude Code is generally available on Team and Enterprise plans, while /code-review runs a lighter local pass. After rolling out the research preview internally, the share of internal PRs receiving substantive review comments jumped from 16% to 54%. Each repository picks a review depth from Quick, Standard, or Deep. Voting on findings: Multiple agents hunt for bugs in parallel, and a second group of agents votes on whether each candidate finding is genuine. Only high-consensus findings survive; pure style and formatting nits get filtered out. Surviving comments post in severity order with Important, Nit, or Pre-existing tags (Pre-existing flags bugs the PR did not introduce). Authors must either fix each finding or close the thread with a written explanation. Security review and required CI: A dedicated security review pass runs alongside bug review, and any open thread from either pass blocks merging. Lint, typechecks, cross-platform tests, and builds are also mandatory, and the PR template requires explicit test and rollback plans. Stacking those layers creates a Swiss-cheese defense where each plate catches defects the previous one missed.
Figure 2. Each plate represents one verification layer, orange dots represent defects, and white holes show blind spots in individual layers. Rare defects that line up through every hole land in fast rollback at the bottom. Source: Original post.
Risk Determines How Many Humans Approve Fixing a documentation typo and changing the auto-updater should not demand the same human scrutiny. The team maps change risk directly to required human approvals:
Risk tier Typical changes Human approvals required Low Docs, copy tweaks, internal-only features, additive code behind a disabled flag Zero once automated and security checks pass Medium Standard product changes, plus sensitive areas such as caching, auto-updater, or system prompts One human High Highest-risk code paths and directories configured to always require dual sign-off Two humans One classifier assigns the risk tier from the diff, and a second independent classifier checks whether an extra human reviewer should still be pulled in regardless of tier. Owner-designated sensitive paths and CI workflow files always require human eyes.
Low-friction paths carry strict guardrails. Only authors on the repository’s trusted list qualify, and an agent approval never counts toward a human approval slot. When an agent opens a PR on someone’s behalf, the human who dispatched that agent becomes a required reviewer. Approvals bind to a specific commit SHA—pushing new commits or resolving a merge conflict by hand resets the approval state.
Protection continues past the merge button. A merge queue re-runs checks with the change rebased onto main so two individually green PRs cannot break the build together. New features ship behind flags to Anthropic employees first, then roll out to the public latest channel before reaching stable. Flags can be killed without redeploying, backed by a weekly on-call rotation. One piece the authors note they have not built yet is an automated circuit breaker that tightens approval thresholds when revert or incident rates spike.
Stopping Endless Agent Review Loops When both the PR author and the PR reviewer are agents, review-and-fix cycles can spin out of control. One CLI PR ran through more than 50 rounds overnight until the human author stepped in and stopped it. Running git blame on the lines flagged in later rounds showed that roughly 59% of them had already been sitting in the diff during round one—the reviewer was barely catching regressions from recent fixes, just surfacing a few more missed issues per pass. Where a human engineer shrugs off a minor comment in seconds, an agent dutifully burns another commit and triggers another full review cycle.
To force convergence, the team rewrote its re-review rules around four constraints:
flowchart TD A["AI review"] --> B{"New findings?"} B -->|"No"| C["Pass"] B -->|"Yes"| D["Fix every instance<br/>of each bug class"] D --> E{"Past round 3?"} E -->|"No"| F["Re-review new diff only after early rounds<br/>Do not repeat prior findings"] F --> B E -->|"Yes"| G["Ask author to<br/>rethink the approach"] Pre-existing bugs lurking in untouched files moved out of PR review altogether into a separate nightly review agent. Those changes shifted internal PR convergence sharply:
Figure 3. Gray bars show metrics before, and orange bars show after the convergence work: share of PRs passing in one review-and-fix round, share needing five or more rounds, and average review rounds to pass. Source: Original post.
The team grades the reviewer itself every day. They curated an evaluation set from historical PRs that caused real incidents, asking engineers familiar with those outages to annotate the exact bug and location. Daily eval runs score recall against that incident set, while precision comes from developer reactions on live PRs—whether an author fixed a comment, marked it wrong, explained it as intended behavior, or dismissed it. They also run the reviewer against known-clean PRs to watch how often it nudges authors toward harmful edits. Their explicit priority order puts catching real bugs ahead of minimizing review rounds.
What Stays With Humans Five responsibilities remain firmly human: deciding product direction, taste, and scope (whether a change should exist at all); reviewing high-risk paths like billing, auto-update, and CI workflows; shaping architectural patterns that other engineers and agents will copy; reading verification artifacts like test logs and UI screenshots; and owning production outcomes. If the attached proof still leaves you unsure what automated checks might have missed, the rule is to request a full human review instead of clicking approve.
Knowledge sharing—the second traditional job of code review—changed form completely. Nobody holds the entire Claude Code codebase in their head anymore, and the authors argue nobody needs to. When an engineer needs to understand an unfamiliar subsystem, they ask Claude for a walkthrough tailored to that question; it arrives in minutes and reflects today’s code rather than stale wiki pages. Skimming a one-line copy diff teaches almost nothing compared with reading a fresh explanation of the module you are about to modify.
Team culture reinforces ownership after merge: whoever merges a small or medium change usually fixes any fallout themselves. That norm works because diffs stay small and most mistakes can be reverted or flag-killed within minutes—putting recovery in the hands of the person who already holds the freshest context rather than hunting for blame.
Takeaways The notes below are this blog’s own interpretation, not part of the original post.
Pairing human-time metrics (approvals, comments, wait time) with outcome guardrails (revert and incident rates) is the sharpest operational idea in the post. Data platform teams can apply the exact same framing to SQL and pipeline reviews: instead of asking whether a senior engineer read every line of a dbt model, map out what schema checks, row-count diffs, and reconciliation queries catch at each layer—shrinking human review down to business-definition changes and high-blast-radius tables.
The finding that 59% of late-round review comments targeted code already present in round one should shape anyone’s multi-agent workflow design. Whenever one agent critiques another agent’s output, build in round caps and diff-scoped re-checks from day one; otherwise, token spend goes toward trickling out missed first-pass observations one commit at a time.
Turning past production incidents into a daily benchmark for the review agent transfers cleanly to internal enterprise agents. Curating real failure cases from your own operations—and re-scoring every prompt, tool, or model change against that incident set—gives you a grounded answer to whether a new agent version actually prevents outages that hurt your team before.
What to Try First Add a short REVIEW.md to your repository capturing the review comments your team repeats most often, plus one sentence per area describing what real failures look like in docs, configs, or application code. Update your pull request template to require explicit fields for test evidence, risk level, and rollback steps. If you already run an AI code reviewer, measure review rounds per PR over the past few weeks and check what percentage of PRs spin past three rounds. Original post: How the Claude Code team does code review
summary: How the Claude Code team—where Claude writes roughly 90% of the code—replaced line-by-line human gatekeeping with six automated verification layers, risk-based approval counts, convergence rules for agent review loops, and fast rollback.
title: Reviewing Agent-Generated Code at Scale: Six Verification Layers on the Claude Code Team

content:
Switching away from a long Claude Code run to check another session often leaves you scrolling back through terminal logs when you return - trying to tell whether the agent is still writing code, stuck on a failing test, or waiting for tool approval.
deadhdis a Claude Code plugin that surfaces progress in a dedicated view. It organizes completed, active, and remaining steps into a checklist, aggregates multiple local sessions onto one page, and offers compact in-terminal status bars when you do not want a browser window open. Here, HUD (heads-up display) means checking live session status without leaving your working screen.
The overview below summarizes features and setup flows documented in the project README rather than benchmarks from a live test run.
Task Steps vs. Session State First, deadhd separates task progress from live session state. Both appear together, but two different mechanisms generate them:
Layer What It Shows Who Generates It Task progress Completed, active, and remaining steps, plus per-step evidence such as files, PRs, commits, and test counts Written and updated by Claude Session state Working, waiting for input, waiting for permission, last tool used, and conversation compaction count Recorded by plugin hooks from session events For example, the task checklist might read “Running tests” while the session state shows it is actually paused waiting for command approval. Seeing both side by side tells you immediately whether a test suite is slow or blocked on your input.
Event listeners called hooks capture session events - firing when a user submits a prompt, when a tool executes, or when a response finishes. Even if Claude forgets to tick off a checklist item, hooks still update permission waits and last-tool activity independently, though hooks alone do not verify whether a task step succeeded.
Picking a Display Mode for Your Workspace deadhd offers three display modes depending on whether you want a minimal line in your terminal or a detailed step-by-step browser dashboard:
Display Mode Location Information Shown band Above the terminal prompt Compact summary of session state, last tool, completed count, and current step statusline Below the terminal prompt Session state plus ticket, PR, next step, and estimated completion html Browser page Full step flowcharts, step cards, and linked completion evidence band fits quick status checks without leaving the terminal, while html works best when inspecting step details and modified files. Apps with a built-in browser pane like Orca can dock the page right beside the terminal, or you can open it in your default system browser.
Image: deadhd repositoryInside the html browser page, you can switch between four layouts without changing the display mode above:
Original: Shows both the step flowchart and detailed step cards. Strip: Condenses all steps into a single row of dots and expands the active step card. Timeline: Lists steps vertically with completion timestamps or time estimates. Tile: Highlights numeric counters first - completed steps, remaining time, and estimated finish. Switching browser layouts re-renders data already loaded in the browser and spends zero extra model tokens, though Claude’s own checklist updates during task execution still use normal session tokens.
Monitoring Multiple Sessions and Parallel Work Instead of opening a separate tab per session, the Hub view collects local sessions on a single page, sorting sessions waiting on permissions or showing no recent signal above actively running ones, with longest-waiting sessions listed first.
Hub is designed to spot local sessions needing human attention on your machine (collecting sessions from version 1.8.0 onward that write status files), rather than acting as a multi-user team server dashboard.
When a single session runs four or more work units in parallel, the Lane Board displays each unit as a row tracking its current step, worker, last signal, and remaining time.
By default, a lane marks itself stalled 10 minutes after its last signal. Because the browser computes elapsed time locally, stalled tasks surface even if the model stopped updating - though a missing signal indicates silence rather than confirmed failure, and rendering the board requires board metadata in the progress payload.
Installing and Opening Your First Progress View deadhd requires only Claude Code and python3 using the Python standard library. You can install it via the plugin marketplace, by copying the skill folder, or through an Orca share link. Starting with the README’s recommended plugin install takes two commands inside a Claude Code session:
/plugin marketplace add lcalmsky/deadhd /plugin install deadhd@deadhd The first command registers the marketplace source and the second installs deadhd itself - registering the marketplace alone does not install the plugin.
Next, run the command inside the session you want to track:
/deadhd:deadhd On first launch, deadhd prompts for where to open the view, display mode (html for browser details or band for an in-terminal bar), theme, and font. From there, Claude updates progress data as steps change.
The README also notes natural-language triggers such as asking Claude to open the progress view or show a checklist. Note that /deadhd applies to manual skill-folder installs, whereas plugin installs use /deadhd:deadhd. Reconfiguring settings or opening the multi-session hub uses subcommands:
/deadhd:deadhd setup /deadhd:deadhd hub Use either the plugin install or the copied skill folder, never both at once - installing both loads the plugin twice and duplicates commands and state updates. For alternative install methods, see the installation section in the README.
Practical Caveats When Reading the Dashboard The browser view polls and re-renders every 15 seconds without reloading the full DOM, preserving expanded cards and scroll position. “Real-time” here means 15-second polling rather than instant zero-latency push.
Completed steps are meant to attach concrete evidence like file paths, PRs, commits, or passing test counts, and the README specifies marking a step done only after verifying execution output. For high-stakes tasks, inspect the attached evidence rather than trusting the completion badge alone.
Estimated finish times also serve as rough guidance rather than hard deadlines, calibrating estimates against actual step durations once 3 or more steps finish.
Finally, the default browser view runs on a local static server bound to 127.0.0.1 accessible only from your machine, whereas publishing an Orca artifact creates an externally shareable URL. Keep local monitoring and external sharing distinct when working on private repositories.
If you juggle multiple Claude Code sessions and regularly miss permission prompts or lose track of active steps, opening deadhd on a single session first is an easy way to see whether a compact terminal bar or full step evidence fits your workflow.
summary: The deadhd plugin visualizes Claude Code step checklists, hook-driven session states, and multi-session progress across terminal bands and browser views.
title: Tracking Claude Code Multi-Session Progress in Real Time with deadhd

content:
On Threads, Jonghun “Dan” Seo (@jonghun__seo)shared a detailed log of testing the AI browser Aside, upgrading to a paid plan in under a week and documenting 100 delegated tasks across a main post and 12 follow-up replies (13 posts total), including candid notes on where the tool still falls short.
Aside is an AI agent built directly into your everyday browser, pitched as “a browser that finishes complex work across websites, accounts, and browsing history.” Because it operates inside existing logged-in sessions, it can open internal groupware, Metabase, and e-commerce sites like Coupang directly.
Grouping 100 Tasks into 10 Categories Seo organized all 100 examples under 10 headings:
Category Count Representative Examples Scheduled jobs that run away from the desk 14 Weekday morning office-cafe coffee orders, syncing groupware events to Google Calendar Single-link analytics inside logged-in accounts 12 Tracing metric drops, building Mixpanel funnels from plain-text prompts Actions right on the active screen 7 Mocking UI improvements over live service pages, finding and downloading printer drivers Multi-tool end-to-end workflows 12 Reading Jira, Slack, Notion, and Mixpanel to write weekly squad status reports Controlling the Mac from a single Slack line 8 Sending tasks remotely via Slack DM, voice commands via Telegram bot and iPhone Shortcuts Parallel multi-agent tasks 5 Splitting dozens of job applications across multiple agents in parallel Local Mac files and terminal tasks 13 Planning to deploying a side project, cleaning server disks over SSH Teach once, reuse as a saved skill 5 Analyzing 63 LinkedIn posts to save a reusable writing-style skill Social publishing and writing 11 Cross-posting and scheduling 9 top LinkedIn posts onto Brunch Personal errands and shopping 13 Reordering and paying on Coupang, booking an optician visit, switching carrier auto-pay Scheduled Routines Away from the Desk The first group covers recurring jobs that run on a schedule without the user sitting at the computer:
Ordering an iced Americano on the office cafe app at 9:20 AM on weekdays, automatically skipping mornings marked with an off-site meeting or public holiday on the calendar. Reading the company groupware calendar hourly, syncing events to Google Calendar, and appending the meeting room name to each event title. Monitoring an X list of AI company accounts every 30 minutes - posting new model releases to Slack immediately and batching everything else into a morning digest. Pulling yesterday’s metrics from Metabase and Mixpanel, plotting charts, and posting them to the team Slack channel, bundling 3 days together on Mondays. After noticing his coffee-chat booking link stayed open on public holidays, Seo also set up a monthly routine that finds upcoming holidays and blocks them out as “Busy” on his calendar in advance.
Analyzing Metrics from a Dashboard Link For product analytics, Seo relied heavily on Mixpanel and Metabase, dropping a dashboard URL so Aside could inspect it using his active login:
Asked “Why do these funnel numbers look off?”, Aside tested three Mixpanel filter variations, discovered a filter applied only to step one of the funnel, and fixed the board. To rename a single Mixpanel property value, it located all 48 events referencing that value and opened 39 saved reports one by one to update them. Given only a visitor-trend board URL, it cross-checked step-by-step numbers and concluded that funnel conversion held steady while top-of-funnel traffic dropped. From a plain-language description (“users pick a carrier, then move to self-signup or consultation”), it built the corresponding Mixpanel funnel chart directly. Workflows Spanning Multiple Tools Given a one-line prompt asking for a squad status report, Aside reads Jira tickets, Slack daily standups, Notion meeting notes, and Mixpanel metrics to draft a single report, then writes it into Notion’s weekly leadership table - creating a fresh page if the target entry was deleted.
Expense filing works the same way: dropping a receipt photo into Slack prompts Aside to look up that day’s attendance log in groupware, take a screenshot, attach both to the expense portal, and submit. Asking it to prep for an interview makes it check the candidate on the calendar, download resumes from the recruiting portal to the Mac Downloads folder, and draft an interview question sheet in Notion.
Beyond the Browser: Local Mac Files and Terminal Aside reaches beyond web tabs to local macOS files and the terminal. Seo delegated an entire side project (“Boomer Slang Dictionary”) from planning, coding, GitHub push, deployment, and admin dashboard setup to finding domain-renewal emails, wiring up the domain, registering on Google Search Console, Naver, and Bing, inserting AdSense verification snippets, and designing GA4 and Amplitude events.
Other examples included SSHing into a personal server to trim disk usage from 90% down to 56%, and exposing an Obsidian knowledge vault over MCP so other AI agents could read and write to it.
Where Human Approval Remains On sensitive actions, Seo stepped in only for identity verification or final sign-off:
Consolidating autopay across 3 telecom lines into one bank account required only his identity check. Signing up as a Toss Shopping merchant required scanning a QR login code. Slack messages waited on his explicit “send” confirmation after reviewing the draft. On Coupang, Aside reordered his usual shower filter from order history through checkout, analyzed 2 years of shampoo purchases to add 3 anti-hair-loss shampoos to the cart, and read a school handout drawing of a kid’s invention to put 10 matching craft supplies into his Coupang cart alongside a separate checklist of household recyclables.
Repeated workflows became saved skills: analyzing engagement across 63 past LinkedIn posts into a writing skill, saving resume-screening criteria refined over chat so daily routines could reuse them, and generalizing a corporate-card expense skill to share as a file with teammates.
Strengths and Current Limitations Seo highlighted five strengths: acting inside logged-in browser sessions, taking remote commands via Slack, running multiple agents concurrently, controlling Mac files and terminal sessions, and reusing workflows as saved skills.
The main limitation is team-wide deployment. Because Aside runs tied to an individual’s accounts and personal Mac, operating it as a shared team agent at work remains awkward - great as a personal assistant, still a step short of a shared team assistant.
Highlights from the Comment Thread Team collaboration: Commenter hiddenest noted that users can already route outputs to team Slack channels via Settings > Channels and that an Organization feature is in development. Seo replied that mixing personal logins into shared workflows remains tricky, limiting what a shared service account can cover today. Free vs. paid tiers: Seo noted that the free tier handles everyday tasks fine, while paid plans lift usage caps, long-research limits, and scheduled-routine counts. Comparison with Meta Muse: While Seo has not used Muse extensively, he noted that doing everything inside his primary daily browser is Aside’s biggest advantage. Before You Try Similar Workflows Because Aside acts with your live sessions and credentials, irreversible actions like payments, account transfers, or bulk deletions deserve extra guardrails. Seo’s own list includes live checkouts, transferring Apple Developer account ownership, deleting hundreds of old X posts, and setting 140 Tistory blog posts to private. Just as he required a manual “send” step before posting to Slack, keeping a human confirmation gate on payments and deletions is the safest default.
Summary Tasks automated with Aside span metric debugging, multi-tool reporting, Mac terminal administration, online shopping, and appointment booking. Because the browser runs tied to personal logins on an individual Mac, shared team operation remains limited for now, though Organization features are reportedly in progress. For irreversible actions like payments or bulk deletions, keeping a final human approval step remains good practice.
summary: Jonghun Seo documented 100 real tasks run in the AI browser Aside across 10 categories, covering scheduled routines, Mixpanel debugging, Mac terminal jobs, and current limits.
title: 100 Tasks Delegated to AI Browser Aside: From Coffee Orders to Mixpanel

content:
An agent that scans Slack channels and GitHub pull requests every weekday morning to post a short action list sounds straightforward on paper. In practice, unattended runs fail quietly: an expired token drops one data source and the agent reports “nothing new today,” a retry posts the same brief twice, or an already merged PR shows up as an open blocker. Because nobody watches a scheduled job run in real time, those silent errors compound unnoticed. This post walks through Anthropic’s reference automation to see how concrete state and permission boundaries prevent each failure mode.
At a Glance Anthropic published a reference implementation on Claude Managed Agents (beta) that reads Slack and GitHub on a schedule and posts only net-new changes to Slack. The architecture separates six concerns: sources, destination, agent definition, schedule, memory stores, and guardrails. Six operational rules anchor the design: read from per-source bookmarks instead of fixed time windows, never report an unreadable source as a quiet day, re-verify every candidate item right before posting, advance bookmarks and ledgers only after Slack confirms delivery, re-read preferences from a store the agent cannot edit, and pair read-only source credentials with a per-run budget cap. About the Original Post Lance Martin and CJ Avilla published this 9-minute engineering guide on October 8, 2026. It walks file by file through a working reference repository while calling out the silent failure modes that appear at each step. Developers automating recurring reports or operational digests with agents can adapt its configuration layout directly. Source: Building effective agent automations.
System Layout and Configuration Files The reference implementation is a declarative bundle of configuration files: agent.md, deployment.md, environment.yaml, two memory stores, and vault.yaml for credentials. Running ant apply with the ant CLI provisions those resources in a Claude API workspace and records their IDs in claude-lock.json. Once deployed, the schedule runs on Anthropic’s infrastructure without requiring your laptop to stay online. Running /claude-api managed-agents-onboard in Claude Code with the post URL walks through setting up the same files interactively.
The diagram below maps how those pieces connect during a scheduled run.
Figure 1. Schedule wakes Agent, which reads Sources, checks Already posted?, and posts to Destination. Under Memory, the agent reads and writes State, while the human Reader edits Preferences and the agent only reads it. Dashed Guardrails bound turns, runtime, spend, and heartbeat monitoring. Source: Original post.
Sources: Read from Bookmarks and Surface Read Failures Credentials live in a vault so the agent never sees raw secret values. For GitHub, an out-of-sandbox proxy attaches the token to MCP calls. For Slack, the agent calls curl from inside the sandbox using a $SLACK_BOT_TOKEN placeholder, and the platform swaps in the real token only when the outbound request targets an allowlisted host.
Hardcoding a fixed window like “the past 24 hours” breaks as soon as schedule timing drifts: a delayed run misses items in the gap, while an early run re-reports items from yesterday. Instead, the automation tracks per-source bookmarks. At the end of each run, it records the timestamp of the newest item read from each source in bookmarks.json inside the state memory store mounted at /mnt/memory/, and the next run picks up from there.
Dead MCP servers or expired tokens cause a subtler failure. The run still starts and logs an error in the session trace, but with that source’s tools missing, the agent sees zero new items and cheerfully posts “nothing new.” Three rules in agent.md block that behavior:
flowchart TD A["Read source"] --> B{"Read succeeded?"} B -->|"Yes"| C["Include new items<br/>Advance bookmark"] B -->|"No"| D["Keep bookmark unchanged"] D --> E["Draft brief from<br/>remaining sources"] E --> F["Append one-line note<br/>naming unread source"] Leaving the bookmark untouched guarantees the next healthy run catches up on the missed window, and the trailing one-line warning tells readers whether a source was genuinely quiet or simply unreachable.
Delivery: Update State Only After Slack Confirms The agent posts its brief with a single curl call to the Slack API via bash, with no human approval step in between. Without strict ordering, internal records easily drift out of sync with the Slack channel. Recording a failed post as delivered advances the bookmark past items that never appeared in Slack, dropping them forever; retrying an ambiguous post without checking the channel sends readers duplicate briefs.
The reference workflow locks down the sequence. Before posting, the agent checks recent channel messages and skips posting if today’s header is already present. After posting, it counts delivery as confirmed only when Slack’s response includes both "ok": true and a message ts. Only then does it update the ledger and advance bookmarks. Each run records its delivery state in runs/<date>.md:
stateDiagram-v2 state "posting" as posting state "posted" as posted state "maybe posted" as maybe [*] --> posting posting --> posted : ok and ts confirmed posting --> maybe : outcome uncertain posted --> [*] : update ledger and bookmarks maybe --> [*] : leave other records untouched When the response is ambiguous, marking the run maybe posted and leaving bookmarks and the ledger untouched guarantees that no source items are silently skipped.
Agent Definition, Schedule, and Memory Split In Managed Agents, an agent is a versioned resource bundling the model, system prompt, and toolset. The reference config runs claude-sonnet-5-5 with web search and web fetch disabled. MCP tools normally pause for per-call approval, which would hang an unattended run where nobody is around to click approve. Instead, GitHub MCP tools are set to always_allow, while the underlying GitHub token itself is restricted to read-only permissions.
Of the eight execution steps in the prompt, the post highlights two that protect brief quality. The first is ruthless filtering: an item makes the cut only if it changes what the reader will do today or alters an upcoming decision, and ambiguous items get dropped. Raw counts like “12 open reviews” never qualify as items. The second is pre-post re-verification: because PRs merge and Slack threads resolve while the agent is still reading, the agent re-opens every selected source item right before posting, drops anything already resolved, and updates lines whose status shifted. Items that cannot be re-verified are omitted from the brief and logged in the run record instead. URLs are copied verbatim from source link fields rather than pieced together by hand.
Scheduling lives in the deployment configuration, which runs on cron 32 7 * * 1-5 in America/New_York for weekday mornings. Computing relative dates from UTC server time causes classic off-by-one bugs—calling this morning’s activity “yesterday”—so the deployment injects the reader’s local timezone directly into the initial wakeup message.
Memory is split across two separate stores with different permissions. The preferences store is written by the human reader and mounted read-only for the agent. It lists which channels and repositories to watch, what topics to mute, and how long the brief can be. The agent re-reads preferences.md fresh on every run, and if the file cannot be read, it halts and alerts rather than falling back to generic defaults. Because ant apply deployment.md provisions the store without populating files, scripts/seed-preferences.sh seeds preferences.md before the first run. The state store is read-write for the agent: alongside bookmarks.json, run logs, and the item ledger ledger.md, the agent writes suggested preference tweaks and per-source operational notes there. Each row in ledger.md records the report date, source, a stable identifier such as a Slack message timestamp or PR number, and the last reported status.
Guardrails: Permissions and Budget Caps Because this agent ingests untrusted Slack messages and GitHub issues written by others, prompt injection is a real risk. The design limits blast radius through hard platform boundaries rather than prompt wording alone: the GitHub token and preferences store are both read-only, and network egress is restricted to an explicit host allowlist. A crafted issue body could still skew a single morning’s summary—or leave a note in state that carries into a later run—but it cannot push code to GitHub or rewrite the reader’s preference rules. Because the Slack bot token needs write access to post the brief, the bot should be invited only to channels it strictly needs.
For cost control, the post recommends setting a per-run spend cap at 3–5x the cost of a normal run and tightening it once real usage data settles. In the example config, "500" is denominated in cents, setting a $5.00 ceiling. A run that hits the cap stops cleanly with status budget_reached rather than throwing an error—which means setting the cap too tight can make truncated runs look deceptively like quiet days.
Takeaways The notes below are this blog’s own interpretation, not part of the original post.
Per-source bookmarks, post-confirmation state writes, and maybe posted states map one-to-one onto incremental ETL watermarks and two-phase commit ordering in data engineering. Unattended agent automations need the exact same discipline as batch pipelines: persist your high-water mark outside the process, and advance it only after downstream delivery is confirmed so retries remain safe.
Rules like “drop when ambiguous” and “drop when unverified” deliberately bias the brief toward precision over recall. That same tradeoff governs internal data-quality alerting: missing two minor anomalies hurts far less than sending one false alarm that trains engineers to mute the channel.
Splitting preferences and state into separate stores with different write permissions is a clean defense against configuration drift. Allowing the agent only to propose preference edits inside state keeps injected prompts from rewriting operating rules. Still, as the authors note, state itself persists across runs—so teams running this pattern in production should periodically audit state notes alongside run logs.
What to Try First Check whether any recurring report or alert automation you run today queries a fixed "last N hours" window; if so, switch it to persist and resume from the last processed item timestamp. Intentionally revoke or break one data source in staging and verify whether your automation surfaces the missing source explicitly or sends a misleading “no updates” message. Run claude update followed by /claude-api managed-agents-onboard with the original post’s URL, then adapt the generated config files to your own repositories and Slack channels. Original post: Building effective agent automations
summary: Walking through Anthropic’s Claude Managed Agents reference automation for scheduled Slack and GitHub morning briefs, focusing on bookmarks, delivery confirmation, ledgers, read-only preferences, and per-run budget caps.
title: Six Rules for Keeping Scheduled Morning Agent Briefs from Failing Silently

content:
A Claude Code session running in your laptop terminal inherits every constraint of that laptop. Opening two sessions in the same repository means sharing one working directory, where concurrent edits and local server ports collide. Every session runs with your full local user permissions, and closing the lid or losing Wi-Fi stops the work mid-turn. Cloud sessions remove all three constraints by moving each task into an isolated virtual machine. This post breaks down how cloud sessions are structured and which tasks belong in the cloud versus on your laptop.
At a Glance Every cloud session boots a fresh virtual machine (VM), clones your repository onto a new branch, and leaves its changes on that branch ready to open as a pull request. Cloud sessions are included at no extra machine charge on Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise plans, drawing from your existing Claude Code usage allowance. Because sessions share neither files nor ports, they fit parallel bug fixes and verification loops that run a test suite dozens of times in a row. GitHub permissions cause most first-run failures: signing in with GitHub and installing the Claude GitHub App are two separate steps. About the Original Post Addy Osmani published this 18-minute field guide on October 6, 2026. Rather than staying abstract, the post runs four real cloud sessions against a small sample repository and shares the actual transcripts, diffs, and wall-clock timings. It is written for developers who already use Claude Code in a local terminal and want to know when to offload work to the cloud. Source: Claude Code in the cloud.
Three Tasks on Three Machines at Once The sample repository, tidepool, is a small Node API that predicts tides across three fictional harbors. It has three separate issues: a test that fails roughly one run in four, API documentation that has drifted from the implementation, and plain string-concatenated logs. The author launches three cloud sessions within 16 seconds, assigning one task to each.
Figure 1. Horizontal axis shows seconds elapsed since launching the first session. Hatched bars mark demo repository setup, where a standard GitHub clone normally happens; each dot represents one tool call. Source: Original post.
Each session ran for 61 to 72 seconds, and all three wrapped up within 87 seconds of the first launch:
Flaky test: Claude traced the failure to a race condition in TtlCache.get, where a second request for the same key arriving mid-fetch triggered a duplicate loader call. It cached the in-flight promise and ran npm test 40 times in a row with zero failures. API docs: Claude started the server, queried every endpoint with curl, and fixed five mismatches between the responses and the documentation. Structured logs: Claude replaced string logs with JSON output and added five tests. When one test failed during verification, Claude traced it to the same cache race condition VM 1 was fixing, left the out-of-scope cache code untouched, and noted the dirty test run in its summary. Because each session had its own repository clone, process space, and branch, the documentation and logging sessions could both boot the API server simultaneously without port conflicts. Isolation has a flip side: the logging session could not see the cache fix happening next door. When splitting parallel work, cut along clean file boundaries and expect adjacent sessions to flag pre-existing bugs that another session is already fixing.
Anatomy of a Cloud Session Inside each session, the VM sits inside a strict boundary while credentials and network controls stay outside it.
Figure 2. Left (START OR CHECK FROM) shows where sessions can be launched—and monitored from browser, mobile, or desktop. Center (FRESH VM PER SESSION) shows the isolated VM, while right (OUTSIDE THE VM) shows the proxies handling credentials and network policy. Source: Original post.
Four architectural choices shape day-to-day usage:
Component How cloud sessions handle it Machine A fresh VM per task; sessions never share files, processes, or ports GitHub token Never enters the VM; a proxy issues a short-lived credential scoped to push only to that session’s working branch Configuration Repository CLAUDE.md, rules, and skills travel with the clone, while your personal ~/.claude stays on your laptop Idle VMs Reclaimed after inactivity; reopening restores the conversation in a new VM, so uncommitted file edits do not survive Cloud sessions do not replace local sessions. Tasks that depend on local-only resources—a local database with test data, internal services behind a VPN, a GPU, or a mobile simulator—still belong on your laptop, as does rapid UI iteration where you check a local browser every few seconds. Organizations under Zero Data Retention policies also stay local-only because cloud sessions are disabled there.
Workloads That Fit the Cloud From the seven workflows in the original guide, four stand out for everyday engineering work:
Firing off parallel small fixes: Run claude --cloud "task description" once per task. Because cloud sessions clone the current branch from GitHub remote, push your local commits first. Write each prompt with three specifics: what is broken, what done looks like, and which command proves it. Demanding proof of a fix: Because the cloud VM burns remote compute rather than your laptop CPU, you can ask for thorough verification—such as running the full test suite 40 times in a single loop to confirm a race condition is gone. Figure 3. The runs=40 fails=0 output at the bottom confirms 40 consecutive clean runs, followed by Claude’s root-cause writeup. Source: Original post.
Foreground bash commands time out after 2 minutes by default (up to 10 minutes max) and can continue running in the background for up to 30 minutes. You can raise those defaults via BASH_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS and BASH_MAX_TIMEOUT_MS.
Planning locally, executing in the cloud: For larger changes, align on an implementation plan interactively on your laptop first, hand execution off to a cloud VM, and pull the finished branch back down when needed. flowchart LR A["Local plan mode<br/>Align on plan"] -->|"Commit and push"| B["claude --cloud<br/>Execute plan"] B -->|"Push branch"| C["claude --teleport<br/>Pull into terminal"] C --> D["Finish by hand"] Running claude --teleport brings both the cloud session’s Git branch and its conversation history into your local terminal. The branch must already be pushed, and your local working tree should be clean—if uncommitted changes exist, Claude Code offers to stash them.
Running untrusted code: Testing an external contributor’s PR or a new dependency’s install script on your laptop exposes local SSH keys and cloud CLI logins sitting in the same user account. A disposable cloud VM holds none of those secrets and lets you restrict outbound network access down to None. Keep two caveats in mind: even with network set to None, requests to the Anthropic API still leave the VM, and the session can still push to its own branch. The guide also covers starting or checking sessions from the mobile app, using Auto-fix to resolve CI failures and review comments on PRs, and scheduling recurring routines from cron schedules or GitHub events.
GitHub Permissions and Environment Setup GitHub access relies on two separate layers. Signing in with GitHub only verifies your identity; repository visibility for private repos comes from installing the Claude GitHub App on the user account or organization that owns the repository. When a private repo is missing from the picker, walk through this check:
flowchart TD A["Private repo missing<br/>from the picker"] --> D{"Claude GitHub App installed<br/>on owning account or org?"} D -->|"No"| E["Install App on that account or org<br/>Org installs need owner approval"] D -->|"Yes"| F["Check App repo selection scope<br/>and SAML SSO authorization"] Public repositories work with GitHub sign-in alone. In the browser flow, private organization repositories appear only after the App is installed on that organization. If you already use the gh CLI locally, running /web-setup inside Claude Code can pass your gh token instead, granting access to whatever repositories that token can reach without the GitHub App—though Team and Enterprise plans require an owner to enable Quick setup first. Auto-fix, GitHub-event routines, and projects always require the GitHub App regardless of setup path.
Once GitHub is connected, the VM needs a working test environment so the session can verify its own changes. The Default image already covers most JavaScript, Python, Go, and Rust repositories. System packages belong in a setup script, which runs as root, must exit 0, and gets cached only if it finishes within 5 minutes. Project dependency steps like npm install fit better in a SessionStart hook inside .claude/settings.json, where both local and cloud sessions execute them identically. Commands for running integration suites belong in CLAUDE.md, since your personal ~/.claude directory never enters the cloud VM.
Takeaways The notes below are this blog’s own interpretation, not part of the original post.
Watching the logging session hit the out-of-scope cache bug, leave src/cache.js alone, and document the failure in its summary is a great model for parallel agent work. Whether you are splitting backend services or data pipelines across concurrent sessions, stating explicit file boundaries in each prompt—and instructing the agent to report rather than fix out-of-scope failures—prevents painful merge conflicts later.
Whether a cloud session returns a PR you can merge quickly depends heavily on the verification command in your prompt. For data engineering tasks, asking an agent to “run a validation query comparing row counts and totals against the baseline table” beats “fix the SQL query” for the exact same reason a 40-run test loop beats a single pass: the session brings back numeric proof alongside the diff.
Leaving ~/.claude behind on your laptop creates healthy pressure for engineering teams. Because cloud sessions only know how to build, test, and lint your project if those instructions live in the repository (CLAUDE.md, .claude/settings.json, shared skills, and MCP configs), onboarding a cloud VM ends up documenting the repo for new human teammates at the same time.
What to Try First Open claude.ai/code, connect GitHub, and verify that the Claude GitHub App is installed on the account or organization owning your main private repositories. Pick two small backlog items that touch separate files, push your current branch, and launch both in parallel via claude --cloud—including an explicit verification command in each prompt. Check whether your repository’s CLAUDE.md states the exact command to run tests; if not, add a one-line instruction today. Original post: Claude Code in the cloud: a field guide to cloud sessions
summary: How Claude Code cloud sessions isolate each task in its own virtual machine and Git branch, which workloads belong in the cloud versus on your laptop, and how to avoid common GitHub setup pitfalls.
title: Claude Code Cloud Sessions: Running Parallel Tasks Beyond Your Laptop

content:
The Codex Update Challenge ships either a feature update or a usage-limit reset every day for 28 days. Here is a breakdown of the week-one changes ranked by how much difference they make in daily development workflows.
1. 500K Default Context and Faster Baseline Speed Using GPT-6.1 Sol in Codex and Work raises the default context window from 272K to 500K tokens - roughly an 80% jump. Fewer compactions mean long sessions preserve task context and subtle constraints much longer. Best of all, subscription usage carries no extra long-context surcharge, and users can manually raise the cap up to 1M tokens when needed. Among all week-one updates, this change makes the biggest practical difference.
Baseline generation speed for subscription GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol also jumped roughly 50%, climbing from 30 TPS to 50 TPS. Partner tools using Sign in with ChatGPT - including OpenCode, Pi, Amp, and Devin - get the same speedup automatically without configuration changes.
2. Agent Supervision and Steering Features Auto-review, which evaluates permission prompts on your behalf, is now free for every ChatGPT account holder and consumes zero plan quota. A secondary agent inspects the main agent’s proposed actions and blocks only risky operations, cutting down approval fatigue. Auto-review previously consumed 2-10% of plan usage, and removing that cost makes enabling it an easy default.
Instant mid-run steering lets the model pivot immediately when you redirect a task in flight rather than burning tokens down the wrong path. Meanwhile, Sol Ultrafast runs up to 8x faster than Sol Standard while staying close to Astra quality. Pairing fast inference with live steering makes directing agent runs feel interactive.
3. Platform Rollouts and Trade-offs GPT-6 and Intelligent UI rolled out to all ChatGPT users as active users across Codex and Work passed 40 million. Codex Cloud also quietly returned with Tailscale integration to reach resources on private tailnets safely, while the Codex desktop app added a Pro beta Composer prediction feature that suggests your next prompt based on conversation flow and writing style.
With three usage resets landing in the first seven days, the event occasionally felt like a reset-voting contest - something even the official account acknowledged. Notably, when Pro users voted between doubling weekly quota with a 5-hour cap versus keeping current quota with no 5-hour cap, removing the 5-hour cap won. Developers clearly value uninterrupted flow over raw weekly volume.
Week one set a clear direction: faster output, longer context, and zero extra surcharges. If the remaining three weeks keep shipping core workflow upgrades like surcharge-free 500K context, feature days will be far more welcome than quota resets.
Summary GPT-6.1 Sol raises default context to 500K tokens with no extra quota surcharge, making long coding tasks far smoother. Subscription throughput rose from 30 TPS to 50 TPS across Codex and Sign in with ChatGPT partner tools. Free quota-exempt Auto-review and instant mid-task steering cut approval fatigue and wasted agent runs.
summary: A week-one review of the Codex Update Challenge covering the 500K default context window, 50 TPS speed boost, free Auto-review, and live steering.
title: Codex Update Challenge Week 1 Review: 500K Context and Faster Throughput

content:
Uploading large documents or images to web converters or launching heavy desktop suites slows down everyday work, and browser tools pose a leak risk for confidential company files or personal records. Filee is a desktop application that runs every conversion directly on your machine with zero cloud uploads, keeping private files local.
Day-to-day usage stays simple: select files in your file manager or desktop, hold a modifier key, and drop them onto the target format. Converted files appear right next to the originals, and a context-menu integration lets you convert directly on right-click. Batch conversion handles 1 or 100 files in a single pass - if one file fails, the rest continue uninterrupted - and built-in bundling can package outputs into PDF or ZIP archives.
Supported Formats and Built-In Engines Filee reads 180 formats across 14 categories, spanning images, PDFs, Office documents, Korean Hangul word-processor files (HWP and HWPX), video, audio, archives, and CAD drawings. Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and HWP/HWPX documents run through built-in engines, so conversions work even on machines without Microsoft Office or Hancom Office installed. Optional heavy backends like LibreOffice and Calibre can be selected during installation or downloaded inside the app later, and Filee automatically detects existing local installations if you already have them.
CLI and Folder Automation Beyond the desktop UI, Filee ships a full command-line interface. Running filee watch monitors a directory and converts incoming files to a target format as soon as they land. Structured JSON output and standard exit codes make scripting straightforward for automated pipelines. Released under the MIT license, Filee is free and open-source with no ads or watermarks.
Engineers and product managers who convert local documents regularly will find it a practical utility.
Summary Runs 100% locally without internet uploads to keep sensitive files private. Converts Office and HWP/HWPX documents via built-in engines without requiring Microsoft Office or Hancom Office. Supports automated folder pipelines through the filee watch CLI command and JSON output.
summary: Filee is a free open-source desktop converter that handles 180 file formats locally via drag-and-drop and CLI folder watching without cloud uploads.
title: Filee: A Free Local Converter Supporting 180 File Formats on Your PC

content:
Running inside Claude Code, showreel is an agent skill that produces finished Korean motion-graphics videos from a single-line prompt. Users do not pick templates or mood boards by hand; the system generates multiple concept candidates, selects the strongest direction, and automates research, scriptwriting, ElevenLabs narration and music, image generation, deterministic HTML rendering, and final quality checks.
Production starts by asking the user only for essential inputs. Claude makes the creative calls directly and writes a 240-to-255-character Korean script for a 60-second video. Audio comes before visuals: voiceover and music are generated first so the timeline script can lock scene transitions to narration phrasing and musical beats. Because the HTML and WebGL REEL engine renders every frame as a pure function of time, parallel workers can render the video deterministically.
Outputs include both a master MP4 and a share-ready MP4 alongside a poster image, SRT subtitles, and production notes capable of regenerating every asset. During assembly, a critique loop scores each segment for generic template feel and pacing, followed by an automated QA report that checks loudness standards and frozen frames. Setup requires Python, Node.js, ffmpeg, and an ElevenLabs API key after cloning the repository.
Summary Delegates creative direction to the agent to produce complete motion-graphics videos from a single prompt. Generates voice and music first so subtitles and scene cuts lock cleanly to audio timing. Runs a critique loop and automated audio/frame QA to deliver production-ready video assets.
summary: Showreel is a Claude Code agent skill that turns a single prompt into Korean motion graphics with narration, music, deterministic HTML rendering, and automated QA.
title: Showreel: Automating Korean Motion Graphics with a Claude Code Skill

content:
Shipping compiled software turns human-readable source code into machine binaries, and reconstructing original logic traditionally required painstaking manual reverse engineering. The open-source project REA automates analysis from high-level app behavior down to native binaries for AI agents, cutting reverse engineering time dramatically.
Agent Integration and Analysis Scope REA connects to coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor as an MCP server. Its analysis spans web apps, consumer appliance firmware, and native binaries through Ghidra integration. Every step runs locally and attaches supporting evidence to each finding.
The DX-Ball Case Study and CLI Usage A reconstruction of the classic game DX-Ball shows REA’s precision in practice. Starting from sound-effect trigger points, the agent traced the underlying algorithms backward and recovered C source code that passed 3,205 tests and recompiled to a byte-for-byte match against the original binary.
For JavaScript applications, the CLI extracts structural metadata with a single command:
npx -y rea-agents@latest analyze-javascript-application /absolute/path/to/app --json The command maps module dependencies and Electron process boundaries into structured JSON output. You can also install the package globally via npm install --global rea-agents.
Limits of Closed Source and New Product Moats Relying on closed source code alone to protect software logic is hitting a wall. As AI agents compress reverse engineering timelines, competitors can map how proprietary features work in a matter of days. Durable product moats increasingly come from proprietary data, operational know-how, and customer trust rather than hidden source code.
As agent-assisted analysis reshapes software engineering, teams need updated security assumptions and clearer product differentiation.
Summary REA connects AI coding agents via MCP to automate analysis of closed binaries and application internals. Verified on DX-Ball by recovering C source code that passed 3,205 tests with byte-exact recompilation. Shifts software defensibility away from closed source code toward proprietary data, operational execution, and user trust.
summary: Open-source tool REA connects AI agents via MCP to inspect binaries and app internals locally, recovering byte-accurate C source code.
title: Analyzing REA: AI Agent-Driven Reverse Engineering and Code Recovery

content:
On Threads, CHOI (@choi.openai)introduced a new app with the line “Google just killed thousands of startups.” Released by Google on October 6, Google AI Edge Foresight is a free macOS app that records and transcribes meetings, summarizes key points, and answers questions across saved documents and past meeting notes.
Paid meeting-assistant SaaS tools already offer these features. What sets Foresight apart is that every step runs locally on your Mac - neither audio streams nor documents ever go to the cloud.
What It Does During a Meeting Foresight captures both your Mac’s microphone and system audio directly. Because it does not rely on calendar bots or video-call integrations, it works equally well with Google Meet, Zoom, or an in-person meeting with a laptop open on the table.
Jot down a rough bullet during a call - such as “recheck Q3 budget, confirm with team lead Kim” - and the app pulls supporting details from the live transcript to flesh out the note. You can view your raw notes side by side with the AI-expanded version.
It also listens for spoken questions during the meeting, detecting them in real time and surfacing answers from your local files right on screen.
What It Does After the Meeting Drop PDFs, Google Docs, Office files, plain text, Markdown files, and web bookmarks into Foresight to build a personal knowledge base. Combined with your accumulated meeting transcripts, you can ask everyday questions like “What launch date did we agree on in the last meeting?” and get grounded answers. Because search is multimodal, it retrieves images alongside text documents.
How Two Models Split the Work Inside According to the Google Developers Blog, Foresight runs on two local models: EmbeddingGemma 2 and Gemma 4. While Google does not spell out every internal call, the division of labor follows a classic library pattern.
EmbeddingGemma 2 acts as the librarian. An embedding model converts text, images, and audio into numerical vectors where similar meanings land close together, letting search find relevant material even when wording differs from the query. Because EmbeddingGemma 2 maps text, images, video frames, and audio into one shared vector space, a single query searches across both audio recordings and PDF files.
Gemma 4 reads the retrieved material and writes the response, expanding shorthand bullets into full meeting notes or answering questions. Splitting retrieval and generation across two models is standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).
Running everything locally works because EmbeddingGemma 2 stays compact at 740M parameters. In Google’s published Pixel 11 Pro benchmarks, active memory usage came in at roughly 191MB for text-only mode and 567MB with image and audio encoders loaded - small enough to fit on a phone, let alone a Mac.
Why On-Device Processing Matters Work meetings routinely cover customer names, unannounced timelines, and personnel matters. Cloud meeting assistants require security reviews before adoption, and many organizations block them outright because audio leaves company devices.
Google states that Foresight keeps all audio, transcripts, and knowledge-base files strictly on-device. That design means the app works offline without an internet connection and carries zero cloud subscription fees.
Things to Know Before Trying It It is an experimental release. Google shipped Foresight as an experimental app alongside the EmbeddingGemma 2 launch rather than as a commercial product, partly to showcase local multimodal RAG on consumer hardware. Apple Silicon Macs only. Foresight targets M-series Macs and does not support Intel-based machines. “Killed startups” is hyperbole, with a caveat. Still, combining zero cost with strict local data retention puts real pressure on paid meeting-note tools, making it an easy trial for teams that previously ruled out AI note-takers on security grounds. You can download the app from the Google AI Edge Foresight page.
Summary Google AI Edge Foresight is a free experimental macOS app that runs meeting transcription, note expansion, live Q&A, and document search entirely on-device. EmbeddingGemma 2 (740M) retrieves relevant context across transcripts and files, while Gemma 4 writes expanded notes and answers. Audio and files never leave the device, enabling offline use, though hardware support is limited to Apple Silicon Macs.
summary: Google’s experimental Mac app AI Edge Foresight transcribes meetings, expands notes, and searches local documents entirely on-device using EmbeddingGemma 2 and Gemma 4.
title: Google AI Edge Foresight: A Free On-Device AI Meeting Notes App for Mac

content:
Advances in AI tooling are reshaping how software and products get built. Beyond basic code generation, developers can now convert token budgets directly into scaled execution capacity.
Iterative Loops and Finishing the Last Mile Shipping a complete product comes down to finishing the last mile. Anyone can reach an initial 80% prototype quickly, but closing the remaining 20% through repeated refinement separates rough demos from real products. Rather than stopping at one-shot answers, AI agents perform best inside verification loops that test outputs and refine the next attempt.
With clear evaluation metrics and higher token budgets, one person can match or exceed the output of a small engineering team. Running multiple agents toward a shared objective through continuous trial and correction creates a clear competitive edge, while setting goals and defining product direction remain human responsibilities.
Specialist Review and Production Quality As implementation gets cheaper, problem definition carries more weight, expanding what generalists can build across the stack with AI tools.
Shipping commercial software that customers pay for still demands the deep judgment of a specialist. Today’s AI agents can get stuck in local optima or introduce subtle defects. Turning agent output into reliable production software requires specialists who can inspect edge cases, give precise feedback, and steer architecture.
Asking the Right Questions and Field Networks Faster implementation raises the bar on logical product design - deciding what to build and why. Pairing a generalist’s broad synthesis with a specialist’s deep domain focus creates durable product value.
Using AI agents to scale execution works best when guided by specialist taste and verification. As raw technical knowledge becomes easier to access, peer networks where practitioners trade real production lessons and collaborate matter even more.
Summary AI agents scale execution capacity by pairing evaluation metrics with iterative verification loops and token budgets. While generalists can build rapid prototypes with AI, reaching commercial product quality still requires specialist review and feedback. As implementation speeds up, defining what to build and maintaining strong practitioner networks become key differentiators.
summary: AI agents let individuals scale execution through token investment and feedback loops, making clear planning and deep specialist review the real differentiators.
title: Scaling Execution with AI Agents and the Role of Specialists

content:
A prompt screenshot from Claude Code head Boris Cherny recently drew attention. In the Claude app, he asked Opus 5.5 to build an interactive artifact for the Home Depot episode of the Acquired podcast. One line stood out:
Make it really good, use lots of tokens and iterate till you’re proud of it.
Dylan Ko (gonnector)highlighted the phrase “proud of.” Nobody knows quite how an AI model interprets pride internally, yet the prompt produces strong results in practice. Teams typically design detailed evaluation rubrics and loop until the agent passes them, which raises a practical question: in loop engineering, does setting “pride” as the stopping goal beat a formal rubric under controlled conditions?
This post lays out the experimental conditions and metrics needed to run that comparison directly.
Three Loop Goals to Compare A. Iterate until rubric metrics pass: Repeat until each metric reaches 90% or higher.
