AI-01 Agreement: Rate at which AI judgments match human expert judgments AI-02 Consistency: Rate at which repeated runs on identical input produce the same judgment AI-03 Explanation usability: Rate at which AI-generated explanations can be used directly in review B. Single-line pride goal: Give only the instruction to iterate until the model is proud of the result. C. Combined A and B: Provide both the evaluation rubric and the single-line pride instruction. Experimental Conditions All three setups tackle the same single requirement - for example, building one support-eligibility review screen - each starting in a clean session. Keep the model, input materials, and harness version identical across A, B, and C, and cap iterations at 10 rounds.
Run each condition 3 times and average the results, since a single run carries too much variance to draw conclusions.
Metrics to Record Quality: Scores on AI-01 through AI-03, plus the number of lines manually edited by a human Cost: Total token consumption and wall-clock time Iteration behavior: Number of rounds before stopping, and the point at which the agent declared itself “done” The decision rule stays simple. If quality ties, pick the condition that spent fewer tokens. If quality differs, pick the condition that cleared 90%. Summarize the results in a single condition-by-metric table for easy sharing.
Summary Boris Cherny’s “iterate till you’re proud of it” prompt delegates the loop stopping decision to the model’s own judgment. The experiment compares passing a formal rubric (A), a single-line pride goal (B), and both combined (C) on the same task and harness. Each condition runs 3 times to measure quality, token usage, and loop count, favoring lower token spend when quality ties.
summary: An experimental design testing whether Boris Cherny’s “iterate till you’re proud of it” prompt outperforms explicit evaluation rubrics in agent loops.
title: Using Pride as a Loop Goal: An Experiment Against Metric Rubrics

content:
Using AI well on your own is very different from getting an entire team to build with AI together. One developer asks only for code implementation while another expects tests and updated docs. Draft proposals get passed around as settled rules, or teams re-litigate approaches they already rejected months ago. Writing for Yozm IT, Jungmin Lee examines how DeepSeek tackles these coordination problems inside the open-source DeepSeek Harnessrepository, an execution environment built for AI models to read files, invoke tools, and ship changes. Original articleLee focuses on how the repository keeps standards consistent even as contributors rotate, letting anyone inspect prior reasoning before making new changes. Rather than maintaining a separate llm-wiki, keeping rules, decision logs, and workflows right next to the code proves simpler for team development - though Lee notes that a public repo alone cannot prove internal collaboration outcomes.
Aligning Definition of Done with AGENTS.md What stands out in AGENTS.md is less the volume of rules than how it binds task conditions to reference material. Before modifying a package, agents read its architecture docs; before pushing, they run matching checks via dsh-pre-push-checks. Prose and comment review rules link out to dsh-prose-standard.
Three rules directly govern team handoffs:
Significant changes must add or update an Agent Note in the same PR to record the decision. Code changes must update related documentation alongside them so the next contributor does not mistake stale docs for current behavior. Verification reports may include only checks that were actually executed. Even if a prompt omits explicit instructions about docs or tests, repository standards still enforce recording decisions and running verification. Completion criteria live in the repository rather than depending on whoever wrote the prompt.
The harness also separates storing guidance from feeding it into context. By default, DeepSeek Harness loads the root AGENTS.md for the working directory and appends subdirectory rules only when working inside those paths. Linked notes and skills are not auto-loaded. Because of that, the rules explicitly state when to look things up - such as searching existing records before drafting a new note.
Organizing Notes into Status Folders Inside .agents/notes, status folders come first rather than chronological files. The folder path immediately tells the next contributor how much weight a document carries:
proposed: Proposals still under review implemented: Decisions actively in effect rejected: Proposals reviewed and declined archived: Historical records kept separate from current standards Within each status folder, subdirectories group notes by topic such as architecture, process, and testing. For instance, the decision to drop a central note index lives at .agents/notes/implemented/process/2026-07-19-remove-generated-agent-note-index.md. The path alone shows that the change is active and governs development workflow.
Transition rules matter even more. Moving a note into implemented requires rewriting forward-looking “we plan to” phrasing into settled “we decided to” statements and updating any changed file paths or defaults. Reversing a prior decision never overwrites the old note to say the opposite; contributors create a new note and link it back to the earlier record so the reason for changing course stays intact.
Why Removing the Central Index Left a Paper Trail The note on removing the central index explains why the current folder layout exists. When independent tasks updated separate notes but also had to touch a shared index file, unrelated PRs constantly hit merge conflicts. The note preserves the alternatives the team weighed: auto-generating the index continuously, generating it on demand, or curating it by hand. They settled on dropping the index altogether in favor of status-and-topic folders paired with repository search.
Lee points out that the lesson is not “never build an index.” The real takeaway is preventing independent tasks from colliding on shared files and recording why that choice was made. When a new teammate or agent wonders whether a central table of contents would be handy, the answer is already in the repo without tracking down whoever was in the original meeting.
Encoding Team Judgment into Shared Skills Shared skills in DeepSeek Harness cover more than code review and documentation - they also codify note archiving, deduplicating proposals, and merging stacked PRs.
Note archiving (dsh-archive-agent-notes) judges notes by whether they help future decisions rather than by age or length. Even after implementation finishes, notes containing key trade-offs or security constraints stay active. Open proposals are never archived; abandoned ones move to rejected with an explanation. The skill forbids optimizing for a target count of archived files and requires flagging ambiguous cases during handoff.
Finding simplifications (dsh-find-simplifications) favors a small set of well-grounded candidates over a long wish list. When pulling ideas from other PRs, agents merge overlapping proposals into existing notes rather than padding the list with weak or duplicate items. Closing duplicate PRs happens only on explicit user request or with clear triage ownership.
Merging stacked PRs (dsh-merging-stacked-prs) handles dependent PR chains in order, with clear boundaries around autonomous actions. If PR authors differ or ownership is unclear, the agent asks the user first. Readiness on a top PR never implies lower PRs in the stack are ready, and branches still targeted by other open PRs are never deleted.
Code Review Starts from Prior Decisions Without Freezing Them dsh-code-review checks code changes alongside shared rules, test policies, and related Agent Notes, while explicitly instructing reviewers not to reject a change solely because it disagrees with an older note. Prior decisions serve as a baseline, and new evidence can reopen the discussion - provided the author checks the original rationale and explains what changed.
Verification likewise separates claims from evidence. Reviewers check whether tests merely mirror implementation details or genuinely fail when the target bug appears, and passing automated lint checks on translated docs does not count as proof of semantic accuracy.
Lee closes by applying the same standard to adopting team-wide skills: a prompt that worked well for one person should only become a shared team workflow after checking what tasks it actually improved, whether it conflicts with existing rules, and whether teammates can apply it consistently.
Summary DeepSeek Harness defines decision notes, doc updates, and executed verification checks as completion criteria in AGENTS.md. Agent Notes live in proposed, implemented, rejected, and archived folders, and reversed decisions link a new note to the old one rather than overwriting history. Records preserve rejected alternatives and rationale, such as dropping a central index to avoid merge conflicts across unrelated PRs. Shared skills for archiving notes, proposing simplifications, merging stacked PRs, and reviewing code set explicit boundaries on autonomous agent actions.
summary: An analysis of the DeepSeek Harness repository covering AGENTS.md completion rules, status-based Agent Notes folders, and shared team skills.
title: What an AI-Native Team Leaves in Its Repo: Inside DeepSeek Harness

content:
On October 7, 2026, the author of Jono’s Corner published a hands-on review after running DeepSeek 4.1 Flash heavily across 12 projects for roughly a month. Without glancing at the model label mid-session, the author could not tell whether DeepSeek or Opus was responding. Conversation flow, code output, and speed felt indistinguishable, making the absence of a 4.1 Pro tier irrelevant: if a model performs like a frontier model, treat it like one. Original postCost per Task Comparison Framing the post as subjective day-to-day experience, the author included an external benchmark chart comparing the weighted average cost in USD to complete a single Intelligence Index task. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash came in at $0.15 with reasoning off and $0.27 at max reasoning. Scaling Claude Opus 5.5 across reasoning effort levels from low to max pushed per-task cost from $0.55 to $1.34, $1.82, $3.46, and $5.98.
Why Are Frontier Labs Not Panicking? The post’s central question mirrors its title. Even if Chinese labs trail Anthropic or OpenAI by a month or two, distilled Chinese models handle the same practical workloads. Addressing claims that Chinese labs distilled Claude outputs, the author notes that Anthropic trained on other people’s data too and skips the IP debate, arguing that working developers care far more about output per dollar.
Good-Enough Models Change How Developers Work Models have crossed the threshold where they produce solid work without constant human supervision, making chasing every new leaderboard release pointless. Handing routine tasks to a top-priced frontier model, the author argues, is like hiring a math PhD to tidy up desktop folders.
Running DeepSeek almost without limits through a $10/month OpenCode Go subscription changed what tasks felt worth automating, from repetitive cleanup to exploratory UI monkey testing. Work that previously cost $1 dropped to $0.003, and single-session estimates rarely crossed $1 even on sessions that ran for most of a workday.
The author splits model roles deliberately. DeepSeek 4.1 Flash handles complex planning and codebase research as well as implementation. Only on high-stakes changes does Opus 5.5 step in for a final review pass to catch a few missed edge cases, which DeepSeek then fixes. Calling Opus or GLM serves mainly to get a second perspective on the same problem rather than higher baseline quality.
Impact of Shrinking the KV Cache by 437x DeepSeek reduced its KV cache footprint to roughly 1/437th of its V1 architecture. Because the KV cache stores prior token activations in GPU memory for reuse, holding that state in VRAM dominates the cost of long coding sessions. That reduction explains how an all-day coding session stays under $1.
The author suspects power and water usage drop alongside memory footprint without citing direct measurements, and notes that Opus 5.5 achieved its own efficiency gains through similar caching techniques.
Sustainability and Access Over Saving Pennies Because the author’s employer already covers frontier subscriptions like Claude and Cursor, the argument is not about personal penny-pinching. What matters is long-term sustainability, predictable planning, and opening capable AI tooling to far more developers.
Criticism lands squarely on industry status signaling - a culture that equates high spend with serious engineering and overlooks major efficiency gains, exemplified by developers load-balancing a dozen Claude Max subscriptions while complaining about rate limits.
On self-hosting, the author remains skeptical. At 4.1 Flash API prices, hardware outlays for cost savings alone will not pay back. Developers worried about privacy are better off waiting: if KV cache compression keeps advancing at this pace, full local execution will soon be practical, whereas self-hosting 4.1 Flash today is technically possible but operationally impractical.
Summary Across 12 projects over a month, the author found DeepSeek 4.1 Flash indistinguishable from Opus in everyday coding sessions. Benchmark per-task costs ranged from $0.15 to $0.27 for DeepSeek 4.1 Flash versus $0.55 to $5.98 for Claude Opus 5.5. Flash handles planning and implementation, while Opus 5.5 is reserved for occasional final code reviews on high-stakes tasks. Shrinking the KV cache to roughly 1/437th of V1 keeps long multi-hour coding sessions under $1.
summary: A developer’s one-month review of DeepSeek 4.1 Flash across 12 projects, comparing per-task costs against Opus 5.5 and examining its 437x KV cache reduction.
title: Why Is the AI Industry Not Panicking About DeepSeek 4.1 Flash?

content:
Finding a specific scene in a photo library or pulling a relevant segment from a meeting recording requires comparing meaning across different file formats. Released by Google DeepMind on October 6, 2026, EmbeddingGemma 2 embeds text, code, images, video, and audio into a shared 768-dimensional vector space. Built to run search directly on smartphones and laptops, the model ships with Apache 2.0 open weights. Google announcementThis post builds on an introduction by choi.openai on Threads, cross-checking the architecture and benchmark numbers against Google’s official announcement, developer guide, and model card.
Comparing Different Modalities in a Shared Vector Space Embeddings represent the meaning of content as numerical vectors. Converting a query into a vector and measuring similarity against stored items retrieves matching content across formats. Because EmbeddingGemma 2 places multiple input types into the same space, a voice memo can match a video scene and a text query can locate a segment in an audio recording. This design removes intermediate steps that previously chained image captioning, speech-to-text transcription, and text embedding in sequence. Google AI Edge overviewThe architecture pairs a Gemma 4 text and code backbone with optional vision and audio encoders. Every configuration outputs vectors into the same shared space.
Active Modalities Parameter Count Text and code 270M Text and code + image and video 440M Text and code + audio 570M Full multimodal 740M Applications that only need text search can skip loading the vision and audio encoders into memory. Adding other modalities later from the same checkpoint keeps existing embeddings compatible without recomputation. Developer guideHigher Code Retrieval Scores and Longer Context In Google’s full-precision evaluations, MTEB Code rose by 9.92 points from 68.76 in the first generation to 78.68. Multilingual text stayed steady, moving from 61.15 to 61.36. For the newly added modalities, image retrieval scored 64.64 on MIEB lite, video retrieval scored 50.67 on MMEB v2, and speech retrieval scored 69.54 on MSEB. Because these are distinct benchmarks, scores cannot be compared directly across modalities. Model cardContext length expanded to 8,192 tokens. Under the default settings documented in the model card, a single-modality input without text fits roughly 5 minutes 30 seconds of audio, about 29 images, or about 58 video frames. Mixed-modality inputs share that same 8,192-token budget. Model cardCutting Device RAM and Index Storage Separately Running quantized weights on a Google Pixel 11 Pro used roughly 191MB of active RAM for the text-only configuration and roughly 567MB for the full multimodal model. Those figures reflect that specific device and quantization setup. Google announcementIndex storage shrinks independently by truncating output vector dimensions. Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) lets developers slice the leading 512, 256, or 128 dimensions from the 768-dimensional output. In the developer guide’s bfloat16 example, storing 1 million vectors takes about 1.5GB at 768 dimensions and about 250MB at 128 dimensions. Those numbers count raw vector storage alone, excluding database index overhead. Developer guideTruncating dimensions trades off retrieval quality. The aggregate MMEB v2 score drops from 59.01 at 768 dimensions to 56.24 at 256 dimensions and 45.65 at 128 dimensions. Google recommends 128 dimensions for large-scale text indexing or first-stage candidate retrieval. After truncation, vectors must be re-normalized, and queries must match the target index dimensionality. Model cardFrom Photo Search to Local RAG and Routing Instant Media Search in Google AI Edge Gallery finds on-device media from text or image queries, while Video Moments Finder indexes video frames and audio tracks to jump to matching timestamps. On macOS, Google AI Edge Foresight pairs EmbeddingGemma 2 for document retrieval with Gemma 4 for answer generation in a local RAG pipeline. Google AI Edge overviewThe model also handles classification and routing. MediaPipe Decision compares an incoming request against pre-written option descriptions by vector similarity to pick the next action, routing requests to functions without separate model training or fine-tuning. Google AI Edge overviewWeights are available on Hugging Face and Kaggle, with runtime support across sentence-transformers, MLX, Ollama, and browser deployments via transformers.js and WebGPU. Running locally eliminates per-call embedding API fees and keeps personal photos and recordings off external servers, at the cost of local compute and storage for model execution and vector indexes. Google announcement
summary: Google’s EmbeddingGemma 2 maps text, code, images, video, and audio into a shared 768-dimensional space with optional encoders for on-device search.
title: EmbeddingGemma 2: On-Device Multimodal Search in One Vector Space

content:
Running multiple AI coding tools side by side quickly multiplies terminal windows and makes tracking work difficult. Because each session runs in isolation, context fragments across tabs. OpenRig addresses this problem by grouping individual agents into a single coordinated team.
How OpenRig Works and Its Core Structure OpenRig adds a team coordination layer on top of multi-model harnesses. Users define an agent team in a YAML file and launch the entire system with a single command, managing Claude Code and Codex together inside the same rig.
The system pairs harnesses with rigs. You communicate with a lead agent to describe the desired outcome, and the lead agent coordinates specialist agents, collects their outputs, and tracks decisions. That structure replaces a sprawl of disconnected terminal sessions.
Installation and Runtime Requirements Running OpenRig requires Node.js 22 or 24 and tmux on macOS or Linux. Native Windows is not supported yet. Because OpenRig modifies workspace settings and provider hooks, backing up existing configurations first is recommended.
Install the CLI globally with npm install -g @openrig/cli, and preview changes before setup by running rig setup --dry-run. You can also run it with Bun, though a Node.js environment is still required alongside it. The installer runs environment checks automatically during setup.
OpenRig fits workflows that scale AI coding to a team structure and brings order to multi-agent management.
Summary Defines multiple AI coding agents in YAML and coordinates them as a single team. Uses a lead agent to manage specialist agents and prevent terminal session sprawl. Runs on Node.js 22+ and tmux, with a dry-run mode to inspect workspace changes beforehand.
summary: OpenRig lets developers define multiple AI coding agents like Claude Code and Codex in YAML and coordinate them as a persistent team.
title: Running Multiple AI Coding Agents as One Team with OpenRig

content:
AI-SQL operators let analysts classify and join unstructured text inside SQL queries using natural-language prompts, yet firing an LLM call per row or per join pair quickly racks up hundreds of thousands of inferences. Quail tackles this bottleneck by co-optimizing the relational query plan and the LLM inference engine together.
Letting the Query Plan Drive Inference Sending row-by-row HTTP requests to a general-purpose LLM server bottlenecks on CPU request scheduling and redundant prompt prefill. Quail couples SQL execution directly with model memory management to cut repeated HBM reads. During semantic joins, it pins an anchor document’s KV states in memory across multiple candidate comparisons and uses KV rewinding to discard per-pair suffixes while keeping shared prefixes intact. CPU batch preparation overlaps with active GPU execution in a pipelined loop to minimize idle gaps.
SQL Compatibility and Benchmark Results Users register Arrow tables or datasets and query them via SQL or a pandas-style Python API. Quail supports Snowflake AI_FILTER and BigQuery AI.IF syntax alongside AI filters, joins, projections, and LIMIT clauses. On an internal benchmark running Qwen3 4B FP8 on a single H100 GPU, Quail outperformed vLLM on 27 out of 29 queries, posting a 1.84x geometric mean speedup with especially large gains on multi-pair tasks like clinical report comparisons.
Practical Trade-Offs Data engineers and analysts running bulk LLM predicates at table scale stand to benefit most, though standard serving engines can still edge ahead on certain simple scan shapes depending on workload selectivity and prompt structure.
Summary Co-optimizes relational SQL query plans with LLM inference to accelerate bulk AI-SQL workloads Uses anchor pinning and KV cache rewinding on semantic joins to eliminate redundant memory reads, achieving a 1.84x geomean speedup over vLLM Supports Snowflake AI_FILTER and BigQuery AI.IF syntax over Arrow datasets via SQL and Python
summary: Quail jointly optimizes SQL execution plans and LLM KV cache reuse, beating vLLM on 27 of 29 AI-SQL benchmark queries with a 1.84x geometric mean speedup.
title: Quail: High-Throughput AI-SQL Engine Co-Optimizing Query Plans and LLMs

content:
Ask an AI coding agent for a system architecture diagram and you usually get boxy generic shapes or tangled Mermaid syntax. diagram-design is an agent skill that outputs editorial-grade, self-contained HTML and SVG diagrams with zero external dependencies.
Restrained Styling and Three Built-In Themes diagram-design strips away visual clutter across three default themes - Minimal Light, Minimal Dark, and Full Editorial - that open straight in any browser without JavaScript or a build step.
It targets a visual density of 4 out of 10, reserving accent colors for just one or two focal elements. Pointing it at a live website URL also lets it extract brand typography and palette cues in roughly 60 seconds.
42 Diagram Types and Semantic Patterns The skill covers 42 diagram types spanning sequence diagrams, flowcharts, and database schemas, with v2.5.10 adding 10 layouts including Sankey, Fishbone, Wardley map, Kanban, and Dependency graph. Semantic patterns decouple system behavior from visual geometry so complex states stay legible.
It can also ingest existing Mermaid or Excalidraw files and redraw them at a chosen fidelity level, defaulting to crisp static output with optional sequenced motion for walkthroughs.
Installing Across Agent CLIs Installation takes a couple of commands across major coding agents. In Claude Code, register the marketplace via /plugin marketplace add cathrynlavery/diagram-design and install the plugin, with optional background auto-updates on session launch.
Codex, GitHub Copilot, Factory Droid, and Pi connect directly through their respective package commands or repo URLs, while enterprise Claude Cowork setups can mirror the repo for automated team sync.
Summary Generates single-file HTML and SVG diagrams with zero build steps, JavaScript, or external image dependencies Supports 42 editorial layouts as of v2.5.10, including Sankey, Wardley maps, Kanban boards, and DB schemas Installs cleanly as a plugin or skill across Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Factory Droid, and Pi
summary: The diagram-design agent skill generates self-contained editorial HTML and SVG diagrams across 42 layouts for Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot without JS or build steps.
title: diagram-design: Zero-Dependency Editorial HTML/SVG Diagrams for Agents

content:
Instead of asking an LLM to “explain like I’m 5,” Andrej Karpathy pointed to ASD-STE100 (Simplified Technical English) as a better way to get crisp technical answers. Originally developed for aircraft maintenance manuals, the standard restricts loose phrasing so instructions cannot be misread.
ASD-STE100 centers on eliminating structural ambiguity: write procedures in active voice, put a single instruction in each sentence, use one consistent term per component, avoid stacked noun clusters, and place conditions at the front of the sentence.
Write procedures and instructions in active voice. Keep one instruction per sentence. Use consistent names for every object. Unpack stacked noun clusters into explicit relationships. Restrict complex tenses and verb forms. State conditions before actions. Break complex information into vertical lists. Preserve exact domain terminology. Karpathy also recommends pushing explanations beyond plain text into diagrams, interactive web pages, or short explainer animations - using diagrams for component relationships, interactive HTML for parameter sweeps, and visual sequences for dynamic concepts.
As AI output volume grows, human review becomes the bottleneck. Pairing strict prose standards like ASD-STE100 with visual formats and a personal research-to-draft workflow shortens verification time.
Summary Prompting with the ASD-STE100 aerospace maintenance writing standard cuts ambiguity in technical LLM responses Enforces active voice, single-instruction sentences, condition-first ordering, and exact domain terms Pairs well with requests for diagrams and interactive HTML pages to speed up human comprehension
summary: Andrej Karpathy highlighted ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English as a sharper alternative to ELI5 prompts for stripping ambiguity out of LLM explanations.
title: Using the ASD-STE100 Aerospace Standard for Clearer LLM Responses

content:
Most AI agent skills live scattered across GitHub repositories. When the author ran a GitHub code search on September 16, 2026, more than 40,000 repositories already carried a top-level SKILL.md file, mostly documented in English for software engineers. Published on WikiDocs, the Claude & Codex Skill Guidebookcurates practical skills in Korean, free to read online with an optional 8,000 KRW e-book edition.
Clear Selection Criteria Before Installation Across 56 chapters, the book covers both popular open-source GitHub skills and custom skills the author runs daily. Every chapter splits good-fit vs poor-fit scenarios into a clear table alongside setup steps, invocation syntax, caveats, and a side-by-side comparison of how Claude Code and Codex load the same skill folder.
Star ratings next to chapter titles condense GitHub star counts into three tiers: three stars for 50,000+, two stars for 10,000+, and one star below that, explicitly framed as a popularity signal rather than a quality guarantee.
Role-Based Roadmaps First Chapter “00-0 Role-Based Skill Combination Roadmap” maps recommended chapters step by step for product planning, marketing, engineering, research, design, and operations roles, alongside the author’s own multi-skill pipeline for building lecture materials.
The book is organized into role-focused parts:
Part Skills Covered 00 Basics Agent and skill fundamentals, Claude Code vs Codex mechanics and specs, glossary Parts 01-06 Business, marketing, data analytics, design, software development, ops automation Part 07 Meta-workflow skills for planning, questioning, memory, and wrap-up Part 08 End-to-end skills for building and shipping web services from natural language 99 Weekly updated Skill Radar Featured repositories range from three-star heavyweights like superpowers, marketingskills, last30days-skill, gstack, and skill-creator to compact utility skills for meeting agendas, blog topic triage, and scheduled macOS jobs.
Recommended Reading Paths Concept chapters 00-2 and 00-3 require zero local setup. They explain an agent as a loop that reads files, runs commands, and checks results toward a goal, and a skill as an on-demand playbook loaded mid-task. Chapter 00-2 diagrams how skills differ from persistent workspace rules (CLAUDE.md), subagents, MCP servers, and hooks.
Non-technical planners, marketers, and business operators are pointed to 00-2, 00-3, and their functional part, while engineers and ops practitioners switching between both tools start with 00-2 through 00-7 before jumping to Part 07 and Part 05. Running the skills requires Claude Code or Codex installed and basic comfort pasting commands into a terminal.
The first edition targets Claude Code v2.1.273 and Codex v0.153.4 (as of 2026-09-17) on macOS Terminal, with ongoing web updates and fresh picks added weekly in “99-8 Weekly Skill Radar”.
Summary Curates 56 GitHub agent skills in a free online Korean guide covering both Claude Code and Codex Breaks down good-fit vs poor-fit use cases, installation steps, invocation commands, and caveats in structured tables Provides role-specific reading paths and tracks newly trending repos in a weekly Skill Radar section
summary: A free Korean WikiDocs guidebook curating 56 GitHub agent skills for Claude Code and Codex, organized with role-based roadmaps, fit tables, and weekly radar updates.
title: Claude & Codex Skill Guidebook: 56 Curated Agent Skills by Role

content:
This LinkedIn postshares a multi-day user review of the Dots agent service, grouping its strengths into three traits - Proactive, Frictionless, and currently Free - while pointing out a frustrating UI constraint.
Proactive Follow-Ups Before going to sleep, the author had Dots send an email requesting a LinkedIn billing cancellation. By morning, Dots proactively notified the author that a reply had arrived, and it also surfaces time-of-day task nudges.
Frictionless Setup and Local Agent Orchestration Existing ChatGPT users can start with almost zero onboarding. Unlike competing agents that demand fresh connector setup from scratch, Dots immediately reads and searches already-linked mail and cloud drive accounts.
It also bridges cloud VMs with the user’s local machine, orchestrating tasks across locally installed Codex or Claude Code instances. A standout UI detail opens a dedicated side thread showing the exact sub-calls and responses exchanged with those local tools.
Generous Free Window on GPT-6 Astra Built on GPT-6 Astra, Dots handles task intent accurately while responding fast, likely with heavy reasoning disabled or dialed down by default. Early access includes a 1-month extended usage window, and standard actions did not burn quota unless they explicitly invoked ChatGPT work or Codex.
The Catch: One Endless Thread The biggest drawback is being forced to work inside a single continuous stream. Having spent 2 years isolating each agent task into separate bounded sessions, the author found a single endless feed awkward for parallel work and easy for both human and AI to lose track of past context - a sharp contrast to multi-bot setups like Grok Bot, even if casual users may prefer a unified inbox.
Even so, the author views Dots as the first consumer-ready productivity agent that makes delegation effortless, noting that bundling unlimited usage into a Pro 200 tier would change its value proposition.
Summary Proactively flags incoming email replies and surfaces time-based follow-up tasks Reuses existing ChatGPT account connections with near-zero setup and visualizes local Codex or Claude Code orchestration in side threads Forces all work into a single continuous thread, making parallel task isolation and history tracking harder for power users
summary: A hands-on review of the Dots agent covers proactive follow-ups, zero-config setup, and local CLI orchestration, plus its single-thread catch.
title: Hands-On with Dots: Three Strengths and One Major Workflow Catch

content:
Ask a standard voice assistant to triage your inbox or research a topic mid-call, and the conversation goes silent while it waits on slow browser actions. Thursday is an open-source voice assistant that hands multi-step jobs off to background bots so live voice conversation never stalls.
Decoupling Live Voice from Task Execution According to the project README, GPT-Live 1 keeps the voice conversation responsive while a Responses model handles immediate tool calls. Any job taking more than a few seconds delegates to background text-model bots with shell, browser, and local file access. Bots split work among themselves, check back when a human decision is needed, and keep running even after you hang up.
Users can ask for live status updates on a later call, inspect execution logs to see what each bot ran, trigger scheduled jobs, or interact over messaging channels. Everything starts locally via npx thursday-agent.
Local Execution Does Not Mean Full Isolation Running on your own machine does not mean audio stays offline: live call audio streams to OpenAI, and background bots call whichever LLM provider you configure. The README also notes that bots execute real shell and browser commands under your user account with no OS sandbox. Stopping right before a checkout button during shopping tasks relies on prompt instructions rather than a hard runtime lock.
Review the security documentationand scope account and file permissions carefully before connecting personal credentials. Architecturally, Thursday offers a clean reference for separating low-latency voice UX from long-running agent execution.
Summary Keeps live voice chat responsive while delegating slow browser, shell, and file jobs to background bots Continues asynchronous tasks after calls end, with full execution history and scheduled triggers Runs under the local user’s permissions without sandboxing, requiring careful credential scoping upfront
summary: Thursday separates live voice conversation on GPT-Live 1 from background bots that run browser, shell, and file tasks asynchronously on your local machine.
title: Thursday: Open-Source Voice Assistant Backed by Background AI Bots

content:
Shipping a distinctive website with coding agents takes a different workflow than typing one detailed prompt and hoping for a finished UI. Generating broad batches of throwaway prototypes and recombining the strongest pieces works much better in practice.
Exploring Broad Variations First When designing their site around product guardrails, the Railcode team paired safety rails with a rollercoaster theme and generated 4 to 10 distinct variations per concept, ranging from restrained layouts to loud experimental takes.
Most generated drafts hit the trash, yet outlier drafts sparked breakthroughs. One overly neon rollercoaster mockup pushed the team past a flat ASCII aesthetic and inspired a full amusement-park direction modeled after Rollercoaster Tycoon. Harvesting sharp visual fragments out of discarded drafts drove the creative direction.
Locking a Visual Anchor with Tight Feedback Loops Early iterations stayed inside a single self-contained HTML file. The team also built a lightweight side-by-side comparison viewer to tweak palettes, typography, and spacing across clones in real time, keeping latency between agent edits and visual inspection near zero.
Once they locked a central Visual Anchor, they expanded outward into themed footer banners, custom icons, and motion details. Agents wrote the implementation code, while humans made every layout and curation call, indexing prompts and prototype snapshots along the way. In this setup, the coding agent supplies high-volume options and the developer acts as art director.
Summary Generates 4-10 broad prototypes per concept and recombines standout visual pieces instead of relying on one-shot prompts Keeps early iterations in single-file HTML with side-by-side comparison tooling for fast visual feedback Uses coding agents to produce volume while keeping final taste, layout selection, and polish in human hands
summary: How the Railcode team generated 4-10 broad variations per concept, locked a Visual Anchor in single-file HTML, and curated agent outputs into a distinctive website.
title: Multi-Stage Prototyping Workflow for Designing Websites with Coding Agents

content:
Logging final AI outputs rarely makes it easy to trace which source facts and intermediate rules produced a conclusion weeks later. Semantica is an open-source Python framework that links facts and decisions inside a knowledge graph so teams can query why a specific outcome happened.
Recording Decisions Inside the Graph According to the Semantica repository, the pipeline ingests documents and structured data, extracts entities and relations, and writes decisions as first-class graph nodes via record_decision(), linking upstream causes to downstream effects. Teams can later query precedent decisions or traverse causal chains.
Lineage metadata exports cleanly to W3C PROV-O, while rule-based inference supports Rete, Datalog, and SPARQL queries. Graph construction and deterministic reasoning run without an LLM, and optional connectors plug into existing models or agent frameworks when needed.
Validate Reasoning Against Real Domain Rules The repository notes that pattern matching inside ReteEngine is currently simplified. Before wiring Semantica into compliance or production policy gates, teams should test match_patterns() against their real rule sets. Provenance tracking guarantees an audit trail, not automatic correctness of the inference rules themselves.
Summary Models facts, AI decisions, and causal chains inside an open-source knowledge graph Exports lineage metadata in W3C PROV-O format and supports Rete, Datalog, and SPARQL queries Ships with simplified ReteEngine condition matching today, requiring validation on real business rules before production use
summary: Semantica records data facts and AI decisions as knowledge graph nodes with W3C PROV-O export and rule-based reasoning, alongside current Rete engine limitations.
title: Semantica: Knowledge Graph Tracking for AI Decisions and Provenance

content:
Improving Performance by Modifying the Harness Retraining LLM weights every time an agent underperforms is prohibitively expensive. Google Research’s RRSI framework keeps model weights frozen and optimizes the surrounding execution environment instead. Agents recursively refine their own harness - prompts, control flow, tool interfaces, and memory management - while regularizing the search trajectory to prevent benchmark overfitting.
Dual Regularization Across Proposal and Selection RRSI splits optimization into a proposal stage that generates candidate edits and a selection stage that filters them. During proposal, the system gradually anneals how many components change at once, checks edit history to avoid repeating failed hypotheses, and redirects exploration toward long-untouched modules.
During selection, a critic pre-validates domain logic and accepts only gains that clear evaluation noise margins. Any candidate that adds inference token overhead must deliver a bigger accuracy jump to survive, and low-impact modules get pruned back out. Across out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluations, this dual regularization outperformed prior baselines by up to 22.9% while cutting policy token usage by more than 30%.
Open-Ended Exploration Managed in Git Worktrees RRSI tracks every harness mutation directly in Git. Candidate harnesses run inside isolated Git worktrees (git worktree), and only changes that pass evaluation merge back into the main branch, keeping the active harness tied to clean commits. Swapping domain adapters lets teams apply the same optimization loop to terminal coding agents, document pipelines, or engineering design tasks.
Released on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license, RRSI offers a structured blueprint for improving agent systems without touching model weights.
Summary Freezes LLM weights and recursively optimizes prompts, tools, and control flow inside the agent harness Prevents benchmark overfitting and cuts policy token spend by over 30% via dual proposal-and-selection regularization Isolates and validates candidate harnesses in Git worktrees so every accepted change maps to a clean commit
summary: Google Research’s Apache 2.0 RRSI framework freezes LLM weights and recursively optimizes agent harnesses via dual regularization and Git worktrees.
title: Google RRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement for AI Agent Harnesses

content:
Long sessions in Claude Code make it easy to lose track of how much conversation context has accumulated, or what a file-deletion command is about to wipe out before it runs. Mods let you attach small custom programs to Claude Code to surface that state or step in before an action executes. Using a weather-style context indicator as the main example, this post walks through how mods run, how to build one, and what to watch out for when sharing them.
At a Glance A mod is a small JavaScript or TypeScript file that runs alongside your Claude Code session. It can inspect session state, modify an action right before execution, or render custom status information in the terminal UI. You can ask Claude in plain language to generate a mod for you, or write one yourself starting from an empty plugin folder. Mods live inside plugins, which package extensions for installation, and connect to session activity through hooks that fire when specific events occur. The post walks through three examples: Token Weather for live context usage, Blast Radius for previewing destructive commands, and Replay Theater for stepping through file edits. About the Original Post Addy Osmani published this tutorial on October 1, 2026. Following the examples requires Claude Code 2.1.287 or later. Because you can start by describing what you want in plain English without memorizing the API upfront, the guide fits regular Claude Code users who want to adapt the terminal workflow to their own habits. Source: Getting started with Claude Code mods.
How Mods Work Under the Hood Whenever Claude Code calls a tool or finishes a response, it emits an event. An event signals that an action is happening, and a hook is the custom handler function you attach to run at that moment—for instance, logging changed files right after an edit completes.
Mod files sit inside a plugin directory, where hooks.json points to the code module to load. Inside that module’s register function, on(event, hook) binds specific events to your handler code.
Multiple hooks run in sequence like middleware. Calling next(e) hands the event to the next handler in the chain; once the chain finishes, Claude Code performs the underlying action. That structure gives each hook three distinct ways to act:
Observe: Let the original action run and record the outcome, such as tracking which files were edited during a turn. Rewrite: Modify the event payload before passing it forward, such as swapping a command for a safer variant. Respond: Return a result directly without calling next, stopping a tool call before it reaches execution. Everything hinges on whether your handler calls next. Calling next lets the event pass through any remaining hooks to the original action and returns the result back up the chain. Returning early without next ends the action inside your hook.
Beyond tool calls, events cover prompt submission, turn start and end, custom slash commands, and ui.render for drawing terminal UI elements.
Modules execute inside a restricted sandbox rather than a browser DOM or a full Node runtime. Instead of standard system APIs, your code interacts with the session and terminal screen through the $ object provided by Claude Code.
Traditional configuration hooks spawn a fresh shell command each time they fire, whereas a mod stays alive for the entire session. Because it persists in memory, a mod can retain state across turns, update status lines, open interactive panels, and register new slash commands or model-callable tools.
First Example: Token Weather The context window is the total span of conversation history and file content the model can hold at once. At the end of each turn, Token Weather reads how full that window is and renders a single status line above the prompt, pairing token counts with a weather label that shifts as usage climbs.
Context usage Label What it signals Under 25% Clear Plenty of headroom left 25–49% Cloudy Context is steadily filling up 50–74% Showers More than half the window is used 75–89% Storm Running low on remaining context 90% and above Compact soon Time to consider compacting the conversation Alongside total tokens used, the bar shows a 12-turn sparkline of recent history and the token delta from the latest turn, making both current capacity and recent growth rate visible at a glance.
The session screenshots from the original post show a 200k context window crossing 18%, 67%, and 81%.
Figure 1. The single-line Token Weather indicator from the original post. Labels progress from Clear through Showers to Storm as the 200k window fills, while the mini bars on the right track per-turn growth. Source: Original post.
Each threshold crossing updates both the weather label and its color: 18% sits in Clear, 67% in Showers, and 81% in Storm.
The fastest way to build it is to launch claude and describe the indicator you want. With hot reload enabled—so Claude Code re-reads modified plugin files without a restart—the new status bar appears as soon as the turn finishes. Follow-up tweaks like lowering the Storm threshold to 70% can also be requested in plain English.
Writing the mod by hand takes roughly 80 lines of code:
Launch claude --plugin-dir to load the plugin under development, reloading automatically whenever you save a file. Read current window consumption via $.session.usage() and store per-turn history in $.state. Plain module-level variables reset on hot reload, whereas $.state survives reloads for the life of the session. Check plugin structure with claude plugin validate and verify behavior with claude plugin test. Saving edits to tweak the UI reloads the module cleanly while keeping the turn history accumulated in $.state.
Sharing Mods and Two Larger Examples To distribute a mod, you publish a marketplace manifest in a GitHub repository listing the available plugins. Other users register that repository with /plugin marketplace add, install the mod via /plugin install, and pick up changes with /reload-plugins.
A mod runs on your machine with the same OS permissions as Claude Code itself, and community-published mods are not official Anthropic code. The module sandbox limits which JavaScript APIs a mod can call directly, not whether installed code is safe to trust. Treat third-party mods like any software package: read the repository first and install only from authors you trust.
The post closes with two larger examples built on the same hook model:
Blast Radius: Intercepts destructive commands such as rm -rf, git reset --hard (which discards uncommitted work), and force-pushes before they run, computes their impact, and opens a confirmation panel with Proceed and Cancel options. In the original example, rm -rf build previews 9 files (1.1 MB) slated for deletion. Because the mod parses only the raw command string, it can miss command substitutions like $(…), shell aliases, or scripts that invoke rm internally. The author frames it as a helpful guardrail rather than a hard security boundary—use permission rules when you need guaranteed blocking. Replay Theater: Observes Edit and Write tool calls during a turn without altering file writes, then lets you press r or run /replay to step through before-and-after diffs one change at a time. Figure 2. Blast Radius lists two uncommitted files that git reset --hard would wipe out, pausing execution until the user picks Proceed or Cancel. Source: Original post.
Figure 3. Replay Theater walks through file edits one step at a time with Prev, Next, and Close controls. Source: Original post.
Non-destructive commands pass straight through without interruption; only flagged patterns pause for human confirmation.
Takeaways The notes below are this blog’s own interpretation and hands-on testing, not part of the original post.
Designing a mod gets much simpler once you decide upfront whether it observes, rewrites, or responds early. File-edit history belongs in a passive observer, whereas destructive commands warrant pausing execution to preview impact. The Blast Radius pattern translates directly to database tooling as well: before an agent runs a query, a hook can preview affected tables or row counts and wait for explicit approval.
Keeping context fill level and recent per-turn growth visible removes the guesswork around when to compact a session. Pairing cumulative totals with recent deltas works well for other operational agent metrics too, such as tool-call latency or retry counts.
Because installed mods inherit Claude Code’s local permissions, a flawed or malicious community mod can affect your workspace directly. Teams sharing internal mods should review authorship, file access, and shell execution paths before installation, just as they would for internal CLI packages.
Rebuilding all three examples directly in Claude Code 2.1.289 surfaced a few practical constraints worth knowing before combining multiple mods:
Only one mod can own the single status line above the prompt at a time. When Token Weather occupies that slot, Replay Theater cannot place its r shortcut prompt in the same spot, so we exposed edit counts in the status bar and opened the viewer via /replay instead. Because Blast Radius inspects only the literal command string, paths containing ~ or $HOME are not expanded and appear only as "not expanded". Remote commit counts for force-push warnings also reflect the last local git fetch rather than live remote state. A single risky command can trigger both the mod’s confirmation panel and Claude Code’s built-in permission prompt back to back. In non-interactive runs such as claude -p, where nobody can answer a prompt, risky commands are always rejected. Running several mods together means sharing scarce UI slots and coordinating pre-execution hooks with built-in permission rules. Check where each mod renders and where it intercepts the hook chain before stacking them in one workspace.
What to Try First Run claude --version in your terminal and confirm you are on 2.1.287 or later before testing the mod APIs from this guide. Pick one metric you want visible throughout a session—for example, ask Claude to build a one-line mod showing current context percentage and the token jump from the previous turn—and watch how it behaves across a real task. Read every file in a mod repository before installing or sharing it with teammates, checking which files it reads or writes and whether it intercepts or executes commands. Original post: Getting started with Claude Code mods
summary: How Claude Code mods work as small in-session JavaScript or TypeScript modules, walked through with the Token Weather context gauge, Blast Radius command checks, Replay Theater diff viewer, and plugin sharing.
title: Extending Claude Code with Mods: Live Context Usage and Risky Command Checks
