Telling a coding agent to “think like a senior engineer” rarely changes its behavior in concrete ways. High-level advice blurs distinct habits like scoping the real problem or spotting failure modes before writing code. A recent project tackles this by decomposing engineering judgment into 23 small, self-contained Agent Skill modules.
Separating the Router from Specific Disciplines The Senior-thinking-skills repository splits responsibilities between a router and focused disciplines. senior-engineer-mindset acts as the router, loading only the discipline files relevant to the current task. Examples include clarify-the-real-problem for questioning surface-level tickets, premortem for listing failure modes prior to implementation, surgical-change for keeping diffs minimal, and measure-before-optimizing for capturing baseline metrics first. Additional skills cover subagent parallelization and recording baseline Git SHAs.
Small Skill Files and Hard Runtime Boundaries Loading a few 30-70 line skill files on demand is far easier to maintain than wrestling with a single 1,100-line mega-prompt. Each skill puts its trigger conditions in the description field and keeps the body strictly focused on concrete actions. The author also draws a clear boundary around what Markdown instructions cannot do: skills shape reasoning habits, whereas hard runtime guardrails belong in a separate Hook layer that blocks unsafe actions deterministically. Keeping judgment guidance separate from hard enforcement makes agent behavior much easier to debug.
Breaking monolithic agent instructions into composable decision units gives teams a clean pattern for steering coding agents across long-lived repositories.
Summary Routing 30-70 line modular skills scales better than maintaining a single monolithic prompt Separates soft reasoning guidance (‘Skills’) from deterministic runtime enforcement (‘Hooks’) Keeps trigger timing in skill descriptions and concrete actions in skill bodies to avoid wasting prompt context
summary: Instead of stuffing a giant system prompt with vague advice, Senior-thinking-skills routes coding agents across 23 focused 30-70 line discipline modules.
title: Splitting Senior Engineering Judgment into 23 Modular AI Agent Skills

Long builds, data migrations, and background scripts stall out if macOS drops into sleep mid-run. Both the built-in caffeinate command and the free menu bar app Amphetamine prevent unwanted sleep, though each fits different workflows.
Terminal-Native Control with caffeinate caffeinate ships with macOS and runs straight from the terminal with zero setup. Core flags block display sleep (-d), system idle sleep (-i), disk idle sleep (-m), AC-power sleep (-s), or declare active user presence (-u). Combining a timeout (-t 3600) or process watch (-w PID) keeps the Mac awake only until a target job finishes.
Wrapping a command directly is straightforward: caffeinate -i npm run build blocks idle sleep for the exact duration of the build. Running caffeinate -i -s on wall power lets the display turn off while keeping background compute alive.
Menu Bar Automation with Amphetamine Amphetamine lives in the macOS menu bar and adds rich conditional triggers without touching the terminal. Sessions can start automatically on schedules, when specific apps launch, or while downloads remain active, as well as on environment signals like Wi-Fi SSIDs, Bluetooth devices, or battery thresholds.
Its Drive Keep Alive feature writes tiny periodic heartbeats so external drives do not spin down, and an optional cursor jiggler prevents corporate screen-lock timers from interrupting monitoring views. When sleep rules depend on changing hardware or network state, GUI triggers beat shell wrappers.
Closed-Clamshell Differences and Thermal Caution Behavior diverges sharply when you close the MacBook lid. On stock macOS, caffeinate -i alone cannot stop hardware sleep the moment the lid closes unless AC power, an external display, and an input device are all attached.
Amphetamine can override closed-display sleep in its session settings, keeping local servers or render jobs running with the lid shut and no external monitor plugged in. Just avoid running heavy CPU or GPU loads inside an enclosed backpack or sleeve, where trapped heat can throttle or damage hardware.
Reach for caffeinate on one-off terminal commands, and pair it with Amphetamine when you need conditional triggers or headless closed-lid operation.
Summary caffeinate wraps terminal commands or PIDs with zero install to block idle sleep during builds and scripts Amphetamine automates awake sessions around Wi-Fi networks, Bluetooth devices, battery levels, and screen-lock prevention Running a MacBook with the lid closed and no external monitor requires Amphetamine’s closed-display override rather than caffeinate alone
summary: A practical comparison of macOS’s built-in caffeinate CLI and the Amphetamine menu bar app across flags, automation triggers, and closed-clamshell behavior.
title: macOS Sleep Prevention Compared: Built-in caffeinate vs Amphetamine

Ask an AI agent to build a data dashboard and it typically dumps hundreds of lines of brittle HTML, JavaScript, and frontend boilerplate. Traditional BI tools lean on point-and-click UIs, leaving little room for code-driven agents. dbt Charts from dbt Labs bridges that gap by defining an entire dashboard inside a single YAML file.
Dashboards Unified in One YAML File dbt Charts keeps data queries and visual layout in one readable spec. SQL handles data fetching, YAML declares chart types and grid placement, Markdown formats narrative text, and Jinja powers variables and macros.
The spec already covers more than 1,000 configuration options and 16 built-in chart types, including composite multi-layer views. Styling cascades cleanly from theme to dashboard to individual chart, and the extends keyword lets teams reuse house style presets without copy-pasting blocks.
Native dbt Integration and Automated CI Checks Placing a charts/ directory right next to models/ on the same Git branch puts the visualization layer directly on top of your transformation DAG. Queries reference upstream dbt models with standard ref() syntax.
Pre-merge validation catches breaking changes early. Running dbt parse && dct validate charts/ in CI flags renamed models or dropped columns right on the pull request. Built-in visual warnings also inspect layout geometry: if bar widths get cramped or tables overflow the viewport, the validator returns concrete fix hints that an AI agent can act on immediately.
Local CLI and Hosted Sync Released under the Apache 2.0 license, dbt Charts runs locally without requiring a cloud account. Install it in Python via uv tool install dbt-charts and run dct skills intro to prime your coding agent with the schema conventions.
An accompanying hosted platform adds conversational analytics and a visual drag-and-drop editor. Edits made in chat or the browser write straight back to the same YAML file in Git, keeping local CLI workflows, CI pipelines, and hosted views in lockstep.
While syntax may still evolve prior to version 1.0, the parser includes automatic migration helpers. Treating BI dashboards as validated code next to dbt models tightens the loop between data engineering and analytics.
Summary Replaces sprawling frontend code with a single declarative YAML file that AI agents can edit and humans can audit Co-locates chart specs with dbt models in Git to catch broken SQL references and layout overflows during CI Syncs edits across local CLI tools, AI chat, and visual editors back into the same version-controlled YAML file
summary: dbt Labs released dbt Charts, an Apache 2.0 YAML dashboard language that unifies SQL queries, chart configs, and CI validation alongside dbt models.
title: dbt Charts: Single-File YAML Dashboards Built for AI Agents and Git

A tiny widget that shows AI usage limits at a glance. If you rotate between Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Antigravity, this tool saves a lot of tab-switching. Codenotch pins a small notch widget to the edge of your screen showing quota consumption and reset timers for each coding assistant. 1. Tracks usage across Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Antigravity 2. Displays 5-hour and weekly quota windows plus reset countdowns 3. Shows whether Claude Code is actively working or waiting for user input 4. Ships a Windows build powered by Rust + Tauri 2 5. Keeps telemetry visible at the screen edge without opening separate billing dashboards. It is especially handy during long Claude Code runs when you want to check whether the agent is still working or waiting on a prompt. GitHub:
Switching between multiple AI coding assistants makes it easy to lose track of rate limits and quota reset windows. Opening separate web dashboards for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and Antigravity breaks concentration, and long terminal runs in Claude Code often leave you guessing whether the agent is still executing or waiting for confirmation.
A Persistent Screen-Edge Usage Notch Codenotch docks a compact notch widget at the edge of your display to visualize quota consumption. Hovering over its progress rings reveals 5-hour and weekly usage percentages alongside exact reset countdowns. For Claude Code, session numbers match the built-in /usage readout.
It also surfaces live execution state, indicating at a glance whether an assistant is actively running tools, finished with its turn, or blocked on user input. Developers stay in flow without hunting through background terminal tabs.
Mobile Companion Sync and Cross-Platform Builds The macOS release runs on macOS 15 or later as a Universal Binary, while the Windows version shares the same feature set on top of Rust and Tauri 2. Companion iOS and Android apps pair over local Wi-Fi via a QR code so you can check desktop agent status from your phone.
The mobile sync path avoids cloud exposure: instead of transmitting API keys, credentials, or raw model responses, it mirrors only the numeric status values shown in the desktop notch.
Engineers juggling multiple AI coding subscriptions at once get a clean, low-friction monitor.
Summary Pins a lightweight screen-edge widget that tracks usage quotas and agent execution state across terminal and IDE tools Pairs over local Wi-Fi to mirror status numbers to mobile apps without exposing API tokens or credentials Supports macOS 15+ alongside a Rust and Tauri 2 Windows build
summary: Codenotch places a compact screen-edge widget on macOS and Windows to monitor usage quotas, reset timers, and live agent status across Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and Antigravity.
title: Codenotch: Screen-Edge Widget for Tracking AI Coding Assistant Limits

content:
“Data modeling should start before you write code.” I recently read a post arguing that you have to understand the business and the structure of your data before writing SQL or defining objects in an ORM. (The author even pointed out real schemas that violated first normal form.)
The topic itself was familiar, so what caught my eye were the seven references linked in the post. I read through all seven and connected their arguments — from the Kimball methodology and history tracking to organizational debt — back to my own modeling work.
Two Decisions Kimball Settled 30 Years Ago The Kimball methodology1 runs in four steps: pick the business process, declare the grain (the unit of aggregation), identify the dimensions (the analytical context), and identify the facts (the measurements). Tools keep changing, yet two of those steps still anchor every design.
1. Declaring the Grain Grain defines what a single row represents. Take a convenience-store sales table. Depending on whether one row represents a full receipt, a single line item on a receipt, or a daily total per store, the questions you can answer change completely. Storing receipt line items lets you check which cigarette brand sells best. Storing only daily store totals makes product-level sales impossible to query, because item-level detail cannot be reconstructed from a daily sum. Leave the grain vague and receipt-level rows end up mixed with daily store totals in the same table, double-counting revenue. That is why Kimball put declaring the grain right at step two: both dimensions and facts depend on it.
%%{init: {"look": "classic"}}%% flowchart TD A["Line-item grain · 3 rows<br/>1 row = one item on a receipt"] A -->|Sum by receipt| B["Receipt grain · 2 rows<br/>1 row = one receipt"] B -->|Sum by store and day| C["Daily store grain · 1 row<br/>1 row = store × date"] Every level above sums to the same 4,000 KRW total. Once you store only the daily total, you cannot recover the item-level breakdown.
2. Conformed Dimensions A conformed dimension2 aligns definitions and attribute values so multiple fact tables share a consistent analytical lens such as Customer. Sales, support, and shipping tables all involve customers. If each system assigns its own IDs and defines customer tiers differently, joining sales with support data produces mismatched counts and broken tier breakdowns. Maintaining one shared customer dimension referenced by sales, support, and shipping solves this at the table level: “VIP” means the exact same thing no matter which fact table you query.
Keeping business concepts consistent across systems is also the point I keep coming back to when explaining ontology. An ontology organizes definitions of business concepts — like Customer or Revenue — and the relationships between them in one place so multiple systems can reference the same model. Putting data from different sources onto one dashboard screen does not unify what “customer” or “revenue” means; combining query entry points and aligning definitions are two separate jobs. Conformed dimensions and ontologies share that goal. Looking back at an appliance company chatbot project where we consolidated several source systems into data marts, we did not call it ontology work at the time, yet most of the effort went into building conformed dimensions and pinning down the grain of each table.
The Kimball Group’s final Design Tipcame out in 2015. Its core principles hold even when you build star schemas as dbt models and manage metric definitions in a semantic layer3 — dbt manages SQL transformations as code, while a semantic layer centralizes metric formulas and business term definitions. Adopting modern tooling does not define table grain or conformed dimensions for you; that work stays with the modeler.
LLMs need grain metadata just as much when generating SQL. Without it, a model will happily join two fact tables at different grains on a shared column name and inflate every sum. Once NL-to-SQL4 pipelines or agents start querying the warehouse directly, consistent definitions matter even more. When explaining why an organization needs an ontology, pointing to that join-and-grain failure mode persuades people far better than saying “because it’s the AI era.”
Four History-Tracking Patterns Used in Practice Principles stay stable, while physical implementations vary widely across teams. Seattle Data Guy’s write-up on real-world data modelingwalks through four patterns the author saw in production — starting with the observation that many teams claiming to use Kimball keep only the fact and dim table prefixes.
1. SCD Type 2 SCD Type 25 (Slowly Changing Dimension Type 2) preserves dimension history and was the pattern the author encountered most often. Whenever an attribute changes, you insert a new row with effective start and end dates. You need this structure when questions ask about duration itself, such as how many days an employee held a given title. To keep BETWEEN predicates clean, the author recommends setting the end date on active rows to a far-future sentinel like 9999-12-31 rather than leaving it NULL. Type 1 overwrites old values in place and loses history; Type 6 hybrids get only a brief mention from a handful of cases.
2. Daily Snapshot Partitions Daily snapshot partitioning6 appears in the article through Facebook’s warehouse conventions. Instead of tracking dimension changes via SCD rows, the pipeline writes a full copy of the table into a new date partition every day. For an employee table, the entire roster for that day lands in its own ds (datestamp) partition. Queries skip BETWEEN range joins on start and end dates and join directly on ds. If you want to know an employee’s title on the day they clicked a page, you match the click log date to ds. Queries get simpler at the cost of higher storage usage.
%%{init: {"look": "classic"}}%% flowchart TB subgraph SCD["SCD Type 2 · New row on change"] direction LR S1["Standard<br/>Start 09-01<br/>End 09-03"] -->|Tier change| S2["VIP<br/>Start 09-03<br/>End NULL"] end subgraph SNAP["Daily Snapshot · Full state each day"] direction LR D1["09-01<br/>C01 · Standard"] --- D2["09-02<br/>C01 · Standard"] --- D3["09-03<br/>C01 · VIP"] end SCD ~~~ SNAP Customer C01 moves from Standard to VIP on 09-03. Here SCD2 treats start dates as inclusive, end dates as exclusive, and NULL as currently active. A daily snapshot alone cannot distinguish multiple state changes that happen within the same day.
3. Date-List Aggregation Date-list aggregation7 comes from a Roblox case study. Rather than scanning raw visit logs row by row, each user record stores an array of dates the user visited. In Roblox’s case, daily scan volume dropped from petabytes to terabytes. Because individual event details are stripped out, this pattern fits retention checks and monthly active user (MAU) counts rather than event-level drill-downs.
4. Handling Fact Corrections Fact correction patterns8 govern what happens when previously loaded numbers turn out to be wrong. Rather than running UPDATE on historical rows, pipelines either append negative reversing entries or route returns into a separate table. Using healthcare claims as an example, when an adjudication adjustment arrives, a team might replace the original claim row, append a negative offset row, or log adjustments in a dedicated table depending on how the upstream system records corrections. If the warehouse model ignores how the source system posts adjustments, queries will execute without errors and still return wrong totals.
Choosing among these patterns always weighs storage cost against query complexity. Today there is one more criterion: whether a human analyst or an LLM writes the query.
Choosing History Tracking When LLMs Write the SQL When most questions ask for daily state and cloud storage costs are manageable, daily snapshots deserve a close look. Because “the state on date X” sits directly inside that date’s partition, explaining the join rule in a prompt stays straightforward. SCD2 requires explaining inclusive/exclusive date boundaries and, if active rows use NULL end dates, making sure the generated SQL includes OR end_date IS NULL9 — omit that clause and every currently active record drops out of the result. Checking a ds filter in generated SQL is much easier, though you still have to verify that the chosen date matches the business question, the join keys match the table grain, and nothing double-counts. If users need intraday state changes, daily snapshots alone will not be enough.
In public-sector or on-premises environments where disk capacity is tight, dimension size and retention windows drive the trade-off. Small reference tables with a few thousand rows and narrow columns — such as organization codes or diagnosis codes — cost very little to snapshot daily even across multi-year retention periods. Copying a beneficiary table with tens of millions of rows every day, on the other hand, hits storage ceilings fast. Mixing history-tracking strategies across dimensions based on row count, change frequency, and retention policy is the practical middle ground.
The Debt That Surfaces Last and Costs the Most Joe Reis’s essaybreaks the cost of modeling shortcuts into three buckets: technical debt, data debt, and organizational debt. There is no free lunch in data modeling.
Move fast with loose modeling and technical debt and data debt pile up first. Once stakeholders start questioning the numbers, trust in the data team erodes too. The moment people start saying “every team brings a different number,” the damage is done — everything the data team ships afterward gets met with skepticism first.
Spend months designing an airtight model up front and you can keep technical and data debt low, yet dragging out schedules without visible deliverables costs organizational trust from the opposite direction. Either extreme leaves you trying to win back credibility. As Reis puts it, having no model is still a model — just a bad one.
His “punch pass” metaphor for organizational patience stuck with me. Every shortcut punches one hole in your card; once the card is full, every deferred problem comes due at once. Broken trust shows up much later than broken pipelines or messy tables, and rebuilding it takes far longer than fixing code.
On one past project, a single mismatched metric during a review meeting reshaped how every subsequent deliverable was scrutinized. Nothing had crashed — two reports simply aggregated on slightly different rules — yet from that meeting onward, every number in the deck had to be re-verified from scratch. Data Warehousing Essentialsmakes a related point: treat data quality checks as part of the modeling deliverable itself rather than a monitoring task bolted on after pipelines go live.
Takeaways 1. Interpret the same question against the same temporal rule “Last month’s revenue from VIP customers” yields two different numbers depending on whether “VIP” means customers who hold VIP status today or customers who held VIP status at the moment of purchase. An ontologycan capture concepts and relationships like Customer and Tier, a semantic layer can hold metric formulas, and technical metadata can record tables, columns, grain, and join predicates. Before handing query generation to an LLM, verify that all three layers point to the same customer definition and the same point-in-time rule.
2. Document which questions you are giving up alongside what you skip storing Keep only daily totals and nobody can answer item-level revenue questions six months later. Whenever you trim detail or coarsen history granularity to save storage, write down the exact questions that design can no longer answer. Having that boundary on paper separates future scope changes from design bugs.
3. Update validation queries whenever a business definition changes Leave validation queries behind that specify how two fact tables must be pre-aggregated before joining and check that row counts and amounts do not multiply afterward. When VIP criteria change, updating the glossary document is only step one — dependent metrics, query rules, and validation checks all have to be re-run together. Operating an ontology means tracing definition changes all the way down to physical data and SQL.
4. Lock down priority metrics first and verify them end to end Rather than waiting for every requirement across the enterprise to settle, agree with business owners on grain, point-in-time rules, and correction handling for the first set of priority metrics and verify the output early. Schedules keep moving while teams debate edge cases, so separating what locks now from what gets revisited later keeps delivery intact.
Looking back at meetings where numbers clashed, you can only explain a discrepancy when the underlying aggregation rules are explicit. Winning back an organization that has started doubting your numbers takes far more time and effort than fixing a single SQL query.
Kimball methodology and star schema: A classic data warehousing approach that separates database structures into facts (numeric measurements) and dimensions (descriptive context used for filtering and grouping). ↩︎
Conformed dimension & ontology: Aligning concept definitions and identifier rules — such as what counts as a “Customer” or “VIP” — across separate systems like sales, support, and shipping. ↩︎
dbt & semantic layer: dbt manages SQL data transformations as versioned code, while a semantic layer centralizes business metric formulas and term definitions so downstream tools query consistent logic. ↩︎
NL2SQL and grain mismatch: A common failure mode when AI translates natural-language questions into SQL and joins two tables at different aggregation levels without pre-aggregating, inflating sums and counts. ↩︎
SCD Type 2 (Slowly Changing Dimension): Preserves attribute history by inserting a new row with effective start and end dates (or a sentinel such as 9999-12-31) instead of overwriting existing rows; requires careful BETWEEN range filtering in SQL. ↩︎
Daily snapshot partitioning: Copies the full state of a table into a new date partition (ds) every day instead of tracking row-level intervals, trading higher storage consumption for simpler equality joins. ↩︎
Date-list aggregation: Compresses user activity history into a single array column of active dates per user instead of scanning individual event rows. ↩︎
Fact correction handling (reversing entries): Corrects historical data errors without UPDATE statements by appending offset rows multiplied by -1 or isolating adjustments in a separate table, similar to accounting ledgers. ↩︎
Missing SQL predicate (OR end_date IS NULL): A frequent LLM query bug on SCD2 tables where omitting the null-end-date check drops all currently active records from the result set. ↩︎
summary: Notes from reading all seven references cited in a post arguing that data modeling comes before code. Covers the principles that outlasted three generations of tooling, four history-tracking patterns used in production, and organizational debt — the slowest debt to surface.
title: 5. Data Modeling in the LLM Era

content:
Per-token model pricing alone rarely explains why enterprise AI agents get expensive. Answering a single user request often resends system prompts and tool schemas, piles query outputs and chat history into the context window, and chains multiple model calls and tool executions.
Three Variables Behind Agent Spend The article splits agent spend into three variables: repeated base input, accumulated context, and call count. Base input covers system prompts and tool descriptions sent on every call. Accumulated context holds tool outputs, intermediate reasoning, and conversation turns. As call count rises, both input and output charges multiply because earlier context rides along on each subsequent step.
Cost control starts by measuring these three variables separately. Teams need visibility into which workflows resend huge contexts, call the same tool repeatedly, or loop through long execution chains before setting optimization priorities.
Managing Base Inputs and Context Growth Shorter system prompts and tool descriptions are not automatically cheaper if ambiguity causes bad tool calls and retries. Instructions must stay specific enough for the agent to pick the right tool on the first try, paired with stable prompt caching.
Leaving raw, oversized query results in history forces every later turn to pay for them again. Teams can keep representative samples, or retain the latest result verbatim while summarizing older outputs. Because over-aggressive compression forces the agent to re-query missing details, teams should track compression ratios alongside answer accuracy.
Ontology Search and Solution Cache An enterprise ontology maps business concepts and relationships across customers, products, orders, contracts, and policies. Narrowing relevant data sources, rules, and tools upfront spares the agent from scanning broad context from scratch on every turn. Finding the right target in fewer steps lowers both call counts and accumulated context.
A Solution Cache stores human-verified answers or resolution paths so similar future questions skip open-ended exploration. Injecting cached paths only pays off when saved exploration outweighs the extra prompt tokens, so teams should validate real cost savings and quality shifts rather than guessing.
Managing Cost and Quality Together Cutting call counts blindly can backfire when wrong answers trigger human rework, approval delays, or customer support errors. Logging which sources an agent read, which tools it called, and how intermediate context was trimmed lets operators govern spend and accuracy together.
LLM cost optimization is ultimately an operations design problem: giving agents the shortest path to the right data and tools while keeping execution traces auditable.
Summary Break AI agent spend into repeated base input, accumulated context, and call count Use ontology search and a Solution Cache to narrow data and tool scope and cut repeated exploration Evaluate cost savings alongside answer quality, retry rates, and human review overhead
summary: How enterprises measure repeated base inputs, accumulated context, and call counts separately while cutting exploration loops with ontology search and a Solution Cache.
title: Controlling LLM Operating Costs for Enterprise AI Agents

content:
Running Claude Code in the terminal can burn through tokens faster than expected. Prompt caching and automatic context management run behind the scenes, yet bills climb quickly if you do not know what drives token consumption. Here is how to inspect and control the main cost drivers.
Measuring Tokens and Managing Context Start by checking where your tokens go. Run /usage in the terminal to inspect session token counts and spend, and run /context to see what occupies the current context window. Clearing clutter before the window fills up keeps per-turn costs down.
Three mechanisms reset or shrink context: /compact summarizes conversation history into key points, /clear wipes prior turns completely, and auto-compaction triggers when the context limit approaches. Compacting periodically during long sessions prevents bloated history from being resent on every turn.
Choosing Models and Trimming MCP Overhead Not every task needs the largest frontier model. Routine edits and file lookups run fine on smaller models or lower Thinking depth settings. Reserve deep thinking budgets for multi-file architecture changes or tricky refactors.
Connected MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers also add hidden token overhead. Every active MCP server injects its tool schemas into the base prompt on each turn. Disable unused MCP servers to shrink baseline context size. Because prompt caching drops cache-read pricing to 0.1x for follow-up requests within 5 minutes, working in focused bursts pays off.
Spend guardrails depend on your billing setup. Teams on Anthropic Console can set hard spend limits to block runaway bills, while AWS Bedrock deployments can tie usage quotas directly into cloud monitoring alerts. Matching context hygiene and model tier to the task keeps daily usage predictable.
Summary Inspect live token spend and context breakdown with /usage and /context Disable unused MCP servers so their tool definitions do not inflate every base prompt Work in sub-5-minute bursts to take advantage of prompt caching, which cuts cache-read cost to 10%
summary: A practical guide to measuring Claude Code token usage, compacting context windows, trimming MCP tool overhead, and using prompt caching.
title: Claude Code Token Tracking and Cost Optimization Guide

content:
Rewiring data prep and execution steps slows down iterative model experiments. Built by Shopify engineers, Tangleis an open-source platform for assembling and running ML and data pipelines visually across a team. Its official documentation focuses on pipeline authoring and fast iteration rather than benchmarking any specific small model.
Visual Authoring and Team Reuse Users drag components onto a canvas, wire steps together, and configure parameters in the browser. Existing scripts wrap cleanly inside containers, so teams do not have to standardize on a single language or ML framework. Teammates can clone, tweak, and rerun shared pipelines without rebuilding environment plumbing.
Reusing Intermediate Outputs Tangle includes a content-addressed execution cache. When an upstream step’s inputs and logic have not changed, Tangle reuses its stored output artifact instead of recomputing it, cutting both iteration wait times and compute bills. Only steps affected by input or parameter edits rerun.
A shared postcirculating alongside the link also mentions Shopify’s internal experiments with small models. However, the official Tangle site does not publish evaluation setups or head-to-head results comparing Qwen3.5-0.8B against larger models, so any model-quality claims should be checked against separate benchmark data.
Summary Provides a visual DAG editor for building and sharing ML pipelines across engineering teams Wraps existing code in containers and caches unchanged intermediate outputs to speed up repeated runs Does not include small-model benchmark claims on its official docs, which require separate verification
summary: Shopify’s open-source Tangle tool lets teams build containerized ML pipelines visually, share workflows, and cache intermediate outputs across runs.
title: Shopify Tangle: Visual Editing and Execution Caching for ML Pipelines

content:
Running local AI on a Mac? Consider oMLX instead of Ollama. oMLX is a local AI server tuned for Apple Silicon. Positioned as an alternative to Ollama and LM Studio, it tiers KV cache onto SSD storage to stretch memory capacity and includes optimizations for Qwen 3.8. With built-in compatibility for Claude Code and Cursor, it fits Mac developers who want to pair local models with coding agents. GitHub:
Running local LLMs on a Mac often hits a wall of memory pressure and throughput drops during long sessions. Existing local runners usually force a trade-off between one-click convenience and fine-grained runtime control. oMLX addresses this gap with an inference server built specifically around Apple Silicon unified memory.
Tiered KV Cache and Continuous Batching oMLX splits the KV cache across an in-memory hot tier and an SSD-backed cold tier. Even when prompt context shifts mid-session, prior cache blocks stay intact for reuse. Long multi-turn coding sessions avoid exhausting unified memory while sustaining fast token generation.
Continuous batching handles concurrent requests cleanly. Users can pin frequently used models in memory, swap heavier models on demand, and adjust per-model context limits and memory budgets straight from the macOS menu bar.
Coding Agent Integration and Developer Workflow oMLX works directly with coding agents such as Claude Code and Cursor. Built-in MCP (Model Context Protocol) support lets local agents pass project context to local models without custom glue code, turning the server into a practical backend for daily development tools.
Installing the menu bar app also sets up a CLI shim for terminal scripts and Apple Shortcuts automation. It requires macOS 15.0 Sequoia or later on Apple Silicon and installs or updates with a single Homebrew command.
Native Model Kernel Optimizations oMLX includes native kernel build flags to accelerate recent open-weight families including Qwen3.5, GLM-5.2, and MiniMax M3. Compiling with family-specific flags boosts local throughput, and registering oMLX as a background service ensures automatic restarts after crashes.
Mac developers looking for both low-level runtime control and sustained local inference speed have a strong option in oMLX.
Summary Tiers KV cache across RAM (hot) and SSD (cold) to handle large contexts without exhausting Apple Silicon memory Connects directly with Claude Code, Cursor, and MCP workflows for local agentic coding Combines a macOS menu bar controller with CLI and Apple Shortcuts support for straightforward daily operation
summary: oMLX brings hot-and-cold SSD KV cache tiering, continuous batching, and MCP coding agent integration to local LLM inference on Apple Silicon Macs.
title: oMLX: Local LLM Inference Server for Apple Silicon with SSD KV Cache

content:
Put simply, if you ask Opus or Codex to build a feature and it normally writes 1,000 lines of code, ponytail brings that down to 100 lines. That grizzled veteran developer persona stops the agent from padding volume with bloated abstractions. Why does that matter? It goes way beyond saving initial output tokens. Where it really shines is modifying existing code. If you tell Opus to update something without guardrails, it often overwrites surrounding logic and introduces bugs (clear task instructions still matter, of course). With ponytail, edits stay surgical and narrow, which keeps error rates low. That is why I use it. By the way, the heavyset guy in the repo art represents an old-school greybeard developer. Pair this plugin with Andrej Karpathy’s coding guidelines link in Codex and ask it to merge non-overlapping rules into AGENTS.MD. The results are night and day.
AI coding agents routinely write far more code than a task requires. Ask for a basic date picker and an agent might pull in a heavy third-party package wrapped in hundreds of lines of boilerplate. The ponytail skill injects a senior engineer’s restraint so agents write minimal, direct code.
Trimming Agent Bloat with Senior Engineering Restraint Instead of adding external dependencies, ponytail pushes the agent toward native platform features like a single <input type="date"> element. Blocking premature abstraction layers and speculative design shrinks a 1,000-line agent output down to roughly 100 lines.
Across 12 feature tickets in a FastAPI and React codebase, ponytail reduced average lines of code by 54% compared to a baseline agent, with peak reductions reaching 94%.
Approach LOC Change Token Usage Cost Task Time Safety ponytail 54% reduction 22% saved 20% saved 27% faster 100% maintained Short control prompt 20% reduction 7% increase 3% increase 2% slower 100% maintained YAGNI instruction prompt 33% reduction 14% saved 21% saved 30% faster 95% maintained Among the tested setups, ponytail was the only option that cut both cost and task duration while keeping a 100% safety score. Structured skill rules outperform one-line prompt reminders.
54% Less Code and Safer Edits The biggest payoff shows up during maintenance rather than greenfield scaffolding. Unconstrained agents frequently rewrite surrounding modules and introduce regressions when asked for a small change. Under ponytail, the agent restricts edits to the exact lines required, lowering defect rates.
Narrow diffs also prevent unintended side effects and make human code reviews much faster.
Pairing with AGENTS.MD in Practice Teams get good mileage by combining ponytail with project rules in AGENTS.MD, such as merging non-overlapping principles from Andrej Karpathy’s LLM coding guidelines.
Developers cleaning up over-engineered repositories or running Claude Code and Codex on production codebases will find it practical.
Summary Steers AI agents away from heavy dependencies and wrapper boilerplate toward built-in platform primitives Restricts code modifications to narrow, surgical diffs that protect existing structure and reduce regressions Pairs well with project-level guidelines in AGENTS.MD, including Andrej Karpathy’s coding rules
summary: The ponytail skill steers AI coding agents toward minimal, surgical code changes, cutting average lines of code by 54% while preserving existing architecture.
title: ponytail: Stopping AI Coding Agents from Over-Engineering

content:
Uber tracks AI agent spend by isolating exactly where costs originate as adoption grows. According to the Uber Engineering Blog, weekly active employees using agent services grew 7x and weekly requests jumped 9.4x since February 2026, yet total spend stayed relatively flat. Rather than relying on a single cost-cutting trick, the team measured and trimmed multiple operational cost drivers.
Breaking Total Cost into Six Factors Uber decomposes total spend into users × sessions per user × turns per session × requests per turn × tokens per request × price per token. The goal is to encourage broader adoption while cutting unnecessary turns, requests, and tokens added by agents. Alongside per-tool user counts, cost per 1,000 requests, and cache hit rates, the team tracks cost and quality metrics per merged PR and per code review.
Tuning Models, Cache Lifetimes, and Tool Calls Separately Uber avoids locking every workflow onto a single default model. The team benchmarks quality against cost on real internal tasks before assigning models to managed agents such as code review. Reasoning effort and default subagent models are also matched to each task profile.
For interactive engineer sessions with longer pauses between messages, Uber extended prompt cache TTL from 5 minutes to 1 hour. Short-lived subagents keep the 5-minute TTL, balancing higher cache-write pricing against actual reuse probability.
Uber also cut the overhead of loading dozens of MCP tool definitions into every session. Agents discover tools on demand through a CLI or tool search at runtime. Repetitive status checks run directly in code and return only a concise summary to the model, keeping turn counts and context growth down.
Making Waste Visible Session status bars and internal dashboards surface cost and usage patterns in real time. Automated session analysis flags recurring waste patterns and feeds into an engineer feedback loop. Because raw savings can mask regressions that shift work back onto humans, Uber always pairs cost metrics with task outcomes and output quality.
Summary Separates adoption growth from per-task unit cost across six multiplicative factors Cuts waste through task-specific model benchmarks, workload-matched cache TTLs, and on-demand tool loading Pairs session cost telemetry with output quality metrics to spot waste without degrading engineering results
summary: Uber kept total AI agent spend stable despite a 9.4x jump in weekly requests by breaking down cost drivers and tuning model routing, cache TTLs, and MCP tool loading.
title: How Uber Controls AI Coding Costs Across Models, Cache, and Tools

content:
When automating workflows with Claude Code and tracking live status, managing a status board in Google Sheets through Google Workspace CLI is far more stable and convenient than vibe-coding a custom web dashboard. Put supporting evidence and run logs into separate sheet tabs, mark GO/NO GO decisions right in the cells, and hand it back to the agent.
Building a custom web UI dashboard every time you automate an operational workflow with Claude Code or AI agents burns unnecessary engineering hours. Using an existing spreadsheet like Google Sheets as your control plane keeps operations simpler and more reliable, and Google Workspace CLI makes reading and updating sheets from terminal agents straightforward.
Dynamic API Discovery and Structured JSON Responses googleworkspace/cli (gws) exposes Drive, Gmail, Calendar, Sheets, and the rest of the Workspace API surface through a single binary. Rather than hardcoding static subcommands, gws reads the Google Discovery Service at runtime to build its command tree dynamically, picking up new Google API endpoints automatically. Alongside human-friendly --help and --dry-run flags, it emits structured JSON by default so LLMs can inspect and mutate Workspace resources without brittle text parsers.
Using Google Sheets as a Claude Code Automation Control Plane Google Sheets works naturally as a shared status board between humans and automation agents: store raw evidence and run outputs in dedicated tabs, and write GO/NO GO gate decisions directly into summary cells. Pairing the 40+ bundled agent skills inside gws with its standard JSON output lets agents keep status boards current without anyone maintaining a bespoke frontend, giving stakeholders immediate visibility into automated runs.
Setup Requirements and Authentication gws runs on macOS, Linux, and Windows via Homebrew, npm, or prebuilt binaries. Runtime setup requires Node.js 18+ and a Google Cloud Project configured for OAuth; running gws auth setup followed by gws auth login walks through granting permissions interactively. Although the project is still working toward v1.0, it already provides a solid foundation for agent-driven Workspace pipelines.
Teams looking for transparent, low-maintenance tracking across AI agent jobs will get far more mileage out of gws plus Google Sheets than maintaining another internal dashboard.
Summary Connecting Google Workspace CLI (gws) to Google Sheets provides a far lower-maintenance agent status board than building custom web dashboards. gws builds its command surface dynamically at runtime from the Google Discovery Service, staying current as Workspace APIs evolve. Default structured JSON output and 40+ built-in agent skills make integrating Drive, Sheets, Gmail, and Calendar into LLM agents straightforward.
summary: Pair Google Workspace CLI (gws) with Google Sheets instead of building custom web dashboards to track AI agent runs, evidence tabs, and GO/NO GO gates.
title: Automating AI Agent Status Boards with Google Workspace CLI and Sheets

content:
Turn every document into one AI knowledge base. This open-source tool gathers PDFs, Word files, presentations, spreadsheets, and web pages in one place so AI can analyze their contents and uncover links across documents. - Automatically searches for relevant details when you ask a question - Returns source links alongside answers - Connects and analyzes information across documents - Runs locally without sending data outside your machine - Fully open source, turning your files into an AI ‘second brain.’ Source:
Teams building RAG systems often struggle with poor retrieval accuracy across scattered files and lost document context. OpenKB is an open-source tool that gathers local documents and compiles them into an interlinked wiki. It converts entire file collections into a structured AI knowledge base without sending data outside your environment.
Wiki Compilation Without a Vector DB Standard RAG pipelines run fresh searches over individual chunks on every query, so knowledge never compounds. OpenKB follows the wiki-compilation pattern highlighted by Andrej Karpathy, automatically generating cross-references and concept pages across documents as knowledge grows. Instead of reassembling fragments at query time, the tool continuously updates the knowledge base itself.
It uses PageIndex tree indexing to reason over long document context without a Vector DB, and it processes charts, diagrams, and images alongside text through multimodal parsing.
Multi-Format Support and Layered Architecture The tool ingests common workplace formats out of the box. It converts PDF, Word, PowerPoint, Excel, Markdown, and HTML files into a structured wiki while syncing extracted entities and concepts under the Google OKF specification.
Internally, OpenKB separates a foundation layer that builds the knowledge graph from a generator layer that applies it. Workflows cover one-off Q&A, multi-turn chat, and custom Skill Factory extraction. Users can also run commands and persist sessions from the CLI.
Built for Strict Data Security and Long-Term Knowledge Organizations bound by strict data governance rules can run the entire pipeline inside isolated local infrastructure thanks to its open-source license. OpenKB flags contradictory statements across documents and attaches explicit source links to its answers.
It fits both individual researchers building a personal second brain and teams designing an internal knowledge platform. Unlike stateless retrieval setups that discard work after each query, OpenKB lets knowledge accumulate over time.
Summary Uses PageIndex tree indexing instead of a Vector DB to track long-document context and process multimodal content Compiles documents into an evolving wiki with automatic cross-references and concept pages rather than running stateless RAG lookups Runs locally as a fully open-source tool across PDF, Word, Excel, and other standard document formats without external data transfer
summary: OpenKB compiles local documents into an interlinked AI wiki using PageIndex tree indexing without a vector database.
title: OpenKB: Turning Scattered Documents into a Connected Local AI Wiki

content:
Suppose a proposal draft generated by AI includes last quarter’s product positioning. Fixing the wording before sending solves that single document, yet leaving the stale reference untouched guarantees the same mistake on the next draft. An AX LABS guidebreaks down a 6-prompt workflow for turning one-off corrections trapped in personal chat logs into shared team operating standards.
From Personal Chat Logs to a Company Map File You do not start by writing a giant wiki from scratch. Instead, team members mine recent AI sessions for factual fixes they made, company context they had to explain repeatedly, prompt constraints that worked well, and reference snippets they paste every time. Keep the exact correction sentences, separate personal style preferences from team-wide facts, and flag uncertain items for verification.
Next comes a short map file that every AI session reads first. It states what the company does, current priorities, which source wins when documents conflict, and where detailed files live. For instance, decisions/ stores decision rationales and superseded choices, policies/ holds standing rules, and learnings.md collects reviewed fixes. Teams running coding agents can use AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md as that entry point, loading detailed docs on demand so old meeting notes never override active decisions.
Routing Fixes and Enforcing the Rule of 3 After editing an AI output, classify why it missed. Stale facts update a dated, sourced knowledge entry; newly agreed directions go into a decision log; proven task recipes become reusable skills; and recurring workflows turn into worker specs with explicit inputs, outputs, and stop conditions. Actions with external blast radius - sending messages, billing, or deleting records - belong behind hard permission gates and human approvals rather than polite prompt wording.
Not every correction deserves immediate promotion to team policy. The guide proposes a 3-strike promotion rule: fix a 1st occurrence inline and move on; log a brief note on the 2nd occurrence; and promote an issue to a policy candidate only when a 3rd occurrence surfaces across different people and tasks, recording its effective date, owner, and any prior rule it replaces so one person’s phrasing preference never hardens into team law.
Specifying Workers and Running Weekly Health Checks Packaging a repeatable job into a worker spec means writing down required inputs, reference files, step-by-step judgment criteria, output format, human escalation triggers, failure signals, and required sign-off roles before external sharing. Before adopting any 3-strike policy candidate, stress-test whether it conflicts with existing rules, applies cleanly across other teams, or carries edge-case exceptions.
Once live, run a weekly review covering unanswered agent requests, conflicting sources, stale citations, repeated manual edits, and unread files. Rather than tracking total file count, the guide recommends tracking source-conflict count as your primary health metric. Pick one recurring workflow, set up its map file and correction log, and run a real task through it - next week’s highest-impact fixes will surface right away.
summary: AX LABS outlines 6 prompts to promote personal AI chat fixes into shared team knowledge using map files, routing rules, a 3-strike policy gate, and weekly audits.
title: Turning Chat Corrections into Shared Team Standards: A 6-Prompt Company Brain

content:
Many teams default to standing up a Vector DB and a Reranking pipeline on day one of a RAG project, driving up operational complexity without always improving retrieval quality. Starting with a simpler search stack often delivers better results faster.
Pairing BM25 Keyword Search with LLM Query Rewriting Combining BM25 lexical search with LLM-based query rewriting satisfies a large share of production RAG workloads. Adding embedding models introduces chunking trade-offs and vector index synchronization overhead, whereas rewriting user questions onto an existing keyword index bridges vocabulary gaps with minimal infrastructure.
When data freshness matters, continuous vector re-indexing quickly becomes an operational bottleneck. High-churn document collections stay much easier to operate on standard inverted indexes, and BM25 also excels on datasets heavy in exact domain terminology, SKUs, or error codes.
Scaling Across 6 Architecture Stages Using 5 Criteria Retrieval architecture should scale step by step across 6 complexity stages matched to five concrete constraints: data freshness, document churn rate, query types, query volume, and engineering team capacity. Validate simpler tiers before adopting heavier components.
Introduce a Vector DB or Reranking layer only after empirical retrieval benchmarks prove lexical search plus query rewriting falls short. Starting at Stage 1 keyword search and adding components incrementally speeds up incident debugging and keeps infrastructure costs low.
Before wiring up a multi-stage vector pipeline, benchmark plain text search paired with query rewriting against your actual queries.
Summary Benchmark BM25 keyword search paired with LLM query rewriting before defaulting to Vector DBs and reranking pipelines. Match retrieval complexity to five operational factors: data freshness, document churn rate, query types, query volume, and team capacity. Add vector indexes and rerankers incrementally only after measured retrieval gaps justify the extra operational overhead.
summary: Start RAG systems with BM25 keyword search plus LLM query rewriting before adding Vector DBs and rerankers, scaling across 6 stages based on 5 data criteria.
title: A 6-Stage Selection Framework for Keeping RAG Architectures Simple

content:
Sharp API price cuts from OpenAI prompted Channel Talk to evaluate switching its production model, knowing a blind cost-cutting swap that degraded support quality would drive customers away. Rather than trusting public leaderboards, the team built a dedicated benchmark running directly inside its production agent engine.
What Public Leaderboards Miss in Live Support Agents Public benchmark rankings rarely predict production agent reliability. Channel Talk’s global support agent ALF conducts multi-turn customer chats while reading knowledge bases and invoking external tools - tasks where math or coding scores do not guarantee clean support resolutions.
Even GLM-5.2, a top scorer on τ²-bench, hit a wall inside the live engine: raising reasoning effort improved pass rates at the cost of pushing average response latency to 17.1 seconds, far too slow for live chat. That gap forced the team to test candidate models directly on internal workloads, including models absent from public leaderboards.
Multi-Run pass^k Evaluation Across Five Agent Capabilities Channel Talk’s internal benchmark tests five operational dimensions under repeated pass^k runs: internal state leakage, step-by-step execution, consistency, instruction adherence, and action fidelity. Any candidate that leaked internal reasoning or tool traces to end users was disqualified immediately.
Two distinct case suites anchor every run: representative support tickets measure overall resolution rate, while regression-prevention cases guard against past production incidents resurfacing. Because the incumbent main model, Claude Sonnet 4.6, scored high on regression prevention, any replacement faced a high bar.
Selecting GPT-5.6 Luna and Rolling Out Gradually GPT-5.6 Luna at high effort won the evaluation: representative ticket pass rates jumped from 40.4% to 51.8%, regression prevention held steady at 71.4%, and unit token cost dropped to roughly 1/13 of the previous model.
Even with clear benchmark wins, rollout followed a staged sequence: migrating lower-risk Agentic RAG components first, validating on testbed channels, and running live A/B tests while auditing provider discount tiers, 272K context pricing cliffs, ZDR data-protection terms, and outage fallback paths.
Reproducing real production constraints inside an internal benchmark turned a risky model swap into a measurable upgrade in both quality and unit economics.
Summary Public leaderboard scores fail to predict multi-turn support agent behavior, making an engine-native proxy benchmark essential. Because reasoning effort trades pass rate directly against response latency, teams should tune effort levels separately for live chat replies versus Agentic RAG steps. Safe model migration pairs quality testing with staged rollouts covering provider discounts, ZDR contracts, 272K context pricing tiers, and fallback routing.
summary: Channel Talk built an internal pass^k proxy benchmark to evaluate quality, latency, and cost, lifting pass rates from 40.4% to 51.8% at 1/13 the token price.
title: Why Channel Talk Migrated Its Production Support Agent to GPT-5.6 Luna

content:
If you use Claude Code, this skill is worth installing right away: it adds native image generation, one capability Claude Code lacks out of the box. Once installed, asking for an image generates it straight into your current working folder using your existing ChatGPT subscription - no API key setup and no per-image charges. You can pass reference images to match an existing visual style or refine outputs across follow-up turns. Installation is as simple as pasting the GitHub URL into Claude Code and asking it to install. 1/ URL: github.com/GENEXIS-AI/gpt-image-skill Paste that URL into Claude Code and ask it to set it up. It requires Node.js 22+, Codex CLI, and a ChatGPT login, and walks you through any missing prerequisites during setup.
When you need UI assets or illustrations mid-session in Claude Code, gpt-image-skill keeps image generation inside the terminal without switching to external web tools or provisioning a separate OpenAI API key, routing requests through an existing ChatGPT subscription instead.
Zero API Key Overhead via ChatGPT Subscription Auth Instead of billing per call through the Images API, the skill authenticates via Codex CLI device login to use your ChatGPT plan quota, saving generated PNG files automatically under the project’s generated-images directory.
Image generation consumes subscription quota roughly 3-5x faster than standard text turns. Splitting multi-asset requests into small batches keeps usage comfortably within plan limits without risking surprise API bills.
Style-Matched Generation and Iterative Edits from Local References Beyond plain text prompts, developers can pass local image paths as visual references to match an existing brand or UI palette. When asked for multiple concepts at once, the terminal agent separates prompts cleanly per variation.
Reviewing generated PNGs and requesting targeted tweaks in follow-up turns happens inside the same terminal session, keeping code changes and visual asset iteration in one place.
One-Prompt Setup Requirements Pasting the GitHub repository URL into Claude Code kicks off automated installation. The environment requires Node.js 22+, Codex CLI, and Git; if any dependency is missing, the installer flags and guides setup automatically.
Completing browser-based ChatGPT device authentication finishes registration, making image generation commands available immediately inside terminal coding workflows.
Adding a single skill turns a text-only coding agent into a unified workspace for both application code and visual assets.
Summary Generates PNG assets inside Claude Code using an existing ChatGPT subscription quota rather than a paid OpenAI Images API key. Accepts local reference image paths for style consistency and supports multi-turn iterative edits from the terminal. Installs automatically on Node.js 22+ and Codex CLI setups by pasting the GitHub repository URL into Claude Code.
summary: gpt-image-skill connects your existing ChatGPT subscription via Codex CLI so Claude Code can generate and iteratively edit PNG assets with zero per-image API billing.

Goldman Sachs open-sourced its quant logic. Originally built as internal risk-calculation infrastructure for Goldman’s options desks, the repo includes standalone modules individual investors and developers can use right away: indicator functions for volatility and correlation, a strategy backtesting framework, and portfolio risk and scenario analysis logic. Instead of coding risk calculators and backtesters from scratch, you can import 25 years of Goldman desk logic directly - worth bookmarking if you are building an AI investing agent.
Goldman Sachs open-sourced the quantitative risk infrastructure originally built for its derivatives and options desks under the gs-quant project. Instead of writing pricing and risk math from scratch, developers can import a Python framework refined across 25 years of market operations.
25 Years of Desk Engineering in a Python Toolkit gs-quant is a Python toolkit built to structure derivatives, run trading analytics, and manage portfolio risk across global markets, packaging production quantitative models authored by Goldman Sachs strats.
Developers can drop its statistical modules into standalone analytics apps or run end-to-end derivatives risk workflows in a single library.
Three Core Modules and Runtime Requirements Capabilities center on three areas: time-series indicator functions such as volatility and correlation, a strategy backtesting engine, and portfolio risk and scenario stress-testing logic.
Running the open-source core requires Python 3.9+ and pip. Connecting to institutional market data endpoints requires a Goldman Sachs Developer client ID and secret, while the underlying quantitative math, timeseries functions, and backtesting framework run freely as open-source Python code.
A Reliable Calculation Engine for AI Investing Agents Coding custom backtesters or risk engines from scratch for an AI financial agent invites subtle floating-point and calendar bugs that take weeks to audit.
Wiring gs-quant in as the deterministic risk and backtesting tool speeds up delivery and grounds LLM financial agents in verified quantitative math.
Teams prototyping quantitative research pipelines or AI trading assistants get a battle-tested calculation backend without reinventing core financial primitives.
Summary Exposes 25 years of Goldman Sachs derivatives pricing and risk management logic as an open-source Python toolkit. Provides ready-to-use volatility/correlation functions, strategy backtesting, and portfolio scenario analysis on Python 3.9+. Serves as a deterministic risk and backtesting tool backend when building AI investing and quant research agents.
summary: Goldman Sachs open-sourced gs-quant, giving Python developers and AI finance agents battle-tested derivatives pricing, backtesting, and portfolio risk modules.
title: gs-quant: Goldman Sachs Python Toolkit Built on 25 Years of Quant

The biggest blocker in enterprise software sales is organizational politics, not product capability. Field lessons shared by a founder and former Palantir engineer show that converting internal skeptics inside the customer org matters more to closing contracts than raw technical polish.
Field-Embedded Enterprise Sales with FDEs Palantir’s FDE (Forward Deployed Engineer) model embeds engineers directly inside customer sites to build alongside domain teams. Early on, labor costs look high relative to initial ACV (Annual Contract Value), yet deep operational integration drives down marginal delivery cost over time and unlocks rapid account expansion.
Executive time allocation reflects that reality. Milestones such as 220 deals above $1M ACV as of Q1 2026 and a 14 trillion KRW US Army contract grew out of this field-embedded motion. Founders selling into enterprises should spend 75% of their working hours talking directly with customers.
Turning Internal Detractors into Champions Enterprise software rollouts rarely stall on technical limits; they stall on risk-averse internal politics. Even inside a 14 trillion KRW program, stakeholders split sharply into supporters and detractors.
Winning adoption means spending more time talking with the people who actively oppose the tool. Work through middle managers to book sessions with vocal critics and translate their operational complaints directly into shipped workflows. Once hardened detractors turn into internal champions, the product locks into core operations.
Front-Loading System Access in Weeks 1-2 of a POC Loss of momentum kills more enterprise pilots than anything else. Focus maximum effort on the first 1-2 weeks of a POC before internal opposition organizes.
Use a Front-load access playbook: request every required dataset, credential, and system permission up front on day one. Dragging access requests out invites political gatekeeping that starves the pilot of real data. Securing early momentum carries POCs across the line into paid production contracts.
Enterprise deals hinge less on code elegance than on reading organizational incentives and earning trust on the ground.
Summary Risk aversion and internal politics derail more enterprise deals than technical product gaps. Seek out vocal internal detractors early and ship fixes for their workflows until they convert into product champions. Front-load all data and system access requests during weeks 1-2 of a POC before political resistance slows momentum.
summary: A former Palantir Forward Deployed Engineer explains how winning over internal skeptics and front-loading data access in weeks 1-2 decide enterprise POCs.
title: Enterprise Sales Lessons from a Former Palantir FDE: Beating Internal Politics

Engineering teams are developing sharper instincts for matching LLM coding agents to specific tasks. Running Anthropic Claude and OpenAI Codex side by side on production tickets for a full week highlighted distinct behavioral defaults in scope control and abstraction density.
Proactive Scope Expansion vs. Strict Literal Boundaries Claude habitually infers unstated intent behind a prompt, expanding scope to introduce helper abstractions or anticipatory structure. Codex sticks strictly to the stated requirements and stops writing the moment minimal changes satisfy the prompt. That difference in restraint directly shapes long-term codebase complexity.
Code Density Differences Inside Ruby on Rails Testing both models on Ruby and Rails repositories made their stylistic gap obvious. Claude eagerly introduces structural abstraction layers, verbose comments, type aliases, and proactive Sorbet type signatures, which can make diffs feel heavy. Codex strips away extra ceremony and writes direct code tied strictly to the ticket, leaving diffs easier to read with less over-engineering.
Matching Each Agent to the Right Engineering Task When exploring greenfield domain models or brainstorming broad architectural options, Claude’s proactive suggestions save design time. Inside mature codebases where surgical refactoring or tightly scoped feature work matters, Codex prevents unnecessary code bloat. Clear boundaries keep review velocity high.
Because each coding agent carries distinct output habits, splitting greenfield exploration and surgical maintenance across the two works well.
Summary Claude infers broader intent and proactively adds abstractions, comments, and type signatures beyond the literal prompt. Codex adheres strictly to explicit task boundaries and produces minimal, readable diffs. Use Claude for greenfield design exploration and Codex for disciplined maintenance and refactoring in established repositories.
summary: A week of side-by-side Ruby on Rails work shows Claude proactively adding abstractions and types while Codex sticks strictly to minimal, literal diffs.
title: Claude vs. Codex: One Week of Production Coding Comparison

content:
Coding agents configured to conserve tokens often clip Korean particles and verb endings, producing telegraphic replies that obscure technical nuance. fluent-korean is an output-style plugin built to prevent that context loss.
Why Korean Sentence Integrity Matters in Agent Loops When an LLM writes degraded, clipped Korean during intermediate reasoning, ambiguity compounds across multi-agent handoffs. Dropping grammatical particles between steps blurs subject-object relationships and lowers task accuracy. Clear syntax keeps reasoning chains unambiguous.
fluent-korean aims for plain, distortion-free phrasing rather than ornate prose. Unlike post-hoc spellcheckers or translationese rewriters, it defines explicit Korean grammar and clarity constraints up front inside the system prompt.
Two Output Profiles and CLI Setup The plugin ships in two profiles matched to your task: fluent-korean, which retains software engineering guidelines, and fluent-korean-not-coding, which strips code-editing rules for product planning and documentation work.
Inside Claude Code CLI, setup takes two commands: run /plugin marketplace add snflkd/fluent-korean followed by /plugin install fluent-korean@fluent-korean. Select your preferred output-style under /config, then run /clear to start a fresh session with the style active.
In web or desktop clients, paste the Markdown prompt body directly into your custom instructions field. Optional extension blocks let you add junior-friendly explanations, custom forms of address, or pre-output self-checks.
Operational Trade-Offs to Keep in Mind Restoring omitted particles and inflections slightly increases output token usage, and the rules occupy a slice of the system prompt in every session. Even so, unambiguous communication outweighs minor token overhead. Double-check exact file names and casing when configuring manually, since typos silently skip loading the style.
Developers tired of deciphering broken Korean in terminal agent sessions can install it in under a minute.
Summary Prevents meaning loss caused by dropped Korean particles and clipped verb endings in Claude Code and coding agents. Ships two output-style profiles - coding and non-coding - so users can match rules to engineering or documentation tasks. Trades a modest increase in token usage for clearer explanations and fewer misunderstandings across multi-agent pipelines.
summary: The fluent-korean output-style plugin stops Claude Code and coding agents from dropping Korean particles and word endings, preserving multi-agent reasoning clarity.
title: Fixing Clipped Korean Output in Claude Code with fluent-korean

content:
MacBooks can now run a 27-billion-parameter multimodal language model locally without NVIDIA CUDA GPUs or cloud endpoints. Developer Jonathan Coretti released Qwen3.8-27B-Uncensored-GGUF, a modified build of Alibaba’s open-weights model tuned to run on Apple Silicon unified memory with substantially reduced refusal guardrails.
Weight-Level Abliteration Without Retraining Instead of fine-tuning on new datasets, this release weakens safety refusals directly in weight space using the abliterated technique, applying targeted mathematical projections to weight matrices to suppress refusal directions selectively.
Refusal benchmarks show a sharp drop: on a 100-prompt harmful-request test suite, the base model refused 98 prompts whereas the uncensored build refused only 12. Even so, “uncensored” does not mean every safety behavior disappears completely.
27B Multimodal Capabilities and Quantization Formats The underlying Qwen 3.8 27B base is a dense 27-billion-parameter multimodal model that accepts text, images, and video inputs, offers a 262,144-token native context window, and supports both tool calling and reasoning modes for coding and research tasks.
To broaden local hardware compatibility, the release ships 2, 4, 6, and 8-bit quantized weights in both GGUF and MLX formats, loading straight into local runners such as Ollama and LM Studio.
Apple Silicon Memory Tiers and Practical Use Cases Real-world throughput depends heavily on unified memory capacity. Even the smallest quantized build requires at least 16GB of unified memory because macOS overhead and long-context KV caches compete with model weights for RAM.
A 16GB MacBook can boot the model at reduced token speeds, while machines with 64GB or more of unified memory sustain smooth offline 27B inference - making it practical for cybersecurity researchers running air-gapped vulnerability analysis or penetration testing.
Offline multimodal LLM testing continues to become more accessible on local workstation hardware.
Summary Weight-matrix abliteration cuts refusal rates from 98% to 12% on a 100-prompt test without additional fine-tuning. GGUF and MLX quantizations (2, 4, 6, and 8-bit) let Apple Silicon Macs run the 27B multimodal model locally without NVIDIA GPUs. Because OS overhead and long-context KV caches share RAM with model weights, 64GB+ unified memory is recommended for smooth offline use.
summary: Qwen3.8-27B-Uncensored-GGUF uses weight-level abliteration and GGUF/MLX quantization to run a 27B multimodal LLM offline on Apple Silicon unified memory.
title: Running Qwen 3.8 27B Uncensored Locally on Apple Silicon Macs

content:
Teams have tried getting LLMs to write raw SQL since 2022, typically stuffing entire database schemas into prompts and hoping the model emits valid queries.
Production analytics workloads follow recurring query patterns. Exposing a fine-grained fact table beneath a Semantic Layer and letting the agent assemble semantic parameters proves far more reliable and flexible than raw text-to-SQL.
When a user asks, “Show me CPA and ROAS for high-spend keywords in a target ad group over the last 7 days,” the LLM never writes SQL directly. Instead, it parses the question into five semantic building blocks: Dimension, Metric, Filter, Order, and Comparison.
The LLM emits those structured components as arguments to a single Tool Call:
{ "days": 7, "dimensions": ["keyword_id", "keyword_name"], "metrics": ["cost", "conversions", "cpa", "roas"], "filters": [ { "field": "adgroup_name", "operator": "contains", "value": "target ad group" } ], "order_by": { "field": "cost", "direction": "desc" } } An internal Python tool or deterministic query builder then compiles those arguments into executable SQL and runs the query.
Pairing 100% Valid SQL Assembly with Agent Autonomy SQL compiled through a Semantic Layer executes with 100% syntax accuracy. Rather than sidelining the LLM, this design shifts its job from guessing SQL dialect quirks to mapping user intent onto clean semantic dimensions and metrics.
Data Modeling Returns as a Core Engineering Asset Data engineering discipline around fact modeling and pipeline governance becomes central again in the agent era. Instead of making data engineers obsolete, the semantic definitions curated by the Human Layer act as safety guardrails, putting years of data lakehouse modeling craft directly to work.
Even a single well-modeled Semantic Layer tool gives an analytics agent broad, accurate coverage. Handing an agent structured assembly blocks works far better than exposing raw table schemas.
Summary Placing a Semantic Layer over granular fact tables beats dumping full DB schemas into an LLM for raw SQL generation. Instead of writing SQL syntax, the LLM extracts Dimension, Metric, Filter, Order, and Comparison arguments into a structured Tool Call. Deterministic query compilation from engineer-defined semantic models guarantees 100% syntax-error-free SQL execution.
summary: Replace raw schema dumps and free-form LLM SQL generation with a Semantic Layer over granular fact tables for 100% syntax-safe analytical queries.
title: Why Data Analysis Agents Should Query a Semantic Layer Instead of Writing SQL
