This comes from a ~25-minute Claude Code workshop video published by the Anthropic Applied AI team (23:25 remaining on the timer in the capture). The slide on screen sums up the core thesis of the session: “Claude Code augments every role across the SDLC” - meaning Claude Code supports every role from planning and design through engineering, security, and marketing, using different capabilities at each stage: PM -> Multimodal: drop in screenshots, wireframes, or competitor UIs and let Claude draft product specs. UI/UX Designer -> Plan Mode + Figma MCP: review an implementation plan first (Plan Mode) and read Figma designs directly via MCP. Developer -> Skills + MCP + Subagents: codify recurring tasks as Skills, pull external docs via MCP, and split large jobs across parallel Subagents. Security Engineer -> Plugins + Hooks: enforce mandatory checks, like pre-commit security scans, whenever Claude takes specific actions. Growth Marketer -> BigQuery MCP: query analytics data in plain language without writing SQL. Notice that every arrow between roles is labeled “Handoff” - instead of isolated individual usage, the PM’s spec feeds the designer, and the designer’s output passes straight to engineering like a relay. On prompting well, the workshop stresses four habits: run Explore -> Plan -> Execute instead of jumping straight to code, document project context up front in CLAUDE.md, give verifiable acceptance criteria (tests or screenshots), and turn repeatable workflows into Skills.
It is easy to think of Claude Code purely as a terminal code generator for individual developers. In a recent workshop, Anthropic’s Applied AI team frames it instead as a shared layer across the entire software development lifecycle (SDLC), aimed at tightening handoffs across roles rather than speeding up coding in isolation.
Role-Specific Capabilities and Handoffs Across the SDLC Pairing each discipline with the right extension changes how work moves from one stage to the next. Product managers pass wireframes or competitor screenshots to Multimodal inputs to draft requirement specs. UI/UX designers review structural plans in Plan Mode before touching code and pull design tokens directly into components through Figma MCP, making MCP the bridge between design files and repositories.
Developers package recurring workflows as Skills and fan out large refactors across parallel Subagents. Security engineers wire Plugins and Hooks so automated security checks run right before commits. Growth marketers attach BigQuery MCP to answer product data questions in plain language without hand-writing SQL. Each stage produces concrete artifacts that pass cleanly into the next role’s Handoff.
Workflow Principles from Exploration to Execution Getting reliable results from agents starts with pacing: step through Explore, Plan, and Execute rather than asking for immediate edits. Keeping build commands and architecture notes in a root CLAUDE.md file spares everyone from re-explaining repository context on every prompt.
Automated verification matters just as much. Giving the agent unit tests or browser screenshots to check its own output cuts silent regressions, a pattern reinforced throughout Anthropic’s cwc-workshops repository examples. Once a workflow proves repeatable, locking it down as a reusable Skill keeps team output consistent.
Treating Claude Code as the connective tissue across product specs, design, security, and analytics unlocks far more value than using it as terminal autocomplete alone.
Summary Claude Code supports PMs, designers, security engineers, and marketers across the full SDLC rather than serving developers alone. Combining role-specific extensions like MCP servers, Skills, Subagents, and Hooks streamlines cross-team handoffs. Following an Explore-Plan-Execute sequence, sharing repo context via CLAUDE.md, and enforcing automated test or screenshot checks keep agent runs reliable.
summary: Based on an Anthropic Applied AI workshop, see how PMs, designers, engineers, security teams, and marketers connect handoffs across the SDLC using Claude Code.
title: Augmenting Every Role Across the SDLC with Claude Code

Reliable coding agents depend on explicit feedback loops and diagnosing why models stall on large codebases. Internal Anthropic engineering walkthroughs show how small prompt and parameter adjustments improve daily output quality.
summary: Anthropic published a free four-hour course walking through how its own engineers prompt Claude, enforce output contracts, and run reliable agent loops.
title: Anthropic Releases Free 4-Hour Course on Internal Claude Workflows

content:
Tracking free-tier quotas and API keys across dozens of LLM providers by hand gets tedious fast. OmniRoute consolidates hundreds of AI models behind a single endpoint running on your machine.
One Endpoint Across 500+ Models OmniRoute serves an OpenAI-compatible API at localhost:20128/v1, unifying more than 268 providers and over 500 models. Out of the box, it connects directly with 26+ developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Copilot.
Its free-tier tracker aggregates roughly 1.5 billion free tokens across a pool of 43 providers in a single view. Every 2 weeks, an automated CI pipeline re-verifies free-token availability against live provider catalogs so dead endpoints do not linger.
Quota-Aware Failover and 18 Routing Strategies Requests keep flowing even when an API quota runs dry or an upstream provider goes down. OmniRoute groups models into combos that automatically fail over to the next available provider, while the default auto mode picks a suitable target on its own.
Users can choose from 18 routing strategies, ranging from priority (draining the top-ranked provider first) to fill-first (exhausting one quota bucket before moving on), or point clients at virtual presets like auto/coding, auto/fast, and auto/cheap.
Prompt Compression and Ecosystem Support To stretch tight quotas further, OmniRoute integrates RTK and Caveman compression to shrink prompt token counts by 15-95% before forwarding requests upstream.
The gateway runs as both a desktop app and a PWA, supports MCP and A2A protocols for agent-to-agent connections, and is maintained by an open-source community of more than 500 contributors.
If you juggle fragmented free tiers across coding tools, running OmniRoute locally keeps keys, quotas, and fallback rules in one place.
Summary Centralizes 268+ providers and 500+ models behind a single OpenAI-compatible localhost:20128/v1 endpoint. Uses combo-based automatic failover and 18 routing strategies to handle quota exhaustion and provider outages. Applies RTK and Caveman prompt compression to cut token consumption by 15-95%.
summary: OmniRoute exposes 268+ providers and 500+ AI models behind a single local endpoint with automatic quota failover, 18 routing strategies, and up to 95% token compression.
title: OmniRoute: Open-Source Gateway Unifying Hundreds of Free AI Models

content:
Getting useful answers from an LLM takes concrete background context, yet typing out paragraphs of backstory on a keyboard feels tedious. Andrej Karpathy suggests bypassing the keyboard with an unfiltered voice dictation session.
A 10-Minute Unfiltered Voice Recording When starting a collaboration with an LLM, Karpathy turns on voice input and talks through whatever is on his mind for roughly 10 minutes. Lean back, speak in a raw stream of consciousness, mention upfront that you are using speech-to-text, or ask and answer your own questions out loud.
How LLMs Untangle Spoken Thoughts Even when a long voice transcript meanders or repeats itself, modern LLMs extract the underlying intent accurately and return a structured response far cleaner than the raw monologue. Front-loading that context aligns the model early and cuts down on back-and-forth correction turns.
Rich Raw Data Over Polished Text Spending energy crafting a tidy prompt is often less helpful than feeding the model dense raw context. Speaking delivers many more context bits per minute than typing, giving the model the details it needs to understand constraints and tradeoffs.
Next time a task feels hard to explain in writing, hit the microphone button and talk through the problem before editing a single sentence.
Summary LLMs excel at reconstructing clear intent and structure from long, unedited spoken transcripts. High-volume spoken context bits align a model faster than short, carefully polished text prompts. Replacing manual typing with voice dictation lowers the friction of sharing detailed background context.
summary: Andrej Karpathy shares why recording an unfiltered 10-minute voice stream of consciousness gives LLMs richer context faster than typing polished prompts.
title: Andrej Karpathy's 10-Minute Voice Ramble Tip for Syncing with LLMs

content:
Recent updates to Claude Code give subagents persistent memory that survives across separate sessions, opening up much finer control over agent context.
Previously, subagents kept working memory only while executing a single call and lost everything once the task returned. Now they maintain independent context over long-running, multi-session projects.
Three Scopes of Subagent Memory Memory permissions split cleanly across three levels. User scope stores and reuses notes across all of a user’s projects. Project scope applies inside the current git repo so teammates share accumulated context. Local scope stays private to the current user within the current project, acting as a personal scratchpad.
Separating shared repo knowledge from personal working notes keeps team conventions synced without leaking local configuration.
Custom Subagent Design and Benefits Subagents keep raw search results and verbose command logs out of the main conversation thread. Each subagent runs in an isolated context window with its own system prompt and tool allowlist, separating codebase exploration from implementation.
Restricting write or shell tools per subagent creates safer execution boundaries, while routing lightweight lookups to a fast, low-cost model like Haiku trims token spend.
Built-in agents such as Explore and Plan follow the same pattern, skipping unnecessary file reads so the main session avoids context bloat.
Shifts in Collaboration Strategy and Use Cases Persistent subagent memory changes how multi-agent workflows fit together. Instead of stitching together separate top-level agents externally, developers can place role-specific subagents - each with its own persistent memory - underneath a single orchestrating session.
Developers who repeatedly type the same project rules or run parallel sessions across repositories benefit immediately from subagents that remember prior runs.
Summary Persistent subagent memory carries context across sessions, cutting repetitive instructions and token waste. Splitting memory into User, Project, and Local scopes balances team knowledge sharing with local privacy. Isolating exploration in subagents and routing lighter tasks to models like Haiku lowers cost while keeping the main context clean.
summary: Claude Code adds persistent memory across User, Project, and Local scopes so custom subagents retain context across sessions without cluttering the main thread.
title: Persistent Subagent Memory Scopes and Design in Claude Code

content:
Gathering and comparing real estate data usually means jumping across multiple public portals to check housing subscription notices and transaction history. The Ipzitalk team has released 27 remote MCP automation skills that let Claude Code and other AI agents query real estate big data directly.
How Ipzitalk MCP Works and Connects Built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the package lets AI agents fetch structured real estate figures over remote APIs without spinning up a local server. Connecting the plugin in Claude Code takes four commands:
/plugin marketplace add chatdaeri/ipzitalk /plugin install ipzitalk@ipzitalk /reload-plugins /ipzitalk:setup Once setup finishes, the skills are ready to call immediately, and any other AI client that supports remote MCP servers can connect in the same way.
Key Analysis Skills and Usage Out of the 27 included tools, the core set focuses on neighborhood research and market trends. Passing an address to location-report compiles nearby infrastructure and transit links into a structured brief, while complex-overview-all evaluates sale price history and valuation metrics for a specific apartment complex.
Housing subscription analysis also gets dedicated helpers. read-notice-report extracts sale prices and eligibility rules from dense subscription announcements, and read-notice-compare lines up two or more notices in a side-by-side table.
For broader regional comparisons, recent-market-trend contrasts price movements across 3-5 administrative districts at once, and presale-report summarizes presale market conditions. Another 21 commands cover tasks such as land registry lookups and actual transaction statistics.
Target Users and Constraints Analysts and planners who normally assemble market tables by hand can query figures in plain language without digging through raw API specs, cutting report preparation time.
Before relying on it for live decisions, check data refresh intervals and rate limits, and keep in mind that response times depend on external API latency and network conditions.
Application details and usage guides are available on the official documentation request page.
Summary Remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) skills let agents query real estate big data in natural language without custom API integration. Commands like read-notice-compare and location-report automate repetitive housing notice comparisons and neighborhood briefs. Four plugin commands connect all 27 tools directly inside Claude Code without running a local server.
summary: Connect Ipzitalk’s 27 remote MCP skills to Claude Code to automate Korean real estate neighborhood reports, apartment price trends, and housing notice comparisons.
title: 27 Remote MCP Skills for Automating Real Estate Big Data Analysis

content:
In data modeling, an ontology defines the core entities and relationships that hold a domain together. Microsoft’s Ontology Playground is a free browser-based learning tool where you can experiment with ontology structures hands-on.
Interactive Graphs and RDF Import/Export The tool renders relationships as interactive node-link graphs so you can design entities from scratch or load existing schemas to inspect their structure. Full RDF import and export support makes it easy to exchange files with external modeling tools.
Because everything runs in the browser without desktop software installation, you can quickly check a schema visually for structural mistakes before translating your ontology into application code.
Industry Templates and Hands-On Examples Ontology Playground includes ready-made domain templates across manufacturing, finance, retail, and other industries. Selecting a template loads a complete graph with standard entity relationships and property definitions already wired up.
Those templates give engineers a concrete reference when structuring unfamiliar domain knowledge or combining schemas across multiple business areas.
A Starting Point for Knowledge Graphs and GraphRAG Schema design is one of the first hurdles when building GraphRAG systems. Ontology Playground works well as a lightweight sandbox for prototyping and validating entity relationships before committing them to a graph database.
Reviewing a visual graph together also narrows communication gaps between data engineers and domain stakeholders, catching mismatched business definitions early.
If you are new to ontologies or want to see how RDF data maps onto a live graph, this playground is an easy place to start.
Summary Interactive node-link graphs make abstract ontology concepts concrete inside the browser. RDF file import and export let teams validate domain schemas alongside existing modeling tools. Industry templates provide ready-made starting structures for knowledge graph and GraphRAG schema design.
summary: Explore Microsoft’s free Ontology Playground for designing interactive entity-relationship graphs, importing/exporting RDF files, and prototyping GraphRAG schemas.
title: Microsoft Ontology Playground: Free Browser Tool for Learning Ontologies

content:
Among AI design skills on GitHub, ‘UI UX Pro Max’ stands out with more than 100,000 stars for a single skill repository. Its most interesting angle is how it defines explicit design rules by industry. Ask for a bank landing page, and it starts by locking in rules like: no playful elements, no AI-style purple/pink gradients, and security UX first. It maps out rules like these across 161 industries: - Healthcare: no neon colors or heavy motion; stick to trustworthy green and blue tones - Luxury brands: no fast animations; a premium feel comes from slow pacing - Education apps: no dark mode and no dense jargon - Kids’ learning apps: conversely, no muted low-energy colors - Mental health apps: no bright neon or motion overload; calm is the feature itself. Notably, the ban on AI purple-and-pink gradients appears across high-trust sectors like banking, insurance, legal, and government. Even if you never feed these rules to an AI, reading through them is a solid UX study resource.
In AI-assisted frontend work, UI UX Pro Max has drawn over 100,000 GitHub stars by focusing on domain-specific UI/UX constraints rather than generic visual flair.
Tailored Design Rules Across 161 Industries The repository breaks design guidelines down across 161 distinct sectors, making it useful reference material for human designers as well as coding agents. Financial services rules ban playful illustrations and AI-cliche purple gradients while putting security cues first. Healthcare rules avoid neon palettes and heavy motion in favor of calm blue and green tones.
Pacing, Color, and Audience Fit Motion speed and color saturation shift according to brand positioning and user needs. Luxury brands rely on slow transitions to convey restraint, kids’ learning apps ban muted low-energy palettes, and mental health apps restrict motion overload so the interface stays calm.
Shared Constraints That Protect Trust High-trust sectors such as banking, insurance, legal services, and government agencies share strict negative constraints, starting with an explicit ban on purple-and-pink gradients common in AI templates. Putting domain credibility ahead of visual trends helps both prompt authors and design-system teams avoid off-tone interfaces.
Design System Generator v2.0 Version 2.0 adds a generator that analyzes project requirements and proposes a tailored design system with layout patterns and style keywords for the target audience. For a wellness brand, for instance, it pairs soft shadows with organic shapes rather than rigid grid cards.
Value for Human Designers Having explicit per-industry “do not use” lists catches tone mistakes early, especially when working in an unfamiliar vertical. Treating the skill’s rules as a checklist alongside human judgment keeps product interfaces grounded in user context rather than template defaults.
Summary Explicit, industry-specific negative constraints help interfaces earn user trust faster than generic styling prompts. High-trust verticals like banking, legal, and government explicitly ban trendy AI purple-and-pink gradients to preserve credibility. Structured rule sets across 161 sectors serve as a practical reference for human design-system work as well as AI prompting.
summary: Examine how the 100K-star open-source skill UI UX Pro Max defines explicit UI/UX rules and visual constraints across 161 industries.
title: Industry-Specific UI/UX Guidelines in the UI UX Pro Max AI Skill

Workpets, an app that lets you use Claude Code like a chat workspace, has officially launched. Skip the black terminal screen: download, install, and chat. Assign tasks in plain language, watch AI staff split the work, and raise virtual pets alongside your projects. Upcoming updates add pet houses, egg hatching, and room decorating. Free to start on PC.
While Claude Code works well in the terminal, a text-only CLI still puts off many users. Workpets is a desktop app for macOS and Windows that lets you run AI agents through mouse clicks and natural-language cards, connecting directly to an existing Claude subscription.
Managing Agent Collaboration on a Kanban Board Instead of terminal commands, Workpets organizes tasks on a Kanban Board. Creating a task card starts an AI agent right away and moves the card across status columns automatically. Because each card runs as an independent session, running multiple tasks in parallel is as simple as opening several cards side by side.
The app pairs the board with a virtual office view: define an agent in one sentence, and an animated character sits at a desk working in real time. A built-in Memory system logs decision criteria and patterns after each finished task and reloads relevant notes on future cards to keep project context consistent.
Gamification and Operational Controls Token usage converts directly into experience points that level up your office all the way to level 999, unlocking interior decor items along the way. Users can collect 80 pet species, decorate rooms, and join one of 6 global factions competing for territory on a shared world map.
Underneath the game layer sit practical operational controls: recurring task schedules, a daily token usage dashboard, drag-to-rewrite partial output editing, and goal loops where agents keep revising until completion criteria pass. Skills, workflows, MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers, and API keys are all managed from one screen.
Pricing and Target Users Core features are free, while a one-time $4.99 purchase unlocks permanent premium access, including Mobile Remote for monitoring and controlling tasks from a phone. On first launch, the UI configures itself automatically in 10 languages, including Korean, based on system locale.
For developers tired of terminal windows or product planners who prefer visual boards over CLI flags, Workpets offers an approachable way to run parallel Claude Code sessions.
Summary Visualizes terminal-based Claude Code sessions as independent cards on a desktop Kanban board. Converts token consumption into office XP, pet collection, and faction map mechanics to make daily agent runs engaging. Includes scheduled runs, partial drag-to-edit revisions, token dashboards, and centralized MCP asset management.
summary: Workpets wraps Claude Code in a macOS and Windows desktop GUI featuring a Kanban task board, persistent memory, scheduling, and virtual office gamification.
title: Workpets Launches a Kanban and Virtual Office GUI for Claude Code

content:
This article explores a deceptively simple question: How do you measure whether sending free products to influencers actually increased sales? The answer is harder than it looks, and rethinking the problem changed what I built.
At first, the approach seemed obvious-use AI to rank influencers by follower count and engagement, then send products to the highest scorers. But measuring success revealed a hidden problem. Coupon-tracked orders told me who received the product, not whether that product caused the sales. The same customer might have bought anyway. The coupon code might have spread to other channels. Concurrent ads or promotions could have driven the same orders.
That gap between “orders attributed to the influencer” and “sales caused by seeding” is the core problem. To bridge it, I needed a comparison-a group of similar influencers who did not receive products yet. By comparing orders from creators who got the product to orders from creators still waiting, I could estimate the true incremental impact of seeding. That is the title’s thesis: without a comparison group, no measurement is possible.
The resulting tool does not predict revenue with high precision. Instead, it enforces rigor. It blocks risky ad copy before it ships, requires company-approved sources only, prevents users from re-rolling assignments when results look unfavorable, and refuses to call a result “successful” when the sample is too small. It admits what it cannot prove.
This project used synthetic data and public information for testing, not real company records. I need to be direct about this: I did not verify any real sales increase. This article is not a proof of impact. Instead, it records building the procedure and safety gates first, so that real validation can start on a foundation that already blocks the common shortcuts and mistakes.
Designing Product Seeding with AI The numbers inside the product are synthetic or drawn from public data. Every candidate, order, and revenue figure shown in this article or its screens is either generated for testing or comes from public sources. None of those figures represents any specific company’s actual creator list, order history, or sales performance. The product data exists to test the design.
The challenge asked me to improve product seeding with AI. My first instinct was to rank creators more accurately. As I built the product, I found that the harder questions came before and after ranking. Before sending anything, the workflow had to stop risky ad copy. Afterward, it needed a comparison that could help explain why orders changed.
That discovery changed what I was building. A creator score could still help allocate a limited test budget, but it could not stand in for evidence that seeding caused new sales.
I Started by Trying to Predict Which Creators Would Sell My first interface looked familiar. It collected follower counts, average views, and engagement rates, then assigned each creator a score. A marketer could compare many accounts quickly and send products to the highest-ranked candidates. Even without a sales model, normalizing public metrics could reduce manual work.
The problem began when I tried to turn that score into a revenue forecast. I had no internal sales history, so I could not train or validate a model against the number of paid orders each creator had generated. High views and engagement showed attention. They did not show that the attention had become company revenue. Adding decimal places to projected return on ad spend would have made the estimate look more certain without giving it a stronger basis.
I also checked the original December 2019 file from a public cosmetics-store datasetfor a behavioral baseline. The file contains 3,533,286 event rows from a public cosmetics-store dataset for December 2019. Those rows record public behavior such as views, cart actions, and purchases. They are not company data, and they cannot replace the missing internal sales history.
I stopped trying to make the forecast look more precise. I kept the creator score only as a way to decide where a limited experiment budget should go first. A separate comparison would evaluate what happened after execution. The product now treated prioritization and measured results as two different things.
Coupon Orders Did Not Tell Me Whether Seeding Worked Dedicated coupons and tracking links still mattered. They let the team count orders associated with a creator-specific path. But coupon- and link-tracked revenue is not the same as incremental revenue attributable to the intervention.
A customer who already intended to buy might use the coupon. A code might spread through another channel. Search ads, messages to existing customers, or another campaign running at the same time could also affect orders. If I counted every tracked order as seeding impact, I would confuse the path attached to an order with the reason that order occurred.
The missing quantity was the outcome without seeding. A coupon cannot create that comparison by itself. I needed a group of similar creators who would not receive products until the measurement window closed. They were not permanently excluded. They formed a delayed-start comparison group that could begin later.
The experiment compared creators receiving products now with creators who had not yet received them over the same period. Google Ads guidance on experimentslikewise describes randomized exposed and unexposed groups as the basis for measuring incremental impact rather than relying only on attributed activity.
A comparison group does not remove every source of bias. Creators may reach overlapping audiences, and concurrent campaigns can contaminate the result. Execution may also depart from the assigned plan. Even with those limits, the design records what was compared instead of treating coupon orders as a causal answer.
I Checked Ad Copy Before Scoring Creators Some candidates should not enter the ranking at all until a person reviews the proposed copy. A missing sponsorship disclosure was one reason to stop. A disclosure paired with wording such as not an ad was another because the surrounding copy contradicted the disclosure. I applied the same pre-publication check to disease-treatment language and claims that were not in the company’s approved material. A high audience score could not offset those risks.
For economic-interest disclosure, I referred to the National Law Information Center’s recommendation and endorsement advertising review guideline. The relationship should be presented where consumers can notice and understand it, close to the recommendation, and the rest of the post should not weaken or contradict it. For copy that could make a cosmetic sound like a medicine, I used Article 13 of the Korean Cosmetics Actas the reason to screen treatment-oriented language before publication.
This was a pre-publication risk screen, not legal advice. Matching a rule or an approved phrase does not guarantee compliance. Jurisdiction, product classification, and the full context of the post still require human review. The product’s job was narrower: stop risky candidates before their reach or engagement scores moved them to the top.
Putting this check first changed the interface. Instead of opening with the highest scores, the workflow first showed which disclosure was missing and which claim fell outside the approved material. It also recorded why a candidate was paused so a marketer could revise the copy and submit it for review again.
I Used Only Data the Company Had Approved A safety check is easy to bypass if the caller can type both the claim and its supposed source. I created a company-approved registry and required product copy to match an approved entry exactly. The same registry supplied a snapshot containing the approver, approval time, and official source. A request could not invent its own copy and approval evidence and present both as trusted input.
Creator metrics needed more than a number as well. The workflow checked a stable creator ID and the time at which the value was collected. It compared the metric name and value with the supplied source file, then calculated a SHA-256 value for that file. If even one byte changed, the calculated value changed too, giving the system a way to detect a later modification.
SHA-256 only supports that limited claim. A matching value can show that the file presented later is the same file that was recorded. It cannot show that the platform or an authorized employee issued the file. Someone could fabricate a file, calculate its hash, and pass the format check. A real deployment would also need an access-controlled source export or a signed export.
I kept this distinction visible in the result. File-content and fingerprint checks belong to the system. Source authenticity requires information about the issuing path and the issuer’s authority. The interface did not combine those two states into one approval label.
I Randomly Split Creators into Seeding and Comparison Groups Only creators who passed the copy and source checks entered random assignment. The product split them into a treatment group receiving products now and a delayed-start comparison group. I also had to protect that assignment from repeated attempts to obtain a preferred result.
If the interface reveals the result before saving it, a user can rename a request and run it again whenever the split looks inconvenient. I reversed that order. The system had to record the assignment before revealing it.
Changes to display-only fields, such as a campaign name or goal description, returned the existing assignment. Changes to inputs that could affect the experiment, including the candidate set, budget, or measurement window, did not create a fresh split. They produced a conflict and stopped the request. That behavior reduced assignment shopping through small input changes.
Budget feasibility had to come before the assignment record as well. The system checked whether every possible treatment combination could satisfy both the minimum execution amount and the per-creator cap. If the budget could not support a valid allocation, the request stopped without saving an assignment. Once the caller corrected the conditions, the first valid request could receive the first recorded split.
For the article, I used a simple absolute rate-difference estimate:
Estimated seeding effect = treatment-group order-event rate - comparison-group order-event rate The groups can have different sizes, so subtracting raw order counts would be misleading. The estimator compares rates instead. I did not treat this formula as the only definition of incremental measurement. Advertising measurement systems may adjust for missing outcomes and report relative differences or confidence intervals. Here, the pre-specified absolute rate difference made the decision structure of a small experiment easy to inspect.
Five Creators Were Not Enough for a Conclusion Five synthetic candidates passed the safety and source checks in the demo. Random assignment put three in the treatment group and two in the delayed-start comparison group. Even if the difference between their order rates looked large, five creators could not support a performance claim.
The sample-size calculation used an 8% baseline order-event rate, a minimum detectable absolute difference of 4 percentage points, a significance level of 0.05, and power of 0.8. Under those assumptions, the approximate requirement was 883 creators per group. That is not a fixed threshold for every campaign. A different baseline, target difference, measurement period, or allocation would change the required sample.
I included a two-sided Fisher’s exact test because it calculates the possible tables directly when counts are small. I paired it with a Newcombe interval, which combines Wilson intervals for the two group proportions to show a range for their difference. The interface presented the test result alongside the sample plan and the interval rather than treating one p-value as the decision.
When I fed the synthetic result into the analyzer, its actual output was PILOT_ONLY_DO_NOT_CLAIM. In product terms, that means pilot only, no performance claim. The analyzer returned the same state whenever the pre-specified sample condition was not met, even if the observed difference looked favorable or a statistical test happened to look significant.
That warning did not weaken the demo. It stopped a five-creator result from being presented as a success story. The smaller the sample, the more direct the product needed to be about what the numbers could not establish.
I Asked AI How the System Could Be Gamed I did not ask AI to decide which creator would produce the most revenue. With no validated sales history, it could still produce a confident ranking, but that ranking would not solve the evidence problem. I used AI to generate attack questions instead.
Could a caller fabricate the approved copy and the approver together? Could renaming a campaign trigger repeated random assignments? Could someone submit past dates and close the measurement immediately? These questions became product contracts. I specified which inputs to reject, when a failed request should leave no assignment record, and when the system had to reuse an existing split.
I also used a separate AI session with no implementation context. That session repeated the attacks and checked whether the behavior described in the documentation matched the behavior in code. Keeping review context separate reduced the chance that the same conversation would explain and approve its own decisions.
AI still did not provide an independent guarantee of correctness. People had to choose the approved claims, approvers, budget, outcome metric, and experiment conditions. The separate review narrowed the material a person needed to inspect. It did not prove that operational data was authentic or that the experiment design was valid for every campaign.
I Tried to Break the Design with 32 Bad Inputs I turned the attack questions into 32 automated tests. A successful request was not enough. The tests deliberately supplied altered records, unsafe copy, infeasible budgets, and attempts to obtain a more convenient assignment.
Category Deliberate bad input Altered source material Mismatch approval details, collected values, source-file contents, and SHA-256 values Risky ad copy Omit or contradict the sponsorship disclosure, or imply medical treatment Assignment shopping Rename a campaign, supply a user-controlled random value, or reverse candidate order Infeasible budget Request a split that cannot satisfy both the minimum amount and per-creator cap Backdated results Use past dates and a caller-created result file to close measurement immediately Small-sample overstatement Demand a performance state from a result that does not meet the sample plan Record-chain tampering Change an earlier record and try to append a new decision I reran the tests from the original submitted project and got 32/32 tests passed. This is not evidence that a company campaign succeeded. It says that the implementation applied its specified stop and reuse behavior to those 32 attack cases.
The tests also made me narrow several statements in the documentation. I had first described SHA-256 as if it verified the source. The test boundary showed that it only checks whether file content changed. I also separated a server receipt time from publisher authentication. A receipt time can prevent a caller from backdating submission, but it cannot prove who created the result file.
Recording what the tests did not verify took more work than reporting that they passed. That boundary was part of the product behavior, not a footnote added after the demo.
What Validation Required from Real Campaigns I did not execute a real company seeding campaign, and I did not have access to the company’s raw sales records. I could not claim that the intervention increased real sales. I also could not show that the same design would produce a similar result across different campaigns.
A result file can match its SHA-256 value while leaving its publisher unknown. A server receipt time can prevent backdating without authenticating the orders inside the file. The system also cannot automatically correct overlapping creator audiences or cases in which execution does not follow the assigned plan.
The next real step would be to register one campaign’s candidates, outcome metric, measurement window, and analysis method before execution. Results should come from an access-controlled source-system export or a signed export. That would connect the recorded assignment to observed outcomes while preserving information about where the result came from.
One properly run campaign would still not justify broad claims. Different campaign conditions require repeated measurement, and each result should report its uncertainty. This project built a structure for starting that validation. It did not produce verified sales impact.
Changing the Question Changed the Product I began with a prediction question: which creator will sell the most product? If I had kept that question, the product would have centered on creator scores and projected revenue. Without internal sales data, a more polished ranking would only have made an estimate look like a confirmed fact.
The revised question changed the main workflow. First, decide whether execution is safe enough to proceed. Then compare the group that received products with the group that waited. Ranking became supporting information for choosing experiment candidates, and results without an adequate comparison or sample did not receive a performance label.
This change also altered when the product should answer. A prediction tool tries to produce one number before execution. My design records reasons to stop and the assignment criteria before execution. It calculates the group difference only after the measurement window ends.
The leaderboard is not the record I most want to see next. I want to inspect a real campaign that followed its pre-registered conditions and kept the same reporting standard when the result was disappointing. At that point, the product would no longer be a tool for guessing who might sell. It would help me review whether the campaign was safe to run and whether the recorded result supported the decision.
summary: Instead of predicting which creators would generate revenue, I redesigned the product around safer execution and a treatment-versus-comparison test.
title: 1. Coupon Revenue Could Not Tell Me Whether Product Seeding Worked

content:
Designing relational database schemas from product specs takes careful manual work, from defining tables to wiring foreign keys without syntax mistakes. StackRender is an open-source tool built to automate and visualize that stage of backend development.
Visual Schema Design and DDL Conversion StackRender runs in the browser with a drag-and-drop canvas for designing tables and relationships visually, cutting down on typos and syntax errors common in hand-written DDL.
You can import existing SQL DDL scripts to render diagrams immediately, or export visual designs straight to target SQL dialects, keeping schema modeling and SQL generation in sync.
Foreign Key Cycle Detection and Multi-Database Support StackRender automatically detects Foreign Key Cycles during design so circular table dependencies do not slip into migrations, and includes built-in index recommendations to catch query bottlenecks early.
Database support covers PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQLite, Oracle, and SQL Server. For local use, running docker-compose up spins up the web UI on localhost right away.
AI Schema Refinement and Cloud Features The hosted cloud version adds an AI assistant that drafts database diagrams from natural language requirements, refines existing schemas, and applies patterns like Soft-delete columns automatically.
Cloud users also get automated table specification docs. Currently in public beta under active development on GitHub, StackRender’s long-term roadmap extends from schema design all the way to automated backend API endpoint generation.
Spinning up the Docker container locally is a quick way to test visual schema modeling and cycle checks on your next backend project.
Summary Open-source visual schema tool aiming to automate backend workflows from database modeling to API endpoint generation. Built-in foreign key cycle detection and index recommendations catch structural mistakes during the design phase. The cloud edition adds an AI assistant that generates schemas and table documentation from natural language specs.
summary: StackRender is an open-source visual schema designer supporting PostgreSQL, MySQL, foreign key cycle detection, index recommendations, and AI-assisted generation.
title: StackRender: Open-Source Database Schema Design and Automation Tool

content:
Hitting usage limits mid-session in Claude Code or Codex CLI breaks focus, especially when switching accounts requires repeated browser logins. Mobius removes that friction from the macOS menu bar.
Automatic Account Switching Flow Mobius tracks sessions across multiple subscription accounts, switches to the next available account as soon as one hits a rate limit, and switches back automatically once the primary account resets. Clicking the menu bar icon shows usage gauges and time remaining until reset for every registered account.
Switching accounts does not open a fresh browser authentication flow each time; clicking an account card swaps the active session immediately. Initial sign-in windows open in isolated sessions so your regular browser cookies stay untouched, and credentials stay on disk with 0600 file permissions without touching external servers.
Priority Ordering and CLI Integration Inside the app, drag-and-drop cards set account priority. The top card acts as the primary account, failing over sequentially down the list as limits are reached. For Codex, running the terminal login command registers the session automatically within seconds.
Mobius also ships its own companion CLI, which you can install from the settings menu or via script. A background monitor watches rate-limit status continuously so you do not have to check usage manually.
Supported Platforms and Limitations The app supports claude.ai subscription accounts and ChatGPT Plus-backed Codex CLI sessions. DMG builds on the official release page are signed and notarized by Apple, so they open without Gatekeeper warnings. Mobius requires macOS 14 or later and does not support raw API keys, Bedrock, or Vertex AI.
For developers juggling multiple subscription accounts, automating local session failover keeps terminal work moving without manual re-authentication.
Summary Automates local session failover across multiple AI subscriptions so rate limits do not interrupt terminal coding. Supports web-subscription CLIs rather than API keys, letting developers alternate across personal and work subscriptions. Stores tokens locally with 0600 permissions and ships as an Apple-notarized macOS binary.
summary: Mobius is a macOS menu bar app that automatically switches Claude Code or Codex CLI sessions when an account hits its usage limit and returns once limits reset.
title: Mobius: macOS App for Automatic Claude Code Account Switching

content:
Five recommended Claude Code plugins. 1. Superpowers (Planning/Design): Enforces a thinking sequence before writing code to raise quality and cut token waste. Refines requirements via questions, gets design sign-off, and builds a TDD plan. Install: /plugin install superpowers@claude-plugins-official. Sample prompt: “I am building a gym check-in mobile web app with Next.js + Supabase. Clarify requirements with questions before coding and show me the design first.” 2. frontend-design (UI Implementation): Moves away from generic AI template layouts to produce consistent UI code with deliberate typography and readability (official Anthropic tool). Install: /plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-code then /plugin install frontend-design@anthropics-claude-code. Sample prompt: “Redesign the home screen of our existing Next.js dashboard with a calm financial-report look while keeping current Tailwind tokens and mobile layout.” 3. code-review (PR Review): Reviews GitHub PR diffs from multiple virtual agent perspectives for bugs and rule violations. Install: /plugin install code-review@claude-plugins-official. Commands: /code-review (check in terminal), /code-review --comment (post to GitHub PR), /code-review --fix (apply fixes locally). 4. Security Review (Built-in Audit): Requires no separate install and checks for SQL Injection, XSS, auth bypass, and API permission flaws from an attacker’s perspective. Command: /security-review. Sample prompt: “/security-review Focus on the updated admin refund API and webhook verification logic, including exploit conditions, impact, and minimal fixes.” 5. Claude-Mem (Long-Term Memory): Compresses conversation context and past decisions into local SQLite and reloads them automatically in future sessions. Install: /plugin marketplace add thedotmack/claude-mem then /plugin install claude-mem. Sample prompt: “How did we decide to handle duplicate payment webhooks in the last session? Summarize the key context.”
Combining the right plugins in Claude Code lets you automate everything from pre-coding design specs to pre-merge security checks inside the terminal. Here are five practical plugins worth adding to your setup.
Superpowers Establishes a structured planning sequence before any code is written. It clarifies requirements through targeted questions, waits for design approval, and drafts a TDD plan. Install it with /plugin install superpowers@claude-plugins-official and pair it with architecture-first prompts.
frontend-design An official Anthropic plugin that writes UI code tailored to a product’s domain rather than falling back on generic AI dashboard templates, keeping layout and readability consistent. Register the marketplace via /plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-code and run /plugin install frontend-design@anthropics-claude-code.
code-review Inspects GitHub PR diffs from multiple virtual reviewer perspectives to catch bugs and project convention violations early. Install with /plugin install code-review@claude-plugins-official, and pass --comment or --fix to post feedback on the PR or patch local files.
Security Review A built-in security check that runs without extra installation. It audits changes from an attacker’s perspective for flaws such as SQL Injection and API permission bypasses. Run /security-review to get exploit conditions, impact analysis, and minimal patch suggestions.
Claude-Mem Stores conversation context and engineering decisions in a local SQLite database, reloading relevant history automatically when you start your next session. Add the marketplace with /plugin marketplace add thedotmack/claude-mem and install via /plugin install claude-mem.
Keeping planning, review, security checks, and persistent memory inside the terminal cuts down on repetitive context setup across sessions.
Summary Enforcing up-front planning and design before code generation cuts unnecessary token spend and rework. Automated PR review and built-in security auditing catch bugs and auth flaws before deployment. Local SQLite session memory preserves past architectural decisions across separate terminal sessions.
summary: Review five Claude Code plugins covering pre-coding design, UI implementation, multi-agent PR review, security auditing, and SQLite-backed session memory.
title: 5 Practical Claude Code Plugins for Daily Development

content:
A shared postintroduces a card titled “11 Rules for Success.” Comments on the post note that the card was not an official company-wide code of conduct for all Apple employees, but a badge-holder insert distributed within a team led by John Brandon. Reading it as one team’s operating principles rather than corporate policy keeps the context accurate.
The 11 Rules Let go of the past and focus on the future. Always tell the truth. Deliver bad news early. If you do not know, ask. Think like a businessperson, not just a salesperson. Do whatever work is needed regardless of job level. Be professional in your words, actions, and follow-through. Listen to the customer. Build mutually helpful relationships. Share information with teammates. Do not take yourself too seriously, and have fun at work. Applying the Rules to Engineering Work The later you surface an outage or schedule slip, the less room teammates have to respond. Rule 3 translates directly into sharing known blast radius and open unknowns as soon as an issue appears. Rules 4 and 10 map to asking questions early and documenting the answers where the rest of the team can find them.
Rules 5 and 8 remind engineers not to stop at shipping code, but to verify what user problem the implementation actually solves. Note that these takeaways are an engineering interpretation of the card rather than a description of Apple’s official development process.
Summary Distinguish between a single team’s badge card and company-wide policy when citing workplace rules. Escalating bad news early, asking when unsure, and writing down answers directly improve engineering collaboration. Checking real customer impact and finishing follow-through work apply just as well to software delivery as to sales.
summary: Review the ‘11 Rules for Success’ badge card shared within a team at Apple and translate its lessons on early bad-news escalation and collaboration to engineering.
title: 11 Work Rules Shared by an Apple Team and Their Engineering Takeaways

content:
Writing domain instructions from scratch every time you set up an AI agent gets repetitive fast. The open-source claude-skills repository on GitHub packages reusable domain manuals that you can plug directly into coding agents.
A Large Skill Library Across 13 Tools Rather than locking into a single client, the repository works across 13 AI coding environments including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI.
The collection spans 355 skills and 602 Python helper scripts. Every Python script relies solely on the Python standard library with zero external package dependencies, so scripts run immediately after cloning.
Controlling Context Cost and Security Risks Loading hundreds of skills does not bloat the context window because the library uses progressive disclosure. Agents keep only skill names and short summaries in memory at startup and read the full markdown body only when a task triggers that skill.
To guard against unsafe third-party scripts, a built-in skill-security-auditor scans code before installation and reports PASS, WARN, or FAIL.
Practical Ways to Apply It Instead of importing the entire repository wholesale, teams can treat it as a structural reference when authoring internal domain guides. Specialized folders covering regulatory compliance or C-level advisory tasks show how to organize complex SKILL.md files clearly.
Every guide follows Anthropic’s official agent skill specification, making it easy to take the skeleton of a skill and adapt the rules to your own stack and policies.
Browsing the markdown files in this repository is a quick way to see how production-ready agent instructions are structured.
Summary claude-skills is an open-source skill library compatible with 13 AI coding tools, including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI. Progressive disclosure keeps context overhead minimal even when hundreds of skills are registered. A built-in security auditor scans scripts before installation to flag risky code with PASS, WARN, or FAIL results.
summary: Explore claude-skills, an open-source library of 355 skills and 602 Python tools compatible with 13 AI coding tools, built with progressive disclosure and security auditing.
title: Sharpening Agent Domain Skills with the claude-skills Library

content:
Running multiple AI coding CLIs at the same time quickly turns terminal windows and working directories into a mess. Orca is a desktop IDE built to solve this workspace sprawl by organizing CLI agents into isolated project views.
A Control Plane for AI Coding CLIs Orca does not bundle its own AI model; instead, it runs and coordinates multiple CLI agents in parallel. For each task, it automatically creates an isolated Git Worktree so concurrent agents never overwrite each other’s files, while linking agent terminals, browser tabs, and code editors in one window.
The desktop app itself is free under the MIT license, while API usage or subscription fees for connected agents follow each provider’s billing plan.
Installing and Starting Orca on macOS macOS users can install Orca with a single Homebrew command:
brew install --cask stablyai/orca/orca After installation, launch the app to pick your default agent and enable desktop notifications.
Turning on notifications lets you know right away when a background agent finishes its run. Installers for Windows and Linux are also available on the official website.
Setting Manual Permissions and Connecting a Practice Repo Before letting agents edit code, switch permissions to manual control. Leaving auto-approval enabled by default risks unintended file modifications. Open Settings, go to the Agents tab, and change Agent Permissions to Manual.
Start by connecting a lightweight local practice repository rather than a production codebase. Multi-repo imports and external integrations can wait until you are comfortable with the basic loop.
Creating Your First Workspace and Running a Task Once a repository is registered, click the button in the top-right corner to create your first Worktree workspace. Give the task a name, choose a base branch, and Orca sets up the Git Worktree in the background. Open an agent tab and test a read-only question first before making file edits.
From there, walk through a small edit, inspect the diff view, and make a local commit to see the full workflow. When a task wraps up, merge only the changes you want back into your main branch.
For developers tired of juggling scattered folders and terminal tabs, Orca cuts context-switching overhead and keeps parallel agent runs tidy.
Summary Orca provides a dedicated desktop IDE that runs multiple coding agent CLIs in isolated Git Worktrees rather than acting as a standalone AI model. Setting initial agent permissions to Manual prevents unintended file overwrites while you review proposed changes. Per-project setup scripts can automate dependency installation whenever Orca spins up a new worktree workspace.
summary: Learn how to install and configure Orca, a desktop IDE that isolates multiple CLI coding agents like Codex and Claude Code using Git Worktrees.
title: Setting Up Orca Desktop IDE to Manage Multiple AI Coding Agents

content:
AI dashboards often look oddly dated because every metric tries to be the main character. That is a classic failure mode of AI-generated UI: an engineer or PM builds something functional, yet in daily work it feels tiring to read. Cards sit crammed together with weak grouping and visual hierarchy, as if every data point is shouting at once. The simplest fix is to hand the AI a reference screenshot instead of nudging layout details one by one. Pass a well-structured dashboard image and tell the model: “Write the data logic yourself, and match the layout and information hierarchy in this image as closely as possible.” Design4Users is a strong source for this. Rather than flashy concept art, it collects practical UI structures that show how designers pare down dense data and group metrics without exhausting the reader. My go-to pattern puts the top-line numbers executives care about most in large type at the top, places trend charts underneath to add context, and leaves detailed item lists at the bottom. If you are not a UI specialist, deciding what to remove is much harder than deciding what to add, so starting from one clean reference saves hours of prompt trial and error.
AI-generated dashboards frequently feel crowded and tiring to scan. Trying to surface every available metric on the main screen creates visual fatigue, which stems from missing information priority rather than bad charting code.
Trimming Screen Clutter Fixing a broken dashboard layout by hand takes non-designers a long time, and asking an AI for a cleaner design through text prompts alone rarely works well. Supplying a strong visual reference solves both problems: let the AI write the data logic while instructing it to mirror the layout and spacing of a proven screenshot.
Good dashboard design depends on subtraction. Deciding what to remove matters more than deciding what to add, because clear screens rely on strict visual hierarchy.
Using the Design4Users Archive Design4Users curates practical UI structures rather than decorative mockups. Its examples demonstrate how experienced designers group complex data and arrange panels to reduce cognitive load.
A top-down summary layout works reliably across internal admin tools and user analytics views. Place the primary KPIs decision-makers check first in large cards at the top, position trend charts in the middle to show how those numbers move over time, and keep granular row-level lists at the bottom so the eye follows a natural reading path.
Proven Dashboard Design Examples Reviewing domain-specific dashboards offers concrete layout patterns you can reuse:
Fuselab Creative advanced analytics dashboard: pairs AI-driven widgets with clear demographic and regional breakdown charts. Virgil Pana SaaS table filter: organizes multi-column data sorting and filtering into a clean toolbar. Sigma Software Design health metrics dashboard: consolidates scattered patient and wellness indicators into a single readable view. Robin Holesinsky booking platform UI: links payment history directly with customer profiles. Conceptzilla logistics dashboard: simplifies multi-step order tracking into a focused operational workspace. Feeding a clean layout screenshot to your coding model speeds up frontend work far more than wrestling with text-only layout prompts from scratch.
Summary AI dashboards look cluttered when every metric competes for attention; effective screen design starts with deciding what to remove. Passing a proven reference screenshot and instructing the AI to mirror its layout beats iterating with text-only design prompts. Placing C-level summary metrics at the top, trend charts in the middle, and detailed record lists at the bottom gives operational dashboards a stable hierarchy.
summary: Instead of tweaking cluttered AI-generated dashboards through text prompts alone, feed verified UI reference images so the model copies a clear visual hierarchy.
title: Why AI Dashboards Look Cluttered and How Reference Images Fix Them
