Prompt library prompts.chat, which has earned over 160,000 stars on GitHub, just shipped a major update with more than 2,000 AI prompts. 1. Expanded prompt catalog - Provides 2,000+ prompts across coding, image generation, video, writing, learning, and business, backed by new categories, tags, filters, and search. 2. AI agent support - Adds 63 AI agent skills, 13 prompt chains for multi-step workflows, and a plugin for Claude Code.
prompts.chat, an open-source repository with more than 160,000 GitHub stars, has rolled out a major platform update. What began as a static collection of prompt templates now serves as a structured library for developers and practitioners managing multi-step AI workflows.
Major Expansion of the Prompt Library The update expands the catalog past 2,000 curated prompts spanning code generation, image synthesis, video editing, writing, and business operations. New tag systems and search filters make it straightforward to narrow down templates for a specific task.
Looking at an image upscaling prompt in the catalog illustrates the level of detail. The prompt instructs the model to raise resolution to 4K while preserving original facial structure, lighting, composition, and clothing, recovering fine details like skin pores, individual hair strands, and fabric weave.
It also pairs positive instructions with explicit negative constraints to prevent plastic-looking skin, distorted fingers, or shifts in perspective. Having concrete constraint patterns like these ready to inspect makes it much easier to adapt templates for production services.
AI Agents and Prompt Chaining Beyond single-turn queries, the update introduces 63 dedicated AI agent skills and 13 prompt chains for multi-step tasks. Each chain breaks a larger workflow into sequential stages.
Tool integration has expanded alongside the library. A new Claude Code plugin brings prompt templates and agent skills directly into terminal-based coding sessions for writing and reviewing code.
Each chain defines task context per step and passes the output of one stage cleanly into the input of the next, offering a practical reference for engineers designing LLM application pipelines.
Conditions for Effective Use The platform fits AI engineers and product planners who want concrete examples of how prompt constraints shape model behavior. Because different models respond differently to the same wording, tuning remains necessary.
Rather than copying templates verbatim, teams get better results by inspecting how each section constrains output and testing modifications against their own service data.
As an open-source catalog, prompts.chat gives teams a solid starting point when drafting domain-specific prompts and agent workflows.
Summary Open-source prompt libraries are moving beyond single-turn templates toward multi-step prompt chains and reusable agent skills. Domain-specific positive rules paired with explicit negative constraints remain key to consistent image and code generation. Terminal plugins for tools like Claude Code bring curated prompt and skill libraries directly into daily development workflows.
summary: Open-source prompt repository prompts.chat (160K+ GitHub stars) expands to over 2,000 prompts and adds 63 AI agent skills, 13 prompt chains, and a Claude Code plugin.
title: Major Update to 160K-Star Open-Source Library prompts.chat

content:
Streamlining Prompt Engineering Getting consistent outputs from an LLM often takes rounds of manual prompt edits. Edmond Francis proposes a Meta Prompt approach where the model designs the prompt itself based on a short description of your goal.
The meta-prompt assigns the model a ‘PromptMaster’ persona focused on precision, accuracy, and minimal hallucination. Instead of hand-tuning prompt techniques, users answer three brief questions and receive a ready-to-run prompt.
Core Structure of the Meta-Prompt The template requires every generated prompt to cover seven elements: Context, Persona, Format, Exemplars, Task, Tone, and Constraints. Defining each element explicitly keeps the target model aligned with the user’s intent.
Users only need to provide three inputs:
Exact goal and expected outcome Specific requirements (tone, length, format, examples, and similar details) Forbidden elements or patterns to avoid From those inputs, the AI applies step-by-step reasoning and self-critique before producing the final prompt. It wraps the output in <start of prompt/> and <end of prompt/> tags so you can copy and paste it directly into another tool.
Full Meta-Prompt Below is the complete meta-prompt from the original post.
You are PromptMaster, the world's most elite, meticulous, and results-obsessed prompt engineer. Your only mission is to craft the single most powerful, precise, and high-performance prompt possible that will force any frontier AI model to deliver exactly the outcome the user wants, with zero fluff, zero hallucination, and maximum accuracy. ============================= ELEMENTS YOU MUST INCLUDE ============================= Your precise, high-performance prompt must include: *Proper Context: Background information that helps the AI understand the situation, audience, or goal. * Persona: The perspective or expertise the AI should adopt * Format: The desired structure, length, and style of the output * Exemplars: Show the AI 1-3 few-shot examples of the desired output style or pattern. * Task: The specific, clear task/action you want completed * Tone: The style, voice, and feeling of the response * Constraints: Add rules to define the format and desired output ============================= USER INPUT ============================= You will ask the user to briefly describe: 1. Their exact goal / desired outcome 2. Any specific requirements (tone, length, format, style, constraints, examples they want included, etc.) 3. Any forbidden elements or things to strictly avoid Then, you will write the final optimized prompt for the user to achieve the exact result for their scenario. Think carefully step by step, and once you understand this prompt, do not add greetings, explanations, commentary, or anything else. Only ask the user to briefly describe the scenario and their end goal according to the three points above in this "USER INPUT" section. ======================================= THE OUTPUT FORMAT YOU MUST GIVE FOR THE PROMPT YOU CREATE ======================================= Your output response must consist of ONLY the final optimized prompt, wrapped in <start of prompt/> and <end of prompt /> elements, ready to copy-paste immediately. Do not add greetings, explanations, commentary, or any text outside the <start of prompt/> and <end of prompt /> elements under any circumstances. When crafting the prompt, apply every advanced technique possible: - Start with a one-line goal the model should achieve. - Assign a highly specific expert role with extreme competence. - Use step-by-step reasoning mandates (chain-of-thought, multi-step verification). - Specify exact output format down to the smallest detail (headings, bullet styles, markdown tables, etc.) - Add anti-hallucination guards and source-citation rules if relevant. - Use delimiters, placeholders, and strict structural instructions. - Force the model to critique and refine its own output before finalizing. - End with a clear “Begin your response now” trigger for the AI to follow. ======================== START ======================== You now have all the instructions. Use the content in this prompt as your source of truth. BEGIN YOUR RESPONSE NOW Prompt Optimization Techniques The template bakes in standard prompt engineering practices automatically. It enforces Chain-of-Thought reasoning, specifies Markdown or table formatting down to headings and bullets, and adds anti-hallucination guards alongside source-citation rules.
Ending generated prompts with a ‘Begin your response now’ trigger gives the target model a clear starting boundary and cuts down on trial-and-error drafting time.
Replacing manual prompt iteration with a reusable meta-prompt helps standardize prompt quality across everyday tasks.
Summary A structured meta-prompt reduces trial-and-error drafting and keeps LLM outputs consistent across tasks. Explicit persona assignment and step-by-step reasoning instructions improve response accuracy. Wrapping generated prompts in delimiter tags makes them easy to copy into downstream workflows.
summary: Feed a structured meta-prompt into an LLM like Claude to generate task-specific, low-hallucination prompts from three short user inputs.
title: Automating LLM Prompt Engineering with a Meta-Prompt

content:
Forecasting future trends from historical numbers alone hits a ceiling whenever real-world shifts start in unstructured events such as earnings releases or policy news. Researchers from Google and Pennsylvania State University proposed Nexus, a multi-agent time-series forecasting framework that reasons jointly over numerical series and unstructured text.
Bridging Time-Series Foundation Models and LLMs Existing time-series foundation models extrapolate numerical patterns well but stay blind to external news context, whereas large language models grasp causal narratives yet struggle at precise numerical forecasting. Instead of forcing a single monolithic model to do both, Nexus splits macro trajectory reasoning and micro step-by-step volatility analysis across specialized agents.
Three-Stage Multi-Agent Forecasting Pipeline Nexus organizes forecasting into three sequential stages:
First, the Historical Context Agent aligns raw multimodal inputs chronologically, linking past numerical inflection points to the textual events that triggered them without overwhelming downstream context windows.
Second, dual-resolution reasoning agents generate complementary outlooks: the Macro-Reasoning Agent sketches top-down trajectories across the full forecast horizon, while the Micro-Reasoning Agent evaluates short-term catalysts and step-level volatility from the bottom up.
Third, the Forecast Synthesizer Agent mathematically reconciles the macro and micro outlooks into a final point forecast with supporting rationale, while a Calibration Agent refines forecasting rules against past errors using walk-forward simulation backtesting so only guidelines validated across multiple historical windows survive.
Leakage-Free Evaluation and Results To prevent training-data leakage, the authors evaluated Nexus strictly on real-world data recorded after a January 2025 knowledge cutoff, forecasting US real estate indicators and closing stock prices of major companies using Gemini-3.1-Pro and Claude-4.5-Sonnet. On the real estate forecasting tasks, Nexus lowered average prediction error by 14.7-15.3% compared to standard Chain-of-Thought (CoT) baselines.
Summary Nexus overcomes pure numerical extrapolation limits by pairing time-series data with causal reasoning over unstructured text events. Splitting top-down macro trajectory agents from bottom-up micro volatility agents stabilizes multi-horizon predictions. Walk-forward simulation backtesting inside the Calibration Agent retains only repeatedly validated forecasting rules to guard against overfitting.
summary: Proposed by researchers at Google and Penn State, Nexus pairs numerical pattern recognition with unstructured text reasoning across a five-agent forecasting pipeline.
title: Nexus: Multi-Agent Time-Series Forecasting Combining Numbers and News

content:
Commissioning a custom portfolio website from a design agency easily runs $5,000, yet developers can ship the same visual polish on their own in about 2 hours with a disciplined stack. Moving past cookie-cutter templates comes down to locking layout hierarchy early and pairing fast component tooling with restrained motion.
Planning and Minimal Grid Layout Shipping quickly starts before opening an editor. Stripping away decorative clutter in favor of a minimal grid puts project work front and center, where typography scale and whitespace carry most of the visual weight. Spend no more than 15 minutes sketching core wireframes in Figma before moving straight into code.
Pairing Modern Frontend Build Tools Combining Next.js with Tailwind CSS keeps component authoring and styling fast without configuration tangles, especially when paired with accessible UI primitives. Exporting via static page generation also drops ongoing hosting costs to nearly zero.
Adding Subtle Motion and Polish Heavy scrolljacking hurts both frame rates and readability; gentle scroll-triggered fade-ins are enough to make a static page feel alive. A few lines of Framer Motion handle natural entrance transitions, followed by a pass across mobile and desktop breakpoints to tighten spacing.
One-Minute Deployment and Custom Domain Connecting the GitHub repository to Vercel or Netlify deploys the site onto a global CDN in about 1 minute, complete with custom domain routing and automatic SSL provisioning.
Summary A 15-minute Figma wireframe focused on typography and whitespace sets clean visual hierarchy before coding begins. Pairing Next.js static generation with Tailwind CSS speeds up component assembly while eliminating server hosting costs. Restrained Framer Motion transitions and 1-minute GitHub deployment on Vercel or Netlify take the portfolio live within 2 hours.
summary: Walk through a practical two-hour workflow for shipping a $5,000 agency-caliber portfolio site using Figma, Next.js, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion, and Vercel.
title: Building an Agency-Grade Portfolio Site in Two Hours

content:
batisay STT (Free) - App download: flow.bati.ai / Models: huggingface.co/collections/batiai/stt. Fine-tuned for Korean on top of OpenAI Whisper (large-v3-turbo): collected 25,000+ hours of Korean audio and trained on roughly 4,300 quality-filtered hours. Runs on-device via whisper.cpp + Metal with zero external audio upload. Domain CER (N=500 benchmark, lower is better): Casual conversation 3.0 / Call-center support 5.7 / General (clean) 7.0 / General (noisy) 8.3 / Meetings 8.9. Note: Call-center 5.7 is measured on an 8kHz call-center benchmark; long real-world calls currently sit around ~15% and are being improved. Usage: Drag an audio file into BatiFlow > Speech Recognition tab for automatic transcription, AI summary, and structured notes. CER numbers come from an internal N=500 evaluation set and serve as directional reference alongside public benchmarks. Speaker diarization is currently in beta (research preview).
Transcribing meeting recordings and support calls in Korean usually forces an awkward choice: stock open-source STT models stumble on colloquial Korean phrasing, while cloud APIs charge per minute and require uploading sensitive audio. batisay addresses both issues with a free on-device Korean STT engine built for MacBooks.
Fine-Tuning on Conversational Korean Audio Out-of-the-box Whisper models often hallucinate repeated phrases on spontaneous Korean speech and phone audio. The batisay team gathered 25,000 hours of Korean speech, filtered it down to 4,300 high-grade hours, and fine-tuned Whisper large-v3-turbo specifically for real-world Korean.
That curation cut repetition loops noticeably. Measured by CER (Character Error Rate) - wrong characters per 100 - the model scores 3.0 on casual conversation, 7.0 on clean general speech, and 8.9 on multi-speaker meeting recordings.
On-Device Execution with Metal Acceleration All inference runs locally on the user’s Mac through whisper.cpp paired with Apple Silicon Metal GPU acceleration, keeping confidential meetings and customer calls off external servers.
On an M4 MacBook Pro, a 7-8 minute phone recording transcribes in roughly 12 seconds, and a 50-minute meeting finishes in just over 1 minute - roughly 38x faster than real-time playback.
Drag-and-Drop Transcription and Summarization Dropping an audio file onto the speech recognition tab inside the BatiFlow desktop app triggers local transcription followed by automated AI summarization and note structuring. Speaker diarization is currently included as a research-preview beta, and 8kHz call-center recordings score a 5.7 CER while long-call accuracy continues to be tuned.
Domain CER (Lower Is Better) Casual Conversation 3.0 Call-Center Support (8kHz) 5.7 General (Clean) 7.0 General (Noisy) 8.3 Meeting Audio 8.9 Both the desktop app and model weights are available directly from the official site and Hugging Face.
Summary Fine-tuning Whisper large-v3-turbo on 4,300 curated hours selected from a 25,000-hour Korean corpus cuts colloquial transcription and repetition errors. Combining whisper.cpp with Apple Silicon Metal acceleration keeps all audio processing local with zero cloud uploads. An M4 MacBook Pro transcribes a 50-minute meeting in roughly 1 minute (~38x real-time), making private business transcription practical at zero marginal cost.
summary: batisay fine-tunes Whisper large-v3-turbo on 4,300 hours of conversational Korean and runs locally on MacBooks via whisper.cpp and Apple Silicon Metal acceleration.
title: batisay: Free On-Device Korean Speech-to-Text Tuned for Apple Silicon

content:
Running multiple AI coding tools side by side quickly scatters conversation histories and token bills across different folders. AgentsView collects local session logs automatically and surfaces them through both a web UI and CLI from a single zero-config binary.
Local-First Architecture and Automatic Session Discovery Written in Go as a standalone binary, AgentsView scans your machine on first launch to discover session logs from over 20 coding agents - including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Gemini CLI - and syncs them into a local SQLite database.
Everything stays on disk with no account sign-up or cloud telemetry. Opening http://127.0.0.1:8080 in a browser lets you search past prompts and inspect token consumption across tools in one place.
Core CLI Commands and Deployment Options Four CLI subcommands handle everyday daemon control and reporting:
agentsview serve: Starts the web server in the foreground. agentsview daemon start: Launches the background SQLite sync daemon. agentsview session list: Lists indexed sessions from the daemon or SQLite store. agentsview usage daily: Prints daily token and cost totals to the terminal. Installation takes a one-line shell script on macOS and Linux, a PowerShell command on Windows, or a single Docker container:
docker run --rm -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 \ -v agentsview-data:/data \ -v "$HOME/.claude/projects:/agents/claude:ro" \ ghcr.io/kenn-io/agentsview:latest You can also point AgentsView at custom local directories for tools like Devin CLI, or connect S3-compatible object storage to aggregate session and spend metrics from multiple developer workstations into one central AgentsView instance.
Summary AgentsView indexes coding agent histories into a local SQLite database without sending session data to external cloud servers. It auto-discovers and syncs local logs across more than 20 coding agents including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Gemini CLI. Optional S3-compatible storage sync lets teams roll up session and cost analytics across multiple development machines.
summary: AgentsView is a single-binary Go tool that discovers local logs from 20+ coding agents including Claude Code and Cursor to track sessions and token spend in SQLite.
title: AgentsView: Unified Local Session and Cost Tracking Across Coding Agents

content:
“Can AI coding build interfaces that feel as natural as an iPhone?” Design engineer Emil Kowalski (formerly Vercel and Linear) open-sourced “Skills for Design Engineers” to bring Apple-style fluid UI and motion principles into AI coding agents, quickly passing roughly 10,000 GitHub stars. What it does: Packaged as AI skills that Codex or Claude Code reference when building interfaces, covering immediate button press response, interruptible animations, swipe velocity continuity, subtler shadows and borders, and accessibility plus performance checks. Why it stands out: AI generates functional UI fast, yet the result often feels stiff and unmistakably AI-made - delayed button feedback, abrupt transitions, unnatural swipe physics, or identical boilerplate effects everywhere. These skills translate motion criteria from Apple WWDC sessions and real shipping products into rules and code patterns agents can follow. Core capabilities: Audits all animations on a screen, prioritizes awkward motion and UI issues, suggests exact files, durations, and easing curves to fix, adapts Apple interaction principles to web UI, and supports both redesigns and greenfield builds. Installation: Run npx skills@latest add emilkowalski/skills, then ask Codex or Claude Code to “make this screen feel as natural as iOS” or “audit the button response and transition animations.” Keep in mind: Attaching a skill does not automatically make every screen Apple-tier on its own; think of it as an expert design guide and checklist that steers the agent toward sharper interaction decisions. Takeaway: The gap in vibe coding is shifting from “can AI render a screen” to “can you teach AI the tactile details that make an interface feel natural.”
UI code generated by AI agents usually works on the first try yet still feels slightly off under the cursor or thumb - transitions snap abruptly, or button press states lag by half a beat. An open-source skill pack from design engineer Emil Kowalski bridges that polish gap by encoding interaction engineering rules directly for coding agents.
Closing the UI Polish Gap in AI-Generated Code Whether a web interface feels calm and responsive comes down to small craft decisions, especially around animation curves and shadow layering. Picking the wrong easing curve on an entrance transition or stacking heavy opaque borders immediately makes a layout feel rigid.
Drawing on interaction design work across developer platforms and collaboration tools, this repository packages concrete motion and styling heuristics as agent-readable checklists.
Five Skills for Natural Web Interactions The package equips AI coding agents with five focused skills that work standalone or together:
emil-design-eng provides foundational rules for animation and UI design decisions. review-animations audits existing UI code to flag stiff or jarring interactions. improve-animations scans the codebase and proposes an actionable motion improvement plan. animation-vocabulary gives developers and agents shared technical terms for specifying motion precisely. apple-design adapts Apple’s fluid motion principles to web interfaces. Adding Design Judgment to Your Repository Add the skill set to your local project with a single terminal command:
npx skills@latest add emilkowalski/skills Once installed, prompting Codex or Claude Code to refine a view directs the agent to check easing curves, interruptibility, and border contrast against the skill guidelines rather than falling back on generic CSS defaults.
Summary Injecting domain-expert interaction rules helps AI coding agents move past functional boilerplate toward polished UI craft. Checklist-driven skills give agents concrete motion vocabulary, easing curves, and review criteria instead of vague aesthetic prompts. Adapting Apple’s fluid interaction principles to the web sharpens micro-details like press feedback, swipe continuity, and view transitions.
summary: Emil Kowalski’s open-source skill pack gives coding agents like Claude Code and Codex concrete checklists and motion rules for fluid, Apple-grade web interfaces.
title: Skills for Design Engineers: Teaching AI Agents Apple-Caliber UI Motion

content:
Many developers upgrading to GPT-5.6 inside Codex have noticed an odd combination of shallower code edits and rapidly depleted API quotas. In most cases, the culprit is not the GPT-5.6 model itself, but default Codex system instructions and subagent orchestration settings. Adjusting config.toml and supplying a clean instruction file fixes both issues.
Removing the 30-Second Reporting Bottleneck in the System Prompt Codex’s default system prompt instructs the model to post a progress update every 30 seconds. Under that constraint, the model prematurely curtails its own reasoning token budget once chains of thought pass a certain length - execution logs show reasoning token counts repeatedly clipping along a predictable ceiling, holding back a frontier model like GPT-5.6.
Replacing the base system prompt removes the 30-second status mandate and grants explicit autonomy to finish the task within the turn, alongside rules to follow existing repository conventions and avoid unnecessary abstractions. Point config.toml to your replacement instructions file:
disable_response_storage = true model_instructions_file = 'path\gpt-base-instructions.md' Dropping the periodic status interruption restores full reasoning depth while cutting wasted status-turn tokens.
Controlling Subagent Spawning to Protect API Quota The second quota drain comes from subagent orchestration. Currently, spawn_agent does not cap reasoning effort or downgrade model tiers for child agents. A single top-level prompt can trigger recursive subagent spawning where dozens or hundreds of full-weight agents load context and invoke tools concurrently, burning through API limits in minutes.
Two config.toml patterns keep multi-agent spend bounded. The first switches back to the V1 multi-agent runner and caps spawn depth at 1 so child agents cannot spawn grandchildren:
[features] multi_agent = true multi_agent_v2 = false [agents] max_depth = 1 max_threads = 6 The second keeps V2 enabled while throttling concurrent threads per session to flatten burst traffic:
[features.multi_agent_v2] enabled = true max_concurrent_threads_per_session = 2 Before blaming a new model release for regressions or cost spikes, audit the harness prompts and concurrency defaults wrapping it.
Summary A 30-second progress-reporting rule inside Codex’s default system prompt prematurely clips GPT-5.6 reasoning tokens and degrades output quality. Unbounded spawn_agent recursion and thread concurrency in multi-agent mode can exhaust API quotas on routine tasks. Overriding model_instructions_file and capping subagent depth or thread count in config.toml stabilizes both reasoning quality and API spend.
summary: Fix truncated reasoning and runaway API quota drain on GPT-5.6 in Codex by replacing the 30-second reporting prompt and capping subagent spawning in config.toml.
title: Tuning Codex Settings to Preserve GPT-5.6 Quality and API Quota

content:
Introducing Three LLM Wikis - The Era of AI-Maintained Code Documentation
Reading unfamiliar codebases and keeping technical documentation current remains one of software engineering’s most neglected chores. A new wave of LLM wiki tools analyzes entire repositories to synthesize architecture overviews, diagrams, and API guides automatically, refreshing docs as code evolves.
Unlike traditional generators such as Doxygen or Docusaurus that rely on docstrings or hand-written Markdown, LLM wikis infer system structure directly from source files. Here is how three representative tools compare:
Category DeepWiki Google Code Wiki OpenWiki Delivery Runs immediately as SaaS Hosted by Google Runs as an open-source CLI Repo Scope Supports public repos (free tier) Supports public repos Supports private internal repos Security Posture Uploads code to external cloud Uses Google cloud infrastructure Runs inside local or air-gapped networks Key Strength Instant access via URL swap Auto-regenerates on code changes Manages context files for coding agents DeepWiki DeepWiki offers the lowest friction for exploring open-source projects: swapping github.com to deepwiki.com in your browser opens a generated wiki immediately with no sign-up.
It includes natural-language Q&A backed by line-level source citations and exposes an MCP server for AI coding agents. Its free tier covers public repositories only, while private repositories require a paid plan and send source code to external cloud servers - making it unsuitable for restricted proprietary code. Even with line citations, teams should cross-check major architectural decisions against the raw source.
Google Code Wiki Powered by Gemini, Google Code Wiki regenerates prose explanations and architecture diagrams automatically whenever commits land, preventing documentation drift. Every claim links directly back to the underlying source files so engineers can spot LLM hallucinations quickly.
Today it supports public repositories only, requires an unofficial CLI wrapper for custom automation, and remains in preview, meaning pricing or retention policies could shift later.
OpenWiki OpenWiki is an open-source CLI built for security-conscious and on-premises teams. Instead of uploading code to a third-party SaaS, it writes wiki files directly inside your repository and pairs with local LLMs for fully air-gapped operation.
Teams wire it into GitHub Actions for incremental doc updates and automated agent-context maintenance. Running it requires a local Node.js setup, an LLM connector, and careful local secret management for API keys.
In practice, DeepWiki fits instant open-source exploration, Google Code Wiki suits live-synced public projects, and OpenWiki serves private enterprise repositories where code cannot leave the network.
Summary Unlike static doc renderers, LLM wiki tools read source code directly to synthesize and update narrative architecture docs and diagrams. DeepWiki gives zero-install URL access for open-source repos, while OpenWiki pairs with local LLMs to support private and air-gapped enterprise codebases. Google Code Wiki uses Gemini to keep prose and diagrams synchronized with repository commits via direct file hyperlinks.
summary: Compare DeepWiki, Google Code Wiki, and OpenWiki across hosting model, repository support, security posture, and auto-sync workflows for code documentation.
title: Comparing Three LLM Wiki Tools That Turn Source Code into Living Docs

OpenAI overhauled its desktop application alongside the launch of its GPT 5.6 Sol lineup, mounting a direct challenge to the desktop agent territory Anthropic staked out with Claude Fable 5 and Cowork. Competition between the two labs has moved past browser chat tabs into owning the desktop workspace and instant web deployment.
Desktop App Overhaul and Agent-First Workspaces OpenAI folded its standalone Codex app into the main ChatGPT desktop app and placed its Work agent mode front and center, relegating the previous chat-only client under the name ChatGPT Classic. Users now manage both general knowledge work and software engineering from a single desktop interface.
Anthropic took an early lead earlier this year with Cowork on desktop and recently added cloud execution so tasks keep running even when a user shuts down their PC. OpenAI’s new Work mode ships with cloud execution built in from day one, narrowing Anthropic’s 6-month head start and raising the stakes across desktop, mobile, and web agent environments.
Model Benchmarks and Token Efficiency The two flagship models - GPT 5.6 Sol and Claude Fable 5 - trade leads depending on workload. On SWE-bench Pro, which measures autonomous software engineering, Claude Fable 5 leads decisively at 80.3% versus 64.6% for GPT 5.6 Sol, backed by Opus 4.8 and Sonnet 5 across Anthropic’s coding lineup.
GPT 5.6 Sol counters on web browsing, token efficiency, and price. It scores 90.4% on the BrowseComp web-agent benchmark, improves agentic coding token efficiency by 54%, and prices API input at $5 per 1M tokens - half the $10 per 1M input token rate of Fable 5, giving cost-conscious enterprise teams a serious trade-off to weigh.
Web Publishing: Sites vs. Artifacts OpenAI’s new Sites feature builds and deploys live websites to a hosted domain straight from chat, aiming at a different use case than Anthropic’s Artifacts. While Artifacts focuses on quick interactive single-page tools, trackers, and internal dashboards, Sites targets public-facing multi-page web publishing.
Build times and output scope reflect that split: Sites takes roughly 40 minutes to assemble a complete multi-page website, whereas Artifacts turns around a working single-page app in about 10 minutes. Choosing between them comes down to whether you need a fast internal dashboard or a hosted public site.
Summary Revamped desktop apps from OpenAI and Anthropic push AI competition beyond chat windows into OS-level agent workspaces with background cloud execution. Claude Fable 5 leads on SWE-bench Pro coding accuracy (80.3% vs. 64.6%), while GPT 5.6 Sol wins on BrowseComp (90.4%), token efficiency, and half-price API input rates. OpenAI Sites targets ~40-minute multi-page public web deployments, whereas Anthropic Artifacts excels at ~10-minute interactive single-page tools.
summary: Compare OpenAI’s revamped ChatGPT desktop app and GPT 5.6 Sol against Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Cowork across coding benchmarks, pricing, and web publishing.
title: Hands-On Comparison: GPT 5.6 Sol vs. Claude Fable 5 Desktop Apps

content:
Training a Personal Language Model in 30 Minutes with GPT-5.6: Designer and developer Pietro Schirano used a single GPT-5.6 prompt to build an end-to-end pipeline that trains a personal language model on his own iMessage chat history. 1. Highlights - GPT-5.6 generated the entire pipeline from data preprocessing through model training - Trained on roughly 8 million iMessage tokens to mimic the author’s texting style - Uses a compact decoder-only architecture with 1.38 million parameters across 4 Transformer layers - Pairs a custom 4,000-vocab BPE tokenizer with a 256-token context window - Completes full training in about 30 minutes on a Mac. 2. Takeaway - With modern coding models, an individual can design and train a custom small language model from scratch in half an hour using a published open-source walkthrough.
Experiments with personal, local-only language models are getting remarkably accessible. Using GPT to scaffold the training code, developer Pietro Schirano open-sourced a complete pipeline that trains a tiny Transformer on your own iMessage archive in under 30 minutes on a single Mac laptop.
Privacy-Safe Preprocessing and Pipeline Design Because personal message archives contain sensitive private conversations, the pipeline never touches the live Messages database directly. Instead, it copies the archive and opens SQLite in read-only mode, strips attachments, and masks sensitive strings and participant identifiers with HMAC hashing before tokenization.
Lightweight Model Architecture To train quickly on consumer hardware, the model uses a 1.38M-parameter, 4-layer decoder-only Transformer paired with a custom 4,096-token BPE tokenizer. Running on Apple’s MLX framework for Apple Silicon, full training across millions of chat tokens finishes on a Mac in under 30 minutes.
Clear Boundaries and Safe Local Storage This tiny model is a style mimic rather than a general assistant. It picks up personal phrasing, cadence, and favorite slang, but it cannot verify facts or handle multi-step reasoning. Because small models can still memorize verbatim snippets from private chats, trained weights and outputs should stay strictly on your local machine.
Summary A purpose-built 1.38M-parameter Transformer trained from scratch can capture an individual’s texting cadence without fine-tuning a massive foundation model. Read-only SQLite backups and HMAC pseudonymization keep sensitive message data local and protected during preprocessing. Apple Silicon acceleration via MLX finishes training across multi-million-token chat histories in about 30 minutes on a personal Mac.
summary: Build and train a 1.38M-parameter decoder-only Transformer on your own iMessage history in 30 minutes on Apple Silicon using MLX and read-only SQLite backups.
title: Training a Personal iMessage Transformer on a Mac in 30 Minutes

Grasping how public administrative systems fit together is difficult when the rules are scattered across dense statutes. A Korean civil servant recently published “Korea 100 Systems,” a project that uses AI to distill 100 major national administrative procedures into single-page visual process maps, turning institutional tacit knowledge into readable diagrams.
Expanding Domain Literacy with AI Rather than treating AI purely as a coding tool, the creator used it to accelerate cross-domain knowledge synthesis. Reading sprawling legal texts and translating them into structured flowcharts by hand would ordinarily take years; pairing domain review with AI compression shortened that cycle dramatically while sharpening domain literacy across unfamiliar agencies.
From Statutes to Real Workflows on a Single Page The catalog lays out the statutory basis and end-to-end operational flow - from initial filing to final disposition - for 100 core public systems. Both civil servants and everyday citizens can trace how administrative procedures actually move in practice, though the charts serve as a navigational reference rather than formal legal advice or binding statutory interpretation.
Administrative Transparency and Visual System Design Clear process maps also provide a blueprint for transparent digital government services. Connecting visual stage tracking to civil petition portals such as e-People (Korea’s national petition platform) could make multi-agency case handling much easier for citizens to follow, offering a practical template for other regulated industries.
Summary The project uses AI to synthesize complex legal and administrative domain knowledge into visual system maps. Condensing dense statutory text into single-page flowcharts improves public access to and transparency around 100 core government workflows. Human-AI collaboration cut years of manual process mapping into a manageable solo documentation effort.
summary: The Korea 100 Systems project uses AI to map complex Korean public administration statutes and workflows into single-page visual process diagrams.
title: Mapping 100 Korean Public Administrative Systems into Visual Charts with AI

Search user behavior is moving rapidly from scanning ten blue links to reading synthesized AI answers in services like Google AI Overviews and Naver AI Briefing. Ranking high in traditional results is no longer enough on its own; GEO (Generative Engine Optimization) focuses on getting your brand cited directly as a trusted source inside AI-generated responses.
How AI Search Reshapes Click-Through Rates Data from SEO analytics firm Ahrefs shows that when Google AI Overviews appear on a query, average click-through rate for the top-ranking organic page drops by roughly 58%, while overall link click share falls from 15% to around 8% because users get their answer directly from the summary.
Brands cited inside the AI answer tell the opposite story: cited sources see 35% more organic clicks and up to 91% more paid clicks than uncited competitors. Earning a source citation inside the generated answer now matters as much as traditional rank position.
Three Pillars of Channel-Specific Optimization Digital marketing agency Kinda Growth structures integrated SEO and GEO programs around three distinct search ecosystems:
On Naver, optimization restructures owned assets across Naver Blog, Cafe, Knowledge iN, and Place into clean, extractable formats that Naver AI Briefing and the AI Tab readily cite - even for brands without a standalone corporate website.
On Google, work centers on E-E-A-T (Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, and Trustworthiness), structured schema markup, and authoritative external references so Google AI Overviews and AI Mode treat key landing pages as primary evidence.
Across standalone LLMs including ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, teams open up AI crawler access and align third-party brand facts across wikis, review sites, communities, and press coverage so models see consistent signals.
New Performance Metrics and Four-Step Execution Because keyword rank tracking misses zero-click AI answers, Kinda Growth tracks Mention Rate, Citation Rate, and Share of AI Voice monthly across target prompts. Execution follows four stages: brand diagnosis, building citation-ready source pages, distributing corroborating facts across third-party channels, and ongoing metric tracking.
Summary With AI search summaries cutting top-rank organic click-through rates by roughly 58%, securing citations inside AI answers via GEO now drives brand traffic. Effective optimization adapts structured content and third-party corroboration separately for Naver, Google, and standalone LLMs like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. Measurement shifts from pure keyword rankings toward Mention Rate, Citation Rate, and Share of AI Voice.
summary: As search shifts from link lists to AI-generated answers, combined SEO and GEO strategies focus on earning brand citations across Naver, Google, and major LLMs.
title: Combining SEO and GEO for Brand Visibility in AI Search

AI agents increasingly run data analyses and generate charts on the fly, yet existing visualization grammars are often either too verbose for LLMs to emit cleanly or too cryptic for humans to tweak afterward. Microsoft open-sourced Flint, an intermediate visualization language built specifically to bridge AI agents and human editors.
An Intermediate Language Connecting AI and Humans Low-level specifications such as Vega-Lite require explicit definitions for axes, layouts, and scales, leaving plenty of room for LLM syntax and schema errors. Flint accepts just the dataset binding and high-level chart intent, while its compiler fills in layout and scale defaults automatically. The resulting spec stays compact enough for humans to read and edit directly.
Smart Compiler and Built-in Chart Templates Flint pairs a type-aware compiler that infers data formats and visual encodings with support for 46 chart types and 83 reference examples. Users specify the chart family and field mappings without wrestling with boilerplate layout templates.
Practical Fit for Data Analysis Agents Available on GitHub as an open-source library, Flint drops neatly into LLM-powered analytics pipelines to lower chart-generation failure rates. Support for complex interactive controls and custom animations is still being expanded, making it strongest today on clean statistical and business reporting charts.
Summary Flint automates low-level axis, scale, and layout configuration to cut chart-generation errors from AI agents. Its concise, human-readable specification lets users and LLMs collaborate on visual edits without verbose JSON schemas. Built-in support for 46 chart types and 83 examples makes it easy to embed in LLM data analysis pipelines.
summary: Microsoft open-sourced Flint, a concise chart specification language designed so both AI agents and humans can generate and edit visualizations reliably.
title: Microsoft Flint: An Intermediate Visualization Language for AI Agents

Data pipelines get brittle fast when structured tables mix with unstructured free text. fenic embeds large language model inference directly inside DataFrame operations so Python engineers can process relational columns and raw text through one unified API.
Ad-hoc regex scripts and glued-together prompt loops become painful to maintain in production. fenic turns AI operations into typed DataFrame pipelines that both human engineers and AI agents can inspect and execute reliably.
Combining SQL and Semantic Operators Alongside relational operations like select, filter, and join, fenic provides first-class semantic operators including extract, classify, and summarize. Under the hood, the query engine manages LLM calls automatically with built-in request batching, token cost accounting, and response caching.
Pipelines Built for Agent Collaboration Pipelines written in fenic stay maintainable as production code rather than throwaway notebooks. The engine includes an explain view for execution plans and row-level lineage tracking, and any pipeline can be exported directly as an MCP (Model Context Protocol) tool so external AI agents can invoke it on demand.
Companion CLI tooling smooths local development as well: fenic skill install teaches coding agents like Claude Code and Cursor fenic authoring conventions, while fenic check runs static analysis before execution - useful for data engineers cleaning messy application logs or support tickets.
Summary Treating LLM inference as native DataFrame operators removes custom prompt-orchestration boilerplate. Pipelines export directly as MCP tools so AI agents can run typed analytical queries on their own. Engine-level batching, response caching, and cost tracking handle production inference concerns out of the box.
summary: fenic integrates PySpark/SQL-style relational operations with LLM-powered semantic operators to process structured and unstructured data in typed pipelines.
title: fenic: A Semantic DataFrame Engine Combining LLMs and SQL

content:
Looking for a cleaner way than raw tmux sessions to juggle multiple AI coding tasks in parallel, the author of the original post set up an Orca ADE server on a Mac mini and shared a brief hands-on note. Below is how that workflow operates based on the official Orca documentation.
Task-Isolated Workspaces Orca provisions a dedicated Git worktree for every task, giving each run its own branch, working tree, and agent terminal. Multiple CLI agents can work against the same repository concurrently without stepping on each other’s uncommitted edits, while the terminal, code editor, preview browser, and diff viewer stay grouped per workspace.
Running on Remote Hardware Like a Mac mini Pointing Orca at a remote host offloads both the worktrees and agent processes onto that machine. You edit files and inspect diffs locally while the remote Mac mini handles heavy builds and agent execution. According to the documentation, remote tasks keep running even if your laptop disconnects and resume cleanly when you reconnect.
During review, you compare changes against the base branch and leave inline diff comments that feed straight back to the agent. Because Orca isolates workspaces rather than guaranteeing passing builds on its own, running verification commands and checking final test results remains the developer’s responsibility.
Summary The source post highlights a smooth parallel AI coding setup running an Orca server on a dedicated Mac mini. Official Orca documentation centers its workflow around per-task Git worktrees, persistent remote execution, and inline diff review. Worktrees keep concurrent file edits isolated, while developers still run final tests and verification per task.
summary: Starting from a developer’s Mac mini server setup, explore how Orca ADE isolates parallel agent tasks using Git worktrees, remote execution, and diff reviews.
title: How Orca ADE Runs Parallel Coding Agents on a Mac mini

content:
New harnesses and wrapper loops for AI coding agents appear almost weekly, leaving engineers wondering whether these extra layers actually produce better software or just burn more tokens. CopyEval is a benchmark built to test coding agent harnesses under realistic development tasks.
Three Criteria Testing Agent Limits CopyEval scores agent harnesses across three axes: problem-solving accuracy, alignment with user intent, and cost efficiency. Tasks start from natural-language requirements verified against hidden test suites, paired with an evaluator-agent feedback loop that critiques intermediate builds.
Alongside pass rates, the benchmark tracks total token consumption and dollar cost across five harness setups: bare-agent, superpowers, opencode, oh-my-openagent, and headroom, using requirements extracted from open-source projects including 2048, hugo, and wordle.
What the Experiments Reveal About Harnesses The benchmark results show that a harness cannot overcome a capability gap in the underlying base model. Problem-solving scores depend overwhelmingly on which LLM powers the run, while harnesses contribute only minor gains within the same model tier.
Cost measurements surfaced sharp trade-offs as well. Stronger Sonnet models used fewer tokens than Haiku yet cost more overall due to higher per-token pricing. Meanwhile, oh-my-openagent delivered average task scores while burning an unusually high volume of tokens.
Even headroom, which markets aggressive token savings, preserved accuracy but delivered far smaller cost reductions on real coding tasks than advertised.
Constraints and Noise in Realistic Benchmarks Running realistic agent evaluations also exposes measurement noise and sandbox friction. When grading UI tasks via raw pixel-diff scores alone, agents struggle to infer concrete CSS fixes and spin without converging. Sandboxed network blocks and pinned toolchains also trigger environment build failures unrelated to code quality, and identical builds can score differently depending on measurement timing.
Even with those constraints, CopyEval gives teams building internal agent loops a grounded way to weigh marginal accuracy gains against real token spend.
Summary Coding agent problem-solving performance is governed primarily by the underlying LLM rather than the surrounding harness. Several agent harnesses spin in unproductive retry loops on unsolvable tasks, driving up token spend without improving pass rates. Realistic agent benchmarks must contend with evaluation noise from pixel-only UI feedback, network-isolated sandboxes, and fixed toolchains.
summary: CopyEval evaluates AI coding agent harnesses and loop systems across problem solving, user intent alignment, and token cost efficiency.
title: CopyEval: Benchmarking Whether Coding Agent Harnesses Actually Help

Drafting a product spec in ChatGPT and copying code back and forth into a local editor gets tedious fast. Integrating ChatGPT directly with the Codex desktop app removes that copy-paste loop, turning planning, rendering, and UI revision into a single continuous workflow.

The Sites feature renders web pages immediately and generates shareable URLs without separate hosting setup. content:
I build DataNexus with several coding agents running at once. Claude Code fixes router logic while Codex fills in test coverage.
The workspace was the problem. With one checkout and multiple terminals, agents step on each other’s files. One reinstalls dependencies while another’s build breaks mid-run. I juggled stashes for a while, then gave up and ran them one at a time. Agents I added for parallelism were running serially.
Splitting the workspace with git worktree Branch switching shares a single directory across branches. git worktree does the opposite: one repository, a separate directory per branch.
repo (datanexus) └─ base ref: origin/main ├─ worktree: fix-nl2sql-timeout ← branch + directory + terminal ├─ worktree: semantic-layer-v2 └─ worktree: rbac-audit One task, one worktree, one agent. Agent A can tear through node_modules without touching agent B’s build. Isolation comes first; parallelism only works after that.
Orca turns this structure into a desktop app You can manage worktrees by hand, but once tasks pile up, tracking which agent runs in which directory becomes its own chore. Orcais an open-source desktop app that takes over that bookkeeping. Stably, a YC-backed team, built it and released it under the MIT license. It runs on macOS, Windows, and Linux, and the GitHub repo had passed 16,000 stars when I wrote this.
One task = one git worktree = one agent terminal = one browser tab
That equation is Orca’s unit of work. Add a repo and the default branch becomes the base ref. Name a task and Orca creates a real git worktree and checks out the branch. You can always cd into the directory and use plain git, so the tool never locks you in.
Installation on macOS is one line:
brew install --cask stablyai/orca/orca On first launch it offers to import ~/.claude and ~/.codex. Subscription auth carries over, so my existing Claude Code setup came up without re-login. Presets cover more than 25 agents, from Claude Code and Codex to Cursor CLI, and you can register any custom CLI.
The race: three different models on one task The official recipeis a race. Create three worktrees for the same task, assign Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor CLI, and paste the same prompt into all three. Watch them side by side in split panels, pick the best result, and delete the losing worktrees along with their branches.
I was skeptical at first because I had dropped this pattern in post 9. Generating three SQL candidates from the same model produced identical results 92% of the time, and the selector never overturned the first candidate. More candidates meant nothing without diversity.
The race starts from a different premise. The models themselves differ, so the approaches actually diverge. Give them the same refactoring task and one extracts an interface while another reshapes the inheritance tree. That is post 9’s lesson seen from the other side: multi-candidate lives or dies on candidate diversity, not candidate count, and model heterogeneity is the most reliable source of that diversity.
It does burn three times the tokens. For fixes with one obvious path it is waste, so I reserve it for problems where the design could go several ways. Losing worktrees disappear with one click, branch and all, which keeps the cost of trying low.
Diff review becomes the next prompt The deciding evidence is the diff. Orca lets you drop markdown comments on any diff line, batch them, and send them back to the agent. Comments like “early return here” or “this test misses an edge case” become the next iteration’s prompt as-is.
Post 11argued that AI answers need their evidence on screen. The same principle applies to development: a human makes the merge call, no matter which agent wrote the code. Commit, push, PR review, and CI checks all happen inside the app, and Linear or Jira issues open directly as worktrees.
The features that stuck Each worktree gets its own Chromium window. In Design Mode, clicking a UI element sends its HTML, CSS, and a cropped screenshot straight into the agent prompt. Explaining a visual bug in words used to take longer than the fix; now it is one click. Heavy jobs can move to a remote machine over SSH worktrees, and per-worktree checkpoints give you a way back when an agent goes off the rails.
There is also an orchestration feature where a top-level agent delegates work to agents in child worktrees. It is still experimental: you enable it under Settings > Experimental, and it ships as the orca orchestration CLI plus an agent skill.
Code stays local. Nothing goes to Stably’s servers, and you can turn telemetry offin settings.
What I am still figuring out Deciding which tasks deserve a race is still gut feel. It takes judgment to spot problems where designs will genuinely diverge. A few weeks of use should give me adoption rates by task type, and I will revisit this with token costs alongside those numbers.

The workspace was the problem. With one checkout and multiple terminals, agents step on each other’s files. One reinstalls dependencies while another’s build breaks mid-run. I juggled stashes for a while, then gave up and ran them one at a time. Agents I added for parallelism were running serially.

content:
Optimizing Project Environments with /checkup As a Claude Code project grows, accumulated skills, instructions, and hooks start eating into both context window space and response latency. The /checkup command automates routine workspace housekeeping that developers previously had to audit by hand.
Key Capabilities and Workflow Running /checkup inspects your current project setup and applies five targeted cleanups:
Removes unused skills, MCP servers, and plugins to free up context tokens Eliminates duplicate instructions between local CLAUDE.md files and checked-in repository files Splits an oversized root CLAUDE.md into scoped subdirectory CLAUDE.md files and modular skills Identifies and disables slow hooks Prompts you to update to the latest Claude Code release when behind Large repositories quickly bloat the baseline prompt sent on every turn, so pruning stale configuration keeps token spend under control.
Operational Benefits Keeping project instructions modular pays off on long-running team repositories. Breaking a monolithic CLAUDE.md into directory-scoped files ensures agents load only relevant context and lowers ongoing maintenance friction.
Disabling sluggish hooks also cuts per-turn wait times so interactive coding sessions stay responsive. Running /checkup periodically is an easy habit for keeping a daily-driver Claude Code workspace lean.
Summary Claude Code’s /checkup command automates context cleanup and removes unused skills, MCP servers, and plugins. Deduplicating and splitting a monolithic root CLAUDE.md keeps instructions maintainable as repositories scale. Detecting and disabling slow hooks reduces turn latency across everyday LLM coding workflows.
summary: Claude Code adds a /checkup command that removes unused resources, deduplicates and splits CLAUDE.md files, and disables slow hooks.
title: Managing Claude Code Projects with the /checkup Command

content:
The term Loop Engineering has started appearing frequently across AI engineering discussions. At first glance it can sound like vendor rebranding for standard agent orchestration, yet a closer look shows it reframes Harness Engineering around day-two operational control.
What Loop Engineering Focuses On Instead of crafting better single-turn prompts, Loop Engineering designs the recurring execution cycle itself. Rather than waiting for a human to issue each command and inspect the output, the system discovers work, executes, verifies results, and logs state on its own - adding explicit repeat conditions and halt rules on top of an underlying agent harness.
Five Questions for Loop Design Five operational questions separate genuine loop engineering from a basic automated script:
What triggers the loop to start? What defines completion? Does verification rely on deterministic tests or an evaluator model? When does the system halt on failure or budget overrun? What state is persisted for the next run? Without clear answers to those five points, a system remains a loose agentic workflow. Higher-order meta-loops where the system modifies its own harness belong to AgentOps or eval-driven operations.
Applying Loops in Production Because production teams still cannot trust raw agent outputs blindly, auto-mutating harnesses carry too much risk today. A practical rollout starts with trace analysis, routes proposed changes through human approval, and deploys updates incrementally. Loop engineering is less a brand-new paradigm than the discipline of defining clear start, verification, and stop boundaries around existing harness components.
Summary Loop engineering layers explicit operational repeat and stop rules on top of an agent harness execution environment. Clear completion criteria, verification methods, failure/budget circuit breakers, and persisted state separate real loops from basic agentic workflows. Meta-loops that automatically refine the harness itself fall under AgentOps and eval-driven operations.
summary: Compare loop engineering with harness engineering and examine the five operational questions that separate real agent loops from basic workflows.
title: From Harness Engineering to Loop Engineering

content:
“Go and boil the sea.” Last week at the AI Engineering World’s Fair, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan gave a 20-minute talk distilling YC’s AI-Native playbook - opening with hard numbers, laying out a concrete methodology, and closing with a bold vision, backed by the fact that YC has funded 94 seed-stage companies that went on to pass $100M (roughly 150 billion KRW) in annual revenue. “Boil the ocean” used to be shorthand for impossibly wasteful scope, yet now is the exact moment to do it. 1. FOMO - Why act now / The numbers: “If you don’t do it, your competitor will gladly eat your lunch.” Garry Tan is rebuilding 20-year-old YC itself as an AI-native org, aiming for 1 person to do what used to take 1,000 - literally, not metaphorically. His personal coding output jumped 400x while still running YC full-time; even penalizing heavily for AI verbosity and scaffolding, that is 8x-80x, while still picking up his kids at 5 PM. Someone getting 2x and someone getting 100x use the exact same Claude, the same weights, and the same API - the multiplier lives not in the weights, but in the wiring. One quarter of the YC Winter 2025 batch had 95%+ AI-generated codebases and became the fastest-growing, most profitable cohort in YC history by treating AI as a workforce rather than an assistant. Examples: Emergence hit 9-figure ARR 8 months after launch and passed $15M with 15 employees; Retail hit $60M with 40 employees - revenue per employee unseen in software, oil, or railroads. 2. Methodology - Rebuilding the org in Markdown: Everything learned building agents maps 1:1 to org design. Skill = one clearly documented capability or job role anyone can run. Resolver table = the org chart and routing rules deciding which .md file handles incoming work (for example, loading tests.md whenever test files change). Filing rules = internal process checks ensuring the resolver complies with rules. Trigger eval = performance evaluation verifying tests.md actually loads. Writing Markdown files is building the organization: sitting in front of Claude Code means hiring, training, and managing a Markdown workforce rather than just writing software. At YC, media, events, and finance staff who had never opened a terminal now write skills and cron jobs; one finance team member consolidated hundreds of Excel workbooks into a single app backed by a Company Brain and agents. “It is not because we work harder, but because we run a different kind of organization.” 3. Computation - Separate where compute happens: Most AI engineering bugs happen when deterministic work and latent-space work live in the wrong place. Latent space handles taste, judgment, and ambiguous intent (steered via Markdown); deterministic space handles state, arrays, and logic in code. For Startup School seating of 800 people, keeping seat arrays in deterministic code outside the context window while letting the LLM handle human seating judgment turned a month-long chore into 10 minutes and a few hundred dollars in tokens. 4. Working memory - The library and the librarian: Human working memory holds roughly 7 items (why phone numbers had 7 digits). An AI agent’s 1M-token window holds 3 Harry Potter books at once - huge yet tiny compared to a whole company library of emails, meetings, decisions, customer calls, and postmortems. Whether an agent acts like a genius or a goldfish depends on who picks which 3 books sit on the desk: Context Engineering, where the Company Brain acts as both library and librarian. Search/RAG is only the primitive; the hard part is deciding what to record, how to link it, what to promote to working memory versus cold reference, and how to resolve conflicting facts. Without curation, a brain becomes a searchable landfill, so the real primitive is memory plus hygiene. 5. Personal signature habit - “Never do one-off work”: When an agent produces a great result, skillify it immediately; asking twice means the system failed. Organizations that preserve learning compound daily instead of waking up with amnesia. Model quality is rented, whereas the brain you build belongs to you. 6. What defines an AI-Native company: Small flat teams, skill files for everything, founders who still write code, and a compounding Company Brain. Tools matter less than concepts - if OpenClaw is a Ferrari, Codex is a great Honda that still gets you 90% of the way there if you follow 4 rules: (1) separate where computation happens, (2) use skill files as employees, (3) build a library and librarian, and (4) never do one-off work. 7. What to build at 25 - Memory Layer: Every company will soon need a memory layer, which is why Garry Tan open-sourced GBrain under the MIT license while inviting founders to build category-defining companies in personal context and company memory. 8. Vision - Boil the sea: A friend of Garry Tan built an 80,000-Markdown-file brain for his son’s rare epilepsy, pushing right up to the frontier of medical knowledge with just one father, a laptop, and a library - proving we can now fix bug-ridden codebases, read massive archives, and boil the ocean.
The Rise of AI-Native Organizations “Boiling the ocean” used to be a warning against impossible scope; today it describes what small teams with AI workforces actually take on. At the AI Engineering World’s Fair, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan shared how YC is restructuring its own 20-year-old operations around AI-native design.
Across YC’s portfolio, 94 seed-funded companies have surpassed $100M in annual revenue, and a quarter of the Winter 2025 batch shipped codebases that are 95-99% AI-generated. Treating AI as an autonomous workforce rather than a typing assistant changes the revenue-per-employee ceiling of a company.
Designing an Organization in Markdown An AI-native organization encodes repeatable operations into Markdown skill files. Each job capability is written down clearly enough for an agent to execute, a resolver table routes incoming tasks to the matching skill file, filing rules check process compliance, and trigger evaluations verify that the right skills load when expected.
This pattern extends well beyond engineering. Finance, events, and media teams at YC pair a shared Company Brain with scheduled agents to automate recurring operations, shifting human contributors from manual execution to managing and refining agent skills.
Separating Computation and Curating Memory Most reliability bugs in AI systems come from mixing up where computation belongs. Ambiguous judgment and intent interpretation belong inside the model’s non-deterministic latent space, whereas state tracking, arrays, and strict business logic belong in deterministic code outside the context window.
Long-term agent quality then depends on the memory layer. Raw RAG search is only a starting point; without active memory hygiene - deciding what to store, what to promote into working memory, and how to reconcile conflicting records - an internal knowledge base degrades into noise. Turning every successful one-off task into a reusable skill lets organizational knowledge compound day after day.
Summary AI-native companies scale output by encoding repeatable roles and routing rules into Markdown skill files. Reliable AI engineering separates non-deterministic model judgment from deterministic state and business logic in code. Beyond basic search, curating memory hygiene and converting one-off tasks into reusable skills lets a company brain compound over time.
summary: Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan outlines how AI-native companies encode operations into Markdown skills and build a curated company memory layer.
title: Boil the Sea: Principles of AI-Native Organization Design

content:
Modern LLM agent harnesses increasingly treat Goal definitions as a first-class feature. Rather than relying on a human to re-prompt the model after every attempt, goal-driven harnesses let the agent iterate on its own until completion criteria are satisfied.
Shifting from Manual Prompts to Loop Design An agent loop repeats a task cycle until the target state is reached. Previously, whenever an output fell short, a developer stepped back in with a follow-up prompt in a classic HITL (human-in-the-loop) workflow. Loop engineering moves the developer out of that inner retry cycle: instead of rewriting prompts on every turn, engineers define the rules that tell the agent when to keep going and when to stop.
Setting Clear, Verifiable Goals An agent can only decide whether to stop if its goal translates into a checkable signal. Vague expectations need to become concrete metrics. When asking an agent to replicate a website’s visual theme, for instance, specifying a color-palette match rate of 90% or higher gives the verification step a clear pass/fail threshold; anything below triggers another iteration automatically.
Even qualitative tasks benefit from proxy metrics. Instead of asking for “good restaurants for a team dinner,” requiring at least 10 blog reviews containing specific group-dining keywords turns subjective taste into a verifiable condition that keeps the loop grounded.
Validator Personas and Maximum Turn Limits When a task resists simple numeric scoring, teams separate generation from evaluation using a worker-validator subagent pattern. An LLM that just produced an artifact tends to grade its own work generously. Spawning a separate validator agent in a fresh context window with a strict reviewer persona and explicit acceptance checklist yields much sharper filtering.
Every autonomous loop also needs a hard cap on maximum turns. If acceptance criteria are too strict, an agent will burn tokens retrying indefinitely. Setting a maximum iteration count at launch bounds worst-case cost - a safeguard most open-source agent harnesses now build in by default.
Summary Moving beyond manual HITL prompting requires loop rules that let agents evaluate progress and retry autonomously. Subjective goals become controllable when translated into concrete proxy metrics or checked by an isolated worker-validator subagent. Enforcing a strict maximum turn count prevents over-strict validation criteria from causing infinite loops and runaway token spend.
summary: Learn how to design autonomous LLM agent loops using measurable Goal definitions, worker-validator separation, and strict maximum turn limits.
title: Implementing Agent Loop Engineering with Measurable Goals

content:
OfficeCLI: Automate Word, Excel, and PowerPoint Without Installing Office. AI agents can now create, inspect, and edit Office files directly without PowerPoint or Excel installed on the machine. iOfficeAI’s open-source OfficeCLI gives agents a CLI-based document automation workflow for Word, Excel, and PowerPoint. Previously, generating or modifying Office documents usually required Microsoft Office, Python scripts, and extra runtime dependencies. OfficeCLI ships as a single executable binary across Mac, Windows, and Linux, automating document workflows with zero Office installation.
AI agents increasingly need to generate and revise real business documents rather than plain Markdown alone. Historically that meant wrestling with desktop Office installations or brittle library dependencies, a gap OfficeCLI addresses with a standalone open-source binary.
Single-Binary Architecture Without Office Dependencies OfficeCLI runs without Microsoft Office installed and ships as a single executable binary for Mac, Windows, and Linux. Because it needs no external Python or language runtime, teams can drop it straight into containerized or local agent environments with a one-line download command.
Visual Feedback Loops via Built-in Rendering For an AI agent to format slides or spreadsheets well, it needs to see what it produced. OfficeCLI embeds its own HTML rendering engine that converts generated Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files into HTML or PNG snapshots.
Vision-capable agents inspect those rendered PNGs, spot overlapping text or broken layouts, and fix formatting issues in a closed feedback loop without relying on rigid pre-made templates.
Coding Agent Integration and Simple Commands OfficeCLI integrates directly with AI coding agents including Claude Code, Cursor, and Windsurf. Running the installer detects local coding tools and registers its skill file automatically, or an agent can read curl -fsSL https://officecli.ai/SKILL.md to configure itself.
Commands stay readable and shell-friendly - for example, officecli create deck.pptx initializes a blank presentation - so agents manipulate documents through standard CLI calls rather than verbose SDK code.
Users who prefer a graphical chat interface can pair it with the companion desktop app AionUi, which translates natural-language document requests into OfficeCLI commands under the hood.
Summary OfficeCLI automates Word, Excel, and PowerPoint creation and editing from a single cross-platform binary with no Microsoft Office or runtime dependencies. A built-in HTML/PNG rendering engine lets multimodal AI agents visually inspect generated pages and self-correct layout bugs. Skill files plug directly into Claude Code, Cursor, and Windsurf so agents control Office files via clean shell commands.
summary: OfficeCLI is a single-binary open-source CLI tool that lets AI agents create, inspect, and edit Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files without installing Microsoft Office.
title: OfficeCLI: Let AI Agents Edit Office Documents Without Microsoft Office

content:
Engineers running Claude Fable 5 often hit rate and token quotas far sooner than expected. Keeping everything on the heaviest configuration burns budget fast; tuning reasoning effort and splitting responsibilities across model tiers cuts usage dramatically without sacrificing output quality.
Lowering Costs via Thinking Effort Settings Dropping the thinking mode from max to high immediately trims per-task spend. On the DeepSWE benchmark, accuracy between max and xhigh barely differs, while task cost drops from $22 on max to $13 on xhigh.
Stepping down to high brings task cost to $9 with less than a 1% dip in benchmark performance, making high a strong default for daily engineering. Sonnet 5, by contrast, currently offers poor cost-to-performance value for this setup.
Splitting Model Roles and Enforcing Control Hooks Rather than running Fable 5 solo for every action, a three-tier setup reserves Fable 5 strictly for high-level planning and task decomposition, delegates code implementation to Opus 4.8, and routes routine chores to Haiku.
Instead of relying on soft instructions in CLAUDE.md, environment hooks enforce this hierarchy directly so subagents cannot escalate back into orchestrator calls and waste tokens. Developers toggle orchestration control as needed with fable on and fable off.
Production Results and Continuity With role delegation and high effort in place, long coding sessions barely dent usage quotas. Across 10 hours of continuous work, 5-hour window consumption stayed around 25%, while weekly quota usage hovered near 7%.
Because the workflow follows Anthropic’s multi-agent delegation pattern, the Opus 4.8 and Haiku tiers keep running smoothly even if Fable 5 quota runs out.
Summary On DeepSWE benchmarks, high thinking effort cuts cost by over 40% compared to max and xhigh with less than a 1% performance drop. A three-tier split - Fable 5 for planning, Opus 4.8 for coding, and Haiku for routine tasks - keeps heavy tokens off boilerplate work. Enforcing delegation through environment hooks rather than CLAUDE.md prevents subagent re-orchestration overhead, with fable on/off switches for manual control.
summary: A practical orchestration guide to reducing Claude Fable 5 token costs by up to 90% by tuning thinking effort and delegating work across Opus 4.8 and Haiku.
title: Cutting Claude Fable 5 Token Usage by 90% Through Role Delegation

content:
Every message sent in Claude Code carries a hidden token tax. Unused tool schemas and bundled system instructions ride along on every turn, often billing tens of thousands of tokens before your actual prompt even starts. A few lines of configuration can strip out that overhead.
Start by measuring where your context goes. Running /context inside a terminal session breaks down context window usage by category, showing just how much space tool definitions occupy.
For a byte-level breakdown, run a local logging proxy (proxy.mjs) and point ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to your local endpoint. Sorting the captured tool schemas by byte size makes it obvious which definitions to cut first.
Disabling Unused Features via Configuration Adding disable flags to settings.json removes heavy feature groups in one step. Place global defaults in ~/.claude/settings.json or scope rules per repository in .claude/settings.json:
disableBundledSkills: Removes built-in skills such as data visualization and code review. disableWorkflows: Removes the workflow tool, one of the single largest token consumers. disableRemoteControl: Removes remote-control tool definitions. Removing Specific Tools and Common Pitfalls To drop individual tools, list them in the permissions.deny array. Add EnterPlanMode and ExitPlanMode if you skip plan mode, NotebookEdit if you do not work with Jupyter notebooks, and SendMessage if you do not need agent notifications.
One detail matters here: specify the bare tool name so Claude Code omits the entire JSON schema from the request payload. If you qualify the rule with sub-options or path patterns just to restrict execution scope, Claude Code blocks invocation at runtime while still sending the full tool schema on every turn.
Restart Claude Code after saving settings.json and run /context again to verify the drop in baseline token usage.
Summary Claude Code sends unused tool schemas and bundled instructions with every API turn, inflating baseline token consumption. Setting disable flags and permissions.deny entries in settings.json strips unneeded tool definitions from the request payload. Denying the exact tool name - rather than a scoped sub-pattern - is required to exclude the schema itself and save tokens.
summary: Cut tens of thousands of wasted per-turn tokens in Claude Code by disabling unused bundled skills, workflows, and tool schemas in settings.json.
title: Trimming Claude Code System Prompt Bloat to Cut Token Waste

content:
Complex engineering work rarely resolves in a single prompt. Real tasks move through research, planning, execution, and verification. Oh My Hermes (OMH) adds a structured workflow layer on top of Hermes Agent to organize those stages.
How OMH Works OMH installs as a runtime skill package without overwriting your existing Hermes Agent configuration. When a user submits a request in natural language, OMH proposes an appropriate workflow path and coordinates coding subagents such as Codex or Claude Code.
Code-heavy tasks pass through an explicit Handoff gate before touching the execution environment. Because code runs only after user approval, OMH prevents unintended edits and premature execution.
Core First-Value Skill Packs OMH ships with five First-value packs designed for common engineering workflows:
Frontend Rescue - Fixes web UI layout issues and runs visual QA checks. Repo First-Win - Maps out an unfamiliar repository and identifies safe, PR-sized improvements. Failure-to-Fix - Triages failing CI builds, tests, or deployment signals and prepares targeted fixes. Visual Deliverable - Turns pull requests or release notes into formatted docs, slide decks, or PDFs. Toolbelt Readiness - Checks that local CLI tools, MCP hosts, and credentials are ready before a workflow starts. Supporting skills including web-research, ultragoal for long-horizon task tracking, and code-review work alongside these packs. Checking local tool readiness up front noticeably lowers mid-run failure rates.
Installation and Initial Setup You can install OMH and register its Hermes skills directly from the terminal:
# Run the OMH installer script curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rlaope/oh-my-hermes/main/install.sh | sh # Configure the environment and run health checks omh setup omh doctor # Add and install the Hermes skill pack hermes skills tap add rlaope/oh-my-hermes hermes skills install rlaope/oh-my-hermes/skills/oh-my-hermes --yes Running omh doctor after installation verifies local binaries and permissions, cutting out setup guesswork before you launch multi-agent tasks.
