Git Version Control and AI-Assisted Drafting Because decks live as plain text files, Git workflows apply naturally. Unlike binary PPTX files, teammates review line-by-line diffs in pull requests, merge edits cleanly without emailing final_v3.pptx attachments around, and keep a full commit history.
Plain Markdown also pairs cleanly with AI coding tools: feeding meeting notes or design specs into an LLM API or Claude Code generates a structured Marp draft in seconds.
Fast Exports for Internal Tech Talks For architecture reviews and internal engineering seminars where clarity beats flashy animations, Marp exports straight to PDF, PPTX, or HTML from the same source file. Custom CSS themes carry over across talks via simple copy-paste, and built-in syntax highlighting plus math typesetting keep code snippets and formulas sharp on screen.
Trading heavy GUI slide editors for a single version-controlled Markdown file turns presentation prep back into straightforward technical writing.
Summary Marp renders slide layouts automatically from plain Markdown (# headings and --- page breaks) so engineers focus on substance over pixel nudging. Text-based decks support line-level Git diffs, clean branch merges, and PR-style peer review. Markdown syntax integrates directly with LLM APIs and CLI agents like Claude Code for rapid slide drafting and PDF/PPTX/HTML export.
summary: How engineers use Marp to generate PDF, PPTX, and HTML slide decks from plain Markdown with Git diffs and AI-assisted drafting.
title: Building Technical Slide Decks from Plain Markdown with Marp

content:
Alibaba has open-sourced OCR, an AI code review system battle-tested over 2 years by tens of thousands of internal developers. Built to address recurring failure modes in general-purpose coding agents - such as silently skipping files on large PRs or miscalculating diff line numbers - OCR draws a hard boundary between deterministic code and LLM reasoning.
Where General-Purpose Coding Agents Struggle on PRs Off-the-shelf agents such as Claude Code or Codex hit predictable snags during large pull-request reviews. On wide diffs, models often skip files on their own, leaving silent coverage gaps. Models also miscount hunk offsets and post comments on the wrong lines, while minor wording tweaks in natural-language review rules cause wide swings in output consistency.
Strict Role Separation Between Deterministic Logic and LLMs OCR’s core architectural rule is role separation: deterministic code handles every structural step that must never drift, while the LLM handles contextual code judgment.
Deterministic modules filter changed files upfront so nothing gets skipped, then group related files via smart bundling to run reviews in isolated parallel contexts similar to subagents. Template-based matchers attach file-specific rules, and a dedicated post-processing verifier checks and corrects LLM-reported line numbers and finding quality to cut noisy misfires.
Within those guardrails, the AI agent applies curated review tools and tuned prompt templates to evaluate logic bugs and contextual risks without worrying about diff arithmetic.
CI/CD Integration and Precision Trade-offs OCR enforces team coding standards and security policies through a 4-tier rule priority chain spanning CLI flags, repository configs (.opencodereview/rule.json), and global settings. Distributed via NPM and compatible with Anthropic Claude environment variables, it runs standalone in the terminal, inside GitHub Actions or GitLab CI pipelines, or as a Claude Code plugin.
Clear trade-offs remain. In benchmark testing, OCR achieved strong defect recall at roughly 74%, while precision landed around 12% due to high false-positive rates. Built-in default rules are also written in Chinese today, requiring teams outside China to pull community English rule repositories.
Reliability in LLM engineering grows in proportion to the surface area where the model is structurally prevented from making mistakes. With deterministic plumbing in place, raising precision by curbing false positives is the next practical hurdle.
Summary Reliable LLM developer tools expand the deterministic surface area where the model cannot miscount lines or skip files. OCR pairs deterministic file filtering, smart bundling, and line verification with parallel LLM code judgment. Benchmark results (~74% recall vs. ~12% precision) show false-positive reduction remains the main challenge for production rollout.
summary: Validated over two years at Alibaba, open-source code reviewer OCR pairs deterministic file bundling and line validation with LLM judgment.
title: How Alibaba's Open-Source AI Code Reviewer OCR Separates Code from LLM Judgment

content:
Tuning chunk sizes and bolting on rerankers still leaves standard RAG pipelines struggling on complex multi-hop questions. Google Research tackled this ceiling with an Agentic RAG architecture centered on collaborative subagents and explicit evidence verification.
Checking Evidence Completeness Before Answering Instead of generating an answer from whatever the first retrieval pass returns - or giving up early - Google’s pipeline inserts a Sufficient Context Agent that inspects whether gathered passages actually contain enough facts to answer safely.
An orchestrator breaks incoming questions into subtasks across specialized roles: a planner maps the retrieval path, a query rewriter turns vague phrasing into sharp search queries, and a fanout agent pulls candidates from multiple sources in parallel.
The Sufficient Context Agent then compares retrieved passages against draft answers to spot missing constraints - such as an unverified allergy detail. When gaps appear, it sends targeted feedback to the query rewriter to launch another search pass with refined keywords.
Multi-Hop Gains and Cross-Corpus Routing on FramesQA Evaluated on the multi-step FramesQA benchmark - including questions that require looking up and comparing broadcast runtimes across separate shows - the multi-agent loop lifted single-corpus accuracy by up to 34% over standard RAG baselines.
In cross-corpus tests mixing separate departmental databases, the planner routed queries across candidate stores and reached 90.1% accuracy, landing right inside the 90-95% target band.
Built-In Auditability and Cost Control Enterprise deployments need clear explanations for why an AI produced a specific answer. Because the Sufficient Context Agent logs every gap check, rewrite reason, and retrieval hop, reviewers get a transparent audit trail out of the box.
Stopping the retrieval loop the moment context passes sufficiency checks also avoids wasted API calls, turning multi-hop retrieval into an auditable, cost-aware workflow.
Summary The Sufficient Context Agent checks whether retrieved passages cover all required facts before answer generation, curbing hallucinations. Reaches up to +34% accuracy over single-corpus RAG baselines and 90.1% cross-corpus accuracy on the multi-hop FramesQA benchmark. Produces step-by-step sufficiency and query-rewrite logs that give enterprise teams a clear audit trail while capping extra retrieval calls.
summary: Google Research’s Agentic RAG uses a Sufficient Context Agent to verify retrieved evidence iteratively, reaching 90.1% cross-corpus accuracy on FramesQA.
title: Google Research's Agentic RAG and the Sufficient Context Agent

How do you build an organization that uses AI well, rather than relying on a few individuals who use AI well? Toss Place is turning AI from a personal productivity tool into shared company infrastructure so individual experiments and lessons become team-wide assets. This article walks through Toss Place’s initiatives toward becoming an AI-native organization: AI Surf Day & AI Surf Club, an environment where anyone can experiment right away, an AI onboarding program, and cross-team adoption through AI Evangelists.
Moving past individual power users to make AI part of company-wide infrastructure takes deliberate cultural engineering. A payment fintech company tackled that transition by pairing open experimentation events with structured onboarding and embedded team advocates.
Lowering the Barrier to Hands-On Experimentation Recurring hackathon-style events such as AI Surf Day encourage employees to turn daily workflow annoyances into working automation scripts. Rather than letting momentum fade after a one-off event, internal study groups under AI Surf Club keep peers sharing new techniques and testing practical use cases together.
In a culture that treats failed prototypes as useful data, non-engineering staff including product managers and designers routinely call LLM APIs to ship lightweight internal tools on their own.
Onboarding Labs and Embedded Evangelists New hires encounter AI workflows on day one through mandatory company-wide onboarding sessions covering prompt engineering labs and internal tooling standards.
To support day-to-day execution, each department also works with an embedded AI Evangelist who listens for local bottlenecks, offers tailored guidance, and proposes concrete automation paths. Whenever a team lands a high-impact workflow, evangelists broadcast the playbook across company channels so neighboring teams can adapt it right away.
Accumulating Shared Knowledge Assets Individual experiments and troubleshooting notes get documented in a central knowledge base rather than staying trapped in private chat histories. Proven prompt templates go into a shared internal library where any employee can pick them up without reinventing the wheel.
Combining shared tooling with repeatable peer transfer frees staff from repetitive admin work and embeds AI as durable company infrastructure.
Summary Documenting personal experiments and failed attempts in a shared library turns individual know-how into company assets. Internal programs like AI Surf Day and AI Surf Club help non-engineers build working LLM prototypes directly. Mandatory AI onboarding labs and embedded AI Evangelists close knowledge gaps across departments.
summary: How a payment fintech company turns personal AI experiments into shared infrastructure through hackathons, study clubs, onboarding, and team evangelists.
title: Embedding AI as Core Organizational Infrastructure

Fast-growing startups often assume hypergrowth automatically requires migrating off relational databases to NoSQL. Instagram scaled its core data store to 2 billion users on PostgreSQL instead, resolving concrete bottlenecks one layer at a time before considering costly rewrites.
Taming Connection Explosions Before Blaming the Database Instagram’s first major scaling wall came from connection exhaustion rather than data volume. As application instances multiplied, open database connections drained server memory. Deploying PgBouncer to pool thousands of application connections down to a small set of active PostgreSQL backend sessions stabilized latency right away.
Teams often blame the storage engine when surrounding connection topology is the real culprit. By isolating bottlenecks methodically, Instagram ran all core metadata on a single machine far longer than conventional wisdom predicted.
Decoupling Logical Shards and Generating 64-Bit IDs Separating logical shards from physical hosts gave the team room to grow cleanly. Data was partitioned by user ID across thousands of logical shards, while a lightweight mapping table tracked which physical server hosted each logical shard. Whenever hardware neared capacity, engineers moved logical shards onto fresh machines without rehashing application keys.
Co-locating a user’s records on a single shard kept per-user reads fast, while a dedicated caching tier absorbed cross-shard fan-out reads. To issue globally unique, time-sortable primary keys across distributed shards without a central coordinator becoming a single point of failure, Instagram implemented a 64-bit Snowflake-style generator inside PostgreSQL functions combining timestamp, logical shard ID, and local sequence numbers.
Squeezing Maximum Value from Native PostgreSQL Features Leaning into built-in PostgreSQL capabilities saved enormous operational complexity. Indexing only the last 30 days of activity via a partial index shrank index footprints dramatically, complemented by functional index definitions on derived expressions and logical replication for real-time downstream streaming.
Adopting an unfamiliar NoSQL engine doubles operational surface area, tooling maintenance, and hiring friction. Understanding your existing database deeply and fixing measured bottlenecks beats chasing infrastructure trends.
Summary Fixing concrete bottlenecks such as connection pooling with PgBouncer beats premature migrations to NoSQL. Mapping thousands of logical shards separately from physical servers lets teams rebalance hardware without re-keying data. Generating 64-bit Snowflake-style IDs inside PostgreSQL and applying partial indexes keeps distributed writes sortable, fast, and lean.
summary: How Instagram scaled PostgreSQL to 2 billion users using PgBouncer connection pooling, logical sharding, 64-bit Snowflake IDs, and partial indexes.
title: How Instagram Scaled PostgreSQL to 2 Billion Users Without Jumping to NoSQL

Adding LLM API calls to an existing product no longer sets a startup apart. A growing wave of teams is rebuilding company operations around AI from the ground up - running agents overnight on routine execution while humans review outputs each morning.
Redefining Execution Speed and Coordination Cost AI-native startups optimize for decision velocity and low headcount friction. Keeping teams small slashes human communication overhead while agents clear repetitive operational queues overnight, shifting employees into direction-setting and quality-gate roles.
In traditional startups, adding headcount drives coordination cost up exponentially and slows shipping cadence. Agent-driven teams replace status meetings with automated pipelines, allowing a focused 5-person team to match the output that once required 50 people.
Compounding Product Gains Through Feedback Loops Durable advantage comes from how fast a team absorbs feedback and updates its systems. Execution logs from agents and live customer signals flow straight into a central database that feeds the next day’s system refinements, tightening product quality every 24 hours.
Engineers spend far less time wrangling routine data exports or watching dashboards manually, focusing instead on refining prompt chains, evaluation gates, and data pipelines. Treating AI as an operational teammate rather than a side tool leaves human judgment focused where it counts: product direction and taste.
Summary AI-native startups compress coordination costs so small teams (such as 5 people) ship at the pace of much larger organizations. Human roles shift from repetitive execution to setting direction and reviewing agent output quality. Feeding agent execution logs and user feedback directly into daily pipeline updates creates a compounding improvement loop.
summary: How AI-native startups cut coordination overhead, run overnight agent pipelines, and turn execution logs into daily product improvement loops.
title: How AI-Native Startups Redesign Their Operating Model

content:
Generative AI is widely expected to lift workplace output, yet early empirical data tells a different story. Examining the first 3 years of workplace adoption, a Bank of Korea report found that employees saved time without producing measurably more output.
Where the Saved 1.5 Hours Went According to the Bank of Korea’s “BOK Issue Note,” workers using generative AI reduced their working hours by an average of 3.8%, or 1.5 hours on a 40-hour workweek. Reinvesting all of that saved time into productive work would theoretically yield a 1.0% output gain. In practice, measured output growth was zero, with a 0.00 correlation coefficient between work-hour reductions and task throughput growth. Researchers concluded that saved hours mostly went toward on-the-job breaks, personal skill building, or lower work intensity.
Productivity Gains Track Direct Incentives and Autonomy Output did rise in specific groups: self-employed workers and specialized professionals. For every 1% reduction in work hours through AI, self-employed workers increased task volume by 1.0 percentage point more than salaried employees, while professionals gained 0.7 percentage points over clerical staff. Both groups share high job autonomy and direct links between output and personal income, giving them clear financial reasons to reinvest saved hours into additional work.
Workflow Bottlenecks and Weak Organizational Incentives For most salaried employees, AI remains confined to isolated subtasks. Jobs achieving more than 20% time savings accounted for just 4.4% of all tasks surveyed, reflecting AI’s role as a drafting or analysis aid rather than an end-to-end process automation engine.
Rigid approval chains also swallow local speedups: even when AI accelerates data analysis, unchanged sign-off layers turn saved minutes into idle waiting time, and flat compensation structures give salaried staff little reason to take on extra volume. Turning individual time savings into real organizational output requires redesigning approval workflows alongside performance-linked incentives.
Summary Generative AI cut weekly work hours by 3.8% (1.5 hours), yet showed a 0.00 correlation with higher output across most salaried roles. Significant throughput gains appeared mainly among self-employed workers (+1.0%p) and professionals (+0.7%p) whose pay tracks output directly. Capturing real productivity gains from AI requires end-to-end process redesign, faster approval chains, and aligned incentive structures.
summary: A Bank of Korea study finds generative AI trims weekly work hours by 1.5 hours on average, yet output stays flat without workflow redesign and aligned incentives.
title: Bank of Korea Report: AI Cuts Work Hours Without Lifting Productivity

content:
The CEO says, “Put together a business proposal - any format works.” Where do you start? Having shared ways to generate PPT decks with AI before, here is how I plan the substance before opening any slide tool (with final slide generation done in MiriCanvas’s Miricle).
The most common mistake on high-stakes decks is starting with visuals - hunting for slick covers, charts, and layouts first. Visuals belong near the end. Start with what you actually need to say: a persuasive deck backs up a spoken argument, so the narrative arc comes before slide layout.
Read the Hidden Intent Behind the Request: Receiving a business-plan request as a team lead is rarely routine paperwork. If the company is restructuring revenue models, the deck directly affects team headcount (TO) retention and hiring. A data analytics team cannot just list routine reporting; it needs market-backed SWOT analysis, 3-4 new growth initiatives, and a concrete calendar with budget estimates, staffing, and IOE scores (Impact, Operational Ease, and Effort/Difficulty) so proposals look executable rather than wishful. Outline the Deck Like a Spoken Pitch: Imagine explaining the plan across the table with zero slides - “Here is what our team delivered this year, what market shifts demand next year, how we will manage budget and timelines over 12 months, and why current workload justifies 1 additional hire.” Turning that natural pitch into sections yields: Chapter 1. Current Work (revenue, customer, operations, brand, data, or product impact), Chapter 2. Problems to Solve Now (SWOT, market/customer shifts, bottlenecks, competition), Chapter 3. Action Items (who, when, what, and success criteria), and Chapter 4. Roadmap and Staffing (timelines, owners, and IOE scores). Sketch a Paper Grid First: Before touching slide software, divide a sheet of paper into rough boxes to map flow - for example: Slide 1: Title -> Slide 2: Full Agenda -> Slide 3: Part 1 Cover -> Slides 4-7: Current Work -> Slide 8: Part 2 Cover -> Slide 9: SWOT Analysis -> Slide 10: SWOT Action Items -> Slides 11-18: Action Item Details -> Slides 19-22: Execution Scenarios and Expected Impact -> Slides 23-25: Roadmap and Staffing -> Slide 26: Wrap-up. Check why each slide exists, whether transitions hold together, where repetition creeps in, and whether the conclusion arrives too late. Convert the Plan into a 7-Part Prompt: Translate the paper grid into structured instructions covering: 1. Role, 2. Context, 3. Target Audience, 4. Core Message, 5. Slide Structure, 6. Required Content, and 7. Excluded Content (or pass a photo of the grid sketch directly to AI to draft the prompt). Feeding that structured prompt into Miricle produces clean, editable layouts backed by MiriCanvas templates and editing tools. Sudden requests to draft a business proposal often send people straight into template galleries hunting for polished slide layouts. Starting with visuals gets the sequence backward; structural planning comes first.
Uncovering Executive Intent and Designing a Spoken Outline Strong proposals address the organizational stakes behind an executive request rather than listing routine tasks. Questions around headcount justification or revenue restructuring need clear answers, framed in the natural order you would explain them aloud to the CEO.
A reliable arc moves from current business contributions to market-driven bottlenecks, concrete growth initiatives, and an execution roadmap. A data analytics team, for instance, gains far more traction proposing at least three new growth initiatives than repeating last year’s reporting tasks.
Turning new initiatives into credible commitments requires explicit schedules, budget estimates, staffing plans, and prioritization metrics. Scoring each initiative with an IOE score - weighing impact, operational ease, and implementation difficulty - gives executives a transparent basis for resource decisions.
Paper Grid Sketches and 7-Part AI Prompts Before opening presentation software, sketching rough slide boxes on paper clarifies why each slide exists and how one point leads to the next. A quick grid review exposes repetitive slides, trims filler, and prevents burying the core recommendation at the back of the deck while eliminating blank-screen paralysis.
Once the paper flow holds together, convert it into a structured prompt built around seven elements: role, situation, target audience, core message, slide structure, required content, and excluded items. Passing that specification to Miricle generates clean, editable slide layouts that teams can refine quickly with built-in templates.
Slides without underlying logic are just empty shells; reaching for a pen before opening a template produces proposals that actually persuade decision-makers.
Summary Clarify the spoken argument and executive stakes behind a proposal request before choosing visual templates. Back new business initiatives with concrete timelines, staffing plans, and IOE prioritization scores. Sketch slide flow on a paper grid first, then convert it into a 7-element structured prompt for AI slide tools like Miricle.
summary: How to outline persuasive business proposals on paper, score priorities with IOE, and convert a grid sketch into a 7-part prompt for AI slide generation.
title: Plan Before Slides: Structuring Business Proposals for AI Presentation Tools

content:
[Free Open-Source Release: Quant Bot Built on the Toss Securities API] Using the Toss Securities Open API, I built a program that applies an LLM momentum quant strategy to generate buy, sell, and hold signals for South Korean equities. Retail traders in South Korea often lean heavily into margin and speculative swings; pairing quantitative rules with an LLM helps curb impulsive trades by grounding overbought alerts and exit calls in objective metrics.
Writing code late at night while US AI infrastructure stocks tumble is a strange feeling. Ironically, backtesting right in the middle of the AI boom shows simple buy-and-hold delivering the strongest overall returns - yet on panic-stricken nights when the VIX spikes, steady quantitative rules act like a lighthouse. The GitHub release includes Toss API integration notes, trading strategy docs, momentum signal-bot source code, and 3 years of paper-trading backtest logs using the Adaptive Momentum Quant Strategy (AMQS). *Note: Live real-time feed wiring awaits final API key issuance, and a dedicated paper-trading sandbox API would be a welcome addition.
Coding through a steep late-night US tech sell-off while the VIX surges highlights why discretionary traders panic at the worst moments. Combining a fintech brokerage Open API with an LLM provides a clean, rule-driven way to strip emotion out of equity decisions.
Momentum Signals Anchored Against Market Panic Feeding quantitative indicators into an LLM establishes an objective baseline when volatility spikes. Built around the Toss Securities Open API, this bot outputs buy, sell, and hold signals for South Korean stocks using AMQS (Adaptive Momentum Quant Strategy), backed by 3 years of backtest logs.
Even though 3-year backtests show patient buy-and-hold beating most active timing during an AI bull run, explicit rules stop panic selling during sharp drawdowns. AMQS scales equity exposure dynamically with trend strength - leaning into confirmed uptrends and raising cash buffers during downturns to control drawdowns more tightly than simple moving-average crossovers.
Working Around Sandbox Gaps in Real-Time Integration Connecting live market streams requires formal API key approval, and the brokerage currently lacks a dedicated paper-trading API sandbox. While the clean REST design makes initial bot scaffolding straightforward, testing requires historical replay until live credentials arrive.
To bridge that gap, the project replays 3 years of historical market data capturing real volatility regimes. Exponential backoff handles API rate limits during ingestion, while a local signal engine refreshes a local database on a schedule with strict network-timeout and retry guards to prevent missing candles.
Constraining Impulsive Decisions Through System Prompts Rather than generating loose market commentary, the LLM evaluates overbought thresholds and exit triggers strictly against quantitative rule tables, with full source code published on GitHub. Explicit system instructions forbid emotional speculation and force every buy, hold, or sell rationale to cite numeric indicators directly - keeping decisions calm even on nights when screens flash red.
Summary Pairs the Toss Securities Open API with an LLM to generate rule-bound momentum signals for South Korean equities. Uses 3-year AMQS backtest logs to adjust cash and equity weights dynamically and curb panic trades during VIX spikes. Bridges the lack of a brokerage paper-trading sandbox with historical simulation, rate-limit backoff, and local DB sync guards.
summary: Building an emotion-free Korean stock momentum bot that pairs a fintech brokerage Open API with LLMs and 3 years of AMQS backtest logs.
title: Emotion-Free Momentum Quant Trading with the Toss Securities API and LLMs

content:
<Bought ChatGPT for Every Employee, Yet Company ROI Turned Negative> - Real AI transformation starts by redrawing the org chart, not buying seats. (Notes from a candid conversation with an industry peer on enterprise AX.)
(1) What Happens When Leadership Just Hands Out Licenses
An executive hears AI hype at a breakfast forum or on YouTube, walks into the office, asks what the company is doing, runs one quick seminar, and buys paid AI accounts for hundreds of employees. A month later, staff use those paid seats to draft routine reports slightly faster and polish PowerPoint slides. Monthly fixed SaaS bills go out for hundreds of seats while total focused work hours actually seem to shrink, pushing company ROI into negative territory. Buying seats is tool adoption, not organizational transformation. (2) Why Employees Put Up Defensive Walls
Dropping new tools onto untouched legacy workflows triggers immediate self-preservation: “If this automates my job well, am I next to be cut?” Leadership has to flip that incentive explicitly - framing AI not as a headcount-cutting threat, but as a way to double output and take home twice the performance bonus. (3) Tear Up the Industrial-Era Org Chart
Functional silos such as Planning, Logistics, and Sales are relics of an older era. AI-native companies reorganize into autonomous, venture-style customer pods (such as Dedicated Team for Customer A and Dedicated Team for Customer B), while AI agents absorb the routine coordination and administrative support those functional departments used to handle. (4) Arm Staff with Semi-Finished Meal-Kit Templates
Handing employees a blank prompt box stalls adoption. Give teams expert-built “semi-finished meal kits” instead: employees follow a simple recipe to run a working baseline automation first, then add custom features for their own daily tasks. Once people experience automating real work firsthand, peer learning takes over. Wrapping an AI label around an outdated org chart changes nothing. Executives across tech companies increasingly share the same frustration: after funding paid AI seats for every employee, company-wide ROI actually turns negative. The root cause lies in organizational structure rather than model quality.
The Illusion of Seat-License Productivity Rolling out paid accounts by the hundreds after a single inspirational seminar turns software spend into dead weight. Without redesigned workflows, employees use premium models to shave a few minutes off routine reports or format slide decks while high-value output stays flat. Fixed monthly license fees accumulate while business metrics barely budge.
Turf Protection and Misaligned Incentives Layering automation onto unchanged departmental boundaries triggers rational defensiveness. Employees quietly worry that documenting and automating their tasks will make their roles redundant.
Breaking through that resistance requires explicit upside alignment: leadership needs compensation structures where higher AI-driven output translates directly into larger team bonuses rather than headcount anxiety.
Customer-Aligned Pods and Meal-Kit Templates Functional silos such as separate planning, logistics, and sales departments slow execution down. Reorganizing around autonomous customer-dedicated pods - backed by AI agents handling routine back-office coordination - lets small teams operate like nimble internal ventures.
On the ground, blank-slate training fails most non-technical staff. Providing expert-built, semi-finished “meal-kit” workflow templates lets employees assemble a working automation first and customize steps for their own tasks afterward. Hands-on wins spread organically across teams, whereas bolting AI subscriptions onto a legacy org chart leaves every bottleneck intact.
Summary Buying company-wide AI subscriptions without workflow changes raises fixed costs without improving business ROI. Keeping legacy functional silos intact triggers job-security fears unless leadership ties AI-driven output directly to employee rewards. Rebuilding around autonomous customer pods and equipping staff with customizable “meal-kit” workflow templates drives lasting adoption.
summary: Why company-wide ChatGPT subscriptions often produce negative ROI, and how customer-aligned pods and semi-finished workflow templates drive real AI adoption.
title: Why AI Subscriptions Fail Without Rebuilding the Org Chart

content:
Building reliable self-service analytics without a human analyst in the loop is harder than wiring an LLM to SQL. Left on its own, an agent easily queries deprecated tables or copies stale join logic. A leading AI lab addressed these failure modes by redesigning its internal data stack specifically around agent consumption.
Warehouse Hygiene That Leaves Only One Canonical Answer Accurate analytics agents start with zero ambiguity inside the data warehouse. Data teams first define canonical datasets, prune duplicate tables, and enforce code-level metadata standards so agents cannot pull numbers from abandoned schemas.
Keeping transformation SQL, the semantic layer, and reference documentation inside a single repository prevents silent drift. Whenever a data model changes, automated CI checks verify whether downstream dashboards or metadata definitions break before the commit lands.
Pairing a Semantic Layer with Business Context Pointing an agent straight at raw warehouse tables invites join and filter mistakes. Directing queries through a verified semantic layer of governed metric definitions - enriched with organizational charts and product roadmaps - lets the agent interpret business intent accurately.
Indexing thousands of raw historical SQL queries rarely helps on its own. Internal evaluations showed that raw query retrieval failed to lift accuracy, whereas distilling recurring query patterns into curated domain guides produced consistent gains.
Teaching Procedural Workflows Through Markdown Skills Knowing what each table means is only half the job; the agent also needs to know how to investigate a question step by step. Encoding tool execution order and disambiguation playbooks as Markdown skills gave the agent explicit procedural guardrails. Analytical accuracy, which hovered around 21-30% without skills, jumped sharply once those procedural skills were loaded.
Reliable self-service analytics depends less on raw model size than on disciplined warehouse curation, governed metrics, and explicit procedural skills.
Summary Eliminating duplicate warehouse tables and enforcing CI-checked metadata in a single repository stops agents from querying stale schemas. Routing queries through a governed semantic layer paired with business context outperforms raw historical SQL retrieval. Loading Markdown skills that specify tool order and disambiguation steps lifts agent analytics accuracy sharply above the 21-30% baseline.
summary: Engineering practices for self-service analytics agents, covering data warehouse hygiene, verified semantic layers, CI checks, and Markdown skills.
title: Designing Self-Service Data Analytics Agents with Claude

content:
Minho Hwang x AI Frenz <Harness Engineering 60-Minute Stimpack> Q&A Session - What are practitioners actually wrestling with right now? Audience energy carried yesterday’s event well past its planned runtime. While the main talk walked beginners from onboarding through the new Dynamic Workflow, the real action happened during the 1-hour Q&A as seasoned harness builders surfaced practical questions on AI workflows and organization-scale agent systems. Notably, Minho Hwang answered most recurring pain points with another purpose-built harness he had already crafted after spotting human-in-the-loop friction firsthand. Methodology matters less than the care and perspective of the person refining the workflow.
Core Concepts People Still Mix Up Q. Is orchestration itself an agent? Who coordinates subagents, and how does CLAUDE.md differ from orchestration? A. You can run an orchestrator as a separate agent, though Hwang implements orchestration as a skill mounted on the main agent so it coordinates subagent roles and execution order directly. CLAUDE.md serves a separate role: storing project context plus harness history.
Fixed Frameworks vs. revfactory Meta-Harness Q. How does this differ from popular frameworks like the oh-my series? A. Frameworks such as the oh-my series, gstack, and superpowers ship pre-polished, ready-made harnesses for common workflows. Hwang’s revfactory project acts as a meta-harness: pre-designed templates generate a custom harness on the fly once you supply your intent. Grab an existing framework when its opinionated workflow already matches your goal; use a meta-harness when you want a custom setup tailored to your own requirements.
Q. After generating a harness in seconds without deep coding knowledge, what does “refining (whittling) a harness” mean in practice? A. Refining means calibrating generated agent and skill Markdown files to fit your exact standards in three ways: 1) editing skill or agent .md files directly to add domain edge cases like an internal playbook, 2) asking your active AI how to tighten the spec (meta-calibration), or 3) running Hwang’s 1:1 coffee-chat/postmortem skill (agent-1on1) to interview a specific agent and fix structural gaps. That discussion also touched on Karpathy-style AutoResearch loops where Claude Code iteratively improves its own skills.
Cross-Tool Portability and Cross-Verification Q. Does the meta-harness work in Antigravity, Cursor, Codex CLI, ChatGPT, open-source LLMs, or OpenClaw? A. Antigravity is already supported and runs roughly 4x faster on Gemini 3.5 Flash, though Claude still edges ahead on final output precision. For Codex CLI, Hwang built a general-purpose skill pack alongside dedicated image-generation skills. ChatGPT lacks multi-agent execution, so no port exists there. Open-source LLMs can run converted standard skills (shared across OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google), though provider-specific agent configs do not transfer cleanly; Hwang has run local VLM servers on air-gapped networks with extra glue work. OpenClaw performs weakly solo, so users often connect Claude Code behind OpenClaw or use dedicated OpenClaw harnesses.
Q. How should teams apply harnesses to brownfield codebases, and when does LangGraph make sense? A. Clarify the objective first - full operations vs. shipping a new feature (such as generating options A, B, and C, simulating all three, and picking a winner). LangGraph fits custom agentic backend services, whereas many teams now embed Claude Code or Antigravity CLI directly and invoke claude -p without pre-wiring rigid workflow graphs.
Q. Can Codex run QA to cross-check work produced by Claude? A. Yes. Instructing a Fact-checker agent to always verify via the Codex CLI skill sets up clean cross-model verification.
Cost vs. Quality and Scaling Agent Hierarchies Q. Can subagents run on cheaper models or lower reasoning tiers? A. Per-agent model assignment is supported, though without a solid evaluation harness to catch regressions, sticking to the strongest model is safer. On reasoning effort, xhigh costs roughly 4x more time and tokens than high, while max runs too slowly for routine use, making high or xhigh the practical range (Opus+high vs. Sonnet+xhigh remains an open empirical question).
Q. How deep can agent hierarchies go, and can swarms reach hundred-person research-lab scale? A. Stacking 3-4 layers of agents above agents breaks down quickly; Claude restricts nested subagent depth to prevent infinite loops and token explosions. Scaling toward large agent teams shifts the challenge toward swarm control: experimental agent teams in Claude Code already add roughly 30% communication overhead, and naive broadcasts can wake 1,000 idle agents at once, triggering massive token bills. Routing messages strictly to relevant agents turns large-scale harness engineering into an organizational design problem.
A recent Harness Engineering session hosted by AI Frenz drew sharp questions from practicing engineers. While the main presentation covered onboarding and dynamic workflows, the hour-long Q&A exposed the real trade-offs teams face when putting multi-agent setups into daily work.
Ready-Made Frameworks vs. Dynamic Meta-Harnesses Unlike opinionated frameworks such as the oh-my series or gstack that lock in fixed workflow patterns, a meta-harness dynamically generates agent teams and skill files around a user’s specific task intent. Pre-built templates make it fast to spin up custom workflows without starting from a blank directory.
Generating the initial files is only the starting line; quality comes from iterative calibration. Practitioners refine .md agent specs directly with edge cases, ask the model for spec critiques, or run interactive 1-on-1 postmortem skills with individual agents to patch structural blind spots. Craft and domain judgment matter more than the generator script itself.
Cross-CLI Verification and Lightweight Invocation Engineers increasingly mix CLI tools and model providers inside a single harness. Running harnesses on Gemini-based Antigravity CLI executes nearly 4x faster, whereas Claude still leads on final output precision. Meanwhile, open-source LLMs share standard skill formats but still suffer from fragmented agent configuration schemas across providers.
Cross-checking outputs across model families has become a practical pattern: Claude drafts code or analysis, and a QA agent invokes a Codex CLI skill to verify facts and edge cases. Rather than standing up heavy orchestration servers for every internal workflow, many teams also invoke CLI agents directly via claude -p inside existing systems.
Swarm Control and Cost Trade-offs Nesting agent hierarchies 3 or 4 layers deep invites runaway loops, lost context, and steep token bills. Until a team builds automated quality checks to validate cheaper tiers, defaulting to top-tier models avoids silent regressions, while reserving xhigh reasoning (roughly 4x the cost of high) for genuinely hard steps keeps spend predictable.
Scaling toward research-lab-sized agent teams turns orchestration into a swarm-control problem. Broadcasting updates to every idle agent triggers severe token waste, demanding selective routing protocols that mirror human organizational design.
Summary Meta-harnesses generate task-specific agent teams and skills on demand, offering more flexibility than fixed opinionated frameworks. Pairing different CLIs and model families - such as verifying Claude outputs with Codex CLI skills or invoking claude -p - keeps production workflows light and auditable. Deep agent hierarchies (3+ levels) and naive broadcasts trigger token explosions, making selective swarm routing and careful reasoning-tier selection (high vs. xhigh) central to controlling spend.
summary: Practical lessons from an AI Frenz Q&A on meta-harnesses vs. fixed frameworks, multi-CLI cross-verification, model tiering, and agent swarm control.
title: Building Agent Teams: Takeaways from a Harness Engineering Q&A

content:
Document splitting is often the first place a RAG pipeline breaks. Even top-tier LLMs return weak answers when poorly placed chunk boundaries sever tables, pronouns, or logical arguments before retrieval even starts.
Five Intrinsic Metrics for Label-Free Chunk Scoring Because documents vary widely in layout and discourse flow, a single fixed chunking rule fails across mixed corpora. Adaptive Chunking evaluates split quality without ground-truth QA labels using five intrinsic metrics. Referential Completeness (RC) tracks unresolved pronouns across boundaries, while Block Integrity (BI) checks whether tables, lists, and figures stay intact.
Intra-Chunk Coherence (ICC) measures semantic similarity inside each chunk, Discourse Contextual Coherence (DCC) evaluates transitions across neighboring chunks, and Size Compliance (SC) penalizes deviations from target token ranges. Scoring candidate outputs across these five signals lets the pipeline pick the highest-scoring splitter per document.
LLM Regex Splitters and Two-Pass Split-then-Merge The authors also add two chunking methods to expand the candidate pool. First, the LLM Regex Splitter inspects document structure once with an LLM to synthesize custom regular-expression boundary rules, avoiding expensive per-boundary LLM calls across long files.
Second, the Split-then-Merge two-pass recursive splitter recombines fine-grained fragments to preserve context while staying within token limits. A post-processing pass re-splits oversized chunks and merges undersized ones so token budgets stay predictable.
For document ingestion, the framework defaults to open-source Docling while also supporting lightweight PyMuPDF and cloud parsing APIs, passing extracted structural metadata straight into the chunking engine.
Measurable Gains in End-to-End RAG Accuracy Evaluated on RAG benchmarks without changing the downstream LLM or prompt templates, switching from a single fixed splitter to per-document adaptive selection lifted answer accuracy from 62-64% to roughly 72%. The number of questions answered accurately jumped by more than 30%, showing how much retrieval headroom sits inside document boundary decisions alone.
Summary Replaces one-size-fits-all splitting with per-document strategy selection driven by document layout and discourse flow. Automates label-free chunk evaluation across 5 intrinsic metrics (RC, BI, ICC, DCC, and SC). Pairs a one-shot LLM Regex Splitter with Split-then-Merge post-processing to lift RAG answer accuracy from 62-64% to around 72%.
summary: Adaptive Chunking scores candidate splits with five label-free intrinsic metrics to pick the best chunking strategy for each document in a RAG pipeline.
title: Adaptive Chunking: Selecting the Right RAG Strategy per Document

content:
A Netflix engineer open-sourced Headroom on GitHub, a context compression layer that cuts AI agent token consumption by up to 95% right before RAG outputs, bulky system logs, or codebases hit the model. Using a CCR mechanism, Headroom stores raw JSON, source code, and logs locally while passing only compact structured summaries plus dedicated lookup tools to the LLM. Whenever the model needs exact raw details, it calls those tools on demand, shrinking input token counts physically without losing underlying data. Teams can also deploy it as a reverse proxy by swapping the LLM endpoint URL with zero application code edits. As frontier context windows expand, middleware that defends API margins is becoming a central battleground.
Expanding LLM context windows make it tempting to stuff entire logs and repositories into every request, driving API bills sharply higher. Released by an engineer at a global streaming company, Headroom sits ahead of the model and cuts input token volume by 60-95% on RAG payloads and system logs.
Lossless Access via Local Storage and On-Demand Lookup Tools Headroom keeps full raw payloads on local storage while sending the LLM compact structured representations paired with dedicated retrieval tools. Built around its CCR mechanism, the layer lets the model fetch exact raw slices only when a step requires fine-grained detail, cutting physical input tokens without permanently discarding source data.
Zero-Code Reverse Proxy Deployment Teams can integrate Headroom without rewriting application logic simply by pointing their LLM endpoint configuration at the proxy, or embed it directly as an in-process library depending on their deployment setup.
Defending API Margins as Context Windows Grow Larger frontier context limits do not make raw context dumping economical. Shipping megabytes of unfiltered text over the wire on every agent turn erodes product margins fast. Middleware layers that compress and index context in transit let teams run capable LLM agents at a fraction of the token bill.
Summary Uses the CCR mechanism to keep raw logs, JSON, and code locally while passing compressed structured views and lookup tools to the LLM, cutting tokens by 60-95%. Supports drop-in reverse proxy deployment via an endpoint swap or direct library integration without application code changes. Protects API cost margins against context bloat as agent workloads and model context windows grow.
summary: Built by a global streaming engineer, Headroom compresses agent context by 60-95% using local storage, structured summaries, and on-demand retrieval tools.
title: Headroom: Open-Source Context Compression That Cuts Token Usage by Up to 95%

content:
Scaling model parameters alone has hit diminishing returns on multi-step agent tasks. Rather than training a bigger model, the Harness-1 team redesigned the surrounding execution environment, enabling an older 20B open-weight model to beat current frontier models on multi-turn search benchmarks.
Separating Reasoning from Bookkeeping In long-horizon search tasks, agents usually bottleneck on working memory and token clutter. Once trajectories pass 20-30 turns, standard agents burn capacity remembering prior queries and filtering duplicate results. Harness-1 offloads that bookkeeping to a stateful external environment and gives the model just 5 focused tools covering search, raw source reading, and result curation.
The stateful harness deduplicates retrieved documents, compresses text, and maintains clean working state automatically. Freed from tracking ledger details in its own context window, the model spends its compute budget purely on search decisions.
Shaping Search Habits with Targeted RL Rewards Clean tools still fail if the model falls into lazy habits. Training via reinforcement learning on financial report analysis, the researchers added two reward signals: a tool-diversity reward that penalizes repetitive search-API spamming, and a curation penalty whenever the agent finds relevant evidence during browsing but forgets to save it into the final collection.
Together, those incentives taught the model to alternate between broad search, deep reading, and explicit curation while pacing its step budget.
Domain Transfer That Beats Much Larger Models Paired with its stateful harness, the RL-trained 20B model reached 73.0% average recall across search benchmarks, surpassing GPT-5.4 recall at 70.9% and Sonnet-4.6 recall at 68.8%.
Even though RL training used only financial filings, recall on unseen domains such as patent search and general web tasks jumped by 17 points. Instead of memorizing domain facts, the model learned transferable search mechanics. Careful harness design and behavior shaping now open a realistic path to running competitive private search agents on compact open-weight models.
Summary Offloads deduplication, compression, and state tracking across 20-30+ turn trajectories to an external stateful harness. Uses RL with tool-diversity rewards and curation-omission penalties to train disciplined search and evidence-saving behavior. Reaches 73.0% average search recall with a 20B model - beating GPT-5.4 (70.9%) and Sonnet-4.6 (68.8%) - with +17-point transfer gains on unseen domains.
summary: Harness-1 pairs a stateful search harness with reinforcement learning so a 20B open model outperforms frontier models on multi-turn search benchmarks.
title: Cognitive Offloading in Search Agents: How Harness-1 Beats Frontier Models

content:
Turning into an AI-native organization is one of the biggest topics in San Francisco right now, sparking active debate on how to make meetings, chats, user research, code, and interviews usable by AI. Similar discussions are picking up in South Korea as well.
The catch is that feature matrices and benchmark scores alone rarely tell you which option actually fits your stack - whether built-in memory in ChatGPT or Claude, Hermes + LLM-Wiki, Garry Tan’s GBrain, or dedicated memory SaaS platforms. After testing and building several approaches firsthand, I put together an open-source repository comparing how these tools handle the full pipeline from ingestion to agent execution across five questions:
How does the system ingest scattered data across apps and tools? How does it transform raw inputs into structured knowledge AI can use? How does it keep stored knowledge current as facts change? How do agents retrieve and apply that knowledge during real tasks? How do teams govern, audit, and trust the resulting knowledge base? Anyone exploring AI-native workflows, agents, or second-brain architectures can use this comparison as a practical reference. #ai-transformation
Engineering and product teams increasingly want every meeting transcript, customer interview, and repository commit wired into an AI-native workflow. Between built-in chat memory, managed SaaS platforms, and open-source stacks, however, surface-level feature checklists make it tough to pick an architecture that holds up in production.
Bottlenecks in Ingestion and Knowledge Structuring The first bottleneck appears when turning scattered collaboration data into representations an LLM can query accurately. Dumping raw text chunks into a vector DB hits retrieval ceilings quickly. Raw feeds pulled from Slack, calendars, and source-code APIs need to be normalized into entities, factual relationships, and timelines inside a structured knowledge wiki before agents can reason over them reliably. Hosted platforms such as Membase automate this ingestion and structuring pipeline, cutting upfront infrastructure work.
Keeping Knowledge Fresh Through Background Sync Loops A knowledge base lives or dies by the synchronization loop that updates existing entries when new context arrives. When stale notes pile up without invalidation, LLMs cite outdated decisions and answer quality drops fast. Self-hosted options like OpenHuman and GBrain give teams full data ownership, though engineering teams must build and maintain their own background deduplication and sync pipelines.
Agent Permissions and Source Governance Giving agents read access to organizational memory in production requires fine-grained permission boundaries and filtering APIs. Without strict separation between private workspaces and shared team spaces - plus clear source citations in the UI - employees stop trusting the system. Running Hermes Agent alongside LLM Wiki locally keeps sensitive records inside an internal governance boundary with zero external data exposure.
Evaluating your organization’s data lifecycle before comparing benchmark leaderboards prevents costly re-platforming later.
Summary Plain vector DB chunking hits accuracy limits quickly; teams gain better retrieval by structuring context around entities, facts, and timelines. Reliable organizational memory depends on recurring background sync loops that deduplicate entries and invalidate stale facts. Production agent adoption requires clear workspace permission boundaries, data-leakage controls, and verifiable source citations.
summary: A lifecycle framework comparing AI memory and second-brain tools across ingestion, structuring, sync, agent access, and data governance.
title: Choosing a Second Brain for AI-Native Teams Across a 5-Stage Lifecycle

content:
You do not need to prebuild a giant knowledge graph to run GraphRAG. Standard GraphRAG pipelines read tens of thousands of documents ahead of time to map every entity and relationship before a single user asks a question. Even minor corpus updates can wipe out hours of preprocessing and hundreds of thousands of KRW in API fees. Researchers at The Hong Kong Polytechnic University introduced LogicRAG, a lazy query-time alternative that builds reasoning paths only when a question arrives.
Live Reasoning Blueprints Instead of Prebuilt Encyclopedias: If traditional GraphRAG acts like a librarian cataloging every shelf in advance, LogicRAG works like a detective investigating on demand. When a complex question arrives, the model decomposes it on the fly and sketches a small directed acyclic graph (DAG) of dependencies - solving step 1 before step 2 - exploring only the paths needed for that query. Untangling Dependencies and Pruning Context: Even a sharp detective stalls when buried in paperwork (context overflow). LogicRAG applies topological sorting to flatten tangled sub-questions into a clean one-way search sequence, and uses rolling memory (pruning) to distill dozens of retrieved pages into concise one-line notes while discarding raw text to save tokens. Strong Accuracy from a Budget Model: Live planning and summarization do not require heavyweight frontier models. Using gpt-4o-mini, the team cut offline graph-building cost to 0 KRW and hit 64.7% accuracy on the 2WikiMQA benchmark - beating HippoRAG2, a leading prebuilt-graph baseline, by 14.7 percentage points. Trade-offs in Premature Certainty and Latency: On reasoning chains of 4-hop depth or deeper, the model occasionally jumps to conclusions before gathering enough evidence (premature certainty). Query-time planning also pushes response latency to roughly 9.8 seconds, more than double Vanilla RAG at roughly 4.2 seconds. Closing thought: LogicRAG challenges the industry habit of pouring budget into rigid, precomputed graph schemas, showing that applying modern LLM reasoning at query time can be both cheaper and more accurate in 2026.
High preprocessing bills and steep API invoices stop many engineering teams from deploying GraphRAG in production. Parsing tens of thousands of documents upfront to maintain a static knowledge graph becomes painful whenever underlying data changes. Proposed by researchers at The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, LogicRAG shifts graph construction entirely to query time.
Building Reasoning DAGs at Query Time Instead of pre-indexing a graph database, LogicRAG drafts an execution plan the moment a query arrives. Given a multi-step question, the LLM decomposes it into sub-questions and sketches a DAG capturing logical dependencies, exploring only the retrieval paths required for the active prompt.
Classical graph ordering and memory pruning keep the context window lean. Topological sorting flattens interdependent sub-questions into a linear retrieval order, while rolling memory summarizes key findings from retrieved documents and discards raw passages to conserve tokens.
Beating Prebuilt Graphs with a Lightweight Model LogicRAG reaches strong benchmark numbers using lightweight gpt-4o-mini rather than expensive frontier models. On 2WikiMQA, it recorded 64.7% accuracy, outperforming the prebuilt-graph baseline HippoRAG2 by 14.7 percentage points while keeping offline preprocessing cost at 0 KRW.
Two trade-offs remain worth watching. When reasoning depth reaches 4 hops or more, the model can exhibit premature certainty by guessing an answer from incomplete clues. Live graph planning and rolling summarization also bring average latency to 9.8 seconds, more than twice the 4.2 seconds of Vanilla RAG.
Rather than locking corpora into expensive static graph schemas upfront, spending runtime compute on structured query-time reasoning offers a lighter, more adaptable RAG architecture.
Summary Eliminates offline preprocessing costs (0 KRW) by generating query-specific reasoning DAGs at runtime instead of prebuilding static knowledge graphs. Combines topological sorting with rolling memory pruning to keep multi-step retrieval within tight token budgets. Reaches 64.7% accuracy on 2WikiMQA with gpt-4o-mini, beating HippoRAG2 by 14.7 percentage points at the cost of roughly 9.8-second query latency.
summary: LogicRAG skips expensive offline graph construction by building query-time reasoning DAGs with topological sorting and rolling memory.
title: Real-Time GraphRAG Without Prebuilt Knowledge Graphs: LogicRAG

content:
Claude Code is widely known as a terminal tool for software engineers, yet its architecture fits product management workflows just as well. Beyond drafting specs, PMs can encode their decision criteria and operating rules directly into files so the agent executes repeatable planning workflows.
Defining PM Operating Principles in CLAUDE.md **CLAUDE.md** acts as an operating manual rather than a basic config file. Writing explicit product goals, target customer segments, and prioritization rules into this file steers the model to evaluate trade-offs like a product owner. Specific constraints sharply reduce generic output. Adding a rule that every feature spec must list estimated engineering effort alongside key risks immediately tightens the quality of generated proposals.
Connecting Workspace Context and Modular Skills An agent loses usefulness when product context stays scattered across separate apps. Connecting Slack feedback channels, Notion requirement docs, and Linear tickets brings fragmented context into a single terminal session. Granting read-only permissions first keeps security risks contained while establishing the data pipeline.
Packaging recurring tasks such as customer interview synthesis or PRD critiques into modular **skills** removes repetitive prompt writing. A single slash command or short CLI invocation then runs multi-step analysis with consistent formatting.
Prioritizing Critique Loops Over Draft Speed Agent adoption succeeds or fails on evaluation quality, not document generation speed. Catching hidden assumptions, weak success metrics, or missing user segments matters far more than producing a polished first draft in seconds.
Practitioners need to challenge model drafts with structured verification questions that test whether a proposed feature actually moves the target metric for a real user problem. Without that review loop, agents simply mass-produce plausible-looking boilerplate. Installing the CLI is just step one; encoding sharp product judgment into the review loop creates the real advantage.
Summary Treat CLAUDE.md as a product operating manual that encodes target segments, scope boundaries, and decision principles. Connect Slack, Notion, and Linear with modular skills so the CLI operates on live product context instead of isolated prompts. Focus agent workflows on assumption testing and metric validation loops rather than raw document drafting speed.
summary: Practical strategies for configuring Claude Code CLI with CLAUDE.md, tool integrations, and review loops to run product management workflows.
title: Turning Claude Code from a Developer CLI into a PM Agent

content:
Autonomous coding agents drive up monthly API bills fast. Profiling real sessions shows that only a small fraction of tokens goes toward generating new code, while repeated context loads burn through the rest of the budget.
Eliminating Wasted Tokens with Context Compression Open-source toolkit claude-ns-hub cuts spend in half by shrinking payload sizes before calling the model. When session histories bloat, models forget earlier architectural choices and repeat dead-end reasoning loops. Instead of resending full file histories on every turn, claude-ns-hub compresses input payloads from 569KB down to 42KB - roughly a 93% reduction.
Cross-session decision memory further reduces redundant work. Storing technical decisions from prior tasks stops the model from re-debating settled questions and firing unnecessary API calls. Across a 2-week test in an active development environment, total billing dropped by half.
Real-Time Visibility via tmux Background Sessions Long-running autonomous tasks often leave developers guessing whether a terminal session is making progress or hanging silently. Running agent processes inside managed tmux sessions exposes live state directly from the CLI.
A companion mobile web view displays idle states, active subtasks, and completion progress at a glance, letting engineers check or steer background jobs away from their desks without opening a full desktop terminal.
Milestone Queues and Safe Remote Access Structured work units keep autonomous runs on track. Injecting lifecycle protocols into project configuration files lets the hub track milestones automatically and pull the next queued task whenever the model enters an idle state.
Pairing the mobile web interface with a VPN or Tailscale network gives developers encrypted remote access to local terminal sessions from anywhere. Controlling token waste and background execution turns autonomous coding from an expensive experiment into a predictable daily workflow.
Summary Compresses redundant input context (such as shrinking 569KB payloads to 42KB) to cut Claude Code costs by 50%. Runs autonomous jobs inside tmux background sessions with live CLI and mobile progress visibility. Combines cross-session decision memory with milestone queues to prevent repeated reasoning and advance multi-step tasks.
summary: Open-source tool claude-ns-hub cuts autonomous coding token bills by 50% through context compression, decision memory, and tmux-based remote monitoring.
title: Cutting AI Coding Agent Costs in Half with claude-ns-hub

content:
Many organizations now emphasize AX (AI Transformation), yet teams rarely share a clear definition or common playbook. People naturally ask whether talking about AX makes sense when DX (Digital Transformation) still feels unfinished, and that confusion shows up constantly in practice.
When invited to speak on harness engineering recently, my goal was not to claim every team must adopt harness engineering today, but to show how far practical AI tool and agent adoption has progressed. Even if full adoption is premature right now, seeing the upper rungs gives teams clear direction. Realizing that AI adoption extends beyond writing clever prompts into tool wiring, role separation, verification loops, and workflow redesign changes how teams plan. Harness engineering is less a mandatory starting line for everyone today than a preview of mature AX.
AX is not simply “using AI tools well.” It means redesigning how work happens so AI reads context, organizes inputs, supports judgment, and executes within approved boundaries. That makes AX a question of workflows, data, permissions, verification, and accountability rather than software licenses. The progression roughly follows seven stages:
Trying AI tools on individual tasks Using prompts for drafting, summarizing, organizing, and ideation Turning recurring tasks into templates and automating personal routines Connecting internal tools and data safely to AI Structuring work procedures so AI can parse and execute them Building agent environments with skills, MCP, and verification loops Redesigning team processes around human-AI collaboration Seen this way, prompt engineering sits near the entrance of AX, not the finish line. Roadmaps also differ by role. Non-technical staff gain traction fastest by speeding up documentation, synthesis, and decision prep. Engineers see quick returns in code generation, verification, review, and test automation. Infrastructure and security teams should start with read-only lookup, summarization, validation, and approval-gated execution rather than autonomous remediation. Leaders and managers add the most value by reshaping team processes into forms AI can handle reliably.
Practically, AX works best when teams start with repetitive, time-consuming, low-risk tasks where humans can spot AI mistakes quickly. Summarizing calendars, emails, Jira tickets, Git issues, monitoring alerts, on-call schedules, and approval queues into a single “what to check first today” digest may not look like a flashy autonomous agent, yet it saves real hours every morning. Small automations like these compound until team habits shift.
Companies also owe employees proper backing. Organizational transformation stalls when workers pay for subscriptions out of pocket and guess at rules alone. Leadership needs to supply AI tools, API credits, GPU access, clear security boundaries on allowed vs. restricted data, and internal training. Instead of rigid short-term ROI scorecards, tracking genuine workflow improvements and rewarding individuals or teams right away builds momentum. When people say they want to try AI but are too swamped with daily work, that overload is the clearest reason to start AX.
Calls for AX echo across the IT industry, yet many teams still wrestle with unfinished digital transformation initiatives. Cutting through the fatigue requires setting aside vague slogans and mapping concrete adoption stages.
From Prompt Writing to Workflow Redesign The real target of AX is redesigning operational processes rather than polishing individual prompts. Mature setups let AI read internal documents, assist human judgment, and act within explicitly approved boundaries. Permissions, verification gates, and clear accountability matter more than picking a chat tool.
Adoption moves in stages: teams start with personal drafting and prompt templates, progress to safe internal data connections, and eventually build agent environments incorporating MCP servers and automated verification loops. Harness engineering represents one of the upper stages on that ladder.
Role-Specific Roadmaps and Low-Risk Starting Points Every department needs a different entry point into AX. Non-technical roles gain momentum through document synthesis, while software engineers capture immediate value in code generation and automated testing. Infrastructure teams stay safe by focusing on verification and approval-gated workflows rather than autonomous server changes.
A daily digest that pulls together email threads and Jira issues to highlight morning priorities delivers more practical value than an ambitious autonomous agent that fails unpredictably. For infrastructure engineers, fast incident context assembly beats automated production mutations. Starting with repetitive, low-risk tasks such as calendar triage or approval-queue summaries lets humans catch errors easily while compounding daily time savings.
Company-Provided Infrastructure and Direct Incentives Leaving employees to pay for subscriptions out of pocket and figure out policies alone stalls company-wide adoption. Organizations need to fund AI tools and API credits upfront while publishing unambiguous security guidelines on permitted data use.
Replacing rigid short-term KPI frameworks with immediate recognition for teams that eliminate real workflow bottlenecks accelerates internal sharing. When teams feel too buried in routine tasks to experiment with new tools, targeted AX on those exact bottlenecks is the fastest way out.
Summary AX goes beyond individual tool usage to redesign workflows around permissions, verification loops, and clear human accountability. Teams need role-specific AX roadmaps that start with repetitive, low-risk tasks where humans can review outputs quickly. Organizations must fund tools and credits centrally, set clear security rules, and reward practical workflow improvements.
summary: A staged roadmap and role-specific guide to AI Transformation (AX), moving from personal prompting to tool integration, governance, and workflow redesign.
title: Why AI Transformation Goes Far Beyond Writing Good ChatGPT Prompts

content:
Many assumptions behind early LLM application stacks no longer hold. Scaffolding layers originally built to compensate for weak model reasoning now weigh systems down, turning yesterday’s helper frameworks into bloatware.
Better Models Shorten the Lifespan of Thick Harnesses Rapid gains in base LLM reasoning have shrunk the shelf life of complex orchestration frameworks. Just a few months ago, models struggled to decompose plans or verify their own work, forcing engineers to wire up elaborate external loops and multi-step controllers. Modern models plan and self-check natively, making duplicate framework logic pure overhead.
Repeating work inside a heavy harness wastes tokens and obscures failure modes. Thin, transparent runtimes are taking their place.
Three Lightweight Projects Built Around Verification Loops Three recent developer projects illustrate this minimalist design shift. lazycodex leaves application code untouched at first, generating only plan files and looping until its self-verification checks pass. gajae-code strips out sprawling toolkits in favor of a tight cycle built around deep requirement interviews and plan critique.
roach-pi extends an existing coding agent with just two additions: explicit goal contracts and validator pass tracking. Instead of locking behavior inside rigid framework abstractions, all three projects rely on the model’s native execution ability paired with a small verification loop.
Designing a Custom Harness for Your Own Workflow Developers get better results by writing a small harness tailored to their own workflow than by adopting a monolithic framework that predefines every step. As models improve, thick abstraction layers get in the way. Wiring the loop and tool boundaries directly keeps latency low and debugging straightforward.
Building the control loop yourself lets you match the runtime to your exact codebase and review standards.
Summary Improvements in native LLM planning and self-checking turn heavy agent control frameworks into redundant bloatware. Recent projects such as lazycodex, gajae-code, and roach-pi strip away thick abstractions in favor of minimal verification loops. Writing a small, workflow-specific harness delivers better control and productivity than relying on rigid general-purpose frameworks.
summary: As base LLM capabilities improve, heavy agent frameworks add redundant overhead, pushing developers toward thin, custom harness runtimes.
title: Why Heavy Agent Frameworks Turn into Bloatware

content:
Implementing KRDS, South Korea’s digital government web design standard, normally takes significant manual effort. Its Figma templates and HTML component kits are well documented for human designers, yet coding agents struggle without machine-readable specifications. Packaging those rules into dedicated agent skills lets AI read the standard directly and publish compliant markup.
Design Guidelines Written for Coding Agents Figma files guide human eyes, whereas tools like Codex and Claude Code need structured rules and explicit constraints. That gap motivated future-krds, an AI-native skill set built around the government design system.
The pipeline splits work across three modules. krds-plan maps UI components and defines accessibility requirements. krds-transform preserves existing site architecture while converting themes and markup to match government standards. Finally, krds-improve checks the rendered output against KRDS rules and patches violations.
Automated Scanning and Feedback Loops With the skill loaded, a single-line prompt produces standard-compliant markup. In a test converting the Korean page of a global web portal from one prompt, the system mapped 74 components with zero errors. Codex generated and validated the full page in just a few seconds.
An automated internal loop drives that consistency: it scans markup, scores compliance, prioritizes violations, patches the code, and re-runs validation. The feedback loop repeats until the KRDS compliance score reaches 95 or higher with 0 failed rules.
Because the underlying design tokens and component boundaries match the official specification, teams can also import the resulting markup back into Figma cleanly. Giving coding agents structured domain skills and an automated validation loop eliminates hours of manual accessibility and markup review.
Summary Converts the KRDS government design system from human-oriented docs into AI-native skills that coding agents execute directly. Chains krds-plan, krds-transform, and krds-improve into an automated planning, markup conversion, and compliance-repair pipeline. Repeats automated scoring and repair until pages hit 95+ compliance with 0 failed rules, cutting manual publishing review effort.
summary: How future-krds packages South Korea’s digital government design system (KRDS) into structured skills so coding agents can generate and validate compliant pages.
title: Building future-krds: Turning the KRDS Design System into AI Agent Skills

content:
Reading long code explanations or architecture summaries generated by an LLM inside a terminal quickly strains the eyes. Dense text walls pile up, and wide Markdown tables wrap awkwardly across narrow windows. Codexplain is a project-scoped UX layer built to fix terminal readability without mutating machine-readable outputs.
Fixing Broken Terminal Tables and Dense Text Walls Codexplain converts raw Codex and LLM responses into structured terminal layouts. Standard terminal streams dump plain text lines that obscure hierarchy and break table borders whenever columns exceed the viewport width.
A width-safe renderer keeps tables aligned inside the active terminal window. When cell text exceeds the available width, the renderer wraps rows cleanly and inserts visual dividers. Instead of printing flat file lists, it also draws architecture maps that show module dependencies and execution flow at a glance.
The tool restrains noisy rainbow syntax highlighting as well. Color applies only to high-priority states such as pass or warning indicators, while ordinary nouns and body copy stay in a calm default tone paired with clear status symbols.
Preserving Raw Artifacts with Project-Scoped Control Formatting passes never alter machine-parsed artifacts such as JSON, source code blocks, test logs, or patch files. Codexplain isolates display transformations behind safety filters so downstream scripts and copy-paste workflows receive exact, untouched payloads.
Setup stays local to each repository. Developers toggle adapters per project without polluting global shell configs, and teams can define custom output styles such as checklists or diagnostic cards.
A built-in terminal configuration UI adjusts rendering rules without manual config-file edits, while a compatibility check command verifies that renderer contracts hold across environments. Tools that make AI output easier for humans to scan while keeping raw artifacts intact solve a real daily friction point in CLI workflows.
Summary Reformats LLM-generated architecture walkthroughs and wide tables to fit terminal widths without broken borders. Protects machine-readable artifacts including JSON, source code, logs, and patch files from formatting mutations. Enables per-project adapter toggles and custom diagnostic layouts without modifying global configuration.
summary: Codexplain reformats dense LLM architecture notes and wide tables for terminal readability while preserving raw source code, patches, and JSON artifacts.
title: Codexplain: A Local UX Layer for Readable LLM Terminal Outputs

content:
Startups designed from the ground up as AI-native organizations are emerging in Korea as well, piping Slack discussions and meeting transcripts directly into internal infrastructure so models track operational context automatically.
Turning Everyday Work Context into Structured Data An internal AI assistant cannot help much if company context disappears into ephemeral chats. Beyond archiving raw meeting recordings or messenger logs, AI-native teams preprocess unstructured discussions into clean, LLM-ready formats so models understand project ownership and current blockers.
Exposing that internal knowledge base over an API shrinks lookup time dramatically: new hires can ask the internal assistant for historical background on any project and get full decision context from a single query.
Building Custom Internal Tools with Tight Feedback Loops Rather than buying rigid off-the-shelf SaaS for every workflow, AI-native engineering teams spin up custom LLM bots tailored to business-unit requests in a few hours. Purpose-built internal tools integrate far more tightly with company schemas and permissions than generic third-party software.
Teams then refine prompts and fix failure cases daily, feeding user feedback straight back into RAG dataset cleanup or fine-tuning runs so internal tools improve continuously with usage.
Cultural Adaptation and Compounding Output Changing ingrained work habits proves harder than wiring up APIs. People naturally default to familiar manual routines, so early rollouts face friction unless the whole company aligns on transparent, recorded workflows.
Once teams push past that initial friction, structured institutional memory compounds productivity over time, widening the execution gap against traditional organizations. Moving toward an AI-native operating model means pairing small pipeline automations with deliberate shifts in how teams document everyday work.
Summary AI-native teams preprocess unstructured Slack threads and meeting transcripts into LLM-ready context stores accessible via internal APIs.
