content:
The barrier to retail algorithmic trading in Korea just dropped. Challenging legacy brokerages that long dominated programmatic trading, mobile-first brokerage Toss Securities has launched its own Open API.
Dropping Legacy HTS Clients for Cross-Platform Web Standards Developers can now build trading systems using standard web protocols without installing heavy Windows-only Home Trading System (HTS) binaries. Instead of keeping a Windows PC running 24 hours a day to maintain desktop sessions, traders can query live quotes and place orders from Linux servers or mobile workflows over REST API and WebSocket connections, cutting infrastructure overhead.
Conversational Portfolio Analysis via External LLMs Investors can connect issued API keys to external LLMs such as ChatGPT or Claude for conversational portfolio analysis. Even without writing complex glue code, users can ask for return breakdowns in plain language against live account data, and automated split-order algorithms can handle overnight US equity sessions across time zones.
Unified Domestic-Overseas Interface and Fee Waiver Toss Securities combined domestic Korean equities and overseas stocks behind a single unified API surface to simplify client code. Existing fee tiers carry over to overseas trades, and domestic equity API trading commissions are waived through June 2026.
Retail programmatic trading is no longer confined to Windows desktop specialists; the tooling is open, and adoption now comes down to execution quality.
Summary Provides OS-independent programmatic trading over REST API and WebSocket without legacy Windows HTS installs. Connects API keys to external LLMs like ChatGPT and Claude for natural-language portfolio analysis. Unifies domestic and overseas stock endpoints while waiving domestic equity API trading fees through June 2026.
summary: Toss Securities enters retail algorithmic trading with a web-standard REST and WebSocket Open API, external LLM integration, and zero domestic fees.
title: Toss Securities Launches Open API for Automated Trading and AI Analysis

content:
Production agents need a runtime that controls local file systems and acquires new skills rather than acting as a thin LLM API caller. Released by Nous Research, Hermes Agent v0.14.0 provides a unified runtime spanning the CLI and 22 messaging platforms.
Three Paths for Provider Authentication Provider authentication is the first setup step when launching Hermes Agent. The runtime supports three paths: placing API keys in a .env file, logging in via OAuth through the hermes model command, or pointing config.yaml at a custom endpoint. Users can also switch providers mid-session on the fly with the /model command.
Faster Cold Starts and Local Subscription Proxies Version v0.14.0 publishes directly on PyPI and introduces lazy dependency loading, cutting cold-start wait times by 19 seconds. A single pip install hermes-agent command finishes the base install, deferring heavy tool dependencies until a tool actually runs. Meanwhile, hermes proxy exposes paid web subscriptions such as Claude Pro or SuperGrok as local API endpoints.
22 Messaging Integrations and Cross-Provider Computer Use A single gateway process connects the agent to 22 messaging platforms including Slack and Telegram, with LINE and SimpleX Chat joining in this release. Even on non-Anthropic models, the runtime powers screen-aware computer_use control through cua-driver.
Agent runtimes have moved well past simple API wrappers, and an open-source runtime that expands its own tools and memory is worth tracking closely.
Summary Supports three provider authentication paths across .env API keys, OAuth login, and custom config.yaml endpoints. Cuts cold-start time by 19 seconds via PyPI packaging and lazy dependency installation. Connects 22 messaging platforms through one gateway and enables computer_use on non-Anthropic models.
summary: Nous Research’s Hermes Agent v0.14.0 unifies CLI and 22 messaging platforms with faster cold starts, local subscription proxies, and computer use.
title: Hermes Agent v0.14.0: A Practical Agent Runtime Guide

content:
The era of ten blue search links is fading as AI systems read web pages and synthesize direct answers for users. Instead of clicking through every result, readers increasingly consume AI summaries and inspect cited sources.
The New Visibility Playbook: AEO and GEO Developers use Answer Engine Optimization (AEO) to target direct answer boxes and Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) to earn citations in LLM responses. Both rest on traditional search infrastructure: Google pulls AI Overviews sources through its existing ranking index, and other AI platforms ground responses in web search indexes as well. Strong search fundamentals still come first.
Crawler Access and Server-Side Rendering Basics If a page fails to appear in standard search results, AI answer engines will not cite it either. Blocking crawlers in robots.txt or hiding content behind heavy client-side JavaScript drops pages from citation candidates. Inspecting rendered HTML in Google Search Console’s URL Inspection tool and serving content via server-side rendering keeps pages readable to crawlers.
Splitting robots.txt Rules by Crawler Purpose Blocking model training while still appearing in AI search answers requires splitting robots.txt rules by bot role. Teams can allow search indexers such as OAI-SearchBot and Claude-SearchBot while disallowing training crawlers like GPTBot and ClaudeBot. Avoid firewall rules that trigger 403 errors or redirect loops on allowed bots, and verify official crawler IP ranges.
Verifying Crawler Access from the Terminal A quick curl check spoofing bot User-Agent headers, such as Googlebot or OpenAI’s search bot, confirms whether your server returns 200 OK. Because operators block spoofed agents in production, reverse DNS lookups and published IP range checks complete the verification.
Web pages now serve not only human visitors, but also AI systems reading upstream sources.
Summary AEO targets direct answer engines while GEO targets generative citation synthesis, and both build on core SEO indexing. Pages missing from search indexes or blocked behind heavy client-side JavaScript rendering drop out of AI citations. Separate robots.txt directives let teams block training crawlers like GPTBot while keeping search bots like OAI-SearchBot open.
summary: How to configure robots.txt, server-side rendering, and crawler verification so AI Overviews, ChatGPT, and Claude cite your site.
title: Getting Cited in AI Answers: A Practical Guide to AEO and GEO

content:
A global fintech company recently cut 40% of its workforce while restructuring operations around AI. The goal is to strip out management layers that bottleneck internal information and run the company around a shared intelligence layer.
Replacing Management Layers with an Intelligence Layer The company compressed a traditional 5-layer reporting hierarchy down to 2-3 layers. AI models ingest internal artifacts across Slack messages, code pull requests, and meeting notes so any employee can query institutional context directly.
Hands-on player-coaches replaced pure middle managers, and roles consolidated around builders and customer outcome owners. With everyone querying the same underlying context, information asymmetry across teams drops.
Running AI at the Core Rather Than as a Copilot Instead of treating AI as a sidekick tool, leadership placed it at the operational core. Coding models crossing a capability threshold on legacy codebases triggered the restructuring, with headcount recalculated around a blank-slate question: how would we staff this company if we founded it today?
Internal meetings shifted from Google Slides decks to live data simulations and working prototypes, while market research moved from speculative surveys toward conversational customer signals captured directly in product interfaces. Decision cycles now run at a noticeably different pace.
Shifts in model capability are now reshaping org charts as directly as codebases.
Summary Replacing traditional reporting layers with an AI intelligence layer cuts internal information distortion. Placing AI at the operational core rather than as an optional copilot accelerates company-wide decision cycles. Teams shift from slide-deck status reporting toward live data simulations and working prototypes.
summary: How a global fintech company cut 40% of its workforce, flattened reporting layers, and modeled internal data to operate around AI.
title: A Fintech Company's Experiment in Becoming an AI-Native Organization

content:
Shipping a weekend project built with AI coding agents often leads straight to a blind spot after launch: users show up, yet you end up writing the next feature on guesswork because you cannot see what they actually do. Running a live service without analytics is like flying without instruments.
Under 100 Users, Observation Beats Statistics When a product has fewer than 100 users, aggregate metrics like DAU or conversion rates carry little statistical meaning. Small sample sizes skew averages easily, and A/B tests lack power. At this stage, watching individual user journeys to see where people stall matters far more than dashboards.
Reviewing session recordings from sign-up through saving a first note immediately reveals where users hesitate and sparks concrete hypotheses to test next. There is no need to force an early prototype into a full AARRR funnel template.
PostHog for Product Behavior vs. GA4 for Acquisition Traffic PostHog bundles session replay and feature flags on its free tier, making it a strong default for early product teams. With 1 million events and 5,000 session recordings free per month, builders can inspect user behavior closely at zero cost, and Next.js integration plus AI agent tooling support are straightforward.
For content-driven sites or ad-funded acquisition funnels, GA4 remains the standard. It processes up to 10 million monthly events free and connects directly with Google Ads and BigQuery, helping teams measure channel attribution on a tight marketing budget.
Alternatives for Data Sovereignty and Deeper Funnels Teams that want self-hosted data ownership without third-party tracking can deploy Umami. Its lightweight script runs cookie-free, simplifying privacy compliance while storing unlimited self-hosted events, though it skips session replay and multi-step funnel charts.
Builders curious about enterprise-style product analytics can also try Mixpanel’s free plan, which handles cohort analysis and retention curves cleanly, though a cap of 5 saved reports hits its ceiling fast.
Just as stepping on a scale does not cause weight loss by itself, analytics tools never hand you product answers automatically; their value comes from shortening the loop between observation and hypothesis testing.
Summary Early-stage products with small user bases learn more from observing individual user sessions than from aggregate statistics. PostHog fits product behavior tracking and session replay, while GA4 suits marketing attribution and ad traffic analysis. Self-hosted Umami covers lightweight privacy-first tracking, and Mixpanel’s free tier offers a taste of cohort and retention analysis.
summary: Why products with fewer than 100 users need session observation over statistics, comparing free tiers across PostHog, GA4, Umami, and Mixpanel.
title: An Early-Stage Analytics Guide for Builders Shipping on Intuition

content:
A global software company has released an open-source 10-step curriculum aimed at cutting trial and error in AI agent development.
Agent Architectures Beyond Basic Chatbots Autonomous agents differ from simple LLM API wrappers by combining reasoning, planning, and memory. Wiring those pieces together gets messy quickly. Using concrete Python examples, the course walks through where single-agent loops break down and how to structure multi-agent orchestration where specialized agents communicate and delegate subtasks.
Pairing System Prompts with Structured Tool Calling Letting an LLM query external APIs or databases reliably hinges on tool calling. Handing search or math off to dedicated tools raises accuracy and cuts hallucinations, and in practice, system prompt clarity plus strict JSON schema definitions determine whether an agent parses tool arguments cleanly without runtime errors.
Evaluation Pipelines and Runtime Tracing Checking whether non-deterministic agents behave consistently requires automated evaluation pipelines. Moving past exact string matching, the course uses LLM-as-a-judge scoring to measure task completion quantitatively. Because agent debugging is notoriously tricky, later modules cover prompt injection defenses and execution tracing wired into modern observability frameworks.
Reading theory alone only gets you so far; running the code and hitting failure modes firsthand teaches much faster.
Summary Multi-agent orchestration architectures overcome the context and reliability ceilings of single-agent loops. Reliable agent execution depends on external API and DB tool calling backed by strict JSON schema definitions. Production deployments need quantitative LLM-as-a-judge evaluation pipelines paired with execution tracing for debugging.
summary: An open-source 10-part curriculum covering multi-agent orchestration, tool calling with JSON schemas, and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation pipelines.
title: [Course] A 10-Step Roadmap for Building Production AI Agents

content:
Left unchecked, autonomous coding agents regularly break production environments. Prompt tweaking alone cannot stop unexpected tool calls or half-finished edits, which is why reliable agent products enforce behavior at the system level.
Closed Loops Matter More Than Raw Model Intelligence Granting open-ended autonomy to an LLM creates operational risk in production. An agent harness constrains the model inside explicit boundaries, centering on a closed loop that executes generated code immediately and feeds test or compiler output straight back into the next turn.
Behind every coding assistant that feels dependable sits strict infrastructure planning and state management. Going beyond raw API wrappers means building task-specific harnesses for code review, test generation, and refactoring, especially in complex domains like retail logistics where domain constraints are tight.
Environment State Management and Deterministic Control The workspace where an agent edits files and runs shell commands has to stay predictable. If file mutations or failed commands leave dirty state behind, the entire pipeline derails, which is why production harnesses run inside isolated sandboxes.
Defining explicit rules and pre/post-execution checks upfront takes effort, yet catching unexpected database schema edits or API endpoint changes immediately keeps systems stable. Engineering around LLMs comes down to wrapping probabilistic model outputs inside deterministic guardrails so operational complexity does not spiral.
Verification Gates and Runtime Observability Coding agents frequently declare a task complete before the job actually works. Stopping premature completion requires combining internal self-checks with external test suites inside the harness so the loop cannot exit until verification passes.
Runtime observability is equally important. Without clear execution traces showing why an agent took a wrong turn, engineers have no way to fix failure modes, and digging through raw trace logs often reveals hidden latency bottlenecks.
Multi-session tasks also depend on disciplined context management that injects only relevant state into each prompt.
Well-designed constraints build far more capable coding tools than unrestricted autonomy.
Summary External control and verification harnesses determine production reliability more than raw model intelligence alone. Closed-loop architectures pairing self-checks with external test suites stop agents from declaring completion prematurely. Real-time runtime observability and selective context injection keep multi-session engineering tasks on track.
summary: System design techniques including closed loops, isolated sandboxes, and verification gates that keep autonomous coding agents reliable in production.
title: [Course] Control Architectures for Reliable Autonomous Coding Agents

content:
Anyone running local LLMs has hit out-of-VRAM errors after pulling a model that barely fits on disk. Cramming the largest possible parameter count into memory neither guarantees fast token generation nor better answers; matching model architecture to your actual hardware matters far more.
Measured Benchmarks Over Raw Memory Fit whichllm detects local compute hardware automatically and ranks open-source models that fit the machine. Instead of picking the biggest model that squeezes into available memory, it prioritizes measured benchmark scores, helping users with high-end GPUs pick fast, capable models over bloated alternatives.
In practice, smaller newer architectures regularly outrank older, heavier models on constrained setups, avoiding the mistakes that come from judging models by parameter count alone.
Live Benchmark Signals and MoE Scoring Because whichllm pulls current benchmark indicators dynamically, its rankings adapt faster than static blog lists. Calibration rules prevent older model generations from staying artificially ahead of newer architectures, and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) scoring separates active parameters from total parameters to weigh generation speed alongside output quality.
A single CLI command prints tailored recommendations for the current machine, and a hardware simulation flag lets you preview what models a prospective GPU or Mac upgrade could run before buying.
Picking a local model tuned to your exact hardware specs now takes seconds instead of hours of trial downloads.
Summary Newer model architectures with strong benchmark scores beat simply loading the largest model that fits in VRAM. whichllm combines live HuggingFace metadata with multi-benchmark scores to stay current beyond static leaderboards. Distinguishing active from total parameters in MoE architectures balances inference speed and answer quality accurately.
summary: How whichllm detects local hardware specs and combines live HuggingFace benchmarks to recommend open-source models that balance speed and quality.
title: Finding the Right Local LLM for Your Hardware with whichllm

content:
The familiar scene of sales reps spending all day typing customer notes into forms is fading. Passive databases built primarily to store records are giving way to AI systems that evaluate context and act on their own. Enterprise software value is moving from record-keeping to active execution.
Execution Over Manual Entry Customer relationship management (CRM) platforms increasingly act as raw backing stores that feed agents rather than workspaces where humans spend their day. Careful manual data entry used to define operational discipline; now models run account research and analyze call transcripts directly. Records become a byproduct of work, while what the system executes takes center stage.
Much like social media users interact with a live feed without thinking about the underlying storage tables, enterprise teams care about real-time API data flows and output quality rather than rigid database hierarchies.
An Intelligence Layer Driving GTM Workflows Sales and marketing gravity is moving from static record systems into an active execution layer. Agents draft routine updates that reps once typed by hand, freeing engineers to tune orchestration logic and shifting middle managers from checking dashboards to auditing automated decision rules.
Intelligent orchestration links previously separate tools into one continuous sequence, from outbound email through calendar booking, while interaction outcomes feed straight back into future runs. Wiring these systems together takes careful engineering, yet the operational step change is unmistakable.
Pipelines Built for Moving Data Modern enterprise architectures prioritize low-latency data pipelines over static table schemas. Information loses value when trapped in silos, so teams pair real-time streaming with vector stores to keep context fresh. Inference accuracy ultimately depends on how quickly current facts reach the model.
Developers consequently spend less time hand-crafting static form schemas and more time designing context selection logic. Deciding which signals to prioritize inside a prompt shapes product competitiveness, and as backend orchestration grows more sophisticated, user-facing interfaces grow simpler.
Enterprise data now behaves less like a still reservoir and more like a live stream, reshaping what business software is built to do.
Summary CRMs are shifting from primary human workspaces into input data sources for AI agents. GTM workflows are moving away from manual data entry toward automated judgment and execution. Software value is migrating from the System of Record layer to the System of Intelligence layer.
summary: Enterprise software value is shifting from passive data storage in CRMs toward AI agents that execute research, outreach, and workflows directly.
title: From Systems of Record to Systems of Intelligence

content:
Users abandon AI products quickly when faced with a blank prompt box and a slow wait for output. Finding real examples that turn complex model capabilities into intuitive screens takes deliberate search, and studying well-organized design reference libraries gives teams a concrete starting point.
Structuring Interfaces Around User Intent Generative features demand interaction patterns that differ from traditional web apps. Forcing every capability through a single empty text input pushes cognitive load onto the user, whereas how a product summarizes and structures generated output shapes perceived value.
Examining paid checkout and upgrade flows on specialized UI reference sites surfaces useful layout cues. Watching where large retail or banking apps place conversational assistants helps teams pick placements that stay out of the way of core data tasks.
Data Visualization and Feedback Controls That Build Trust Whether users trust AI output depends heavily on how easily they can react to it. Small placement adjustments to regenerate or edit controls shift user satisfaction, and latency-sensitive workflows need interaction details tuned down to sub-second transitions.
Inline citations that expose source evidence directly raise transparency. When visualizing dense entity relationships, simplifying node-and-edge clutter keeps cognitive load manageable; enterprise financial dashboards offer strong examples of organizing dense data cleanly.
Bridging Backend Constraints Through UX Skeleton screens and token streaming keep waiting intervals from feeling broken. Product managers, designers, and engineers need to align backend response timing with frontend transitions early, because backend execution characteristics show up directly in interface polish.
When reviewing reference libraries, treat each screen as the final rendering stage of a data pipeline. Trace how user input transforms before landing on screen, since clear interfaces guide users without extra instructions.
Sharp judgment about core user workflows elevates interface quality far more than stacking flashy features.
Strong AI UX moves beyond a bare chat box to structure both prompt inputs and visual outputs. Pairing skeleton UI states with streaming responses masks real-time inference latency. Visualizing complex data structures such as GraphRAG requires explicit user feedback loops built into the interface.
summary: Design patterns and reference analysis techniques that turn unfamiliar AI features into clear, responsive product interfaces.
title: Using Design References to Make Complex AI Interfaces Intuitive

content:
Even when employees use ChatGPT every day, company-wide capability often stands still. Individual wins stay trapped on personal machines instead of flowing into shared team knowledge. What matters now is not seat distribution, but how fast an organization turns individual experiments into shared assets.
Why Personal Productivity Gains Fail to Compound Across Teams Handing out licenses no longer differentiates any company. Staff across retail and finance already keep AI assistants open all day, yet hard-won prompts and failed experiments rarely reach teammates sitting one desk over.
Gaps widen because adoption happens inside isolated personal loops rather than team workflows. One employee cutting report drafting time in half does not speed up the company as a whole, and unshared verification steps mean coworkers keep paying the cost of solving the same problems from scratch.
Personal time savings never turn into organizational assets automatically, and traditional change-management cadences move far too slowly to keep up with AI workflows that shift every week.
Shifting Metrics from Token Volume to Organizational Learning Using token consumption as a primary KPI backfires quickly, encouraging noisy, low-value API calls just to hit targets. Leaders get better signal by asking what teams learned and changed as a result of AI spend.
Connecting employee feedback and workflow friction signals directly into company-wide priorities serves a very different goal than publishing a token usage leaderboard. Tracking which tasks repeat across teams and where people lack guardrails creates concrete evidence for enablement.
Designing for Shared Growth Rather Than Surveillance Ranking individuals under the banner of collecting learning signals shuts participation down. Measurement should stay at the team level, tracking collective progress and reusable workflow assets, while top-down adoption quotas for executive slides only make teams defensive.
Guardrails should strip personal identifiers and aggregate metrics strictly by team. Dropping raw seat-activation targets in favor of weekly failure logs, bringing shadow AI tools into the open, and publishing tested workflows in an internal catalog builds durable habits.
Estimating department budgets upfront also helps teams plan transitions realistically. Rather than chasing vanity usage numbers, organizations need structures that answer what the team learned this week.
Summary Raw adoption rates and token-volume KPIs distort incentives and hinder genuine organizational learning. Turning individual productivity gains into shared company assets requires a loop intelligence hub that captures workflow learning signals. Metrics should exclude individual tracking and focus on team-level learning velocity and registered reusable assets.
summary: Why broad AI tool rollouts stall at individual productivity, and how teams can replace token-usage KPIs with shared organizational learning loops.
title: What to Check When Enterprise AI Adoption Fails to Deliver Results

content:
Spending all night scrolling Pinterest for UI inspiration no longer pays off. Pairing generative models with structured reference databases has changed how product teams gather and apply interface patterns. Here is what stands out when treating design references as structured data in practice.
Data-Driven UI Benchmarking Stronger search filters across UI reference platforms have cut benchmarking time dramatically. Curating structured reference sets upfront raises output quality, as seen in retail app teardowns that now take a fraction of the time they once required.
Viewing mockups as object trees rather than flat pictures exposes logic gaps early. Abstracting UI components to check structural consistency matters far more than surface polish. When generative tools can produce dozens of variations in minutes, curation judgment separates strong product teams from the rest.
Systematizing Assets and Team Handoffs Mobile UI patterns already behave much like structured data. Comparing AI-proposed layouts against technical specifications beats drawing every screen from scratch and cuts repetitive busywork. Translating vague visual preferences into concrete parameters also clears up handoff bottlenecks.
On large projects, managing design assets via APIs has become standard practice. Mapping complex payment flows in fintech apps visually makes edge cases easier to spot and cuts unnecessary back-and-forth across product, design, and engineering.
Replacing hardcoded hex values and pixel spacing with design tokens removes drift. Once models work directly with those tokens, they can generate on-brand screens on demand with minimal variance, enabling high-volume workflows like generating retail promotional pages programmatically.
Prompt Analysis for Reproducible Output Working reliably with image and UI generation models requires inspecting prompt structure closely. Analyzing seed numbers and style-reference parameters treats visual generation as an engineering problem rather than guesswork, which is the only way to get reproducible results.
Visual curation goes beyond picking attractive screens; it encodes business priorities into repeatable prompt weights. Keeping structured experiment logs gives designers and PMs shared ground when collaborating with engineers.
What sets teams apart is how they wire tools together rather than which tool they pick, and outputs backed by structured data carry far more weight inside an organization.
Effective AI design relies on analyzing the data relationship between prompt parameters and visual outputs rather than chasing ad-hoc inspiration. Turning visual assets into structured data via the Figma API and design tokens lowers cross-functional collaboration costs. Reverse-engineering prompts through reference libraries such as Lexica helps teams reproduce generative results consistently.
summary: Combining generative models with structured UI reference data speeds up product planning, asset management, and reproducible prompt design.
title: Designing AI Product Workflows Around Structured UI Data

content:
OpenDesignis an open-source workspace that produces design artifacts using locally installed coding agents or user-supplied model API keys. Starting from a short prompt, teams can generate prototypes grounded in a design system, collect feedback, and iterate inside the same project. Adopting it cleanly requires distinguishing local app usage from hosted model billing.
Connecting Coding Agents and Design Systems According to the official README, users can wire up existing local coding agents as the design engine or plug in their own API keys. Projects can attach design systems, templates, skills, and plugins tailored to team conventions, and users can preview and edit generated web screens or slide decks right inside the workspace.
Because the source code and assets ship under Apache 2.0, teams can inspect and adapt the setup to match internal standards. Rather than shipping the first generated screen as-is, the workflow centers on checking brand rules and user flows across iterative passes.
Separating Free Local Use from Model Costs The official pricing pagenotes that the free plan supports local CLI agent connections and BYOK. However, the free tier does not include recurring hosted model credits. Connecting an external API key incurs usage charges directly from that model provider, while paid OpenDesign tiers bundle hosted model credits based on usage volume.
Open-source licensing and local execution do not make model inference free. Before rolling it out, check your installation path, connected model provider, and credit budget.
Summary OpenDesign runs design workflows through existing local coding agents or user-provided API keys. Teams can apply design systems, preview generated screens or slides, and iterate together in one workspace. Free local usage, paid hosted model credits, and external API provider billing cover separate cost scopes.
summary: OpenDesign connects local coding agents and BYOK API keys to design systems, separating free local workflows from paid hosted model credits.
title: OpenDesign: A Workspace for Generating Designs with Local Coding Agents

content:
Extracting plain text alone breaks the structural links between table rows and columns, chart axes and legends, and mathematical formulas. This RAG-Anything overviewintroduces HKUDS’s multimodal RAG pipeline, which handles text, images, tables, and equations together. Built on LightRAG, the system indexes non-text elements directly as first-class retrieval targets.
Preserving Document Structure in a Graph RAG-Anything parses PDF and Office files into text, image, table, and formula chunks, generating searchable descriptions and entity summaries for each item. It then merges the cross-modal graph and text graph around shared entities. When a query references a table or figure, retrieval combines structural graph relationships with semantic similarity to surface candidates. During answer synthesis, the pipeline passes both the text descriptions and the original visual crops to a vision-language model.
This design pays off when locating the exact cell where a fiscal year meets a line item in a financial statement, or when distinguishing axes and legends in multi-panel figures. Flattening a table into a single string strips out spatial relationships that the graph preserves.
Benchmark Results and Remaining Constraints In the experiments cited by the post, RAG-Anything reached overall accuracy of 63.4% on DocBench and 42.8% on MMLongBench, compared with LightRAG’s 58.4% and 38.9% under the same setup. Those numbers reflect specific document QA benchmarks rather than a blanket guarantee across every RAG workload.
Performance gains widened on long documents, though clear limitations remain. Retrieval can still over-favor text chunks on questions that require visual evidence, and tables with merged cells or irregular column borders can confuse spatial parsing. Teams considering adoption should benchmark the pipeline against their own document layouts and query types first.
Summary RAG-Anything links text, images, tables, and equations in a shared entity graph for joint retrieval. The pipeline retrieves via generated text descriptions and passes original visual elements to a vision-language model at answer time. Alongside benchmark gains over LightRAG, teams should test against failure modes on complex merged-cell tables.
summary: HKUDS’s LightRAG-based framework links text, images, tables, and formulas in a dual graph, posting gains on DocBench and MMLongBench.
title: RAG-Anything: Multimodal RAG Across Text, Images, Tables, and Equations

content:
When AI-generated UI screens feel off, checking how live products solve the same problem is the best starting point. Lazyweb’s agent guideintroduces an MCP tool for searching real mobile and desktop screens alongside user flows. Multi-screen journeys like sign-up or checkout require inspecting the entire sequence rather than copying a single static screenshot.
Searching Screens and Multi-Step Flows Through Lazyweb, an agent can search screens matching a prompt and trace consecutive steps inside a real product. When designing onboarding, for instance, you can inspect input states through completion screens instead of imitating only the welcome screen. Still, layout choices and information hierarchy in reference apps remain reference points; teams still have to judge whether those patterns fit their own data model and user tasks.
Lazyweb’s current site also highlights product research features covering growth experiments, competitor teardowns, and conversion flows alongside visual references. Treating it strictly as a UI styling plugin misses half of what the service currently covers.
Separating Free MCP Setup from Paid Report Access According to the official documentation, browsing and setting up the MCP server start free of charge. Free installation, however, does not mean unrestricted access to every research artifact. Full growth reports sit behind paid plans, and available depth varies by account tier.
In practice, the cleanest workflow is to search target screens and flows first, check whether deeper paid reports are worth unlocking for the task at hand, and then feed those grounded references into your design decisions.
Summary Lazyweb MCP lets agents search real product screens and inspect multi-step user journeys. Beyond UI visual references, the platform includes product growth and conversion flow research. MCP setup and basic browsing are free, while full research reports depend on paid subscription tiers.
summary: How Lazyweb MCP searches mobile and desktop screens, multi-step user flows, and growth research, plus what separates free access from paid reports.
title: Researching Real Product Screens and User Flows with Lazyweb MCP

content:
A PDF conversion tool open-sourced by a Korean software company recently reached #1 on GitHub Trending. Decades of specialized document engineering earned recognition from developers worldwide, and that result came from deliberate product strategy rather than luck.
Processing Speed and Hybrid Efficiency The benchmark numbers stand out immediately. The tool processes roughly a page in 0.015 seconds, a job that took tens of seconds with heavier pipelines. At scale, that gap changes what teams can realistically run.
Data cleaning jobs across massive document archives that once took hundreds of days now finish in a few hours. For teams building ingestion pipelines, projects that were previously cost-prohibitive become practical.
The speed comes from a hybrid architecture. A fast rule-based engine handles plain text layouts right away, while AI models step in only on complex structures. Instead of running heavy inference across every single page, the pipeline reserves compute for pages that need it, making large-scale document processing viable even on modest infrastructure.
Data preparation has long been a bottleneck in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. Document formats rarely optimize for machine parsing, turning basic tasks like detecting table boundaries into tedious work. This parser reconstructs accurate reading order even on dense multi-column pages, giving enterprises a reliable path to turn legacy archives into machine-readable text.
Exporting Core Capability Instead of a Bundled Suite In the past, the company tried selling a full office software suite abroad, and results fell short because a single global incumbent already held 95% of the market.
This time, the team unbundled its strongest asset: document decomposition. Years of working through complex local document formats paid off, because the structural patterns accumulated over decades formed the backbone of the parser.
That domain foundation also opened doors to partnerships with global AI companies looking for reliable document ingestion. Releasing the core engine under an open-source license lowered adoption friction and aimed straight at becoming the default standard.
The business model seeds open infrastructure first and layers commercial services on top. As developer adoption grows, paid enterprise features follow naturally.
Turning Niche Expertise into General Infrastructure Engineering solutions built inside an isolated domestic market translated into broad utility once reframed for AI pipelines. Teams that define clear technical standards hold an advantage as competition over agent infrastructure heats up. Specializing deeply in hard document edge cases created lasting value in a new market.
Summary Modularizing core document parsing tech into an open-source release proved effective as a GTM strategy for setting technical standards. Combining a rule-based engine with targeted AI inference cuts compute overhead while keeping extraction accuracy high. Domain expertise accumulated in specialized document formats translates well into general-purpose AI data infrastructure.
summary: A Korean software company hit #1 on GitHub Trending by open-sourcing its PDF extraction engine instead of selling a monolithic office suite.
title: How Decades of Document Parsing Tech Topped GitHub Trending

content:
Over the past month, I ran Claude Code and Codex side by side in the same repository on production tasks. I wanted to test whether pairing two coding agents actually improves day-to-day output beyond the hype. Here is the setup that worked after a few weeks of trial and error.
Logical Separation Between Writing and Review I set up the workflow so Claude Code writes the implementation while Codex reviews from the side. Asking the same model to review its own output tends to reinforce its initial assumptions, so splitting models across roles matters. Having one model question the assumptions made by another noticeably reduced logical blind spots.
Keeping the reviewer purely advisory is what makes this setup sustainable. Even when Codex flags an error, the push itself goes through so momentum never stalls. The moment a false positive blocks a commit, the pipeline grinds to a halt and developers start bypassing the hook altogether.
Distinct Configuration Files per Role Author and reviewer configuration files need completely separate instructions. One file defines implementation conventions and code style, while a separate file lists only verification checks. If both files start looking alike, take it as a warning sign that role separation is breaking down.
File path patterns and inline regular expressions act as a separate safety layer. Security-sensitive files trigger an immediate hard stop, whereas model review findings stay at warning severity. Preventing security incidents and improving code quality sit at different risk levels and need distinct enforcement rules.
I also defined routing rules based on task sensitivity. High-risk changes such as SQL modifications or payment logic always pass through cross-review. A lightweight wrapper script manages agent invocations and exits cleanly so the surrounding Git workflow stays stable.
Operational Efficiency and Pre-Merge Catch Rate When a change touches many files, the wrapper switches execution modes automatically. Reading full Git context directly works well on small commits, but large diffs burn tokens and time quickly. Passing only the modified hunks keeps larger reviews practical.
Since introducing this dual-agent setup, pre-merge bug catches have climbed noticeably. A typical example is Codex spotting a race condition in code that Claude wrote with high confidence. Spending less mental energy re-reading my own diffs feels much closer to working alongside a sharp human peer reviewer.
I also spend far less time opening yesterday’s code with regret the next morning. Because an independent model already scrutinized the diff once, regression checks take much less effort. Building multiple perspectives into the loop pays off directly in code quality.
Summary Splitting author and reviewer roles across two different models catches logical blind spots far better than single-model self-review. Keeping the advisory reviewer non-blocking prevents false positives from stalling commits or tempting developers to bypass hooks. Maintaining separate context files for the author (CLAUDE.md) and reviewer (AGENTS.md) enforces distinct perspectives.
summary: Separating author and reviewer roles across Claude Code and Codex catches blind spots before merge without blocking developer workflows.
title: Building a Cross-Verification Workflow with Claude Code and Codex

content:
Spending more time rewriting AI instructions than doing actual engineering work is an easy trap. Vague requests trigger off-target outputs, burning both wall-clock time and API credits on retries. Prompt Master is a Claude skill built to tighten prompt structure on the first pass.
Every Token Should Earn Its Place Longer instructions do not automatically produce better answers; every word in a prompt should change the output. Prompt Master decomposes an incoming request across 9 intent dimensions, including task scope and explicit constraints, asking follow-up questions only when required context is missing before proposing a tightened prompt.
Filler modifiers that do not alter model behavior get stripped out to save tokens and keep generation focused on the target deliverable.
18 Tool Profiles and 35 Anti-Pattern Checks Prompt Master automatically detects the target AI tool and selects from 18 tuned profiles spanning coding agents through image generators, picking a matching prompt structure without manual template hunting.
In real time, it also scans drafts against 35 common failure patterns, catching weak verbs or missing acceptance criteria and turning vague asks like “help me with this code” into concrete, testable instructions.
Model-Aware Prompting Without Redundant CoT Forcing explicit Chain-of-Thought instructions onto reasoning models like o1/o3 often degrades output by clashing with their internal reasoning loops. Prompt Master intentionally omits redundant CoT scaffolding on reasoning models and prioritizes clean XML tag boundaries and explicit grounding rules instead, blocking unstated assumptions when environment details are incomplete. Installing the skill takes a single zip upload or repository clone.
Summary Prioritizes token efficiency where every word shapes output rather than padding prompt length Deliberately omits redundant CoT prompts on reasoning models such as o1/o3 so instructions do not clash with internal reasoning Combines 9-dimension intent decomposition with 35 anti-pattern checks to produce clean outputs with minimal back-and-forth.
summary: How Prompt Master decomposes requests across 9 intent dimensions, matches 18 tool profiles, and catches 35 prompt anti-patterns before execution.
title: Prompt Master: Cutting Retries and Token Waste with a Claude Skill

content:
Smart Chunking Strategy
When a RAG pipeline returns off-target answers, overly fine fixed-length text chunks that sever surrounding context are usually to blame. Before swapping embedding models, teams get far more mileage out of redesigning how documents are split and enriched during preprocessing.
Preserving Context with Heading Hierarchies Carrying a document’s table-of-contents hierarchy into chunk metadata keeps semantic links intact. Attaching parent section and subsection titles (H1, H2) to every chunk noticeably sharpens embedding retrieval because the retriever knows exactly where each paragraph sits inside the broader document.
Preserving structural hierarchy consistently beats flat text slicing on retrieval precision.
Converting to Markdown for Cleaner Reasoning Converting complex source files into Markdown gives LLMs explicit structural cues such as heading levels and emphasis markers instead of a flat wall of text, improving downstream reasoning accuracy.
Tables benefit even more from staying in Markdown: keeping rows and columns together inside a chunk lets the model answer numerical lookups directly rather than forcing you to serialize cells into awkward prose.
Layout-Aware Splitting and Dynamic Overlap Rather than applying a rigid percentage overlap everywhere, layout-aware chunkers detect natural sentence, paragraph, and visual block boundaries first. Dynamic overlap carries across only the bridging context needed for the next chunk without slicing thoughts mid-sentence.
Refining chunking and preprocessing logic almost always delivers better cost-to-accuracy gains than chasing the newest frontier model, making data preparation a core architecture decision rather than cleanup work.
Summary Attaching document heading hierarchies (H1, H2) as chunk metadata preserves retrieval context. Converting source documents to Markdown directly improves LLM reasoning accuracy over tables and structured sections. Dynamic overlap driven by fast layout analysis resolves the context breaks of fixed-length chunking.
summary: Why fixed-length text splitting breaks RAG context, and how heading metadata, Markdown conversion, and layout-aware dynamic overlap fix retrieval.
title: Smart Chunking Strategies That Raise RAG Retrieval Accuracy

content:
Every data engineer knows the morning routine of waking up to a broken crawler because a target website renamed a single CSS class overnight. Scrapling is a Python scraping framework built to cut down that manual selector maintenance.
Adaptive Element Relocation Across UI Changes Turn on the adaptive flag, and Scrapling relocates target elements even after a page redesign by comparing structural position and element attributes against previously recorded snapshots. Instead of halting the pipeline every time a frontend deploy shifts markup, the parser scores candidate nodes by similarity and recovers the match automatically.
Automatic selector generation helps during initial authoring too, building resilient paths through deeply nested DOM trees backed by high test coverage so engineers can focus on downstream data logic.
Anti-Bot Bypass and Checkpoint Resumption Scrapling ships StealthyFetcher to spoof browser fingerprints and clear common anti-bot gates such as Cloudflare out of the box, paired with built-in concurrency controls and proxy rotation for larger crawls.
Crawl state persists across runs so interrupted jobs resume from the last checkpoint rather than restarting tens of thousands of requests from zero. Lazy loading and fast serialization keep memory usage low under heavy traffic, while built-in ad and tracker domain blocking trims wasted proxy bandwidth.
Plugging Directly into AI Agent Workflows With built-in MCP server support, Scrapling connects directly to editors and AI agents, extracting targeted page fragments instead of dumping raw HTML so token usage and latency stay low.
Its async-native Python API processes batches of URLs concurrently with per-domain rate limits and custom delays, while session objects handle cookies and authenticated state cleanly. An interactive shell also lets you test selectors live before committing scraper scripts.
Summary Similarity-based adaptive parsing relocates DOM elements automatically after web UI changes, cutting selector maintenance. Combines StealthyFetcher fingerprint spoofing with proxy rotation to clear anti-bot protections like Cloudflare. Exposes an MCP server so AI agents can extract targeted web data with lower token overhead.
summary: Scrapling tracks moved DOM elements automatically when websites change class names, combining anti-bot stealth, proxy rotation, and MCP agent integration.
title: Scrapling: Adaptive Python Web Scraping That Survives UI Redesigns

content:
If you run the Hermes agent, take a look at Hermes WebUI. It brings the existing Hermes agent cleanly into the browser. Multi-profile support lets you spin up separate AI “staff members” per workflow and switch between them, solving the chronic context pollution that happens when every memory and tool piles into a single chat thread. Conversations started in the TUI or Telegram continue uninterrupted on the web, with file browsing and long-term memory management in one place. Because it acts purely as a UI layer, existing local data stays untouched, and remote servers connect easily over SSH. A dedicated native macOS app also shipped recently.
Staring at a black terminal window waiting on an autonomous agent gets opaque quickly. Pure text streams hide workspace state and break focus whenever you have to inspect generated files elsewhere. Hermes WebUI wraps the Hermes agent in a browser workspace designed to make those internals visible.
Isolating Context Across Specialist Profiles Asking one agent session to write backend code in the morning and run ad-hoc data analysis in the afternoon quickly muddies its long-term memory. Hermes WebUI solves this with isolated profiles per domain, giving each persona its own dedicated toolset and memory store.
Switching profiles loads the right specialist context immediately, and existing conversation histories from Telegram or the TUI carry over without manual migration. A single host machine can serve distinct workflows without cross-contaminating instructions.
Integrated File Browser and Visual Tool Cards A file tree in the right-hand panel exposes the server directory layout directly, so you can inspect and edit code the agent just wrote inside the browser without bouncing to an external editor.
Keeping chat and filesystem views side by side preserves momentum, while project-scoped sessions and tags help organize high-volume data tasks. External API calls and tool invocations render as distinct visual cards rather than raw log lines, letting you trace step by step how the agent reached its output.
Zero-Build Python + Vanilla JS Architecture Skipping heavy frontend bundlers in favor of Python and plain JavaScript keeps startup time near zero with no complex build step. Remote agent hosts connect securely as if they were local via SSH tunneling, and a native macOS wrapper app makes daily access even quicker.
A live status ring along the bottom bar tracks resource consumption at a glance, and outputs from scheduled background jobs appear as formatted reports the moment you open the dashboard, bringing memory inspection, cron outputs, and file editing under one roof.
Summary Multi-profile isolation prevents context pollution across tasks by separating tools and memory per specialist role. A zero-build Python and Vanilla JS stack keeps deployment and maintenance lightweight. Combining long-term memory controls with an inline file browser gives clearer visibility than a terminal-only workflow.
summary: Hermes WebUI brings the Hermes autonomous agent into the browser with isolated specialist profiles, visual tool-call cards, and built-in file editing.
title: Hermes WebUI: Multi-Profile Context Isolation and Browser Control for Agents

content:
Opening a sprawling Google Sheet just to update overseas stock holdings gets old fast: manual entry is tedious, and sheet-side price formulas break constantly. firma moves personal portfolio tracking into the terminal instead.
Keeping Financial Records in Local SQLite Portfolio holdings are sensitive data. Instead of syncing balances to a third-party cloud service, firma stores every record locally inside ~/.firma/firma.db, eliminating external data-leak worries.
Market quotes pull directly from the Finnhub API with no middleman service in between. Running firma show portfolio prints current unrealized P&L and position weights right in the terminal.
Buys, sells, dividends, and tax entries all log through firma add txn. As transaction history accumulates, monthly net-worth curves and cash-flow breakdowns sharpen automatically, and firma report renders quick visual summaries.
Turning the CLI into an AI Portfolio Assistant via MCP Registering firma as an MCP server in Claude Desktop turns the tracker into a conversational portfolio analyst. A single firma mcp install command handles wiring, letting you ask about sector weights in plain language or cross-check holdings against recent ticker news.
Because the model queries your local SQLite database directly, asking why cash outflows spiked this month returns a concrete month-over-month breakdown. Logging new trades works through natural conversation too, removing friction from day-to-day bookkeeping.
Scriptable JSON Output and Lean Setup Every read command supports a --json flag, making it easy to pipe output into custom price alerts or personal dashboards, while firma show earnings parses company financial metrics cleanly.
API keys configure in one line via firma config set, and minimal runtime dependencies keep installation light for developers who live in the terminal.
Summary Stores all holdings and transactions in a local SQLite file (~/.firma/firma.db) to keep financial data private. Uses MCP (Model Context Protocol) to standardize the interface between the CLI tracker and desktop LLMs. Supports both natural-language portfolio queries and conversational trade logging through Claude.
summary: Replace fragile Google Sheets stock trackers with firma, a local SQLite CLI and MCP server that lets Claude query and log trades conversationally.
title: firma: Managing Stock Portfolios from the Terminal with SQLite and MCP

content:
Combining OpenAI’s image generation with conversation-history awareness unlocks a fun format shift: feed in a single photo or rely on your existing chat history, and ChatGPT renders a personalized report directly as a formatted image card.
Here is a prompt collection compiled by @choi.openaithat you can paste straight into ChatGPT.
From Conversation History
“Based on our conversation history so far, generate my Four Pillars (Saju) fortune report as an image.” “Based on our conversation history so far, generate my MBTI report as an image.” “Based on our conversation history so far, generate a CIA psychological profile report on me as an image.” “Based on our conversation history so far, generate an evaluation sheet written from an ex-partner’s perspective as an image.” “Based on our conversation history so far, generate an internal HR performance review report on me as an image.” From a Photo
“Look at my photo and generate my personal color analysis report as an image.” “Look at my photo and generate a hairstyle recommendation sheet for me as an image.” “Look at my photo and generate a celebrity look-alike and vibe match report as an image.” “Based on my photo, generate an appearance rating report card answering ‘How does my look score?’ as an image.” “Based on my photo, generate a fortune report (romance, career, wealth, etc.) as an image.” Combining Both

Using accumulated chat history and user photos as inputs opens up a wide range of personalized prompts. summary: A ready-to-run collection of ChatGPT prompts that turn your chat history or a single photo into shareable visual report cards.

content:
Three multi-candidate experiments from post 9produced no meaningful improvement. Before moving on to the Schema Binding Plan, I wanted to test one more hypothesis: model tier as the bottleneck. I expected Gemini Pro to improve the current 56% accuracy baseline over flash-lite. I also ran the error-type classification and Spider experiment as part of that test.
Switching to Pro Made Things Worse Prompts, context, and pipeline stayed the same. Only the model changed, and the same 50 BIRD questions ran against it. The metric is EX (Execution Accuracy): whether the generated SQL produces the correct result when executed against the database.
Model EX gemini-flash-lite (baseline) 56.0% gemini-pro 48.0% Δ -8.0%p.
Three previously wrong questions became correct, but seven previously correct questions regressed. Most regressions came from the Czech financial database. QID 168 required only a 2-table JOIN, but Pro constructed a 4-table join, apparently seeking a more exhaustive path, which missed the correct answer. QID 39 produced no SQL output at all. flash-lite generated SQL for the same question without difficulty.
Pro performs slightly better on the in-house 30-question benchmark. However, that benchmark uses familiar database schemas and question patterns, so it is hard to compare directly with BIRD’s 50 unseen databases. For measuring generalization, BIRD is the more credible signal.
Model tier is not the direct bottleneck for this pipeline.
Classifying 19 Errors Into Six Types The same 50 BIRD questions from post 9 were re-run. 27 came back wrong, but 4 of those were grader artifacts; the same SQL scored differently across grader versions. The remaining 19 represent genuine pipeline failures.
Category Count Rate COLUMN_BINDING 6 31.6% VALUE_BINDING 6 31.6% DERIVED_METRIC 3 15.8% HIDDEN_JOIN 0 0.0% GENERATION_FAILURE 2 10.5% LEXICAL_NORMALIZATION 2 10.5% COLUMN_BINDING: The wrong column was selected for a JOIN or SELECT. In a question asking for the percentage of blue female superheroes, the LLM joined on eye_colour_id when the correct answer required skin_colour_id. Both column names look similar and both reference the colour table, and the schema alone does not indicate which one to use.
VALUE_BINDING: The value used in a WHERE clause was a wrong guess. A question about cash withdrawal transactions in a Czech financial database expects the actual stored value VYBER, but the LLM wrote cash withdrawal. No rows matched, so the result was empty. This happens when the model has no knowledge of what values are actually stored in the database.
DERIVED_METRIC: The derivation strategy itself differed, producing genuinely different results. Two patterns exist here. One is a calculation strategy error: when the gold SQL uses INTERSECT to compute an intersection but the LLM approaches it with a JOIN, duplicate handling can lead to different outcomes. The other is an evaluation boundary case: expressions like SUM(CASE WHEN ...) vs COUNT(CASE WHEN ...) usually agree, but diverge in the presence of NULLs; even execution-based grading can produce false negatives depending on the data. The higher rate in Spider is explained by the prevalence of INTERSECT/EXCEPT questions in that dataset.
HIDDEN_JOIN: Cases where reaching the target table requires passing through an intermediate table not mentioned in the question: “to connect column X in table A with column Z in table C, you actually need to go through table B first.” There are proposals to solve this via graph traversal over the schema, which is why it was tracked. Zero cases appeared in the 19 BIRD errors. Not a significant source of failures here.
GENERATION_FAILURE: The model declined to generate SQL at all. First observed during the Pro tier test; flash-lite produced SQL for the same questions. More cautious models appear more likely to decline SQL generation in ambiguous situations.
LEXICAL_NORMALIZATION: Lowercase text from the question made it into the WHERE clause unchanged, mismatching the casing of the stored values. For example, querying with 'active' when the database stores 'Active'.
COLUMN_BINDING and VALUE_BINDING together account for 63.2% of failures. The bottleneck is the schema grounding layer, where natural-language concepts get mapped to the actual columns and values in the database, not the SQL generator. These are not syntax errors; they arise from an incomplete interpretation of the schema.
Running Spider Produced a Different Distribution Spider, published by Yale NLP, is another Text-to-SQL benchmark with simpler database structures and more general domains than BIRD. The same pipeline ran against Spider: 50 questions, SQLite, 20 databases.
Spider EX: 72.0% (36/50)
That is 16%p higher than BIRD. The raw accuracy gap mattered less than the shift in error distribution across categories.
Category BIRD Spider COLUMN_BINDING 31.6% 50.0% VALUE_BINDING 31.6% 0.0% DERIVED_METRIC 15.8% 42.9% HIDDEN_JOIN 0.0% 0.0% GENERATION_FAILURE 10.5% 0.0% LEXICAL_NORMALIZATION 10.5% 7.1% VALUE_BINDING dropped to zero in Spider. Unlike BIRD’s Czech financial database, Spider does not contain domain-specific values that are hard for the model to guess. Most Spider databases use general, English-language data where value inference is relatively straightforward.
DERIVED_METRIC jumped sharply in the other direction. Spider includes many questions based on INTERSECT/EXCEPT set operations, and failing to express those operations the same way as the gold SQL lands in this category.
All 14 Spider errors fit within the existing classification. No new category was needed, confirming that the taxonomy holds across both datasets.
The same pipeline produced a different failure profile on each dataset. VALUE_BINDING was prominent in BIRD due to the Czech financial domain; DERIVED_METRIC dominated in Spider due to the prevalence of set-operation questions. Which error type appears most often depends more on the database characteristics than on the model.
What Two Weeks of Testing Covered Direction Attempts Result Pre-prompt hint injection 4 No effect, some reversals LLM multi-candidate 3 No exploration diversity Execution-based selection 2 No discriminating signal Model scaling 1 -8.0%p Accuracy measurements across the series, in chronological order:
Measurement Benchmark Model EX Post 8 start (DDL + Glossary) In-house 30Q flash-lite 66.67% Post 8 peak In-house 30Q flash-lite 80.0% Posts 9-10 baseline BIRD 50Q flash-lite 56.0% Model swap BIRD 50Q gemini-pro 48.0% Benchmark swap Spider 50Q flash-lite 72.0% Post 9 covers the first three directions in detail, including their experimental results and failure modes. The shared conclusion was that selecting after execution does not work; the correct column and value have to be identified before generation begins.
Model scaling was the additional verification in this post. Swapping the model did not change the underlying problem, and the result was -8%p.
One point is worth clarifying: these experiments were not run without an ontology in place. By the start of post 8, Vanna already had DDL and a Glossary YAML with 25 business terms trained in. 66.67% was the first measurement under those conditions, and 80% was the peak built from that baseline.
The issue was scope. That Glossary was built for an e-commerce domain, and BIRD is a benchmark that spans 11 domains, including Czech financial databases, superhero databases, and others. Against domains the Glossary was never trained on, it does not help. Its presence makes no measurable difference.
BIRD 56% is not a number that is low because the ontology is missing. It is evidence that an ontology, even one that is present, has no effect on domains it was not trained on.
The upcoming Schema Grounding redesign follows directly from this conclusion. Pre-defining knowledge in YAML hits a clear ceiling against unseen databases. A separate layer is needed for interpreting value-level semantics: not just column selection, but understanding what values are actually stored in the database.
Closing The next step is Schema Grounding redesign: improving the stage where the system maps natural-language concepts to the correct columns and values. The work moves into implementation from here.
33 error-labeled cases remain (19 BIRD, 14 Spider), ready for direct use in prioritizing the next phase. COLUMN_BINDING and DERIVED_METRIC are structural problems that deeper schema understanding can address. VALUE_BINDING is a different problem: values like VYBER cannot be inferred from the schema; the system needs a separate mechanism to enumerate what is actually stored in the database. Schema Grounding targets the first two types first; VALUE_BINDING follows in a later stage.
WikiSQL is a candidate for additional validation, but that falls after Phase 1.
